Now usually I'm a very opened minded sort of guy that doesn't shy away from most games. There are two kinds of games I like, ones with a meaningful narrative that also works into the game play, that's "Oneshot", and one with fast paced kick♥♥♥♥♥game play, that's "F.E.A.R". Now sometimes those can mix together and make a deformed hybrid of a child that has tourettes
that's your postal 2, which I personally think is one of my favorite games. Too bad that the country I lived in completely forgot the time that they were trying to be important like America
.
Now "UBERMOSH" falls into the latter category and I'm happy to say that what it says in the trailer is what it is. It's a fast paced hack and shoot game that is based around your reflexes and judgment skills, and you have to survive waves upon waves of morons for a certain time.

The gameplay is based around your usage of the sword and gun. your sword can cut enemies and deflect bullets back at them, and a gun does what you think it does. There is very little variety in what gun does what and fall into a line graph of the worst to the best. Now you only have 90 seconds to survive which may not sound much, but it does feel like an eternity. Enemies are relentless and will constantly make you twitch around the screen to check your every angle, making it pretty enjoyable for anyone who wants a challenge in less than 5 minutes.

Then you got your classes, you got your classless that starts with a sword, and can grab a gun. Your Kensai that has more health but can't pick up guns. Your gunner that has automatic fire with guns but can't use the sword and has less health and your warlock that starts with the best gun but with the least amount of health. Now obvious problem start to rise like, why would you need a gunner when she fires as fast as when you mash the mouse and why do I need a warlock when I can easily pick up the best gun in seconds. You are most likely to pick classless as your only class because of the variety of options you have and with a decent amount of health. There's probably no reason to pick the other classes unless you want the achievements.

The ai in this game is your standard brain dead, go in with numbers sort of guys. They will come in waves in an attempt to kill the player and even then over a hundred of them are already dead. What they make up for is their twitch movements they try to mimic the player making them unpredictable and some of them have a faster or slower attack speed. They all have one health and only carry guns, so it's nothing to talk a lot about, all you need to know that there are hundreds of them to kill.

There's not really a lot to talk about, I usually talk about atmosphere as well and as interesting as it looks it not necessary. The game has very little content but what it makes up for is it's arcade like action. It's a really cheap game that will take you at least close to two hours to get all the achievements and is not for everyone. If you like fast gameplay like the old "Quake" and "DOOM" games get it if you want to. Your not really missing anything out but if you think it looks good buy it, probably get it on sale. If nothing interests you and you want story narrative games go look at "Lisa", "Undertale" or "Oneshot". I even made a review on "Oneshot" so if you want to know what the game is like, go check out the review.

UBERMOSH (all caps) is a style-over-substance twin-stick shooter with a difference: your best weapon is your sword, which can reflect enemy shots.
The story behind UBERMOSH is limited, but there seems to be a degree of 'lore' surrounding the game and other similar ones by the one-man development team, Walter Machado. I won't try to delve into it other than to say that you play an armoured-up woman with a very big glowing sword and in each short (90-second) game you have to try to survive against hordes of gun-toting enemies.
Graphics have a retro, pixel-graphic appeal to them. They're okay, but not the best pixel graphics I've seen. Animations are okay, too.
The level graphics are fairly bland and uninspired, but I think it is supposed to be a desert, so I guess that fits. In any case, the background gets splattered with gore fairly quickly.
There are no graphics options -- not even a full screen / windowed toggle -- but I found that ALT-ENTER does work for entering windowed mode, in Windows 10 at least, and from there you can resize the window if you want to.
The music is really not my thing. A lot of people love it, but I really didn't. Sound effects are okay, and even somewhat useful in helping you get into 'the zone' given the difficulty of the game, but since there are no volume settings, and I don't want to listen to that music anymore, I've had to mute the sound effects while playing as well.
UBERMOSH is a simple twin-stick shooter played in 90 seconds, if you can survive that long. You're dumped in the middle of a procedurally generated level with nothing but your armour and sword, and very shortly after that the game throws hordes of bad guys, aliens, and who knows what else at you.
Killing an enemy leaves a lovely pool of red slop behind, as well as the enemy's weapon, which you can pick up. There are a few different weapon types, with the best undeniably being a gun that fires five red shots in an arc, covering a fairly good portion of the field in front of you. Unfortunately there's no way to lock a weapon once you've picked it up, and with the battlefield quickly becoming littered with blood, gore, and enemy weapons that you'll unintentionally pick up when you run over them, you won't always be able to hold on to your red death for very long.
And that's basically it. There are a few different modes ('character mods') that provide you with different starting weapons and health ('respawns'), and Steam achievements to aim for if just trying to survive for 90 seconds or beating your previous score isn't enough for you. But there's no advancement or reward for playing other than a sense of satisfaction and relief. There doesn't seem to be any online score keeping or anything like that, either, so some fans have started a 'best score' thread with screenshots in the Steam discussions for the game, in case you want to brag.
There's no zooming in or out and the camera moves with you, keeping you in the centre of the screen. Given the aspect ratio, this means that you have less sight range between your character and the top and bottom of the screen than you do at the sides, so enemies coming from the top or the bottom regularly get the jump on you; you'll often find a run ended by an enemy spewing the five red beams of death at you from one of those directions.
For a game that's obviously focused on reaction time and precision, the controls feel a bit sloppy to me. Playing with a keyboard and mouse is a bit frustrating, but the controller is worse. Stick to keyboard and mouse.
Pros:
+ An interesting setting, but one that's not examined in enough depth
+ It's very hard and unforgiving; some people like that
+ Achievements and trading cards
Cons:
- It's very hard and unforgiving; some people don't like that
- Unpleasant music, with no separate sound/music volume settings
- Controls could be a bit tighter
- No advancement or improvement, just the same thing each time
- Its name is in caps
I'm a fan of most things 'cyberpunk' and I love science fiction twin-stick shooters, so I'd had UBERMOSH on my wishlist for a long time. The store page didn't suggest it was anything but a one-hit wonder, so I wasn't disappointed in the lack of depth in the game, but I had been hoping to enjoy the core gameplay more than I did. As far as the 'cyberpunk twin-stick shooter' genre is concerned, UBERMOSH is the game that I've had the least fun playing.
That said, it is what it is and it doesn't try to pretend to be anything else. You can regularly pick it up for just under 50 cents, sometimes including the soundtrack (not that that's a good thing, from my point of view), so it's also the cheapest game that I've played in the genre.
Given the discounted price and subject matter, it's hard to not recommend UBERMOSH in spite of its shortcomings. But be aware: it's difficult, repetitive, more frustrating than it could be, and there's really not much to it.

Spoilers ahead. If you don't want to be spoiled on the game's plot, turn your lantern off and walk away.
Largely dull and unintuitive with many stock scares. While I do applaud the developers for trying out something unique with this in the whole "everyman vs monsters" being played completely straight in that you don't have a chance in hell against them and your only tactic is to hide, the combination of several factors makes it fustrating:
- You can't look at the monsters without going nuts
- You can't hide in the darkness without going nuts
- You can't hide in enclosed spaces without going nuts (i'm possibly mistaken on this one)
- Going nuts has a higher chance of attracting monsters to you
- If the monsters find you, you're as good as dead
So... i'm meant to avoid the monsters while not looking at them and AVOIDING the best hiding places because they'll make me go insane and attract the monsters to me anyway? Either this isn't the greatest of game designs or the player character is actively and violently suicidal.
The plot and setting itself... eh. While I appreciate that the developers do seem to have made sure everything fits together well for the setting and time period, the actual plot hooks and elements just seem a bit too over-edgy and contrived. The whole "torturing innocent people to death" thing is supposed to be horrific and sickening but the poor presentation fails to really evoke a response from me.
As for the horror.. nah. Not feeling it. While certain elements were well-done (hiding from creatures that know you're around somewhere, the area with "unnatural darkness" where light doesn't behave properly, the invisible water creature, and the sound design throughout is absolutely stellar), most of the game attempts horror through a medium of jump scares and sudden spooks. Being jump scared is not horrifying - it's startling. Being startled isn't really what horror is about.
This all said, it's obvious the developers were trying to go for something new to see if it works, and while in my opinion it didn't pan out this time, if nobody tried anything new we'd all be much more bored for it. I'm willing to bet this development team will really shine once they hit on an idea that they can get more out of. Maybe tomorrow, devs.
As a post-note, writing reviews like this one make me kinda sad. I hope people will actually read this full review rather than just see the big red thumbs-down and assume i'm going "THIS IS BAD AND THE DEVS ARE BAD". I may not recommend the game, but it's honestly kind of a mild discommendation. If you have a vested interest in the game it'd certainly be worth getting, if only to keep the dev studio running so that their future works might turn out a bit better.

is arguably the best psychological horror game ever created.
The story begins as the protagonist, a young man named Daniel, awakens, bereft of memories, in what appears to be a gloomy medieval castle. The player will quickly discover a Memento-style note to self, exposing that Daniel himself has wiped his memories, giving him a mission to "put things right" by finding someone called Alexander and killing him, and warning him that he is being followed by "a living nightmare."
Stage set, the player is set adrift to explore the vast, creepy, run-down castle. The game makes excellent use of darkness as a mechanism to balance tension: when the player remains in the dark for too long, Daniel begins to be frightened, which eventually damages his sanity àla Call of Cthulhu. However, the only two sources of illumination, tinderboxes for lighting stationary items such as candles and torches, and an oil-devouring lantern Daniel carries with him, both leave the player exposed and are only available in limited supply. Therefore, much of the game is a constant conflict between shivering in the murky blackness and taking brief refuge in temporary light.
Advancement is achieved via exploration, unveiling pieces of Daniel's forgotten past, and solving strongly thematic puzzles: repairing decrepit machinery or creating alchemical concoctions. These puzzles, while reinforcing the player's immersion, also force her to scrounge the darkest, most forlorn corners of the vast, decaying edifice for tools, parts, and ingredients, collecting mementos, letters, and fragments of journal entries along the way.
The visual and aural ambience blend perfectly to submerge the player in her surroundings: Daniel shakes, breathes heavily, and suffers from distorted vision when he's frightened; the building creaks and groans as Daniel traverses its dusty corridors; and nameless beings emit unspeakable utterances, hopefully in the distance.
There are a number of hostile beings lurking in the darkness - not many, but given that the only defenses available to Daniel are hiding in the gloom or running desperately for his life, the prospect of a horrifying demise looming suddenly out of the shadows is sufficient motivation to keep the player creeping nervously from room to room, afraid to make a noise or light a lamp.
The Dark Descent clearly draws inspiration, in terms of subject matter, psychological application of horrific elements, and malleability of the player's sanity and overall mental state, from the works of H.P. Lovecraft - in turn, it breathes new life into Lovecraft's concepts by exposing them to new generations via a new medium nearly a century later.
For fans of modern psychological horror, Amnesia: The Dark Descent is a
- the epitome of the genre.
For newcomers, it would be difficult to find a better starting point.

- Maps look nice for little effort involved. Automatically created jagged edges and such look great, as in the examples given on the store page.
Cons:
- It isn't particularly a time saver compared to sketching boundaries or labeling stuff with a pen. That will always be fastest and you can control how much the players see that way.
- While you can import icons, the current icon set is very sparse. Importing icons is time spent searching for tiny chairs and the like.
- Most the tiles demand to be fully colored in, which sucks for printing. You can't just convert the desert tiles, for example, to printer-friendly black and white squiggles representing dunes or something.
- Shortcuts are helpful, but slightly archaic. Every key means something.
Conclusion is that at under 5 bucks, it's ideal for GM's who have time to prepare their maps beforehand to play online. I would much rather use a pen and reveal terrain as it's explored for in-person campaigns. Make sure you fall into one category or the other before buying it.

Offworld trading company is in my opinion the best non-combat RTS on the market. It's not M.U.L.E. but it takes that core concept and give it's a fresh modern spin. It is a well balanced blend of risk vs reward which is simple to learn but challenging to master. A lot of attention and love has been poured into the game and it shows.

Considerations:
* Game is fast paced.
It's a not a case who ever issues orders the fastest wins like most RTS but the game is about balancing you income and the market environment which influences that income is in constant flux and you must be constantly on your game to adjust your strategy and make choices as the climate shifts if you wish to stay on top of your competitors. It eases you into it buy things get more frantic as things go on as you are juggling more and more avenues open up for players to sabotage each other. Point being there isn't time to relax in a match like their would be in a turn based strategy. Most people think a quick game is a good but this is a preference you have to weigh up for yourself.

* The extra campaign features are just for single player.
It is a constant gripe of mine that competitive games that offer mechanics for campaign map don't accommodate multiplayer. Sometimes you want spend to an afternoon with a couple of friends competing for a long game of back and forth struggle. As usual that's not an option. The campaign mode offer a fun and in depth expansion to gameplay experience by incentivising you to continue playing successive matches and thus is makes a good introductory experience to the game and augments your single player experience so it's more then just death match skirmishes with AI bots. Just a shame death match skirmishes is the only experience you can share with your friends.

* Competitive play will take practice.
The downside of simple to learn difficult to master means that without putting the time in you simply will not be able to compete with experienced players. The AI is very well developed at this point as a training tool but you are still going to take a beating before you can compete with regular players.

* Replayability.
The game has a solid core mechanic with a good deal of depth but that's the extent of it. The different factions all follow the same core rules they just each get to break specific rules, meaning learning to play one means you can play them all, you just have different ways to apply their advantages to different strategies. There isn't a lengthy/branching tech tree and if you've played one 30 minute match you've seen all the game has to offer. It's not that it lacks content (it's packed with it) it's just that the content is focused on a specific experience. It's fair to equate it to a game of speed chess. How many matches can you play before you get bored? For some people it depends on the opponents, others just love and can't get enough of the game while other just enjoy a single match every now and then. When you buy the game you a buying a quality board to play with. It's up to you to assess how much playtime you'll get out of the board.

If these considerations do not concern you then I can heartily recommend this title. It is solidly built, well polished and has benefited from rigorous balance testing. Also it's fun, which is what matters most. If you are unsure if it's a fit for you or not remember you can always buy the game, play a few matches to see what it's like and then refund it. 2 hours playtime is plenty of time to get a feel for the core mechanics. For many of us it's exactly the revival of this niche genre we have been waiting for.

Escape Dead Island is the best Dead Island game in the franchise. This is on the basis that while it is technically worse than Dead Island and Dead Island: Riptide, Escape Dead Island does not take 40-60 hours to complete, and it does not require roping in three friends who will disown you after having wasted so much time on a terrible action RPG in search of loot drops so you can kill zombies for the EPIC WINS AND MEMES. Unfortunately for the Dead Island franchise, being the best Dead Island game is like being the best corpse pulled from an alcohol-fueled fiery car wreck/explosion.
Escape Dead Island is not a traditional game in the Dead Island series, so there's no co-op and no loot drops to be had. But somehow, it's even more poorly written and constructed. You're playing as an incredibly whiny and stupid spoiled rich kid with short cropped brown hair and even stupider friends who decide to single-handedly travel to an island full of zombies to find out THE TRUTH BEHIND THE ZOMBIE OUTBREAK IN DEAD ISLAND, which is the single most valuable piece of lore in video games ever. So if you're looking for more poorly written reasons to explain why zombie outbreaks happen, you're gonna get your money's worth here. Oh yeah, and there's also a heap of irritating daddy issues from the protagonist to go with it, all of which don't really get resolved. They're just there to be dispiriting, like most of the flavor text of Dead Island.
Some of your favorite zombie types from Left 4 Dead are here, like The Tank, The Hunter, The Spitter, and even the Siren from Killing Floor makes an appearance! And you're going to meet them all inside of a game that doesn't know whether it wants to be a stealth game, a brawler game, or a survival horror game. Seriously - it tries to be all three, but it's a terrible stealth game because it keeps pushing you towards terrible, unskippable combat scenes, it's a terrible brawler game because fighting zombies basically comes down to mashing quick attack as fast as ♥♥♥♥ing possible, and it's a terrible survival horror game because you're not running out of ammo for your strong melee weapons and any damage you take eventually regenerates if you wait a while and take in the beautiful jungle resort view. (I'm being facetious, of course. Everything looks like it's been wrapped in clingfilm and marked on with a Sharpie.)
The game is dull as dishwater through most of the six hour run time. I didn't really feel the crazy difficulty spike that made Justin McElroy cry in his Polygon review, but that was because I accidentally stumbled into the Underwater Labs DLC that Fatshark so graciously provided to players as a free update (like a second, smaller fart deployed to distract from the massive atomic blast someone let off at the dinner table), and that hour of ♥♥♥♥ing dullness netted me an assault rifle that ate through all of my shotgun ammo, but took care of the most difficult monsters in seconds. (Also, in one of the final sections, zombies can charge off the crystal platform).
I paid four bucks for this game during a Steam sale, and I still feel like I got ripped off. It's not even a good bad game, like Ride to Hell: Retribution - it's ♥♥♥♥ing dull and dreary and unrelatable, everything I expected from a ♥♥♥♥ing Dead Island game, but somehow managing to be worse than the norm. I don't feel bad at all for the people who saw this and said "Oh boy! Another Dead Island game, except it's single-player and they're promising access to the Beta for Dead Island 2, a game that's stuck in development hell and the developer filing for insolvency! Gonna drop my fifty bucks on a pre-order right nowwww!", because this is an object lesson on why pre-order culture is awful and benefits only the publisher.

Above all, this game tought me one important lesson: If it's not fun, stop playing!
In short: Not recommended, unless you like torturing yourself with bad mechanics, or bland stories which don't get to real conclusion.
-Lots of backtracking
-Combat mechanics are rather flawed
-Fails to be fun
-+Story is twisted, which is good, but gets weaker and weaker at some point, to an unsatisfying ending which leaves many holes open
-+A rather short game, mostly linear, has small map, but that isn't necesarrily bad. Depends on your taste.
+Good graphics
+Good soundtrack
+Good free DLC
+Collectibles are..alright
While not being 100% disastrous it is also not too far from that point, and that's a shame because it has potential for something more.
And no, I didn't fall into the trap of expecting it to be like Dead Island or Riptide. I knew, or at least thought I knew, what I was getting into. I knew this is NOT RPG, I knew that it is mainly an 'action' title, with a small map, short length, etc..
And these are true, and personally I have no problem with them. It's perfectly alright, and ever since I saw the trailer when the game was about to come out, it got my attention. Therefore I quickly grabbed it when it was finally on sale.
While I guess you could say this game is worth at least those 4 bucks, and you'd be right, I still feel my time was terribly wasted.
This game is simply not all that fun, and, sometimes it does so in a cruel way.
Gameplay-wise, you would mainly run around some other zombie-infested island - a mostly linear experience - advancing with the story and smashing zombies along the way.
As I said earlier the island's area is relatively small, although appropriate for the game's type and length. YET somehow the developers arranged the game in a way that makes you BACKTRACK A WHOLE LOT. I Hate backtracking. And playing through the game, you'd find yourself walking through the same areas, threading the same caves, climbing the same ladders, using the same ropes, crounching under the same foliage, over, and over, and over, again.
Did I miss something?
Oh yes, you won't JUMP over anything.
Our hero is capable of sending zombies to their ultimate deaths but cannot jump.
This may sound like a minor detail, and if the game was done correctly it could have been. But doing all this backtracking just to run around some annoying not-too-giant obstacles just makes you think WHY CAN'T YOU JUMP CLIFF? WHY????
The combat, which is a big part of the game, won't save things either, for the simple reasons of it being repetitive and monotonous, but above all, way too laggy! The controls would always respond in delay, the combat mechanics feel flawed and clunky.
Also, our hero would die SO FAST. No matter how much medkits you'd collect along the way, (and these would tell yo that you've raised your max health, yeah right!), you'll just keep dying quickly, without even realizing what's happening!
At first these buggy mechanics are bearable, but later in the game on the parts which are meant to be more challanging, it becomes a pain in the butt.
Switching weapons is also not too quick or responsing, and the result is a combat which is not flowing at all, and you'd pray to end it as quickly as possible.
Yes, you will pray. Or just quit. Or just break your computer, as I almost did.
There are also MANY collectibles throughout the island. usually these are logs\recordings\etc you'd have lying around and well hidden, there are also snapshots which you can take with your camera. I actually found this aspect nice and enjoyable, but it grew tired soon enough, and didn't make up for the rest of the game.
The one thing which really kept me from leaving this game mid-way to rot in the depths of my "Don't Like" category on Steam, was the story. And as much as it hurts to say, it wasn't too good or worth it, as well.
It is very twisted, which is actually a good thing in my opinion. It is also very bland at some points, which is neither good or bad for me, and can be easily made into superb plot with just one single strong ending.
There wasn't.
I guess the concept was alright and a somewhat original twist to the classic zombie stories (Some evil corporation spreads the virus because it wants to rule the world\it is just plain stupid), but still, the story is not getting too clear throughout the game. For many of the events, you'll never figure out if they ACTUALLY happened or are simply a fruit of our hero's rather limited imagination.
The ending doesn't properly close the game, there are many holes and questions unanswered, and it is simply not justifying the time spent on.
No need to say the chatacters have no depth or any development (storywise).
My expectations were high because this game is supposed to be "the missing link between Dead Island and Dead Island 2" as the description said. But it didn't really surprise or bring anything good. Oh, and there's one very notable connection to the previous titles: (again, storywise) Xian Mei (hope I wrote that correctly) would be our guest star, her purpose not too clear, and while on previous games she seemed like the kindest person on earth, here she's mostly an annoying ♥♥♥♥♥ with an annoying accent.
Not being racist here.
So, there it is, with a heavy heart I would definitely NOT recommend this game, unless you like torturing yourself. There are some bright sides which are worth mentioning, although they fail to save the game from being what it is.
The graphics are actually pretty good, not too demanding and not too fancy but has a cool comic-style which is very refreshing to the series and I always like to see in video games.
The soundtrack is splendid! Feels like a waste for this game, but, it really keeps the atmosphere in a good place, very dramatic and tense, very fitting, very epic, simply great!
Unfortunately, these make the game look like a nice package while the inside is an utter mess.
The Underwater Labs is also worth mentioning, for being a free DLC, it is quiet good and mostly enjoyable. While it doesn't have much connection to the main story, it would take you aside to an hour or two of something...else. It is probably the only portion of the game which was actually creepy for me. There was a special emphasis on sneaking around instead of storming your enemies, it was bizzare and twisted, tense, and, well, good. Until the game mechanics ruined it and it's final section almost made me quit the game for good.
Maybe I should have.

Before I begin it is necessary to reiterate that this game is NOT complete yet. If you don't have the patience to allow the devs time to fix things as they go, don't bother. No one wants to hear you complaining about an unfinished game being unfinished anyways. The vehicles are glitchy, there are some keymapping/control issues though relatively small, the in game mic system is pretty poor, etc.
Now, this game is great, but not for the faint of heart. You will die, you will have to start from scratch. This will happen to you over and over and over. The good news is you have a decent amount of permanent storage to save gear, there is now an account leveling system that keeps you from starting completely at 0, and once you get the hang of the game you'll find that leveling and earning gold is relatively easy. As of now the one down side would be staying entertained, the good news is this is one of very few games where you can tell the devs are actually regularly and steadily adding features, fixing bugs, and making the game better.
You can group with friends to hunt other members in game (be assured everyone you don't know IS hunting you) it is rare to run across a friendly face outside of a safe zone, but you will learn to be stealthy as well as how to defend yourself quickly. You can battle boss nethers, run packages, fix safe zones, gather gear at loot drops, etc. No playing experience will be the same twice. I highly recommend this game, especially seeing as we have good indicators that this game is only going to get better and better as the devs continue their work!

This game was quite disappointing for me. While the gunplay and weapons are great, everything else seems to be falling apart due to rushed development and general lack of inventiveness. I don't feel like writing a long review so I'll just make the usual list of pros and cons:
PROs:
+ Fun, satisfying gunplay and melee combat.
+ Extremely wide arsenal of available weapons, even if several ones are simply improved versions of already existing ones.
+ Fast-paced combat, faster than the previous title.
+ Fun to play in co-op.
CONs:
- Procedurally generated levels. I ♥♥♥♥ing hate those. Every level looks the same, there's practically zero level design and it all gets boring incredibly fast. Even secrets are placed in the same spot when you get in the same area template, so there's very little incentive to exploration. Horrible.
- Brain-dead enemies that require no particular strategy or skill to be defeated. Even bosses are nothing more that huge bullet sponges that rush you and simply require to be stuffed with lead until they die. In the previous game you had monsters that could only be damaged if hit from behind or after having their shield destroyed, bosses that were only vulnerable in certain moments etc. None of that is present in this sequel.
- Non-existent difficulty. Enemies will kill you a few times during the first hours by outnumbering you and throwing you♥♥♥♥♥♥from all directions, then you'll exp up, find better weapons and get powerful skills and everything will become incredibly easy even at high difficulties. The dumbest thing here is that there is no level cap, you're supposed to choose your skills wisely but you can just keep farming karma and skill points until you become completely OP.
- Tons of useless side-quests blatantly made to keep the player busy with zero effort.
- Overly-exaggerated and unbalanced powerup system that gives you an insanely huge amount of gems to use or craft in order to give special powers to weapons. It's fun for the first couple of hours, then you get really tired to look at all those literal hundreds of items and you just throw in the ones that give you more damage or DPS. Which is the best thing to do anyway. There should have been WAY less items to find around but of better quality and maybe it all would've made some sense, but as it is it's needlessly dispersive and tedious.
- Poor optimization, there are random FPS drops even in situations with no big hoardes of enemies or effects on-screen.
- Lame story. Narration was obviously not the main course of the previous title but it got surprisingly interesting in the end, plus Hoji was a great sidekick. Plot is straightforwardly uninteresting this time, and Kamiko is an unbearable little floozy. The ending sucks big time, too. Devs unexplicably wanted to throw in a lot of utterly useless lore written into notes scattered around, but reading all that stuff breaks the action and honestly nobody really cares. This is not a RPG. A small bunch of trivia like the Doom logs would've been more than enough.
If you just want to brainlessly shoot stuff every now and then I can recommend to buy this game on sale, but if you're looking for a challenging and captivating shooter you should really look somewhere else. A shame, really. I loved the first Shadow Warrior remake so much and I expected this sequel to be at least as entertaining as the predecessor, but my expectations weren't met.

Beamng.Drive is probably the only game of its type. This is the only soft-body game that gets the feel right in that the cars feel like cars and not some box with god like handling. Drive has monthly updates that do not disappoint, The development team are really involved with Drive unlike some other soft-body game devs.
All the maps are very well detailed with lots of places to go and explore.
The cars are very well detailed both aesthetically and "physically" as in all the parts/panels/ect are modeled and attached together so when you crash it all fly’s apart like a real car.
All cars are fully adjustable and can be modified to your desire
The cars handle and dive like the real deal but the downside to this is that they are difficult to drive with a keyboard, you'll need a controller. The user interface is simple and easy to navigate.
In gameplay you can add or remove "apps" like the speedo, tach, cruise control, pitch and roll and more
Game engine wise it's very optimized for what it is. Running a desktop gen 3 I7 and a gtx550ti I can play this game with 3 cars in the map easily. The physics are rendered at 2000 ticks/sec which is quite impressive and being able to slow the game time to x100 is nice for slomos. The game engine is solid and has rarely crashed. The bugs are minimal, However improvements can be made.
Graphically ng.Drive is very good and easy to run.
Story wise I have nothing to say. The scenarios are fun but not story drivin.
Modding wise, it’s easy, Drag and drop and the game dose the rest
Overall I found it very fun to mess around and is quite a fun driving sandbox with soft body.
I'm very invested in the future of Beamngs Drive more then I have been since 2014 when I got the game.
You can download a demo from Beamng's website.
Would I recommend this game?
It depends. If this is the type of game for you and if you liked the demo then Yes.
Some people would find this game fun. Others will find it boring.
Overall I would rate BeamNg.Drive 93/100.

Offworld Trading Company is easily the most exciting new real time stategy game I've played in years. I haven’t had as much fun as this playing a new game since the original version of Starcraft came out over 15 years ago
It's seems to combine the fast-paced gameplay style of Starcraft, with the strategic ups and downs of a game of settlers of Catan (including hexagonal tile grid!), all set on a futuristic Martian landscape with cool background music and sound effects.
In Offworld you aren't directly attacking other players, rather you are competing with them to make the most money. Therefore you aren't susceptible to the plethora of cheap rushing strategies that seem to plague military-based RTS games. (such as zergling rushes in Starcraft)
The single player campaign is pretty basic, although with the developers allowing the ability to mod the game there is a huge scope for different game modes and challenges to be worked on. Daily challenge mode is currently available for those too nervous to test themselves head-head to online.
However it is the multiplayer of Offworld that is one of the most intense, engaging and challenging of any RTS I've played.
The action in a multiplayer game starts immediately with an initial frantic rush to grab what you think is the best spot for your base. This is analagous to the start of a game of settlers (the board game version) on steroids, where you literally have about 15 seconds to weigh everything up as the debt counter plummets, before placing your building and getting started. If you are too finicky in deciding the absolute perfect spot, you will often be punished by an opponent taking that spot just as you go to click on it. This puts you on the backfoot immediately, unless you've already planned a back-up spot to land.
There are so many variables to weight up simultaneously, in so little time, that even top players can get caught out at this early stage. Is there one large deposit of carbon that would be ideal for a scavenger base? If so, do you think your opponent has spotted it and how long do you think you can afford to wait for the initial debt level to come down before you grab it (hopefully before your opponent).
Is there only one small area of silicon on the map that if you can monopolise you will effectively win the mid to endgame by hacking the prices of silicon, glass or electronics up and your opponents will be powerless as they watch you rake in the cash and buy them out.
Or maybe the map has barely any water, in which case you plunk your robotic headquarters over that one little oasis, destroying most of it in the process, and slowly sell the remaining water to your opponents at an exhorbidant price.
The gameplay is fast-paced, engaging and always full of surprises. It appears to be extremely well-balanced between the 4 factions, with very few strategies that are obviously nerfed. In the midgame you have the choice between 5 advanced buildings which can have a dramatic effect on gameplay depending on which you choose to invest in.
I'd recommend this game to pretty much anyone.

Escape Dead Island is a spin off title of the Dead Island franchise, but will this be worth your time ?
Escape Dead Island takes place after the events of the first Dead Island game. We play as Cliff. Him and his two friends Linda and Devan travel to a island Narapela to discover what happened in Banoi.
The game takes a different approach in the story telling department. The story takes center stage and it adds mystery elements making you question what's real and what's fake.
Focusing on the story is this games biggest weakness. The story is a total mess and it's just all over the place and not to mention it doesn't fit into the franchise.
The gameplay is horrible. It's mostly a stealth game where you can go loud and it becomes into a beat em up. You have the same stamina bar that's in the original Dead Island games.  The stealth in this game doesn't work. The game expects you to go around the zombies or stealthily get to your objective, in reality the game spawns zombies in front of you so it's impossible to go around them and they spot you even when you are behind them.
The game has one thing I enjoy and that is the cell shaded look. I love the art style, but I can't appreciate it fully because of the terrible character models and the texture pop ins that happen way too often.
This game is also quite difficult. Zombies can take you out in two hits and checkpoints are far from each other, so you need to beg to God you have a run which doesn't mess you up.
The game took me 4 hours to finish. It's incredibly short and there's no replay value what so ever. So don't expect a second playthrough.
In the end I might say Escape Dead Island is one of the worst games I have ever played. The story is horrible, the gameplay is boring, the stealth is broken and not to mention the game is beyond broken. There is no reason to own this game cause it's a horrible. It's not even worth owning for hardcore fans of Dead Island.
Final Rating:
2/10 - Do not buy

I found Arma 3 to be my favorite Arma game played. It's a fun simulator that supports mods (which can bring in even more realism).
*TLDR is at the bottom*
Unlike Arma 2, you can customize your whole entire person. You can put hats on your guy, place different scopes on your gun, wear a mask if you want. It's amazing!
Now one of the problems I have with the game is the DLC. It isn't required to get the DLC, but highly recommended. If you wear any DLC items that you don't have, there will be ads popping up in your face, which is a big no. BUT I do understand why Bohemia does this.
I do want to get the Jets DLC and LoW DLC, but I currently don't have any money to spare for them. But that doesn't stop me from enjoying this amazing game.
Another problem, which happens with everyone, is low framerate. This game is awful with its framrate. At silent, and calm points you can get up to 50 frames. But once you go into the battlefield, you're getting a max of 30 frames, sometimes dipping down to 10 frames. There isn't really any way to fix this permanently, but a buffy computer could help?
After playing with the game for a while, you'll get used to the horrid framerate, and play it properly.
My last problem (which is also VERY MINOR) is the walking, and running. If you have to walk from point a-b without a vehicle, then your ♥♥♥♥ed. This part of the game is what I'd like to call "Walking Simulator". You just walk for 10 minutes straight doing jack-all.
TLDR: Arma 3 is a fantastic game, but it's not optimized to its max, and has a few bugs and problems. It does support a lot of mods which can make this game even better. I would highly recommend buying this game if you have the money, and you're into simulators.

I have come to thoroughly enjoy this game. I participated in the open beta and loved it. This game contains 4 classes currently, for each of the 3 factions. Each class controls and acts very differently from any other, the only characters which can be compared to others in terms of playstyle is any hybrid type class. Most classes are balanced very well and require a lot of skill and practice to be good with. The fighting system of the game is very simple, but very hard to master. There are few game mechanics I would judge as unfair, but personally I would say that Shugoki should be staggered like other characters, and that bleed damage type combos were more difficult to use, to avoid spam of DoT.
I've noticed this game has been getting hate bombed recently, due to having microtransactions. It's very simple to debunk the argument over this very easily though. You can use real money to buy steel, 1,000 steel is equal to $1 US dollar. Steel can be used to buy cosmetics, equipment, and easy access to the "feat" system, which is a powerup system that allows each hero or character to achieve impossible feats by gaining kills. Alternate feats are available through leveling up your hero or simply spending around 3500 steel to get it done immediately. Feats can turn the tide of a battle, but have a long cooldown, along with requiring kills beforehand. Equipment for each hero is a sidegrade to your original armor, which includes new cosmetic appearances. Stat bonuses and negatives are only used in the "Dominion" and "Skirmish" gamemodes and are ignored elsewhere. Only custom matches can enable equipment stats and feats without being in either of those modes.
At the moment this game includes many connection issues, due to Ubisoft not giving the game designated servers. This is likely an attempt to save money in case the game failed. The game is very prone to freezes, crashes, disconnects, and errors. The game is always online, so even then you can experience connection loss or an error. As an example, right before writing this review, a friend and I finished the final mission on realistic difficulty ( a mode where there is no UI and enemies are beefed up). We both experienced an error on the credits and received none of the rewards for finishing the story. Despite this making me upset, I cannot deny the joy this game has brought me.
TL;DR This game is really fun, not p2w, but has connection problems.

Now if you're like me, and not really one for jumpscares, this is a great game to get into for horror, or if you want horror that is  not in-your-face screamers that'll have you flying out of your seat (like how most nitoriously do). No, the most you'll get in this is chills and a few spooks as most of the edge will come from atmosphere (lights flickering or shutting off, sounds of monsters nearby, sometimes doors may open when they were closed...) with the thrills of having to hide and/or run from enemies.
It's not a triple A title, but for $30 it is well worth it and not a disappointment as the story as everyone else has mentioned is one that is deep and will have you questioning concepts that may very well be reality for us human kind in the future. It starts out a little confusing as you'll be wondering what the heck is going on and what you're doing, you'll be mind♥♥♥♥ed for a while, but as you play, things clear up so bear with the game.
As for cons:
--The AI has much room for improvement, some of the deaths from enemies feel cheap at times when they come at you even though you are hidden. It's not bad but it's not fully polished but it's not something that'll ruin the whole experience; it's forgiveable once you get the hang of figuring them out. But even still things like distracting the enemies by say maybe throwing a cup or chair into another room to distract them kind of feels useless because even if you do, they will not respond to it, and if they do go to the sound, they'll just go, then come right on back and run into you.
--There should have been a karma system added, as the game gives you somewhat choices to make in the game in reguards to morality. But what you do dosen't really effect the outcome so many have told.
--Some characters and minors plots in the game that could add more depth are completely forgotten. I know in good horror games, too much social interaction, and you don't feel alone. But things like your wife or maybe a few other characters you meet are never mentioned again and it could have been put in to just help fill in plot holes and add depth as mentioned.
Still  8/10 for this game and hope there will be more from these people!

Galactic Arms Race is built around a really cool core idea. Weapons, thousands (millions? trillions? bazillions?) of them are procedurally generated and evolve based on your preferences. As a tech demo for an advanced kind of procedural content generation, GAR is impressive. As a game, not so much.
The weapons, which are the sole focus of the game, are at the same time impressively varied and boringly repetitious. The variety of projectile patterns is astonishing: your shots may be concentrated straight ahead, in a spread pattern, out behind your ship, in a circle around it, in a snakelike wave pattern, in a seemingly random corkscrew, in a defensive wall in front of you, and other patterns that I don't have words for. The variety of colors, while maybe not astonishing, does seem to cover the entire range of human visual perception, so there's that. So what's the boring and repetitious part? For all the variety in their movements and colors, in almost every other way,
is identical. They all fire three shots. Those shots all do the same damage. They all have the same rate of fire. Their projectiles all have the same lifetime.
So although some weapons are objectively "better" than others, it's only because of their movement pattern. No weapon fires faster, or fires extra shots, or does more damage. I understand the
appeal of GAR (and indeed these guys are academics who have an upcoming article about it in an IEEE journal), but in my opinion it doesn't translate into a fun
. I never really get to feel more powerful. Every sector looks the same and all the enemies are similar. I have to look at the numbers on the screen to see that I'm making any progress. I didn't get any new abilities until level 50, which took a couple of hours to reach, and when I did finally get that warhead launcher, I was totally underwhelmed. I quit playing shortly thereafter.
As an academic myself, I found some interest in reading about their cgNEAT algorithm and CPPN's (compositional pattern producing networks). But as a gamer, I have to say that its low price only serves to put GAR into that increasingly crowded category of Steam games that are not exactly a waste of my money, but are certainly a waste of my time. Pass on this one, and get a game that's an actual game, not a research project. Trust me.

Ah, Duke Nukem Forever. One of the most infamous titles in history for its prolonged development cycle and the rather savage beating it took in the press once it finally was released. In 2011, I just took everyone's word for it that the game was a total disaster and stayed away. That wasn't easy for me since I had been a huge fan of the series, even going as far back as the first two DOS platformer games. I know I'm late to the party on this one, but when you've been waiting since 1998? Waiting 6 more years to finally put hands on the unholy grail of vaporware doesn't seem all that long.
Overall, I would have to say that I was pleasantly surprised. For a game that's almost universally reviled; I was expecting much worse. I'm not really sure what people were expecting from a game that can't help but have one foot in a previous decade. If this had come out even close to being on time, say 2001 to 2004 at the latest? I think its reception would've been significantly better. It possibly would’ve even been considered groundbreaking if it had beaten Doom 3, Unreal 2 and Half-Life 2 to market as intended. The graphics are perfectly serviceable and in keeping with the overall visual style of the previous games. Nearly all of the classic alien monsters are back with fresh designs that look great! Some might find having to repeatedly bash the space bar to break free from enemies when they're right in your face to be gimmicky, but I didn't mind. The gunplay is good, at least with the weapons it has in common with Duke 3D. Your mileage may vary with the new laser based firearms that dead enemies drop. My experience was also benefitted from playing this updated PC version that allows the player to carry 4 guns as opposed to the 2 of console versions.
That's not to say that it doesn't have its problems. What passes for humor is consistently childish, boorish and chauvinistic. All of the pop culture pastiches are oddly anachronistic; either referencing things not fitting the time of its early development or things outdated by the time it was finally released. The level known as The Hive does feature some uncomfortable moments where the player has to kill bound women who've been impregnated with aliens. However, none of these things were nearly as distracting or offensive as I had been led to believe. Duke 3D wasn't so different in terms of adult content and it's considered an all-time classic. I think it's more that the world has moved past such things and Duke hadn't kept up.
Despite enjoying most of the finished product, I can't help but feel that the real tragedy of this entire saga is the older versions we missed out on. The E3 2001 trailer in particular was mind blowing to me at the time of its release. I couldn't wait to play THAT game! Most of the backgrounds from Duke’s casino in Las Vegas, to the Nevada desert and the Hoover Dam did make it into the game, but what about all those cool moments and characters? Would it have been that hard to include the pick-axe wielding miner character in the desert section, if just for a cameo? I mean for being a focal point of early screenshots, you think he would’ve made the cut.  Where was Duke’s female companion, Bombshell? Upon beating the game, I couldn't help but wonder... what about this took 10 more years to complete?! If they spent over a decade tweaking and refining the game, why is so much missing from what we were promised? It seems all the delays were mainly spent scrapping and entirely redoing the art assets; trying to be competitive visually with whatever game Valve, Epic MegaGames or ID Software had on the horizon. Although the downloadable content episode did eventually include Duke’s original nemesis, Dr. Proton, and the Terminator-esque robot characters, even that didn't find a way to fit in all the missing content we'd been shown from the 1998 and 2001 demos.
I suppose we'll never know what could've been if the management at 3D Realms had been more disciplined in their approach. After 14 years of hype, it would’ve truly had to been the greatest game ever made to live up to everyone’s expectations. Although it often succeeds on its own merits, the unnecessary delays and multiple graphics engine switches negatively impacted the game. Perhaps that's why it was lambasted in 2011; other games had already long since done was this is trying to be and do. In particular, one can obviously tell the developers were greatly influenced by the original Half-Life's cinematic approach. Trading in Duke 3D's exploration based levels for fixed action set pieces didn't have to be a bad thing, but the execution left something to be desired. They were never going to win the race by standing in place and observing what the other runners were doing, telling themselves that they'll reach the finish line "when it's done".
In summation, if you've ever enjoyed a Duke Nukem game in the past; give this a try. I guarantee there will be a moment or two that makes you remember how much you loved those games. If you're easily offended by sexist jokes, cartoonish gore or dangerously hyperbolic levels of machismo? Stay far, far away. If you're looking to play a modern first person shooter with up to date graphics and game play? This probably won't be your thing either. However, if you're interested in the process of game development, I.E. why certain projects descend into so-called Development Hell? This is a fascinating object lesson. Truly an anomaly in the computer game industry as a product released out of its proper place in time, it's worth experiencing at least once. You might be surprised how much fun you'll find yourself having. Check your unrealistic expectations at the door, recalibrate your mindset to the early 2000’s and as Duke would say, “Come get some!”

I haven't played this game that much, but from what i've seen so far, i'm very impressed.
I watched a couple of gameplay footage 1 or 2 months ago and i wasn't a fan of the game at all but i came across another series (little plug: pyschadelicsnake's intense nether diaries) and that series made me buy this game.
Now about the game: The atmosphere is awesome. Especially if you spawn on the map at night and you go into the subway. Everything is dark so that you can barely see, the music is aggrieving, you hear nether screaming from above you and maybe gunshots from other people defending themselves against other nether.
I like the scavenging in this game, you can enter pretty much every building in this game and the fact that loot is... at least most of the time relatively common. At least in terms of food and melee weapons.
The little side-quests in this game are fun. You basically go to a safe zone, you pick up a package that you have to bring to another safe zone. If you do that, you get money and lots of xp. That's a pretty cool feature, because that way you actually have a goal than just "surviving."
The only negative point i have is the pvp system. I mean yeah, it's a survival game, but as soon as you find other people outside of the safe zones, 90% of the time these players have either a pistol or a rifle and 99% of the time they are hostile and shoot on sight. As i said, i understand it, because it's a survival game, but it's massively pvp based and pretty much everyone is hostile. I think i have encountered about 7 players outside of the safe zones and every single one of them shot on sight.
All in all i enjoy this game. The atmosphere is awesome. Fighting nether (especially with pistols) is a lot of fun as well as scavenging the area for food, weapons or ammo. I would definitely recommend this game.
But as i said: Be aware that the game is heavily pvp.

Perhaps the best choice of each MTG game available on steam. MTG 2015 has deck building as well as origins; yet this is the quickest of them all to aquire all of the allowed cards. 2014 would probably be the slowest to unlock every card (out of 2014/2015/Origins) since you only unlock 1 card for each win; and only for the deck you are using. In MTG Origins you play matches to earn coins to purchase 6 cards, which can take quite a while or spend money to purchase their coins. For 2015 you unlock a random booster pack after each win.
Mtg 2015 has cards that I would prefer were in MTG Origins. Origins has their pause button in the bottom right corner (where you would recieve a steam message). Mtg 2014 has 2 headed giant; yet are forced to use dual color premade decks with slight ability to make them better out of about 15 cards you must unlock per deck. About half of the unlockable cards per each premade deck are good.
MTG Origins had probably the most enjoyable story mode; as in the story....yet the most annoying campaign to actually play through considering that you are forced to play a surperior deck (while having some cards that are basically useless against) with no way to sideboard. MTG 2015 expansion campaign is quite annoying during the last match (which can be difficult).
Of the 3 MTG games mentioned, I'd have to say I enjoyed 2015 most. Less stressful to unlock cards. Enjoyable to tweak with the allowed playable cards to make a deck more suited to your play style. Origins has potential, if you plan on spending money on their coins or simply have plenty of spare time to waste. 2014 is a good game if you are horrible at making decks, or just do not want to spend the time and effort to make a deck that is more a part of you and your style of play.
The only thing I dislike about these mtg games is that at times it feels too fast, as in at end steps when a player plays a creature that then at that time you could finally use an instant card yet your mouse curser is too far from the pause button or you have too slow of reflexes. In a way they are helpful in learning at which time to play certain cads at what time; yet again, they are just as frustraing in they at times can seem to trick you when you are waiting to play a card in a countering manner. *but that is just the manner of a person or city or just a manner of speaking*

With everything you've already heard about Amnesia, know this - you can only take its hype so far. Yes, it's a delightfully scary game with a real sense of accomplishment after every puzzle you complete and monster you run from. But it's not so scary that you should immediately dismiss it if it's "not your genre" or you're "too scared".
Any adult gamer owes it to themselves to pick up this game up if only for how well it is able to create a believable atmosphere with simplistic visuals, conveying information through text (an obvious limitation), and one of the best-sounding indie games of its time. AAA titles and indie games that want to venture into horror game making can take something out of this from a sound design standpoint.
Visually, it's delicious. The textures and effects work to display an ominous ancient castle in the 1880s with a steampunk aesthetic for its puzzle elements. The use of props, mechanics, and an inventory system works. It doesn't fare against today's AAAs, but it's going to look damn good on whatever you're playing it on. If you also play it on the correct brightness level (you'd only be cheating yourself), it adds another level of immersion.
The puzzle mechanics are great, but can get needlessly redundant and complex if you don't read some of the lore. If the papers are in the Notes section, they're worth reading. Sprinting mechanics and how the controls work when you're going insane felt strangely natural. Monsters spooked. The pick up, throw, and move object controls were also relieving - sometimes you just wanted to hurl a chair, a skull, or a body of other props in the air for no good reason other than to see it fly away.
The only way you could tell this was a budgeted game was through its use of limited narration in its story texts. Most information is conveyed through what's written down on pieces of paper, and a limited voiceover from a few characters on a few documents (not all are voiced over) made me lose interest. But there were times in the journey where the your world would slow so that the protagonist could remember moments that were mostly delivered only through dialogue and sound. Those moments more than balanced out the chunks of text that were both spoken and unspoken.
With its limited scope and mechanics for it being a budgeted title, the length felt right. It has 3 types of endings, which fit within its lofty lore that surrounds it. The checkpoint system was forgiving, and I wouldn't have had that any other way. Another gripe was that once you died or initially encountered the same few monsters, it felt less spooker than I anticipated. But the scores and sound cues that accompanied their presence hooked me back into it.
TL:DR
++ P H E N O M E N A L  sound design in every step in the process, whether you're using on board audio or a top-notch sound card.
+ Short, but sweet game w/ interesting puzzles
+ Fresh spin on old environments with great visuals
+ Simple mechanics in a complex world
+/- Most information delivered through text, can feel a bit like a visual novel at points
- Characters not as memorable as the setting, which I found to be a missed opportunity
- Monster interactions got tedious and boring at points
8.5/10 - A great game for anyone coming from any genre background. This game also has a semi-active modding community on modDB that can provide tens of hours of new stories and campaign that reaches from Amnesia's rich backstory. One of my best Humble Bundle fringe purchases to this date.

Important:  Each game is a match that takes 20-40min to complete.  There are options that allow for longer games but the design is based on short cutthroat matches over long empire building.
That being said the game is fantastic!
The single player enviroment is rich is choices.  You can play a campaign at a difficulty of your choosing that goes through 7 matches each with carry over conditions and abilities.  This forces you to mix up your playing style and adjust to different situations.  You will be restricted in building choices as well, so learning to make do with what you have is important.  The game ends after a final showdown where you are allowed to buy out your rivals.  This mode is very fun and less stressfull then the other match types.
Skirmish and multiplayer allow you to buy out your rivals from the start (this is how you win the game).  With a dynamic market then the game is all about spotting oppertunities and taking advantage or knee capping your opponents with targeted special abilites on their structures.
The game has a setting that allows you to hide the real identity of each player to prevent grudge matches from getting out of hand for a reason!!
The game is fast, but very deep, you tend to get time to think about your decisions despite the time pressure.  Production chains are rather simple, but the overall interaction of the market and the 13 resources allows for immense possibilities.  No two matches are ever alike.
The game is pretty unique and I really do not have anything else that scratches the same kind of itch (Anno series comes the closest, but the markets are pretty stale in comparision).
If you like schemes like shutting down your rivals water production shortly after causing a spike in water prices with the ultimate goal of making their food production too expensive to compete with yours, then well, you have found your dream game.
To me this game is a 10/10 for this type of game, but it is not for everyone, expecially people who do not like competitive games.

This review is most if you're a single player type gamer such as myself.
I have purchased all Magic games for Steam, and always loved it. I know there have been complaints, but I loved the single player campaign and such - just a nice way to pass time and destress. I have bought all and was planning to buy the game every year - but because of this one, I won't. I refuse to give them my money now. I'll explain why.
The core is the same. It's not a AAA game, the animation is so-so, but it's Magic, we all know it and love it. The cards and decks are great.
However - NOT when you have to GRIND for your deck. That's right. Forget the previous games, with this one you have to either buy or grind boosters until you collected enough for a pre-made deck. Insane. It makes the campaign and multiplayer rather boring - because you can't switch decks as easy and change tactics were as appropriate.
It's an insanely greedy, unneccesary step, only to bring in more money because the grinding is painstakingly boring.
There are more complaints such as mediocre storyline, The menu is horrific. Looks pretty, but the usability is horrible, there's just no oversight.
The worst complaint I have is for the expansion where you play as Garruk. Pretty cool - only for the fact if you follow the single player story line you can NOT change decks. You play only with Garruk's deck. And guess what - they made your opponents in a way they COUNTER your deck.
And you cannot change! This is a classic example of extremely poor gamedesign. It has become a game of luck. You have to get JUST the right cards and hope your opponent (AI) doesn't get theirs in order to win. F*ck being clever or involving strategy, them not allowing you to pick your own deck was the worst they could do. In the expansion it's all luck and no skill - which is extremely poor as game mechanic, but even more so in a strategic game as Magic the Gathering.
It's sad. I really had fun for a while with the other parts. Them going for the option to cash in doesn't sit right with me as life long fan. I don't want ingame transactions to make it more fun with Magic. I paid for the game - let me enjoy all of it damn it.
Just play the old games - and ignore this one and future games. I wish I had listened.

Fun concept. The meat of the game is learning what to build for each character and what to build based on what randomly drops (taking advantage of opportunity), so once you learn the crafting trees and locations that are likely to have items you need to craft things, you'll reach a skill plateau. While not technically "pay to win" because you are unlocking options that can be unlocked by grinding the game, there isn't enough game here to make that interesting for me - and I'm guessing most gamers. This concept works with games like League of Legends because they have amazing replayability - but this is just a novel concept casual game made for cellphones. If this were a $5 stand-alone one-time-purchase, I'd probably get it, but it isn't interesting enought to replay often enough to unlock them through a grind and I'm not paying absurd amounts of money to unlock features in what should be a $5 casual game.

I found Arma 3 to be my favorite Arma game played. It's a fun simulator that supports mods (which can bring in even more realism).
*TLDR is at the bottom*
Unlike Arma 2, you can customize your whole entire person. You can put hats on your guy, place different scopes on your gun, wear a mask if you want. It's amazing!
Now one of the problems I have with the game is the DLC. It isn't required to get the DLC, but highly recommended. If you wear any DLC items that you don't have, there will be ads popping up in your face, which is a big no. BUT I do understand why Bohemia does this.
I do want to get the Jets DLC and LoW DLC, but I currently don't have any money to spare for them. But that doesn't stop me from enjoying this amazing game.
Another problem, which happens with everyone, is low framerate. This game is awful with its framrate. At silent, and calm points you can get up to 50 frames. But once you go into the battlefield, you're getting a max of 30 frames, sometimes dipping down to 10 frames. There isn't really any way to fix this permanently, but a buffy computer could help?
After playing with the game for a while, you'll get used to the horrid framerate, and play it properly.
My last problem (which is also VERY MINOR) is the walking, and running. If you have to walk from point a-b without a vehicle, then your ♥♥♥♥ed. This part of the game is what I'd like to call "Walking Simulator". You just walk for 10 minutes straight doing jack-all.
TLDR: Arma 3 is a fantastic game, but it's not optimized to its max, and has a few bugs and problems. It does support a lot of mods which can make this game even better. I would highly recommend buying this game if you have the money, and you're into simulators.

Mount & Blade: Fire and Sword is the third game from the game series of Mount & Blade. A sandbox game that takes players to control a character in an open world map with multiple  major and minor factions.
Those who have played the previous/other games from the same series will know exactly what I am talking. If not, take a look at my Review related to M&B: Warband for a complete knowledge of what the series and its games are about:
That lack of such feature before your adventure can even begin, gives you the feeling that you will be playing with a completely random character. Unlike of what happens to all the other previous games in the series, Fire and Sword does not have a custom character background history.
There is absolutely nothing new in Fire and sword that wasn’t been already seen and experienced in M&B: Warband. From the graphics and textures, what changes are that only muskets and matchlock pistols were added as a main weapon in the field of battle.
In few words, this game feels like an average community made mod/expansion, and not an actual game produced from a company who managed just before, to release the best game from its series that defined the whole concept of what a true sandbox game should be.
Despite Warband having some issues with some insignificant bugs and errors that could be easily fixed most of the times, in Fire and Sword, not just it has the same bugs and errors but also other more bugs when you wish to do an action, but also in the quests themselves that can ruin your entire gameplay if you are unlucky enough not to create a save file before you accept that quest.
Even when both games follow the same concept of sandbox with a very similar if not the same gameplay style, the way the campaign map is designed being only made of grassland and more grassland instead of the 4 elements seen in Warband, such as the Desert, Snow, Grassland and Montains.
Despite being interesting at the beginning, once you have invested some time in the game and in your campaign progress, you will realize that the game ends up by making you looting villages, sell items, hire troops and fight.
The players routine in the game to achieve success and power is a never ending repetitive loop.
The music in this game is wonderful I must admit, to hear the piano and the violin while you shoot and slain people is very pleasing and mixes perfectly with the time period where the game is based on.
The addition of firearms and armies based on it in a Mount & Blade game is unique and indeed a surprise to players who enjoy shooting and slashing down opponents!
I would rate this game a 20 out of 100 or a 1,0 out of 5,0 stars. The same exact graphics and game mechanics as in Warband in a game that could easily contain success, but failed miserably... a huge disappointment.

Just finished the story. For those who want the short answer: it's a great fast paced shooter that's definitely worth your time and money.
To put it a bit longer, Shadow Warrior 2 is something of a strange combo of video game mechanics. Not a bad thing at all, in fact, the game's direction and design lend itself to a lot of replayability, which is something that's hard to hit in these types of games without any sort of PVP multiplayer. Basically, take Duke Nukem, make him Chinese, take the combat of Doom 2016, throw in sword play, and take the looting of Borderlands, as well as it's co op and throw it into a game. This defintely has its own twists, but this is the best way to describe it. You play as Lo Wang, a curiously named Chinese fellow who likes comic books, his car and killing things. In an accident that resulted in some girl's body being corrupted by some black magic stuff, you accept her soul into your head to save her as part of a "owed favor" kind of deal. The story has a lot of twists and turns and is fairly enjoyable. Some of the acting is a little awkward at times, but it's easily forgiveable.
Story is hardly where Shadow Warrior 2 shines though. The combat is where this games shines without a doubt. It becomes frantic as hell with sequences involving the right combination of dodging, shooting, and slashing, all centered around switching between guns and swords. It becomes super addictive quickly as well. You feel like a badass ninja everytime you finish a shootout almost, though sometimes enemies with larger health bars will feel a little more grindy. The looting I mentioned earlier gets really deep as well, monsters and people you slay will drop ammo, healthpacks, and upgrades for weapons and your character. Weapons can be equiped with certain elemental upgrades which deal increased damage and have  specialized abilities on certain enemies. There aren't any tutorials regarding these things other than a tip on a loading screen from time to time, so it will take a little bit of messing around in menus for anyone who wishes to figure it out (I played most of the game without doing much regarding upgrades and weapon tweaks) I played the entire game through on single player, and while the game does seem to offer co-op through most of, if not all of the game, it always felt like the combat was better for solo play, though I couldn't be for sure. The only thing off-putting about this is that even when playing in single player, death seems still more co-op oriented. Rather than having enemies reset and starting back at a checkpoint to take on the task again, you respawn at the checkpoint to continue working on the sequence you were just in, and the enemies have the same health. It felt offputting mainly because it took away the urgency of not dying, because death had no effect on my progress thusfar. I mean you lose money and some things, but never that much. When I've respawned, it would say "enemies health restoreed" but when I returned to the area they were in, they would have the same health as before I died. Maybe it's a bug, maybe it means something else, I dunno.
Level design seems pretty alright too. It's a step back from that of the first game because instead of making a linear set of levels, the designers made a bunch of open levels that different missions will spawn objectives in. You spend most of your time going between your base of operations and the wilderness/industrial zone where the missions are. It's not an open world, as you teleport between the hub and the level the objectives are in, but there is some continuity between levels, so it feels as if you're traveling to different parts of a region. The one thing I found was off putting about this was that it took away focus from navigating and finding secrets and a path through the level as you did in the predecessor and simplifies it to following a trail on a minimap (which gets a little confusing on occasion). Another thing that I liked less about this is that sometimes enemies will hold objectives, and the game doesn't do a very good job of letting you know that you got it. For instance, if an enemy holds a key to a gate I need, but the game just says "retrieve the key to the gate" I'll go to the location, enter a combat sequence and kill the enemy that was holding the key. Because you pick up things automatically by walking over them, or by aiming at it and pressing X (playing on controller here, feels quite good btw), I would often times end up finishing the combat sequence and wondering aimlessly for minutes before realizing I already got the key. There are notifications on the side, but I just feel as though it could be managed in a way that's less prone to distractions. One time (today in fact), the end objective of a side mission was being held by an enemy, so after I killed it I remained in combat for the next ten minutes or so as more enemies approached before I realized that I picked up the key ten minutes ago and wasted ten minutes killing enemies I didn't need to kill.
So even though I kind of ragged on a few issues I had with it, it was still a great game. Regarding it's central focus, it's nearly flawless as the combat flows so perfectly, and Lo Wang's commentary throughout is memorable to say the least. Near the end of the story you'll grow a little more attached to the main characters, but it took longer than I expected. The gameplay however kept me hooked throughout, can't say I ever got bored of it, even when more grindy enemies came into the mix. If you're a fan of shooters, maybe you liked Doom and wished it had a more light hearted story going on, definitely give this a spin. And if you've played the first one and felt the combat got a little stale after a while, maybe give this a shot, it's tweaks have had massive impact and it feels much better,
