The fact that this game has mixed reviews says more about the people writing the reviews than the game itself. This game is a concept that you have to buy into to properly enjoy it and once you do it can be the most fun, rewarding and challenging game you can play. if you come into this game with a history exclusively of playing CoD and your prerequisite of fun is immediately gaining the title of super-army-soldier-squad-leader-fighter-man where the learning curve last less time than losing your virginity...you probably won't be a fan. Two main complaints I have read are excessive grinding and abusive server GMs. Again, this game is a concept you have to buy in to. If you were one man trying to build a huge keep, it would take you a long time, so yes, going alone in CoD mode #killstreak #lonewolf is going to get very tedious, especially if you have a low attention span. There are options to deal with this, play with friends, or join a collective of players on any of the many volunteer run servers with real RP elements. Which moves to the next complaint, abusive GM's. it's been sad to see how many people I have seen go onto servers (run by volunteers), get kicked for behaving like spoilt children when they break server rules and then come on steam and give the game a bad review, like it's the game devs fault that they couldn't muster the mental wherewithal to do or say anything amounting the more than "lol xd i burn ur howse" and then throwing themselves into the sea in a state of perpetual confusion. Felt a bit like a rant, but it annoys me because this game does deserve a higher positivity in it's reviews. Hats off to the dev team.
tl;dr: Great game, for slightly more discerning gamers. patience and imagination required.

As a server owner/operator I have decided to review LIFEYO from a game operation and maintenance standpoint. As you can see by the hours I have invested in this game, I love it. The critique I give here is out of love for the game and desire for improvements and is not meant to scare players or owners off. Consider it more of a this is what you will face as an owner statement.
LIFYO is a grind both in play and in server operation. It is not for the impatient who want to get the best now, player or owner. Over the last year the Developers have made several changes to the menus of the game and the game itself so I will start with some of the menu changes.
Be prepared to make several furnaces and forges. Before you are high enough level to make repairkits which need nails you will blow up many in the process. The forge and anvil used to last much longer before needing repair than it does now and in my view not much of an upgrade from the furnace in its current state. The crafting levels to make basic repair kits are too high in my opinion and should be a beginning level skill. Repair kits for a furnace that takes clay water and plant fiber to make, shouldn't need nails, so the devs should make a repair kit specific to those items or again make small repair kits a 0 level skill.
Floor lamps being moved to the art crafting skill was silly. While I agree they shouldn't have been in construction, I think they should have been moved to the smelting tools menu and the skill level is too high. But that is just my take on it because I love lamps and hate the dark. The changes to torches were a blessing. Thank you Devs.
The changes to raising and lowering items to combat log ladders and dirt ramps over walls. With the monument system the way it is these changes really weren't necessary in my view. They put a damper on creativity. There are not many servers for LIFYO that allow KOS or that have set judgement hours for these things to really matter.
The way I see it is in a judgement hour situation if someone is making the effort to cut trees and lug logs to the walls of your claim and you aren't shooting them with every arrow you have thats on you. Same goes for dirt ramps and spirited horses. Yes, I get that most people find the jump factor of a spirited warhorse unrealistic but I find it fun and really not everything in the game has to be grindy and real life. It is a game after all. If someone is taking the time to make a ramp to my walls and im not killing them that is also on me.
When I first started running the server there was a setting in the WorldID_1 file that allowed you to limit the height things could be raised. What they should have done is taken paintings and art type things off this setting and left it for the height of logs being floated. This would have solved the problems, but really anyone that didnt like the fact that you could raise and lower logs and float them like that could have fixed the problem by changing the setting in the file rather than complain.
Now that the devs got rid of that option to adjust the height of things, beveled stone stairs dont stack right and clay is now nerfed making it harder to put in roads down mountain sides or build in high places. Again putting the damper on creativity in a game no new items are really coming out for.
GM Mode. up until this last year gm mode as far as flight went worked great. Now dropping out of the sky in a spot you choose doesnt happen. You get dumped in the ocean. stuck above the horizon or dropped miles from where you flew to. Sometimes you now take fall damage or die from it. As a working Gm this is an annoyance especially when you get to the forest changes in the game. It has also become harder to maintain monuments for those on vacation as you can no longer feed a monument in gm mode. Having to create characters and take over a monument is a pain and eventually when there is more than 64 characters created on the server it starts throwing errors and ghosting messages in the console. I have also experienced fall damage teleporting to players.
Mines, I love that they decay on their own. I wish unmonumneted settlements and unbuilt on terriforming as well as dirt piles from mines did to. Mines are killing players when they fight to get in and out of them. They throw you in the air sometimes to death. And they sometimes collapse on you while you are digging them if you aren't reinforcing from the get go.
Players sometimes take fall damage getting off their horse. Horses wont go through some gates and you have to get off them and they throw you at unseen obsticles on the map. these can be as simple as a dip in the road or hillside.
Decay, I don't know what happened, but it used to be that I could amp up player monuments, turn on decay at a reasonably high rate and the decay would take out terriforming, roads and unmonumented claims without burning down monumented ones. This isnt the case anymore and it doesnt seem to remove terriforming causing owners to either work like crazy fighting fires or work like crazy to undig old claims to get the grass back for new players without wiping the server.
Last but not least and the biggest issue in the game is the forest algorithem. In theory this was a very nice idea to promote tree death and new growth to keep us from having to run tree scripts once or twice a month to thin the forest.
In my view the tree script was less work and a better solution to the problem than what we have now. New owners beware. 220 days after server creation you will have a massive tree death in the west and south. You will lose almost all your hardwood, mullberry and apple everywhere. The description of how the algorithem works to balance trees to have lush forests with trees of all types is not factual. At 220 days in you will lose your player base because trees will die off at alarming rates leaving the west and south coasts almost barren and your players will go with them unless you edit your cm_forestry_maintenance.xml file changing that 220 rate to something in the thousands. The devs certainaly did not test this algortihem for the LIFYO map. While mass tree death may be good in the mmo on our tiny map it is devastating and a ton of work to restore things every 220 days leaving new players without hardwood to build with.
Editing your xml file comes with a new set of problems. Lets say you change 220 to something like 1200. You will still experience tree death at alarming rates in 1200 ingame days If you are a no wipe kind of owner like me, which is another thing players hate, you will be fighting this issue at some point in your game no matter what you do. If you change these rates your forests will become over grown again at some point with no good tree script to help you fight the thickness of things as we were warned not to use the old scripts with the new algorithem.
I think the devs need to revamp the trees on the LifYo map again making them all different ages in every map position so death and regrowth are not in huge areas at one time. The Lif Yo Map is too small for barren lands and nobody will build there. Case in point we see little building in the north because of the lack of resources and flat terrain. and speaking of resources it would be nice to have a granite source in the southern region. Lugging 180k granite from the big mountain down to the south for a castle is more than just a grind its a pain. I'm not complaing about the amount of mats needed mind you just the distance with no good rate of carry and no horse drawn carts as promised.(Sorry had to slip that in there somewhere)
This is a good game, I personally love the game. I understand that the mmo was the Devs first dream but LIFYO was born and exists first and has a life of its very own and it DESERVES just as much attention as the MMO.
While I recommend the game to players and owners alike I just wish the Devs would live up to their promises in the game and stop neglecting YO.

Played this for a little over a year throughout the Early Access. Can't recommend it enough. Here are just a few of the assorted points as to why I love it so much:
- The AI had been dramatically improved over the time and is quite, quite competent now. To a point that a newer player might struggle with it quite a bit until he really gets the hang of the game.
- Getting the hang of the game might seem challenging - the learning curve is quite steep and usually that's a sign of a deep game. And trust me, this game is deep in spite of what some people might say. I can see how playing AI can get repetitve but in a multiplayer every game is different and every game presents you with plenty of important and difficult decisions that you need to make quick.
- There is no one way to victory. Every game you have to adapt to the ever-changing environment, fluctuating prices, resource spread and geography, shortaging, colony growth etc.
- I have very little RTS experience. In fact nearly none and I am hardly at all inerested in the genre. Yet somehow when I first saw Offworld I got interested in it and after watching a whole pile of videos I realized that I HAVE to play it.
Now, I understand it's not a feeling everyone will have, not immediately for sure. But I think that if you like RTS, if you want something new and different, if you like a highly competitive game, you should definitely give it a shot.
UPDATE
My opinion on the game hasn't changed, still love it; this is an update on the game's expansion:
It's pretty good. 2 new factions create even more strategic options to the game, with even more depth, especially given that you normally still choose from only 4 options (randomly chosen out of the 6), making for even more variety for founding. It is, however somewhat more challenging for new players to get into, since you get access to both the expansion and the Ceres Initiative DLC when playing ranked even if you don't own them (there's a 50% chance you'll play on Mars and 25% for either Io or Ceres), so even if you don't plan to get either of those it might be difficult to play ranked at first (though you should have no problems in either Single player or with Lobby games).
Also, since I hadn't mentioned it in the original review, the discord community is very helpful to new players and pretty active in general, organizing regular tournaments and competitive events for players of all skill levels.

This is a decently fun game overall and does not deserve all the hate it gets. The reviews slating long load times and dodgy frame rates must be referencing the console versions because, on PC, none of this is the case, the game was incredibly smooth on my meagre setup so you shouldn't have a problem getting it to run well on most systems.
The game is a flat out stupid affair in terms of plot, characters and references to other games. The plot is that aliens invade, take the Duke's girls and he follows in pursuit doing what he always does once he runs out of bubblegum. The references themselves are poorly implemented, hamfisted ones but then again what else can they be if inserted within a comedic game? I guess what appeals is how audacious the game's tone is and how I can't really fault it when it comes to pacing. It's a fast moving game that takes in a good variety of settings, adds simple puzzles and . One of the things I really liked was how messing with the environment gifted you with more health, meaning that not everything break from combat felt like pointless scene-setting up to the next gunfight.
Like most modern shooters, health regenerates which sucks but isn't a complete deal breaker. At least the idea has run its course for the most part these days and developers are slowly re-establishing the much better idea of having health packs in their shooters. This makes combat relatively uninteresting for the most part; its made up for, however, by the weapon selection which is near identical to that of Duke Nukem 3D. They are all overpowered, fun to use, punchy and cathartic and really help make every combat encounter just one long relentless blast-fest like all the early 90s shooters were like.
Overall, the game is basically functional and relatively exciting to play through, though it has plenty of half baked ideas, like the mostly useless alien weaponry found in abundance, a driving sequence which unfortunately becomes very monotonous to the detriment of the otherwise good pacing and some bland boss fights, characteristic of most 90s shooters. There is also some bad platforming sections but thankfully are over quickly before you get too annoyed by them.
I'd say it was definitely worth playing for the tiny amount I payed for it (less than a quid). If you can't get it for as cheap as that, less than £5 is decent price to pay. It's certainly an adequate game, with enough strong elements to keep you invested, and isn't technically broken as reviews suggest (my guess is that is has been patched to hell and back).
Solid 6/10 game.

A huge disappointment of the last 1/4 of the game or longer. It made it all feel like everything I had accomplished, weapon upgrades and story progression, were all for naught. UBERMOSH, an extremely simple, yet balls to the wall hard game with an amazing rocking soundtrack & a top-down view of the action. Story is simple & quick to the point, cyberpunk utopian future colony where violence, crime & poverty is a non-issue but violence is a “basic need”, so what better way to blow off much needed stress than dropping you in a hostile environment. That is basically it, you are armed with a sword, which you can use to deflect enemy bullets back at them or slice them. Guns are dropped by enemies, simply running over them picks them up. The guns are nothing special, each have their own bullet spread and there is a total of 5 different guns. The game has a simple premise, basically your difficult to survive horde/score attack type of game. You are given 90 seconds & 4 lives on the basic mode of play. There are 4 modes or class mods as the game call them: Kensai, limits you to only use your sword, Gunner only guns & Warlock, which gives you the “best” gun as well as the being able to use your sword. Your amount of lives varies between each mod. Gunplay is average serving more to thin the numbers rather than being your main method of attack, the sword being your main weapon & “shield”, with its ability to deflect bullets, against the onslaught. Despite the enemy bullets coming in hard & fast, they are brightly neon colored so you have a decent chance of being able to evade/deflect them.
Ubermosh can be played with both a mouse/kb & controller. It does not feature a graphical setting menus or any other menu for that matter. The game is extremely short considering it doesn’t really have story to tell & consists of nothing more than fighting the horde of enemies for 90 seconds or your death. There was a minor flaw involving the walls, in which having you move next to them it just stops your movement & gets you stuck to them which is an annoyance in such a fast paced game. No leaderboards as well, so you will have to resort to sharing score the old fashioned way.  All in all, despite that minor flaw, it is a decent time waster with a pretty cool soundtrack that will have you head banging along to the beat as you slice & dice your way through the horde.

A worthy successor to Amnesia: The Dark Descent, SOMA is a visceral and engaging experience that wades more deeply into the dark waters of speculative Sci-fi than traditional Horror (though there's absolutely no shortage of physical and psychological ghastliness on display) through the unpleasant ambiguities it asks the player to face.  More often than not these ideas bubble up slowly over time, with only a small numer of heavyhanded moral or expository moments scattered across the 8-12 hours of play.  From a mechanical perspective it follows Amnesia fairly closely, deviating most in that (unlike Amnesia) you can in fact be killed by the creatures you encounter, and that there is more than one variety of enemy stalking you through the game.  The design is almost uniformly excellent, so much so that the few merely passable segments stand out in sharp contrast with the rest of the experience.  To this I'll speak with encouragement and also warning to prospective players: the sections directly before and directly after a certain elevator are by far the least pleasant part of the journey in terms of unintentional frustration.  They feel like they were designed very early on in the game's life cycle and never effectively revisited.  There's much more game to be had beyond them, though, so bite your lip and muscle through.
Buy this game!  Play it!  If only so that I can have more people to discuss it with.

DAMN. This game was amazing, wouldn't have expected nothing less from Frictional since this game was under development for five years! They basically started to work on this almost right after Amnesia The Dark Descent was released. Good work, Frictional!
The story was... really great and many times, especially towards the end I got this unsettling feeling inside, really making me think how to actually define the human being. The game really sucks you in and with the horror elements it's easily one of my favourite games. I spent 12 hours on the main story and since we have mod support (Amnesia's Custom stories), we can expect some great user content to really extend the play time one can get from this game!
The graphics aren't AAA-level, but after all Frictional Games isn't a huge studio, but everything was still a pleasure to look at. The graphical effects were also really cool and makes this game unique graphics-wise.
I absolutely loved Amnesia: TDD's Finnish-made soundtrack and effects. Gladly Frictional Games still uses Tapio Liukkonen's sound effect services and Mikko Tarmia's eerie soundtrack. The game is amazing for your ears too, helping to find the right atmosphere for the current situation.
The gameplay is quite similar to Frictional's previous games. We've got a great physics engine and really, one thing I missed in A Machine For Pigs (Shame on you thechineseroom) was the interactibility. I spent the first 10 minutes of the game throwing stuff around in Simon's apartment. Oh, it feels great!
The monsters in this game are unique. All of them move and react differently, making you wonder how to get past this one. Once you get the gist of one, it isn't hard to overcome the situation, but damn it's still scary since you can't know if it reacts in other ways too.
Full 10 out of 10. One of my favourite games.
One thing I'm still wondering though. How did Simon get the flashlight?
A true dynamic and visually stunning game! Worth the money I paid.

Rush Bros. is the rare type of game that manages to fail at its core mechanic. It is a rhythm platforming game where an algorithm determines the pacing of traps and projectiles based on the beat of a song. Unfortunately the developers have chosen to make the soundtrack a variable, meaning that every person who plays the same level will be met with a different experience and, more importantly, a different level of difficulty.
The level design often betrays itself and the player; where a certain coloured platform may be safe to stand on, another platform of the same colour will instantly kill the player. Similarly, traps may fly across the screen and kill the player in a manner you never would have expected. Nothing is ever clearly explained or defined before the player encounters an obstacle, which means you'll often have to play through a level multiple times before understanding how it actually works. It's a level of artificial difficulty created by the developer as more of a joke on the player rather than competent game design.

PROS: More of the same from Shadow Warrior 2013. Same great melee (now with chainsaws!), great gun variety, fun Chi powers, and skills to customize your play style.
Well optimized game engine yields high performance with beautiful visuals with very minimal slow down.
Wang's one liners lighten the game up.
Looting upgrades seemed like a chore at first but quickly became a fun game feature, as it allows the player even further customization of how their weapon is used. With 8 weapon slots, the player can have two weapons for each damage element (fire ice electric poison) for use against enemies with resistances and weaknesses. The upgrades seem designed such that optimization is there if you want to make the effort, but simply throwing in a random assortment of upgrades usually does the trick as well.
Plays wonderfully with Steam Controller but requires a bit of thoughtful configuration to make it play perfectly since there's a lot of hotkeys.
CONS: Long in-game cutscenes are okay at first but towards the end of the game I started to skip them. Would be better if there were a choice for which quip we want to make as a dialogue choice.
Finding secrets is a bit of a chore, I liked SW2013's take on finding low-poly Build Engine-esque rooms more than SW2's approach. I have found 15 secrets in 25 hours and I'm not going to go for the 50 secrets achievement, it's annoying trodding around the levels looking for secrets.
I recommend this if you liked SW2013, want a tongue-in-cheeck FPS, want to play coop, or enjoy FPS melee.

I really like this game! This is an awesome strategy game with a nice mixture of real-time strategy and a boardgame-like turn-based strategy. It seems very simple but it's not! You can decide between two different modes: The (in my opinion) better mode is to conquer whole europe, the second mode is to get as many points as possible until  the year 1800 (not sure if really 1800 or some other year). You can decide between 5 different countries: Prussia, Great Britain, France, Russia and Austria. Every country has it's pros and cons. For example: Great Britain is an island so you have to build ships to get your troops to another country or Russia has many forests so it's easy to get some wood to build hospitals, barracks etc.
Another cool thing about this game is the Sympathy-system: If you attack another country without declaring war, teh other countries will then start to hate you, but if you declare war with a country, they will "forgive" you (except the country you're attacking of course :P).
So that was a short review about this game. Imperial Glory has many more features which i can't list in this review because it then will get about 5 pages long.
I hope thsi review was helpful for you!
P.S: I forgot to mention something: When you're getting to the end of the game, meaning the stage when you have conquered nearly every country, the game wil start crashing when you have finished a real-time battle. it can only be "fixed" if you let the computer fight against the invading country. It will not get fixed, but then you can fight about 3 battles without crashing, but then it will keep crashing again and you have to let the computer fight. Eidos published a Patch 8 years ago, but it doesn't do anything.

This game was infamously incomplete upon release, with a ton of cut content and numerous bugs which can infrequently rear their ugly heads. At times (albiet not in a long time for me, and on the old 4-disk version, not Steam), it became literally unplayable, blocking me from progressing the story or even being a jittery, graphical mess that's liable to crash from the get-go. But although it can be really frustrating at times, if you're willing to press on, which I highly recommend you do, what we have here is an astounding Star Wars game with a wonderful sense of atmosphere, and a terrific, really dark story about the aftermath of huge wars.
While a lot of content is missing from the game (and should you not be willing to try the Restored Content Mod for whatever reason), the stuff that's there is still amazing. The voice actors do a tremendous job and the writing is very solid. In short, gameplay allows you to explore several parts of this war-weary galaxy, learn more about their history and current situations, and even choose your own outcomes - light or dark, adding to replay value. I've lost count of how many times I've played through the entire thing, and whatever the actual number is, it is guaranteed to rise in the future. Despite its problems - and they are big problems, I admit - this has become my favourite game of all time.

Despite the franchise’s rough reputation, Deep Silver aren’t afraid of milking the Dead Island brand for what it’s worth. In addition to the main game and semi-sequel, we’ve also got a proper sequel in the works, a MOBA, and now a third-person action adventure game. Escape Dead Island is the latter. Swedish Fatshark are at the helm this time. The result is a more story-driven game. This franchise seems to be cursed, so this game comes with its share of problems as well. The audiovisual presentation is all over the place. It’s not really a bad-looking game, but the cel-shading is so overdone that the game looks extremely simple at times. One can wonder what it would look like if the cartoony filter was removed. The music is alright, but the voice acting is generally subpar. And once again, we’ve got a zombie game that takes itself far too seriously. So you can’t just wave it off and call it “unintentionally cheesy”, either.
Most striking of all, is the complete departure from Dead Island’s core mechanics. No longer will you roam an open world, freely craft and upgrade your own weapons that you use to hack up and loot zombies. This is more or less linear experience, where you hardly find any weapons at all, and there are no RPG-elements to be found. Looking at the screenshots, you’ll be forgiven for thinking it’s some sort of interactive story á la Telltale fare. It certainly is more story-focused than any previous Dead Island games, but there’s much more actual gameplay here than in a Telltale game; but the gameplay is so simplistic and repetitive, you’ll wish there was none at all.
The story presented here isn’t all that bad. It’s nothing prize-worthy, but it definitely taps into some interesting things with its character gradually going insane. And it satisfyingly ramps up towards the end, too. You, as the player, will start second-guessing what’s actually happening and what’s only in protagonist Cliff’s head. It reminded me of Spec Ops: The Line; it’s got that same sort of “The gameplay is so mundane but I really want to see what happens next in the story!” vibe. Only here, the story isn’t nearly as good. And the gameplay is even less rewarding. And at nearly twice the price compared to what Telltale charge for their much better adventure games, Escape Dead Island is a damn hard sell. I’d only recommend it if you get it on a sale. And even then, you might end up bored.

If you are looking for a different kind of RTS this is it!
I am a both a big Civ and RTS fan (growing up on Age of Empires etc.) and I have found OTC to be a very nice balance between these two types of games. So if you like strategy like Civ but with the adrenaline and frenzy of an RTS this is your game.
I won't go into the mechanics of the game as you can read plenty of that and there are great tutorials online alread. I do want to address the comment of the game being "too simple" without a lot of depth. People who say this are only thinking in terms of learning all the rules and mechanics, and once they figure that out in a few hours they think there is not much left to the game.
Dead wrong!
You need to think of OTC more like a real-time and complex board game, like chess. Yes, learning the rules and how the different pieces in chess doesn't take long, but the game is infinitely complex. OTC is similar, once the mechanics are down the fun begins! I actually like that the game is 'limited' in some ways - the map is only so big, there are only so many options for attacking your opponent etc. But the variation is infinite and it is all about moves and countermoves and improving your gameplay and skill.
The best kind of game is one that has elegant rules and gameplay but provides for a lot of imagination. Combined with the fact most games only take 20-40 minutes and it hits a nice sweet spot of a satisfying experience without dragging on for hours like Civ (hey, I like Civ, but it is nice to have a quicker game!)
Give it a chance to really learn the strategy and I think you won't be dissappointed.

The game 15 years in the making...
Granted this game has been torn apart by critics, and Duke fans alike... is it really as bad as they make it out to be? Actually no in my opinion, Here is why
The game was released in 2011, around 15 in troubled development. Forever is a direct sequel to Duke Nukem 3D. The game was first announced in 1997, reannounced in 2001, and again reannounced in 2007. The game then saw life breathed into it around 2009 as they (Gearbox Software) confirmed they were finishing the game. The game plays like a game from that era of FPS games. Limited weapons, sometimes overwhelming enemy numbers, but I personally find it enjoyable like that. If you do not like the limited weapon numbers, you can change it in the ingame options menu. The gameplay is just fine, it is nothing super special, but it functions on a basic level and can actually be pretty fun at times, when enemies try to surround you, and you have to use the right weapons in the right circumstance. The game also runs well in my testing of the game. Without V-Sync enabled (highly suggest you use that) the game can hit access of 1500 FPS, while with vsync, the game is locked at a very stable 60. The game also has many varied environments, but the colors used are kind of washed out, and overly dull in my opinion.
Another thing that has always bothered me about this game is the rebounding health bar. I get that when it was released, those were and still are the most common way of health regeneration in these types of games, but for a Duke Nukem game, that was a questionable decision. Although it really does not affect gameplay to much. The voice dialouge by Jon St. Jon (voice of Duke) is honestly really good. I think this is the best version of Duke, even if he does say some of the lines a bit to often, or if he repeats some of the older games lines, they are still enjoyable to hear. The game also loads so much faster than the console counter-parts in my playtime of the game.
Overall, the enjoyment factor for you may vary when compared to me personally, and that is alright. The game is really not as bad as people make it out to be. The controls work, and are actually pretty good. The weapons are standard for FPS games, and the variety in environemts is actually a nice change of pace for this game. The voice acting for Duke himself is also a highlight. Negatives include repetitive gameplay, some cheap deaths, the extremely crude humor (not really a negative for me personally, but some people may not like it to much.) The pointless side activites, and the overall lack of replayability. I say if you can find this game dirt cheap, give it a shot. I personally enjoy the game, and maybe you will too if you actually give it a chance.

tldr; great game, easily worth the full price.  Some wonkyness in terms of bullet spawn and hitboxes, but it's consistent and predictable with some practice, and fun from the start.
If you consider yourself a twitch gamer, this gem will test your mettle.  If you consider yourself patient, this game will cause you to re-evaluate.  If you like a challenge, the achievements associated are a feather for your cap (especially Kensai CM).
This game has stones - big ones.  And rage.  And an awesome soundtrack.
Games last 90 seconds or less - if you're a winner it'll end at 90 seconds no matter what.  Short, simple, video arcade runs are the only thing this game is; variations include random spawn, 4 class mods (CMs), 5 types of gun (sounds low but it's more than enough), and a couple of different maps (always random).
There is some predictability to enemy movement but they'll surprise you, too.  A small visible area  is a *feature* of the game designed to make it twitchy, but to compensate, bullets move slow enough that you can
outrun them... but not quite.  In other words, it's balanced.
VERY nice work, devs!
~Controls are both simple and intuitive
~Game action is smooth and uniterrupted
~Excellent soundtrack, appropriate to game action
~Game has NEVER crashed or glitched in ~13 hours play
~Some will find hitboxes glitchy, but it can be learned and compensated for
~Some will not like bullet spawn being in front of the gun, rather than enemy giving indication of firing
~Some will not like minor screen shake upon being hit by enemy fire
~Player cannot slide along walls, meaning, you can't move diagonally in the direction of a wall that you're already touching; you have to clear the wall first
***A note as to the "Cons" - having a dozen hours of playtime invested, I have found these things to be
rather than negatives, because they are predictable and one can adjust play to compensate.

Full disclosure: I've been playing this game frequently enough on Android via Google Play and consider myself decent at the game. I have also spent zero dollars on this.
As far as mobile-to-Steam ports go, this is a very good 1:1 port of a game. I was concerned once I read that Archbears was going to port the game to Steam since it's kind of an odd game to consider playing on a computer. Part of me was worried that the community here was going to draw comparisons to PUBG despite the game being around for longer (how much I couldn't tell you since I don't know nor do I really care to know). Part of me was worried that the unusual method of gameplay was going to turn people off since it usually amounts to dice rolls on you getting what you want and avoiding what you don't want. I'm glad that through a cursory glance that this isn't really the case and people here seem to enjoy it.
The addition of hotkeys is, I feel, something that's necessary to keep it playable on PC compared to on a phone or tablet. Decisions must be made quickly and the increased distance, even if it's only in inches, can have the potential of ruining a solid run in the game. The fact that the game can be played without clicking at all is a testament to the usefulness behind these hotkeys (although I would recommend to use the M+KB in tandem considering it's right there).
I'm not particularly interested in the IAP model, but I don't feel that it's necessary in order to get by in the game and this is the stated intent by AB. Gems can buy you characters, skins for said characters, gold, and boosters to assist you. Ultimately, this won't matter if you're not good at the game in the first place. The rotation has been varied enough that it caters to all weapon playstyles and the starter character is almost insulting in how good and dangerous he is in the right hands. The free weapon and armor booster can actively screw you if they don't match the playstyle of the character you've chosen (Rosalio doesn't need a gun, for god's sake) and the free food booster isn't going to matter in the long run. The only worthwhile one is the extra bag slot. Not to mention all boosters are free until you hit carnivore league, meaning it'll be a while before gems and gold come into play.
As for backstory, it becomes available on completing certain tasks per character. Do enough damage, make enough of this or that, etc. Along with pieces of plot, you get free boosters of the food, armor, and weapon kind, meaning you don't have to spend money yet again. I will say, though, with nine other people in the way, it is really hard to get at some of these tasks and it'll be a while before you finish off a character's list, if ever.
Overall, the port is as good and even better than it was on mobile. The price for gems is reasonable and the devs want you to not feel like you have to spend anything to get anywhere. They just want you to have fun trying to deal with other people and that's something I can get behind.

A worthy successor to Amnesia: The Dark Descent, SOMA is a visceral and engaging experience that wades more deeply into the dark waters of speculative Sci-fi than traditional Horror (though there's absolutely no shortage of physical and psychological ghastliness on display) through the unpleasant ambiguities it asks the player to face.  More often than not these ideas bubble up slowly over time, with only a small numer of heavyhanded moral or expository moments scattered across the 8-12 hours of play.  From a mechanical perspective it follows Amnesia fairly closely, deviating most in that (unlike Amnesia) you can in fact be killed by the creatures you encounter, and that there is more than one variety of enemy stalking you through the game.  The design is almost uniformly excellent, so much so that the few merely passable segments stand out in sharp contrast with the rest of the experience.  To this I'll speak with encouragement and also warning to prospective players: the sections directly before and directly after a certain elevator are by far the least pleasant part of the journey in terms of unintentional frustration. This isn't a bad game nor is it the worst Duke Nukem game. Sure, it's not great and its a bad Duke game when compared to the likes of DN3D, it's prequel, but there's fun to be had here. I can see why it wasn't well received and♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥people off. I wouldn't pay full price for this on launch. Not to mention the changes they made to the gameplay after launch (more weapons slots) were pretty significant. Very significant.
Let's get one thing out of the way first. The Visuals. They are nothing to write home about but won't make your eyes bleed either. There's a distinct lack of colour even when i bumped up the vibrance in my GPU settings. I can only imagine how dull this looks without the extra colour vibrance. On the PC, the textures are a huge step up from consoles. There are still some ugly ones but overall not really that bad to look at. This game gets a lot of♥♥♥♥♥♥for its crappy textures and I can assure you most of them come from console players or reviewers. Not every texture is a sore to look at.
I have nothing much to say about the audio besides the fact that its lacking a whole lot in everything. The music isn't engaging and the guns all sound pathetic. They lack punch in terms of effectiveness in game and the sounds they produce. One thing I really appreciated and liked is Duke's One liners and Banter. I chuckled quite a bit but then again maybe it's nostalgia. I don't care. I liked it.
Now let's get to the meat of this review. What matters in a video game of this type. The gameplay. It's easily the worst aspect of the game and that's bad news for a video game. It's such a mess of mixed ideas. The initial 2 weapon limit was absolutely stupid. Who thought that would be a good idea. Granted they patched in 4 slots but 4 slots are not enough to do justice to Duke's badass arsernal. To add insult to injury, the weapons all lack punch. You're not sure if you're shooting actual bullets or nerf bullets. Even the Devastator feels weak. It takes away all the fun in the gun fights. The gunfights themselves are boring af. At first I thought there was a certain sense of strategy involved in the fights but then I realized all I did was hide behind ♥♥♥♥ing cover. This is especially true thanks to the EGO meter, which I don't mind as much, but It kinda seems like the whole gameplay was designed around accomodating the EGO meter. This isn't Call of Duty. Boss fights can be infuriating at times and I found myself often exploiting the game environments to defeat bosses.
The gameplay isn't restricted to gunplay. There are puzzles in store which although are quite easy to solve and often times tedious, was a good distraction from the god awful gunplay. I liked the inclusion of it. The pacing could have used more work though and the loading screens are far too many but hey at least on PC its quick to load. I bet it lost points for that on consoles. Speaking of consoles, this game oozes of console design choice. Heck, even the control schemes seems skewed towards using a controller over a keyboard and mouse. There's this dreaded mouse smoothing which can be minimized but it still feels like trash to use. What's worse is the god damn way weapons are switched with no clear slot for your weapons so you'll have to shuffle through till you find what you want even if you bind some hotkeys.

Creative ideas in there but fighting while shrunk is a whole other pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ Still, I like how it tries to be old school with its interactivity and design in certain areas.
All in all, a lot of the♥♥♥♥♥♥this game gets can be equated to the platform it was played on, some console focused design choices, lackluster gameplay at times, the state on launch and the price paid on launch.

Feesh is a unique arcade-style game with minimalist visuals and a chill, ambient soundtrack. The game was made by Tj Hughes, an up-and-coming indie dev & musician from St Louis, as his first commercially released project. Tj began work on Feesh at age 16, which explains the tounge-and-cheek-natured writing on the game's store page and in the in-game instructions.
The objective of the main game (Arcade mode) is to eat other fish smaller than you so you can evolve to a new form and move on the the next stage. Stages get progressivley more difficult and each one introduces a new gimmick that you can use to your advantage.
You have to eat fish smaller than you, otherwise you'll get eaten yourself and lose a life. There are many different kinds of fish, some have unique ways to hamper your progress, others give you perks like shrinking larger fish that are nearby.
It's a very difficult game, seeing as you have no idea if a larger fish or shark is nearby, meaning you have to react quickly. It adds an element of survival, and with the floaty controls it feels somewhat like Sinistar (Google it), which I happen to like.
The game also has a Chill Out mode where you can sit back and watch the AI-controlled fish glide around and eat each other. There's also Shark Attack mode, a brutally difficult gamemode where you're being hunted down by a huge swarm of sharks.
Overall, Feesh is a nice little game, and a promising start for a young, self-taught developer.
I should note that Tj Hughes is currently working on an experimental art-game called Nour, which just so happened to surpass its $25k Kickstarter goal the other day. Having backed Nour I'm really excited to see how much Tj's skills have improved since he made Feesh, once the game comes out early next year.

Some of the reviews for this game (the negative ones) surprise me. This is a really wonderful game and one of my favorites of the "last" generation.
It's a very simple premise. You are a sniper with the United States military and are tasked with going deep into the heart of Germany during WWII and sniping people. It's a very good looking game with robust sound and graphical effects with the kill cam being a highlight. It's from the third person perspective and I found the controls to be very responsive.
The game is not without its faults. A sniper is basically a stealth unit, killing people at long range. The fault with this game is that I find the AI's ability to locate you after one sniper shot (even if change positions) relatively easily.  It can get "annoying" (for lack of a better word) and it seems that the entire German army (and some Russians) are also crack shots. While this is a hindrance occasionally, it never took away the fun of the game for me.
The story itself is not very deep, but you're not playing this game for the depth of its story. You're playing it to snipe nazis from afar. I think of this game as a very good B-movie. Its not perfect, but you'll want to play it more often. Heck, even the DLC is fun!

Alrighty, another review! Amnesia: The Dark Descent is one of those games that you see everywhere and wonder how creepy/eerie/scary it might be. Well you just come to the right place if you want to either♥♥♥♥♥♥your pants or learn a fascinating yet gory story. You wake up as Daniel and have no recolation as to where or how you got to where you are when waking up. As the story progresses (and I will try not to have any spoilers) you pick up notes and random journal entries that you had written before passing out and waking up in the beginning. As your memory gets better, you realize you had been working for an evil mastermind named Alexander who kidnapps victims and tortures them to be "experiments". Once found out this, you do whatever you can to stop Alexander. The rest is up to you to find out, besides everyone likes suprises.
Now, when playing this game I was scared within 10 minutes of playing because of the creepy music, random voices and noises, and of course visuals which I will not spoil. If you turn your sound off completely though, it doesn't phase me one bit. So basically, if you are chicken♥♥♥♥♥♥then you should turn off your sound so you can focus on the main objective instead of focusing on what pair of underwear you need to wash from playing this.
In all seriousness though, I would only reccomend someone who has a strong stomach since most of the game is quite gory and if dissassembled body parts freak you out then you shouldn't even be playing this game. I would like to add is that this game is medium length which I don't mind. I wish it was slightly longer but you can only do so much with a story and a horror game.
Something to also add, this game has medium to hard difficulty puzzles which some had taken me days to figure out. So if you are one to rush and add cheats to the game well you are out of luck buddy because there are no cheats except for walkthroughs on the game online, and you must have patience.
I would rate this game a 8/10 and reccomend anyone 16+

SOMA captures a harrowing shade of existential dread in a way that only a smaller development team could accomplish. Similar in tone to the films Moon and "9" with many obligatory nods to Alien, It actually plays very similarly to Alien: Isolation. Even spookier than Bioshock seafloor vibes with amazing writing, believable dialog, clever  pacing that is always taking surprising turns, and very nice voice acting. It deals with many questions of both human identity and machine consciousness in a way that is very sophisticated, well informed and not at all watered down. There also seems to be a theme here of being forced to adjust your expectations in order to deal with the overwhelming harshness of reality. Its super fun and rewarding to explore the beautifully designed maps and learn more about the various habitats and their past. When it comes to the horror aspects of the game, although I am rarely truly disturbed by games or fictional films, there was at least one moment where my hands were shaking too badly to continue playing. I'm pretty sure this exaggerated reaction resulted from the attention paid to the games sound engine that ramps up the tension as sharply as possible when a monster approaches, speaking of which SOMA HAS THE BEST SOUND DESIGN!  I would go so far as to say that this game is a borderline masterpiece, and would be complementary to a fine cut of steak, seafood, pasta or Alien: Isolation.
Final verdict: 9.5 out of 11

Absolutely horrible game. If you have any interest in crafting, stay as far away from this game as you can.
Want to make a sickle? You need 30 forging. But wait; you need 60 in smelting before you can get 30 forging. But wait; you need 90 in materials preparation to be able to get 60 in smelting. Materials preparation has very few recipes and you will not need more than one of any of them and less than one of some of them. This means an endless grind of junk that is not needed.
Want to be a jeweller? You will need 60 in digging and 30 in prospecting just to be able to use the jewellry skill at all. We all know that medieval jewellers mined and smelted all of the metals they used.
There are sliders that can be used to allow skills to progress faster. The problem with this is that some skills progress way faster than others so turning it up for the slow ones makes the quick ones way too quick.
You can also just GM command your skill levels up. I did this twice, but when I saw I was going to have to do it yet again, I decided it was better to forfeit the money that I paid than the future time I would pay to play.
If you are interested in animals, forget this game. Even with the slider at maximum you will likely play for days without seeing more than an animal or two. The animals you raise you cannot see.. They are just icons when you open a stable or coop. You can make fencing but it is absolutely meaningless.
The only part of the game I would call finished is the graphics. The rest of the game needs serious work.  I really doubt much is going to be done to fix this. I have read forum posts from years ago decrying the horrible skill trees.
Please study the wiki before you buy this game. If you study it well, you will be able to discern just how bad it is.

SOMA is another outstanding horror game from Frictional, even though its a bit light on horror. What makes this game so impressive is the incredibly natural pacing, storytelling and puzzles where it is pretty much always clear what you need to do/where you need to go despite a complete lack of any sort of UI or objectives screen. Even during the relatively open ocean-walking sequences I never became lost, almost as if the devs intuatively knew which way players would go. Puzzles are of similar quality; generally you aren't really told what needs to be done, but it can be quite easily figure it out based on the context.
The story is also a highlight, diving into some similar themes as last year's The Talos Principle. While I didn't find the narrative quite as thought provoking as that game, the way the story is told is masterful. Conversations with another character move the central plot forward, but there is a incredible amount of often very important detail to be found in exploring the environment and interacting with various computers/documents that are lying around. It is all done in such a non-gamey way that this science fiction game manages to feel more grounded in reality than many games based in todays real world.
All of this adds up to make the game incredibly immersive. This is aided by stellar sound design that is responsible for much of the tension throughout the relatively lengthy game (for this genre). There are still some terrifying sequences, with a couple of memorable ones later in the game I will likely not forget any time soon. I would say that SOMA is the pinnacle of immersive story-driven gaming, with near-AAA production values (they just need to work on character models) making it easy to forget this is coming from a small indie developer.
Frictional have once again proven themselves to be masters of their genre, and waiting to see what they do next will be a painful process.

SOMA is something that could only be delivered by Frictional Games. After Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs, I wasn't entirely sure what to expect from the studio, albeit I still had plenty of faith in them after playing not only the original Amnesia: the Dark Descent, but also the entire Penumbra series. I can gladly say that SOMA is everything i expected it to be, and I refrained from hearing any news on it online, and also watching any trailers so I would come in knowing nothing about the game and that it would be a fresh experience, and quite frankly, SOMA delivers something so chilling and thought provoking that the original Amnesias fell short of.
Visually and asthetically, SOMA is beautifully dark and somber. While I found a few textures here and there that weren't exactly up to par with the textures elswhere in the game, it wasn't enough to detract from the beauty of the game entirely(It could've also just been my settings though). The look of the underwater facility you explore is entirely unique to me and the odd electronic cancer growing throughout the place is one in it's own. Keep in mind I'm trying my best not to spoil any details of the game. All in all, I found the game to look wonderfull, and even breathtaking at certain segments, having me stop to take in views and truly think about the environment and the situation this game had placed me in.
The gameplay I think is brilliant, and at certain points has the sort of feel that A Machine for Pigs could evoke, only much stronger and enjoyable. Now, I'm not in any way saying this game is alot like AMFP, but the game definitely learns from the mistakes of The Chinese Room's previous installment in the Amnesia series. I was dissapointed with AMFP, just to get that out there now. SOMA is very much comparable to both The Dark Descent and the Penumbra series, at times seemlessly combining the asthetics and gameplay from both of those games and building onto it. I've heard a decent amount of complaining about the monsters and the tactics used in the game, but I much prefer it this way over the whole scripted feel of AMFP, as that game had encounters few and far between, and didn't instill the same type of horror encounters in SOMA and The Dark Descent do. The segments I found most satisfying were sifting through what was left of the underwater facility, and piecing together the mystery of what was left, where i was, and even
I was, more on that later though. I disagree with critics opinions on the whole monster bits and the mechanics used, and in each scenario I found myself horrified, and coward for quite a bit(My first playthrough took me 14 hours). While monsters typically are unique in each encounter and have their own exploits, you witness quite a few throughout the entire game, with some being repeated only a few times throughout. I enjoyed all of this thoroughly and think very highly of the way this game was executed.
Combined with the gameplay, the story is what I think really sets this game apart from most other horror games. Unlike Outlast, a game in which you spent most of your time running from threat to threat with little to no breaks or relief in between, this game offers alot of time spent just rummaging around and so many of the objects in the environment are interactable, it really immerses you and gives you a sense of place. You can walk from room to room, inspecting the contents in each area and even piece together parts of the story just by looking through things and examining the setting thoroughly, and unlike in games such as
, and
, this part of the game is engaging and very interesting to me. At certain segments I longed to hear the comfort of a companions voice while I sifted through rooms piecing together the puzzle that was the story, only to really be cowering behind objects straying from the horrifying monsters that lurk within the games corridors. Now don't get me wrong, I don't think this is a bad thing, in fact I think it's a very good thing. The game switches things up every now and then and the encounters really help you to appreciate the time you get to spend in peace in the game figuring things out for yourself, and in no way is this a bad thing, its exactly what sets this game apart from Gone Home, AMFP, and even
.
SOMA is a surreal and extremely enticing experience and it really doesn't do it justice to just use the word story, as it's more than just a deep and philisophical story told through text or audio clips. Its something you experience, and in doing so provokes thoughts about mankind, our own selves and the consequences that specific decisions could have on not only others, but even oursleves and who we seem to think we may be. It begs the question;

The Good: Fun Comic Book Art style, combat and stealth are fun, Sound Effect Popups
The Bad: Short (3-4 hours without collectibles), Hidden Ending, story feels salvaged,
The WTF: Shifting World that feels hindered by lack of flushing out
Escape: Dead Island is an amazing game hindered by a lack of faith in it by the publisher. What results is a short hobbled version of a grander planned experience. Deep Silvers lack of faith radiates sharply with a complete lack of advertisement for the game leaving my discover of its release solely to pure luck.
The game is short, roughly 3-4 hours if you don't care at all about the collectables. I do, obsessively, so with them you can grind out an additional 2-3 hours. During which you'll be treated to a 3D metroid style world with hidden weapons, collectibles, and health upgrades galore. Through the collectibles and pictures you take with the camera you'll receive the majority of the back-story, of the virus's lore, the villains motivation, essentially everything.
On the other hand, the main story  is hobbled, short, and feels salvaged. It and its characters would be entirely forgettable without the flushing out the lore collectibles provides them. Without spoiling the ending, I must say it doesn't resolve anything, but there is a hidden ending. Unlocking it is as mysterious as unlocking the 4 bunkers in game, and help for doing so as of this writing is entirely none existent.
Gameplay wise the game does well. There is a simple stealth system that you will rarely use, but the main combat mechanics (Melee and guns) flows fluidly, with each blow results in a reaction from any creature. Once timing is perfected for the harder enemies they're easy although time consuming to dispatch. Dodge mechanic is responsive and a pure requirement for combat. Without its use enemies will auto lock onto you, rarely missing.
Stealth is deadly, especially after recovering the knife allowing for instantaneous takedowns. Sneaking up on unaware enemies allows for stealth kills, dropping the enemy instantly regardless of class. It is extremely satisfying to get a higher tier mutant this way. Unfortunately level design often hinders stealth, levels are often narrow and compact leaving little to no room to sneak behind enemies with only a few exceptions. Important linear areas typically boil down to combat only, with a few opportunities for thinning the horde.
Aesthetically the games comic book, heavy black lines and pop up sound effects give the game a fantastically fun feel. Hit walls, sound effect, hit enemies, sound effect, steam coming out of a pipe, sound effect. Without a doubt the sound effect popup were my favorite feature. Details are not skimped on, characters are detailed, while mutants/infected have a few variations are largely the same class to class.
I had fun with Escape Dead Island, but what stops me from recommending this game is the lack of conclusion it has. It's something that is nearly impossible explain without spoiling what happens after the end so spoiler warning :
There are hints that something else is going on, but answers and satisfaction are relegated to the hidden ending. Price wise I feel good about the game, but I got it last minute prepurchase while on sale, giving access to Dead Island 2 beta and a first issue of the Dead Island comic. Without these perks I'd wait till the game hits around $20 to pick it up.

The basic premise of the game is simple. The tiny feesh has to eat smaller feesh to grow in size, whilst avoiding being eaten by bigger feesh. Some have special skills, such as producing child feesh. Some are more aggressive than the rest, such as the sharks that will track down the player feesh.
Arcade mode is the main one I played. After reaching a certain size, the feesh evolves into a different type. My main criticism here is that this doesn't unlock the new type permanently. I'm never going to be good enough to play through all the different creatures in one game, so it'd be nice if I could start with a later creature. That way, I'd have a chance to eventually play all the available types.
I liked the way the other feesh are doing the same thing as the player feesh. Sometimes one of those feesh will end up growing very large, as they successfully manage to eat loads of tiny feesh. It creates the feel of a working ecosystem, where the player is no more important than any of the other feesh. Eaten feesh respawn elsewhere, so there will always be other feesh around to continue the game.
The art style is fairly minimalistic with a whimsical flair. I'd note there are some flashes of light at times, though it's more of a gradual increase in light rather than a strobe effect.
This is the sort of game for playing a round in odd moments. It doesn't have a whole lot of depth, but what it does have is nicely done. It's cute and I enjoyed the feel of the art and the funny descriptions of the feesh.

Fire and Sword is the third game from mount and blade franchise, it changes a lot of features from the first two games, some for good and some for worse, either way this is a must have game if you liked the first one, although it's not as fun as warband you can still get a lot of hours of playtime from this.
The map this time is based around the zone of Russia , i don't understand much about history but i think this story arc is about how russia federate was born or something.
Graphical wise it looks a lot better than the vanilla mount and blade, and there's quite a lot of armor and designs this time around, there's still some glitches around like your neck being attached to your shoulder but it's all ok.
Unlike the previous games you can now recruit infantry,marksmen or cavalry at mercenaries camps, each faction having their own kind of mercenaries, can also buy them better armor , weapons and more, where in the previous games you had to recruit militia from villages and train them a lot via battles or trainer skill until they become somewhat battle worthy.
You can no longer retire and get a "rank" when you want to quit, this time to win you have to conquer all the world playing as one faction, 3 of them have a special storyline also quite challenging to do, secret of the black mace, the deluge and the false Dmitry all based on historical events.
This game also comes with gunpowder weaponry hence fire and sword name, pistols, carbines and muskets are quite overpowered, a bandit can pretty much one shot a veteran mercenary on full armor set if they get a clear shot, but so can you use that in your advantage.
There's more stuff to build in towns/castles like bank to deposit money and gain a % per month, armor/weapon crafter to get special stuff, i personally recommend getting enough strenght to use crafted armor set it's awesome looking, horse breeder to get an awesome horse, academy to train your companions if you have any and more, oh and you can send trade caravans now for a lot of profit if you know how.
Game is easily worth the full price even if you don't like the gunpowder aspect of the game, if you have the extra money buy the whole collection you won't regret it.

The Vikings are a more comedic approach, with one particular mission going full action packed D-Day.

The multiplayer can be broken down into multiple modes.
Duel - 1v1.
Brawl - 2v2.
Elimination - 4v4
Skirmish - 4v4 with npc who you can kill for a small boost in points.
Dominion - 4v4 with multiple places to capture like king of the hill.
Faction board - On top of all the game modes, every game you complete gives players "War assests" which can be used to take control of areas on the map, essentially this is like chess.
Winners of the Faction Board get exclusive prezzies and runner ups also get a little gift.
The combat system in For Honor is really indepth, Light/Heavy attacks, Dash attacks, Unblockable attacks, Stun attacks, blocking, parrying and of course those sweet sweet combos that come in between.
Players also get "Feats" which are pre-game buffs you can unlock and select through the pre-game menu.
You can get things from Crossbows to catapults as well as buffs that allow you to heal team mates with a certain area, or even drain your enemies stamina.
For Honor has a big learing curve which is easy to learn, but most certainly hard to master.
Good game, well played.

TLDR: This game is incredible fun. <-- Yes that was very uninformative, let's get down to it.
The Introduction:
When playing this you quickly become familiar with terms like, "DEUS VULT" or "weebs".
There are 3 factions to pick from, and the players seems very passionate about their faction for the most part.
When you launch the game for the first time, it asks for you to pick a faction. I felt uncomfortable picking right away, because the game hadn't introduced me to anything about the factions, or if the choice was permanent or not. Thankfully you can always change which faction you fight for at a later point.
The faction you pick, does not limit your choice of classes to pick from, so regardless of which faction you choose you can pick any class. If you want to get all lore and immersion, feeling it breaking either of those, then I'd argue you're wrong, there could always be mercenaries of either side. So it would make perfect sense either way.
The Game Mechanics:
So what is this game like? Well it's like a fighting game really.
It got some Dark Souls vibes, but not really like dark souls, yet it feels like it.
It's like chivalry, but only in the sense of the setting and the very in-depth combat mechanics. However the combat mechanics in For Honor are much deeper.
Essentially it boils down to an almost fighting game, button combos and what now.
So you gotta memorize button combos to execute certain moves, sounds like a fighting game right?
Feels like a fighting game in some aspects, but then not again really.
There's also objective based game modes etc. It may feel a bit like TF2 at times, speaking of TF2 let's move onto the elephant in the room.
Microtransactions:
Yes, there is microtransactions. Microtransactions inherently got a rumor to be bad business, but in cases like Dota2 microtransactions are acceptable. Equally so for CS:GO among others.
This game is a bit like CS:GO and TF2 when it comes to its microtransactions, it's mostly for cosmetics only.
I don't feel there is much more need to go further on this subject, as I've pretty much said everything there is to it.
You can buy Steel (in-game currency) and for these you can buy "Lootboxes" - A premium loot box costs about 500 steel, and by playing for a few hours you have 2-4.000 steel, which is enough for 4-8 lootboxes which gives you 20-40 items, for each class!.. that's more than enough to fully gear yourself to begin with. - Also note, you don't have to buy the classes, to actually play them!!! - Many people miss that.
The items is mostly like items in TF2, the end.
Controls:
Mouse & Keyboard VS Controller, the question everyone cares about.
Yes, you can play this game with both, it's easier to learn via a controller, but hard to master. While on mouse and keyboard it's hard to learn but easy to master. Since you'll have more direct control of your actions.
So as you can clearly see there is advantages and disadvantages of both.
Should you buy a controller for this? Why don't you own a controller already!? And you call yourself a PC gamer?.. pfft!
No really, but serious question: Do you need a controller for this? - I've already answered, learning curve vs mastering.
Longevity:
Feels like there are plenty of hours of gameplay.
I've played the game for 48hours, still haven't even touched the singleplayer campaign, it's not that I don't want to. It's just that I'm having so much fun with multiplayer, but I really have to play it at some point to unlock some cosmetic stuff.
I could easily get 100 hours out of this.
Price:
I'd say it's fairly expensive.
Is it worth the price, well it depends on how you value money. For instance, a 60€ price tag needs to provide me with at least 100hours playtime, that’s not including partial afk periods in the menu etc, but actual play time where you actually want to play the game and not forcing yourself to play something, just because you paid for it.
But as for me, if I can fulfill my minimum of 100hours, then yes, I’d consider it worth it.
However, there is microstransactions and a season pass, I don’t know how BS the dlc will be, or if it divides the playerbase. But it can quickly become very expensive, however if you just settle for a class to main, it doesn’t feel all that bad, there is a lot of things that’s locked behind actual play, and not pay. Again that’s cosmetics, where you have to complete singleplayer campaign for instance or reach a certain level with a class, so it’s not like you can buy everything with money.
Future DLC aside, the game seems good for the price, it’s very well optimized and runs extremely well. I feel like the quality control of the game and it’s performance including how much content there is, the 60€ price tag seems reasonable. I was very uncertain if the game was something for me or not, and I kinda took a gamble on it, and it paid off. I’m liking the game a lot.
Conclusion:
The game seems to present itself with a Chivalry vibe to it, but also looks a bit like Dark Souls at some point, yet anyone who played both would say it’s not really like Dark Souls at all. It really depends on the class you play, I’ve played a lot of Dark Souls pvp(played over 1000 hours), and to some aspects the game feels a like, however each class in this game is like a premade character for you in dark souls, the big and heavy feels like you are fat rolling, feels unplayable and you get angry at yourself for being ♥♥♥♥ing fat and you can’t dodge for♥♥♥♥♥♥ If you’re like me you likely strive towards the lighter and faster classes, they are quicker and feels more responsive, less fat to go about. But instead of just having a light and strong attack, you can combo the buttons for a better result, and it starts to feel a bit like a fighting game at that point. I don’t mind the fact that it feels like this, I’ve always been fascinated by fighting games, but never really been into one. Not until now, if you can even count this as one. Perhaps it’s because of the setting, I’ve personally always preferred the fantasy setting.
I have yet to fulfill my minimum requirement of 100 hours, but there’s a lot of people who’s in doubt about whether or not to buy this game or not, I thought I’d try to be of some assistance, maybe I have, maybe I’ve not at all. But you can spend a lot of hours with just a single class, and takes a long time to fully master one, I’ve still mastered none with 48hours in, I’ve tried a bit of everything to try and find my main.
What I’m trying to get at is, arguing for the value you get for your money, I make up the value in time spend playing. But the product also has to be of a certain quality and this game feel very well optimized, it feels very rare that you actually get such as good and well optimized game nowadays.
Yes, there is also a field of view slider.
At its current state, without any DLC or content patches, but just the main base game at this point. The game feels like it’s worth the money, however I may chance my stance on this depending on how they handle their upcoming dlc.

Arma 3 is a great military simulator sandbox. The game is build upon the community and the games modes they make. You can find everything from King of the Hill to Role-Playing servers to loot-to-survive(called wasteland) game modes and many more. There are some offical servers that offer basic games and draw some traffic but the real center of Arma 3 is private servers. These privately owned servers usually have their own dev team if it is a role-playing server for example. They will progress their servers features and activites indepenent from other servers. Many of my hours have been logged in these RP servers. They offer progression systems and a challenge to newcomers.
Learning shooting techniques has a steep learning curve but can feel rewarding when lining up shots. Gameplay is slower in nature and heavily tactics based typically. There are times when I spend 30 minutes to an hour climbing a hill and setting up a shot to kill one person. It is the best feeling when these plans work. All vehicle controls are pretty solid and decent damage models too. Sometimes the fps element leave something to be desired but are not killing.
The game becomes most enjoyable with friends and groups when you get organized to do a mission or something like that. There are military sim units that can be joined and there are always people to be found.
Pros:
-Great sandbox
-Many unique game modes
-Fantasic mod support
-Vehicles are fun
Cons:
-Occasional bugs/glitched
-CPU based game makes it hard to get high FPS even on nice rigs
-Gunplay could be better

From the below you can read my thoughts about the game.
I would recommend this if you like:

- solid controls
- weapon/skill modding like hell
- looting and little bit more _looting_
- inappropriate humour
- co-op fps

- original shadow warrio game (1997) -> get the Shadow Warrior (2013) if you haven't already ;)
- limited accessories
Open word:
Shadow Warrior 2 isn't the same thing than the first modern Shadow Warrior. Great graphics, solid controls and versatile enemies. Anything is kind of right but still there are some things that doesn't kind of fit in the picture.
Dragon Mountain and teleporting:
The game has some kind of "home area/town" where you can buy ammo and stuff. The weird part is that you can teleport there during the mission. The first part had great level design. You really didn't need to access shop during the level and I think that you really shouldn't need that. It kill the flow, destroys the immersion of the level. Maybe this has been done for Co-op to balance players equipment during mission.
RPG/looting/etc.:
Shadow Warrior 2 has loads of more RPG elements in it. Not really that what I expected for old school fps successor (like the first one was). Lots of looting and lots of weapon modding. Different power ups like fire, poison etc. familiar stuff from RPGs.
Levels:
Levels are wide almost open world levels. There are some old school design elements like keys.
__Menus are a mess__ UI design looks like it was made cheap and fast. The first one had better UX design.
Dying/Challenge (Thanks for stephenronline about corrections):
If you die during the mission you automatically spawn again to the nearest checkpoint (not far where you were). You will lose your karma (level up progress) and shadow fury but you wont lose your money. Maybe dying should punish you little bit more. Max out the difficulty you won't lose a lot if you die.
Overall:
Shadow Warrio 2 is mix of old school action and Borderlands series. I would rather take stricter level design and less menus. But I would still recommend it. It is still Shadow Warrior and there really isn't too much co-op fps games around. I prefer Shadow Warrior 2013. This sequel isn't exactly the shadow warrior I would like to see. Nevertheless it is a impressive game that has lots of content.

As someone who came from the mobile version, I can highly recommend this game.
The game is free, but there's almost no pay-to-win content, many people have already compared it to league, PUBG, etc. Like many round based games, one round does not effect another and every player starts out on the same level(no items, level 1).
Through the Herbivore Ranks(Mouse -> Elephant) which is essentially the tutorial phase to get players more accustom to the game, the developers are insanely generous, giving out free revives, gold for every rank up, etc. The perks are insane just so players could feel like they're on the same playing ground when they step in to Carnivore Ranks(Fox->Dragon), or ranked when the points are actually recorded every season.
Now, the biggest concern of the game appears to be a concern that it is like a mobage game where it starts free then quickly becomes "pay to win" or "pay to play". It is a valid concern, after all the developers must make money somehow. However...
the majority of the income of the game comes from SKINS which are completely optional.
Some people might argue about the revive gold, but it is literally 1 dollar per month for free unlimited revive all month, and even that is optional because gold is earned through just playing the game, and through my 3 month of playing this game I have never had an issue where I "ran out of gold to revive my character".
Overall, you can't find many games more generous than this one, and the gameplay is almost entirely skill based, obviously there are some luck factor but it is a minor part of the gameplay.

Games like Amnesia are pretty rare. Where Silent Hill faded in quality after more iterations due to ignorance of its roots Amnesia took the best parts of Penumbra and refined them into silky-smooth physics and added a Lovecraftian plot filled with gruesome imagery and
.
PLOT
Sadly I can't really say much about the plot, the whole idea is that you're slowly recovering from amnesia and discovering where you are and why you're there, so spoiling it would gimp the experience a little. Don't worry, it unfolds perfectly through your actions.
DESIGN
Visually Amnesia is stunning. Some of the textures are a bit low-res but they're usually unimportant. The lighting is incredible, it feels almost painted on to the environment. A perfect example would be the hall area with the creepy fountain. The castle areas are freaky and unsettling and look almost photorealistic in some places. The design gives a claustrophobic, terrifying atmosphere to every area and you'll be on the edge of your seat (Unless you use a walkthrough, PÜSSY).
SOUND
The sound design is also amazing, one of the most important parts of the game. Echoing screams reverberate around the chamers of the castle, the sounds of the castle slowly crumbling around you, the moans of the servants creeping in the darkness.
