Just finished this game so I feel qualified to speak for this particularly controversial title & I'm keeping it short.
It's nothing as openly mindless laced with a sort of story background as Duke 3D was, instead we have a Halo + Half-life knock off mix with a duke paint job. But is it good? Well for most part I found it surprisingly entertaining, Not blown away, more like watch a B-movie kind of entertaining if you get my drift. This clearly had the potential to be much more with very little effort i.e textures brought up to date, better meshes, make even better use of such a solid engine & revisit some dubious decisions like locking the game down, no map editor, no mod support etc.
My most surprising take from this perhaps is that this title can still be saved if it's taken by it's publisher, rehased & re-released with the suggestions above plus a few more to make it more community friendly but should I recommend it? If you have it already, sure! Do give this game a chance & dive into it without expectations... you may well be positively surprised (if you can make it through the very slow start), from those who don't have it.. buy it only if it's under $5.

8/10
I admit I was expecting something more like Outpost... but it's not the surviving that's difficult. Base-building is deceptively simple, yet has subtleties that aren't immediately obvious - like connecting buildings to your HQ gives you free transport to them, while grouping them together gives bonuses to production but makes them easier to sabotage.
Once you start to grasp the way the competition works, though, and realise it's all about monopolies, resource manipulation and making good use of your scarce sabotage opportunities to outdo your opponents it really starts to shine.

I do check in from time to time, but there has been no news for years, and the most recent reviews regularly say the same thing; this game is dead.

I don't like survival horror games, but got this based on the positive consensus. Absolutely loved it. If there are other horror games like this, I want to know about them.
Gameplay = 9/10; it felt like a mixture of Half-Life 2 and Bioshock, with good puzzles and incredibly tense stealth scenarios. No hand-holding. Very rarely did I get frustrated or confused. Very often did I get scared and excited.
Graphics = 8/10; a combination of really impressive locales with some relatively poor human graphics. The detail in the locations were usually great but often repetitive.
Story = 10/10; took a strong premise and fully committed to the story and characters. The voice acting was effective and consistent, probably some of the best I've ever heard in a video game. While the progression was linear, the world felt fully realized through all the minor details. Most importantly, the story never felt like a series of manufactured "choices"; nothing was done for shock factor. It actually had a story to tell and let the player feel each consequence for his or herself.
Only Con: consistent game crashing bugs which forced me to search online for solutions and led me to some minor spoilers.

First off, this is NOT my kind of game. I'm the kind of player who prefers to spend time investing in one persistent game (as in Cities:Skylines, Dark Souls or an MMO), rather than a match-based game like this one.
That said and given the premise of the match RTS subgenre, I have to say it's a very refreshing IP. No combat whatsoever, but instead an all-out trading system where you manipulate the market and make sure you produce, buy and sell the right kinds of resources for maximum profit and the detriment of your opponents (who share your market).
As for resources, they do feel a bit few and "slapped onto" the game. There's no explicit tree structure or overall design that makes me feel like I should care (possibly because of the said match-based gameplay, which makes everything feel rushed).
I guess I just wish that this kind of trade-focused game would be more fleshed out, with greater array of goods, upgrades, services, alternatives and just general depth. The game feels like a one-man indie game project.
Overall, I have to say that the idea is pretty good and, for its premise and its price, the game plays decently (but not excellently). I can recommend this game, although just barely (I wish there was a third choice haha). The game does have major potential, and I do think the devs may deliver on some of that. I also haven't seen any major bugs with this game yet, but I haven't played it too much either so idk. But I do wish the game was just a few notches better than it is.

I play quite a few stratagy type games so jumped straight into a single player game. It did not go well and was bought out by rival corps pretty quickly as my stock price was low and I amounted a large amount of debt! So I hit up the tutorials which cover very basic gameplay and could do with hints on the way to improve stocks prices or reduce debt/cancel out debt all together.
Yes there are diferent classes which have there own benifits/restrictions. For instance Expansive (human) require large amounts of food/water followed by power and oxygen. Robotic eats through Silicon and Power whereas Scavenger eats Carbon like theres no tomorrow!
So what have I learnt in the past 10hrs of play..?!
Ping quick at the start so you can find the best resourse spot on the map.
You can plant your HQ down ontop of a resourse which adds it to your starting inventory but will not regenerate the resourse like it would if you just planted a mine ontop of the resourse.
Try and keep modules attached to the HQ that way your not charged to transport across the map (Power also = fuel)
Solar panels are good but shutdown at night and thats where debt can mount up quick if your transporting alot! Wind turbines work day and night which give a steady trickle of power. Geo thermal plants work best as they operate day and night and dont require transports but are expense!

There is a lot to say about this film. First of all, I would like to mention that this is a film that wasn't made by a big name studio. That doesn't mean it's bad though. I feel like the story and concept had and still has an amazing amount of potential. However this is a film that was made on a low budget, and it suffers from that sadly. I will say that there is a certain charm about films made on low budgets. For instance, in the beginning, the movie you are greeted with the main character and a nice long stargaze followed by a car ride. SOMA captures a harrowing shade of existential dread in a way that only a smaller development team could accomplish. Similar in tone to the films Moon and "9" with many obligatory nods to Alien, It actually plays very similarly to Alien: Isolation. Even spookier than Bioshock seafloor vibes with amazing writing, believable dialog, clever  pacing that is always taking surprising turns, and very nice voice acting. It deals with many questions of both human identity and machine consciousness in a way that is very sophisticated, well informed and not at all watered down. There also seems to be a theme here of being forced to adjust your expectations in order to deal with the overwhelming harshness of reality. Its super fun and rewarding to explore the beautifully designed maps and learn more about the various habitats and their past. When it comes to the horror aspects of the game, although I am rarely truly disturbed by games or fictional films, there was at least one moment where my hands were shaking too badly to continue playing. I'm pretty sure this exaggerated reaction resulted from the attention paid to the games sound engine that ramps up the tension as sharply as possible when a monster approaches, speaking of which SOMA HAS THE BEST SOUND DESIGN!  I would go so far as to say that this game is a borderline masterpiece, and would be complementary to a fine cut of steak, seafood, pasta or Alien: Isolation.
Final verdict: 9.5 out of 11

Offworld Trading Company is exactly the kind of game I want to see more of. It reminds me a bit of a resource based board game (Power Grid, etc.) but done in real time. This comes down partially to the stock purchasing mechanic and partially to the UI being somewhat rudimentary. If the fact an opponent was about to buy you out was somehow *much* more visible maybe everything would be fine. As it stands there is no late game tension unless you know where to look for it. Compare this to combat based RTS games where its obvious your base is under attack and you are about to lose.
This game /is/ in early access so I do have hope that the above problem can be addressed in some fashion. Until then, you do get used to if after a while.

I love time travel movies, in fact I am a time travel group host, its the reason I bought this film.  I seek out every time travel film/short film and watch them, regardless if they are low budget, big budget, amateur or professional films.
Sadly, this was so so very tedious and utterly sleep inducing for the first half hour but I manage to stick with it all the way if only out of neccessity, being a TT fan.
The only thing keeping me watching (whilst battling the urge to nod off), is the excellent indie 80s style soundtrack.  I actually really enjoyed the soundtrack, I will be seeking out some of the tracks given on the end credits links.
But the film could so easily have been edited down to a more 15-20 minute short film.  Instead, we have a series of music videos, played in complettion to our protoganist driving around, or walking in a building, or staring into thin air...and then again on repeat.   I get art. I get slow burn.  But this is excessive and excruciatingly tedious.  Things happen from the half hour point and a new fun quirky character enters the scene.  The lead actress is very monotonous but I am not holding that against her, as it actually serves the narrative, somewhat.  However, a film like this which heavily focuses on one lead character to carry the movie really needs a more compelling performance, though.  The actress is clearly not of the ability to carry such a film.
This is clearly very amateur work on the whole but despite my "tedious" criticism, it has my respect for its efforts to narrate an interesting "loop" style of time travel (despite the theme being done so many times, it feels as if this genre itself is trapped in a loop).  There is a certain influence of Donnie Darko in some sequences which I liked.  The conclusion is terribly unoriginal but at least makes the effort to give a clear message with additional scifi concepts mixed in.
All the best to the film makers, there is some talent here but they need to be mindful of pacing and keeping viewers engaged.  Dont try to be too clever for the sake of art at the sacrifice of engaging the viewer.
If you are tolerant of amateur film making and want to support indie film making then give this a shot and be wary of the tedious pacing and amateur-ness.  Perhaps you might be a fan of Primer (which I am not but I appreciate its complexity), then you might dig this.
If you are not so tolerant but in the mood for a serious time travel film then pass on this one and go for a more professionally made movie such as Looper, Donnie Darko, Butterfly Effect etc.
Personally, I always encourage everyone to make their own mind up and not to depend on reviews!

SOMA is another outstanding horror game from Frictional, even though its a bit light on horror. What makes this game so impressive is the incredibly natural pacing, storytelling and puzzles where it is pretty much always clear what you need to do/where you need to go despite a complete lack of any sort of UI or objectives screen. Even during the relatively open ocean-walking sequences I never became lost, almost as if the devs intuatively knew which way players would go. Puzzles are of similar quality; generally you aren't really told what needs to be done, but it can be quite easily figure it out based on the context.
The story is also a highlight, diving into some similar themes as last year's The Talos Principle. While I didn't find the narrative quite as thought provoking as that game, the way the story is told is masterful. Conversations with another character move the central plot forward, but there is a incredible amount of often very important detail to be found in exploring the environment and interacting with various computers/documents that are lying around. It is all done in such a non-gamey way that this science fiction game manages to feel more grounded in reality than many games based in todays real world.
All of this adds up to make the game incredibly immersive. This is aided by stellar sound design that is responsible for much of the tension throughout the relatively lengthy game (for this genre). There are still some terrifying sequences, with a couple of memorable ones later in the game I will likely not forget any time soon. I would say that SOMA is the pinnacle of immersive story-driven gaming, with near-AAA production values (they just need to work on character models) making it easy to forget this is coming from a small indie developer.
Frictional have once again proven themselves to be masters of their genre, and waiting to see what they do next will be a painful process.

SOMA is something that could only be delivered by Frictional Games. After Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs, I wasn't entirely sure what to expect from the studio, albeit I still had plenty of faith in them after playing not only the original Amnesia: the Dark Descent, but also the entire Penumbra series. I can gladly say that SOMA is everything i expected it to be, and I refrained from hearing any news on it online, and also watching any trailers so I would come in knowing nothing about the game and that it would be a fresh experience, and quite frankly, SOMA delivers something so chilling and thought provoking that the original Amnesias fell short of.
Visually and asthetically, SOMA is beautifully dark and somber. While I found a few textures here and there that weren't exactly up to par with the textures elswhere in the game, it wasn't enough to detract from the beauty of the game entirely(It could've also just been my settings though). The look of the underwater facility you explore is entirely unique to me and the odd electronic cancer growing throughout the place is one in it's own. Keep in mind I'm trying my best not to spoil any details of the game. All in all, I found the game to look wonderfull, and even breathtaking at certain segments, having me stop to take in views and truly think about the environment and the situation this game had placed me in.
The gameplay I think is brilliant, and at certain points has the sort of feel that A Machine for Pigs could evoke, only much stronger and enjoyable. Now, I'm not in any way saying this game is alot like AMFP, but the game definitely learns from the mistakes of The Chinese Room's previous installment in the Amnesia series. I was dissapointed with AMFP, just to get that out there now. SOMA is very much comparable to both The Dark Descent and the Penumbra series, at times seemlessly combining the asthetics and gameplay from both of those games and building onto it. I've heard a decent amount of complaining about the monsters and the tactics used in the game, but I much prefer it this way over the whole scripted feel of AMFP, as that game had encounters few and far between, and didn't instill the same type of horror encounters in SOMA and The Dark Descent do. The segments I found most satisfying were sifting through what was left of the underwater facility, and piecing together the mystery of what was left, where i was, and even
I was, more on that later though. I disagree with critics opinions on the whole monster bits and the mechanics used, and in each scenario I found myself horrified, and coward for quite a bit(My first playthrough took me 14 hours). While monsters typically are unique in each encounter and have their own exploits, you witness quite a few throughout the entire game, with some being repeated only a few times throughout. I enjoyed all of this thoroughly and think very highly of the way this game was executed.
Combined with the gameplay, the story is what I think really sets this game apart from most other horror games. Unlike Outlast, a game in which you spent most of your time running from threat to threat with little to no breaks or relief in between, this game offers alot of time spent just rummaging around and so many of the objects in the environment are interactable, it really immerses you and gives you a sense of place. You can walk from room to room, inspecting the contents in each area and even piece together parts of the story just by looking through things and examining the setting thoroughly, and unlike in games such as
, and
, this part of the game is engaging and very interesting to me. At certain segments I longed to hear the comfort of a companions voice while I sifted through rooms piecing together the puzzle that was the story, only to really be cowering behind objects straying from the horrifying monsters that lurk within the games corridors. Now don't get me wrong, I don't think this is a bad thing, in fact I think it's a very good thing. The game switches things up every now and then and the encounters really help you to appreciate the time you get to spend in peace in the game figuring things out for yourself, and in no way is this a bad thing, its exactly what sets this game apart from Gone Home, AMFP, and even
.
SOMA is a surreal and extremely enticing experience and it really doesn't do it justice to just use the word story, as it's more than just a deep and philisophical story told through text or audio clips. Its something you experience, and in doing so provokes thoughts about mankind, our own selves and the consequences that specific decisions could have on not only others, but even oursleves and who we seem to think we may be. It begs the question;
Poor Mans Bad Company 2

This game provides great entertainment in small bursts of 90 seconds with a resonable price of 2$.
Visually, the game is heavily inspired by cyberpunk themes. Colorful sprites, striking menu artwork and even the font all help bringing its Sci-fi asthetics home. Most of the tracks in the OST are heavily inspired by heavy metal, featuring distorted guitar riffs and crisp drum-and-bas that never fails to get your blood pumping hand your head banging.
Gameplay wise, Ubermosh takes place in the Ultakaar desert. You have one goal, and one goal only: SURVIVE. Right off the bat, the game's flaws began to rear its ugly head: enveloping the desert is the enemy spawnpoint, referred ingame as Extraction Zone. The player will be kicked to the menu after staying in this area for a certain amount of time. This creates a surprisingly small playground for the player to maneuver. In keeping with the small scale theme, the weapon roster is fairly humble. The most basic weapon in the game is the sword. This weapon is especially effective because all enemies in the game dies in one hit, either of their own bullets or strike of your sword, and bullets penetrate indefinitely. There are only 5 ranged weapons in Ubermosh. Most of them are fun to use in their own rights, with each having different bullet patterns. But once you get your hands on the best weapon in the game, you'll find yourself never using other weapons ever again. This is made difficult by the fact that, once you walk pass a gun dropped by an enemy, your character will automatically pick it up and use it. Avoiding unwanted weapons on the floor now becomes an active gameplay element as a result. Ubermosh is heavily dependent on reflexes. Enemies spawns are randon and usually outside of your viewing range. There are no visual indicators to suggest impending enemy fire, which makes dodging and reflecting bullets immensly challenging and heavily dependent on luck. Ubermosh provides players with the option of different modifications of your character. There is "Kensai" mode, where the only weapon the player could use is the sword. Being the opposite, "Gunner" mode completely remove the sword, leaving the player with the ability to shoot all guns automatically. "Warlock" mode gives the character the best weapon in the game and the sword, along with significantly reduced HP (reffered as "Respawns" in game). The game could also be switched to Hardboiled Mode, increasing the number of enemies in a level. Controls in Ubermosh are simple, snappy, responsive and perfectly serves the purpose of the game, a straightfoward arcade shooter.
To wrap this review up, Ubermosh is an immensly entertaining game, especially for its price. Although it's flaws are quite glaring, the core gameplay is fun enough to make you forget about them. A great game to spend 90 seconds of your life on.

**update** Just recently finished the first playthrough, so I've updated my review.
**SOME SPOILERS AHEAD**
Let me preface this with this, I love Dead Island and Dead Island Riptide. They're both just really fun games, despite any flaws. Didn't bother with the Dead Island MOBA.
A lot of my time was spent inspecting almost everything, dying a lot, trying to stealth... It starts a bit slow but it's a pretty interesting game. Don't go into it thinking it will be like DI or DI:Riptide.
**GRAPHICS / LOOKS**
It looks like a comic book, kinda a bit like Tell Tale's TWD. I like the looks and you can certainly see why this look was chosen as the story progresses.
**STORY**
TL;DR + spoiler -
---
Takes place 6 months after the events of Dead Island. There is a brief tutorial at the beginning where you play as some agent (who appears to also be a ninja) sent to collect intel of what happened on this island and what this company Geo Pharm has to do with it.
In the main storyline, you play as Cliff Calo and you're part of a 3-person group going to investigate and write a story about what happened on Banoi. You start off exploring the island, taking photos, and then things start to get weird...your boat mysteriously sinks and you think you can save it but start to drown, then you wake up in a cargo container far from the beach, friends nowhere to be found. It is now you actually run into zombies and have to make your way back to the beach. Once there, cargo containers start falling from the sky and hits you. You then wake up inside a container on the beach. You are bandaged and your friend says they saved you from the sinking boat. From here on out, it will jump back and forth in time, and you deal with different zombie types along the way. But that's only the start of the mindbending story,
**GAMEPLAY**
It kinda felt like it could end up playing like the original DI, but it only kinda did. Light and Heavy melee attacks, a couple guns, explodable barrels, some of the same special infected...no weapon modding, but you can find upgraded weapons as you progress.
The gameplay is linear and pretty simple but requires some good timing to quickly avoid attacks and then attack. I like the stealth aspect. It allows you to sneak up and silently kill zombies. Zombies lying on the ground will get up if you attract attention. If stealth isn't an option or you choose to attract attention, be prepared to fight off a couple zombies at a time. This is where the dodging might get tricky. But don't worry, you will regain your health. As for when you die, I think it's pretty cool how they handle that. You DO start back at the last checkpoint, but the transition seems pretty seamless. It's like you fall to the ground and then stand back up and you're back at the checkpoint. No waiting at traditional loading screens.
I played with a controller and the weapon swapping is a gripe, mostly when surrounded, but it could maybe be changed in settings, but I didn't bother to check and just dealt with it.
**VERDICT**
All in all, my verdict is it's kinda slow to start but then the story gets very interesting and trippy and the graphics help the story.
Will recommend for those who love Dead Island and those who like mindbending stories.

Hi I've played this game maybe over a hundred hours by now on other platforms and although I am reccomending the game, please understand that my reccomendation is under the assumption of this game being an Early Access game, AND because the game is quite fun no matter which platform you play on IMO.
Anyway if I had to describe this game it's like PUBG or other types of Battle Royale games out there, but with a RPG spin on the whole thing as opposed to being FPS like most of it's counter parts.
Ultimate goal of the game is to be the last one standing out of 10 people. The more general goal to achieve this is to punch, stab, and shoot people so you're the last one remaining. To aid you, you'll search for items and craft them into more powerful items and level up from crafting and fighting. Overall the game is quite strategic and often demands both methodical play and flexible play with a light dash of luck in order to come out on top.
It's really a hard game to explain, so my best advice is to give the game a shot for a bit and see if you like it, but I think it's really quite fun once you grasp the basic mechanics of the game. And it's actually much faster paced than one might think even though it's been ported from originally being a "phone game".
Next I'm going to review the pros and cons of playing this on Steam versus playing it on an android/ios and other platforms *cough* emulators *cough*
Pros of Steam:
-Much smoother. I've experienced higher framerates than I've been able to get on my emu- android.
-It is also much more responsive. Take for example:
If I crafted or searched for items using my ehem; android, I'd be liable to not picking up the item or closing my crafting panel if I mashed my hotkey too hard. I've never failed to pick up and item yet using the hotkeys of this game not matter how much I mash the button.
-The art is much more crisp. I've noticed my "android" has less defined art, especially regarding older art assets.
-Hotkeys are available compared to ios/android
Cons of Steam:
-Hotkeys are available on my "android" as well so that removes a pro.
-Said hotkeys are not rebindable. This is a shame as it is a basic feature of PC gaming imho.
The developers have said they haven't added hotkeys for certain things out of balance concerns. Since all players ios/android/Steam play on the same server I can understand that, but that does not justify being unable to rebind existing keys.
-If you're an existing player and mistakenly transfer your fresh steam account onto your ios/android, you lose all of your progress. They do not have a back up system in place for this at the moment, so exercise caution. Not a TRUE con, but it is a big one if you make a mistake, and mistakes happen.
-No way to adjust volume in game.
You can adjust the general volume using your PC's volume, but... come on. You still don't have a way of adjusting volumes for various aspects like the announcer, voicelines, skill effects, music, and so on.
-No revives using ADs!!!
This one doesn't matter if you're still a newcomer and are playing in the Herbivore league, but reviving with gold is a large expense that adds up over time once you reach the Carnivore league. On the android/ios you could watch an ad for 30s or less and revive. 250 gold in comparison is like 10-15 minutes of survival in an actual match you have to pay attention to. A large gap here that I hope they change.
Overall I like the Steam version for what it brings, but they could do so much more. Hopefully when it leaves Early Access some or all of the cons will have been addressed in some way.

So simple, yet so complicated, yet so fun.
I've been playing this game since the android version was launched.
What first caught my eyes were simple interface with great graphical sense of the developers
which makes the game very easy to learn.
The game is mostly about 'click to advance', and graphics I just mentioned helps you learning the game.
Rule is simple as well. Survive, but in order to survive, you'll have to find items that would help you.
The game limits players by providing very limited number of items the bag can hold,
'stamina' system and 'restricting area' limits your movement throught the game.
In order to win, you need to consider lots of things at once, including few things I've just mentioned.
And that's where the fun comes from. Simple to play, but it asks you much to give you, 'win'.
Also, it is 'pay to boost' but not 'pay to win'. Unlocking more characters requires to play lots of game, or just pay to buy.  Talking about characters, I wouldn't say the characters are 'well balanced', seeing how one character is being preferred on another, but developers are getting there, and I can see that they are not planning to make money out of 'unbalanced character', which is hard to expect from Korean developers.
If you are trying this game out, keep in mind that the current(6th Dec 2017) interface is direct copy of mobile verision, and might be inconvinient for keyboard-mouse users.

Magic: The Gathering is a habit-forming, easy to play, quick to learn trading card game that is essentially inexhaustible in its replayability. Many will find this edition of the franchise enjoyably entertaining. However, if you're more than just a casual player, AVOID this product. The bugginess will drive you mad; you've been warned.
Pros:
*Compete against MTGers from all over the world, anytime.
Cons:
*Suffers from the main identical flaw of the real world game - the more you spend, the more powerful your deck. There needs to be an implementation of parity.
*VERY buggy (some cards are simply unplayable and cause the game to crash). Rather than fixing bugs, Wizards of the Coast/Hasbro simply applies corrections to the next years release (I have played DOTP 2012-2015). I have called them personally on numerous occasions to make them aware of issues, and they only apologize and offer to send me free swag, which I gladly accept (their ‘technical’ team is a joke). They either need to correct issues as they arise or implement more testing before release.
Tl;Dr:
Enjoyable, but you're better off playing MTG: DOTP 2013 or playing IRL and waiting for them to create a superior product.

I'll put this out there to start: I picked this game up on sale for $20, which after having played it feels about right. This is a recommendation based on the $20 pricetag, I do not feel it's worth $40 quite yet.
+Interesting concept that is (mostly) executed well.
+Four different faction types that are relatively balanced.
+Good level of mechanical depth that makes the game more enjoyable as you learn.
+Multiplayer is fun, particularly co-op
+Winning is satisfying - there's no other way to put it. When you buyout your last competitor, you feel like you've earned your monopoly.
-Tutorials are bare bones at best, useless at worst. On top of not covering very basic but vital mechanics (using claims without building, the usefulness of upgrade buildings such as the offworld market/patent office, etc) the last three tutorials simply throw you into a standard game and tell you to win with a given faction, with barely a blurb about that faction's unique traits as a guide. You will need to suffer through a lot of trial and error before you feel skilled at the game.
-The market essentially functions the same way every game. Certain goods (electronics, chemicals, food) are basically always the most expensive on the market, so a strategy of "spam electronics late game" is always viable, and ruins the charm somewhat.
-The Black Market, as it is currently implemented, is a big drain on the game. It refreshes too fast, and you are constantly being bombarded in all directions by pirates, EMP's, and dynamite. Honestly, for a game that claims to remove the military elements of the RTS to focus on economics, it detracts from your economic game and forces you to focus on what is essentially guerilla military ops.
-The difficulty settings are such that you can only functionally choose to apply bonuses/handicaps to yourself. The AI always plays at the same (fairly high) level, which makes it difficult to keep up as a newbie.
Overall the game is still very rough around the edges, but what's there can be fun, particularly with some friends to co-op with. However in it's current state it absolutely feels $20 too expensive at it's standard price of $40. If you can get it on sale, it's worth a look.

This fast-paced game will really put your twitch reflexes to the test. Each run lasts about 90 seconds, but they'll be the most intense 90 seconds ever. Enemies around every corner, forcing you to be fully aware of your surroundings. There is a wide array of guns to help you along the way, but once you get the best gun (The one that shoots red bullets), the fight really begins. You can also slice bullets with your sword, and fling the enemy's bullets back at them while slicing them in half. One word: badass.
--
There are a lot of challenges that will keep you coming back and playing this game again and again. In this game, you get 4 classes total: Green (No class mods), Kensai (Sword only), Gunner (Guns only), and Warlock (Best gun on spawn, sword, but 2 lives). Mastery of each class requires that you get 150 kills for the one you chose. This is more than enough to provide a challenge, so that you master each different playstyle under varying difficult conditions. You also get other challenges, like surviving 7 rounds without running out of respawns (Very difficult), and scoring 200+ kills 7 times (Gets easier the more you do it, but still extremely fun and challenging). There is also a different game mode if you want to go more hardcore called "Hardboiled mode".
--
After playing this, I find myself more aware in other games I play, and performing a lot better in general. I got this game for $0.50, and that's a steal. I'd gladly pay the full $2 for this game. Gave me hours of fun, and improved my reflexes. I highly recommend it to any skilled gamer seeking a challenge. It's well worth your time, and can be a good stress reliever once you get good experience at it.

I had no expectations when I started playing this game, however I am very familiar with all of the Dead Island related titles released so far, so here are my impresions from that perspective:
* the graphics are caught somewhere between "Borderlands" and TellTale's "Walking Dead" game.
* the gameplay is different from the previous Dead Island titles; Jump has been removed and now you have a dodge maneuver using the space bar. Combat happens from a 3rd view perspective and attacks require more timing, however attacking is fluid enough once adapted to it. Stealth is a main component in this title and is implemented in a simple but efficient manner.
* there are no RPG related elements like currency, custom weapons, item collection, leveling up, etc.
* the game is more linear as in you need to get certain items and complete objectives in an order so the next area can be unlocked.
"Escape" is an entirely different game experience from the previous titles which I found quite enjoyable and welcome. The game offers a lot of background information into the epidemic and some of the characters involved thus filling in some of the gaps. I recomend this game but be aware it does not play or feels like the previous Dead Island titles so do not purchase if you are expecting something close to the earlier installments or you might be dissapointed.

For Honor is the most fun I have had in a game since the release of Mount and Blade: Warband. For Honor is an immensely enjoyable, challenging pvp arena with the most developed combat system I have ever seen in a game. The learning curve is a bit steep but if you have any experience with games like Mount and Blade, War of the Roses, or Dark souls you should pick it up quite easily.
The story mode/single player in the game is great even though this game is definitely based around multiplayer with nice plot twists and relatible characters that make you understand each of their motivations for fighting in the brutal war machine. The story mode was a welcomed suprise as the game would have succeded without one, this does not mean that it is just a cheap addition that isnt engaging... cough cough Titanfall cough cough... and also has the posibility to play coop with a friend.
The music and battlefields you encounter throughout the game are gritty and feel authentic. The character animations are very smooth and feel refined with the devs obviously putting a lot of effort into the gruesome executions and emotes for each hero/champion/class.
The only reason that this game is somewhat bad is that the server system put in place by Ubisoft is peer to peer. Meaning that if the host leaves mid game or someone’s internet crashes then the game will pause everyone else in the game to wait for a reconnect or will outright just kick the whole lobby. This aspect is SO FRUSTRATING and if you’re about to finish dominating a 4v4 or dominion then all your exp and rewards are lost. Ubisoft needs to make this system a dedicated server as it is not acceptable to have a fast-paced fighting game with a point on fast reactions run with peer to peer. The devs of For Honor have said that they are actively watching the community and will listen to what the players want so I look forward to seeing how the game improves.
The three main factions in the game feel genuine and represent what I think they would be like in history. Each faction, at this point, has 4 different classes relating to Vanguard, Heavy, Assassin and Hybrid class types. Every champion has their own feel and individual playstyle, which opens up to high skill caps and expect play from people who play a lot of one class. Each champion has their own moves and combos unique to them, making the game always interesting.
For Honor is a constant challenge as no two people play the same forcing you to adapt to every new opponent as you encounter them. This game is excellent to play with friends as it always proves entertaining as you cheese each other on ladders and 1-2 your enemies off bridges.
For Honor has massive potential to invlovle compeditive play and launch itself in the eSport scene, although they have to fix the server issues first

Arma 3 is a great military simulator sandbox. The game is build upon the community and the games modes they make. You can find everything from King of the Hill to Role-Playing servers to loot-to-survive(called wasteland) game modes and many more. There are some offical servers that offer basic games and draw some traffic but the real center of Arma 3 is private servers. These privately owned servers usually have their own dev team if it is a role-playing server for example. They will progress their servers features and activites indepenent from other servers. Many of my hours have been logged in these RP servers. They offer progression systems and a challenge to newcomers.
Learning shooting techniques has a steep learning curve but can feel rewarding when lining up shots. Gameplay is slower in nature and heavily tactics based typically. There are times when I spend 30 minutes to an hour climbing a hill and setting up a shot to kill one person. It is the best feeling when these plans work. All vehicle controls are pretty solid and decent damage models too. Sometimes the fps element leave something to be desired but are not killing.
The game becomes most enjoyable with friends and groups when you get organized to do a mission or something like that. There are military sim units that can be joined and there are always people to be found.
Pros:
-Great sandbox
-Many unique game modes
-Fantasic mod support
-Vehicles are fun
Cons:
-Occasional bugs/glitched
-CPU based game makes it hard to get high FPS even on nice rigs
-Gunplay could be better

-There are a few framerate drops but only minor ones...
-Mods work perfectly (they are not in steam workshop)

Shadow Warrior 2 is in no way a revolutionary game. The easiest way to describe it would be a mash up of something like Borderlands and Doom. It is a very fun first person shooter with lighter role playing elements that can be played alone or with up to 3 friends in its entirety.
GAMEPLAY
When looking at the structure of the game it is quite easy to draw parallels to Borderlands in that there are tons of loot drops and bullet spongy adversaries. There are also your typical fares of MMO type side quests that can be skipped for the decent and often times whacky main story missions. After missions the player comes back to a hub world to resupply, sell unwanted goods and talk to NPCs before moving to the next mission. The shooting mechanics feel pretty good with a nice fast paced action oriented feel to them. In other words, don’t bother aiming down sights, just point and shoot until the humanoid or demonic enemy drops dead. Weapons can be upgraded to inflict more or different types of damage and your character can also unlock different abilities to buff health and chi, which is used to perform special moves that come in useful against certain enemies or in certain combat situations.
7/10
STORY
The story is not going to move you to tears or offer you any moral conundrums. The narrative is pretty straight forward, which lends itself well to the overall fun tone of the game. As mercenary Lo Wang you are tasked with what starts out as a simple rescue mission. Needless to say things don’t turn out peachy and the remainder of the story is spent hunting down a certain being while uncovering some hard truths about other characters. The tale does what it needs to and adds a couple of much needed surprising moments in between the flow of standard “go here kill this” action sequences. It is a fun, and darkly humorous plot that can be enjoyed easily especially if you are okay with the often juvenile jokes. If you are just playing the story it can run you about 8 hours.
7/10
GRAPHICS/PERFORMANCE
The graphics are great and the art direction leans more towards something like Doom 2016. The way that the weapons are designed aesthetically is very Doom like with machine guns and chainsaws adorned with sci-fi doo-dads or skulls. Enemies tend to look like some sort of hell beast or armored humanoids. In terms of performance, on a GTX 1070 FE, 16 GB of DDR4 RAM, and an i7 6700k, you will have no trouble cranking max settings at 1440p.
9/10
Overall Shadow Warrior 2 is a fun shooter with some dark often juvenile humour and game design elements reminiscent of a Borderlands title.
FINAL
7.7/10

If you loved Battle Royale (if you haven't seen it, watch it) you'll love this game. It's the exact same premise, but with a bit of a MOBA twist. Each character has a different set of skills and traits, and they definitely play uniquely from each other. Sure, attacking is all the same when it boils down to it - you're either going to be shooting, stabbing, bashing or breaking each other into bloody little tidbits. It's the skills of these characters that make them wildly unique. My favorite - Jackie, the 22 year old serial killer from the UK - has a skill that reveals areas on the map without players. Another character double taps people with whatever gun she's holding. Yet another character can set an area ablaze, making it dangerous for other players to move around in it. It all boils down to play style.
If you're still on the fence about trying it because "Ugh, another port of a mobile game" - it's literally around a 180MB download and it's free. Hell, if you want to try the game out and team up, you can add me as Z4KU in game.
To the developers, thank you for porting this amazing game so that I can finally play it on something with a resolution larger than my smart phone screen. Also, a side note - minor complaint - some of the menus need arrows added, they still act like they require a swipe. This is more of just an inconvenience though, since you can still simulate one by holding down the mouse button and dragging. Maybe a more linear inventory menu in game too - the cylinder was fine on touch screen, but makes decision making a tad bit slower on PC.

The only Magic games I have played on PC in the past were Magic Online and the old Microprose game. I still dust off the Microprose game every now and then as it plays so well. The sealed tournaments vs AI are a lot of fun.
I'm mentioning this as it establishes what I was looking for in the game when deciding on which version to get - a good single player experience, deck building options, a decent cardpool. I don't care about playing multiplayer online and I have only been playing the campaign so I can't talk about that yet.
Magic 2015 ticked a major box for me compared to the others : deckbuilding. Picking up new cards and tweaking your deck I find very enjoyable. I bought the Special Edition which gave me some foil packs to start with. Some nice usable cards in there which can give you a leg up early on but many I'm replacing as I get better cards. I went with the red/black deck and its not bad as a starter anyway.
The gameplay in duelling was a bit slow and awkward at first. I adjusted the graphics settings and it helped. Sometimes when you click on something it doesn't work first click. An annoyance but one I can live with. I still haven't worked out how to cvhange which lands you tap for casting stuff as its not very intuitive. Personally I liked the Microprose system of single click asnd tap lands manually or double click to tap lands automatically.
I do like how the spacebar is wired so you can pause gameplay to get effects and instants in. Problem is it can feel a little dumbed down as once allies are in the red zone in combat it wouldn't let me do anything, only after intended moves are declared. Feels a little dumbed down and removes a lot of intricate play.
I like the black and white aesthetic. Given a lot of the creatures and planeswalkers revolve around horror elements it suits well. The playfield in duelling feels a little futuristic however.
I'm only 6 hours in but I am enjoying Magic 2015 immensely. So far it ticks all the boxes I was looking for when looking for a more modern single player Magic game. I would have liked something like Shandalar in the Microprose game but I can live without it.

People need something good, something to remind them of what horror is and even though its a shame this game has aged it never loses its charm.

Amnesia plays opon phycological horror in the sense that you fear the unknown. The main enemy in this game, you are never told anything about it, what its call, what it looks like, nothing. The fear looms in the back of your mind like an itch you cant seem to scrach. The music also helps to amp up the tention in moments when the "monster" is hunting you and i say "monster" because i honestly dont even know if its human anymore, or even ever was but ill refer to it by the name Grunt from now on.
The game also has a sanity system which the longer you are in dark areas or looking at Grunt/s your sanity drops causing you to hilusinate and draw the grunts closer to you,if  your sanity drops too low you begin crawling along the floor helplessly with your ears ringing and your heart pounding.
Amnesia might not be a pretty game, the engin might not even be all that great but by god when i say this game is good, its dam good. I dont like horror games, i get scared easily and ive seen grown men turn away from this game, so im not the only one. I did manage to finish the game twice over..well over 4 months.. but i did it and i was proud.
There is so much i could tell you about this game and even more id like to show you, but i wouldnt want to spoil such an amazing experience for any soul willing to delve into the depths of Amnesia: The Dark Descent.

Soma is a deep, intriguing atmospheric horror game from the developers of the survival horrors Penumbra and Amnesia.
The game tackles a variety of themes, ranging from isolation, suicide, relationships and what it means to be human.
It’s interesting how everything comes together by the end of the game. I felt that there was a bit of a slow start and I wasn’t really feeling that scared until a few hours in. I think you’ll appreciate the pacing of the game as you continue playing through it.
There were times where I felt genuinely uncomfortable performing certain actions. You will discover these as you play through the game.
One thing to note is that this game lacks the typical ‘survival’ elements of horror games, so no health bar, inventory management, delectable resources etc. I think this works in the game’s favour though, because it helps keep things flowing in the more narrative-driven style of play.
Recommended.

It's very hard to write something coherent about this game. It is very smart and very depressing game (unlike Amnesia TDD or Penumbra). Casual horror fans might find it a bit lacking in bombastic scares, but it's the story that will keep your mind racing for weeks after you finished it. I just collected my thoughts to recommend this game here. As I'd definitely recommend this game to anyone with IQ high enough to keep the discussion with it, but it's hard to explain why. Yeap, this game is an open discussion, dialog with the player, developers talk to you through gameplay and story. Talk about things you weren't up to talking about. The game is not scaring you, it forces you to scare you by your own thoughts. It's that type of horror that make you double-check what you think is right, to reevaluate your beliefs. And just like in real life you'll always be wrong and sooner or later you'll regret your decisions.
Long story short: this game is philosophical and ethical discussion in a vein of The Talos Principle. But instead of puzzles you get monsters. What makes us human? What death really means? Is there death at all?
I'm pretty sure if you are that type of person you'll ignore some of the game's flaws. Be it sometimes bad dialogs or scares just for the sake of scares. The game has very immersive atmosphere, great sound and visual design. Also has great sense of going deeper and deeper down the ocean. You might loose an arm in the process. I recommend this game to everyone with open mind, not only horror fans.
p.s.: the ending will leave a scar. I warned you.

Frame rate skipping problems galore, mousing problems on a solid mid-level system (which would be considered ultra high end when this game came out), and long loading times from an SSD. The character models look a few steps and notches better than the plastic models in Postal 2 - but this game came out only in 2011 and should have looked much better. Lighting was terrible - any shadows cover up the color completely and everyone just looks dull in the dark.  So there are some pretty major technical problems, and then there is the gameplay.  Hit boxes are terribly defined. It feels like your just shooting the air and hoping some of the bullets will connect - part of this is because of the mouse lag though. I could tell this wasn't going to be very fun or worth my limited gameplay time, so I stopped once I got the handgun.  Refund requested and granted.  Duke Nukem certainly deserved better than this heaping pile of trash and vomit.

Duke Nukem Forever is a first person shooter action game that has been stuck in development hell for years, 12 years to be exact! The game turn out to be a disappointment in my opinion. The gunplay is decent but there are only a small variety of weapons to play with. The same enemies are reused over and over again in almost every level which feels pretty cheap. The boss fights are also pretty weak as the bosses usually reuse the same attack patterns over again until they are dead and this make those fight not really challenging.
The levels can be quite confusing at times and you might spent awhile thinking about what to do or how to go pass an obstacle as there are no hint regarding what to do, especially during those "puzzle" sections which can be very frustrating. The mandatory driving in this game is horrible as the vehicle feels really lightweight and would flip over at almost every collision and this would require you to exit the vehicle to flip back up the vehicle in order to use it. The multiplayer aspect of this game is also pretty much dead as there are almost nobody playing it at the time of this review.
The good thing about this game is that there are many "easter eggs" hidden throughout the game that references other popular games and movies which is pretty cool. Oh, there are also lots of virtual topless women and aliens with♥♥♥♥♥♥shown. Other than that, I have nothing good to say about this game. If I were to rate this game, I would give it a 3/10 as it is a pretty terrible game and would not recommend it to anyone unless you are really bored or a huge fan of duke nukem.

For Honor is the most fun I have had in a game since the release of Mount and Blade: Warband. For Honor is an immensely enjoyable, challenging pvp arena with the most developed combat system I have ever seen in a game. The learning curve is a bit steep but if you have any experience with games like Mount and Blade, War of the Roses, or Dark souls you should pick it up quite easily.
The story mode/single player in the game is great even though this game is definitely based around multiplayer with nice plot twists and relatible characters that make you understand each of their motivations for fighting in the brutal war machine. The story mode was a welcomed suprise as the game would have succeded without one, this does not mean that it is just a cheap addition that isnt engaging... cough cough Titanfall cough cough... and also has the posibility to play coop with a friend.
The music and battlefields you encounter throughout the game are gritty and feel authentic. The character animations are very smooth and feel refined with the devs obviously putting a lot of effort into the gruesome executions and emotes for each hero/champion/class.
The only reason that this game is somewhat bad is that the server system put in place by Ubisoft is peer to peer. Meaning that if the host leaves mid game or someone’s internet crashes then the game will pause everyone else in the game to wait for a reconnect or will outright just kick the whole lobby. This aspect is SO FRUSTRATING and if you’re about to finish dominating a 4v4 or dominion then all your exp and rewards are lost. Ubisoft needs to make this system a dedicated server as it is not acceptable to have a fast-paced fighting game with a point on fast reactions run with peer to peer. The devs of For Honor have said that they are actively watching the community and will listen to what the players want so I look forward to seeing how the game improves.
The three main factions in the game feel genuine and represent what I think they would be like in history. Each faction, at this point, has 4 different classes relating to Vanguard, Heavy, Assassin and Hybrid class types. Every champion has their own feel and individual playstyle, which opens up to high skill caps and expect play from people who play a lot of one class. Each champion has their own moves and combos unique to them, making the game always interesting.
For Honor is a constant challenge as no two people play the same forcing you to adapt to every new opponent as you encounter them. This game is excellent to play with friends as it always proves entertaining as you cheese each other on ladders and 1-2 your enemies off bridges.
For Honor has massive potential to invlovle compeditive play and launch itself in the eSport scene, although they have to fix the server issues first

I really love this game and I would advise anyone interested to check it out even though there are problems right now.
Simple list of the Pros and Cons and other issues that will hopefully be worked out later on.
Temporary Cons.- List of things the development team needs to work on but are easy enough to work around.
-The game has some issue with index in english. This is a game with very many different languages supported, however not all of them are completely there. A couple of the character guides are still in korean.(or japanese) This isn't major as it is nothing you absolutely need, but it is still a problem.
-This is a port for an App so an indepth options menu is missing, mostly options for Full scene and resolutions are not here yet.
-You can not rebind keys yet. There is also no map for what the key bindings are in game.
-While you can link your account to the one you have on your phone, It does make you waste a couple minutes having to skip through the opening and tutorial. Again not a big thing as you can exit the the tutorial by giving up the game.
Pros
-Theme is simple but effective. Battle Royale with just enough backstory to be interesting.
-Very fast paced with little down time. Even when you're healing you are constantly planning your next move.
-Matches are not long, the longest being around 20 minutes if you win or come in second.
-Simple enough crafting system once you get the hang of it. The game also has a nice feature of being able to have a small index in the upper left that tells where the item or items you are looking for are located.
-A good number of different Characters that support different styles of play. There are a number of characters available to play as for free for a limited time, kind of like Leagues champion rotation.
-Matches are fought with people around your expience level for normal matches.
Cons
-While the tutorial if fine, it needs to make mention of a few more details about the game. I went through a few hours not knowing that while an item may be found in three different places, it is twice as likely to be found at one of them.
-Getting new characters takes a bit of time. You will need a few hours to get the really expensive ones give or take how fast you level. (You get a good chunk of gold when promoting)
-Trying to find certain items can get very frustrating.
-Character promotion is an annoying system that makes the characters require a bit more gold. While low star charcters are not unplayable vs high level ones, it is still something frustating
Very lovely game over all. Glad to see it on Steam

Another game that didn't need a loot system. Too many items, and too much time spent on the menu micro-managing what upgrades to use.
Then in the next mission, you realize you just spent all that time for nothing because you found even better upgrades. The trend just repeats with each mission, so on and so forth. It becomes a ♥♥♥♥ing chore to have to remove upgrades so you have better ones.
When you break it down, it essentially forces you to use different elemental types/different weapons to attack enemies that are vulnerable to certain elemental types. So if an enemy says "Electric vulnerable", you're forced to switch to an electric elemental weapon in the heat of battle, which just gets extremely annoying...especially when you don't have the elemental type yet.
Then the game just throws constant waves of monsters at you. You can easily ignore them and proceed with whatever the objective is. No amount of monster waves can mask the bland "go from point A to point B" approach that each mission gives to a high degree.
The game gives you co-op characters, but none of them really have voices, nor does your first person view change when you're playing a character in someone elses game. You're always Lo Wang, but to your co-op partner, you look like another generic character with no sense of personality. They're absolutely mute. It's like they just threw in the option for co-op, and the option to adjust the difficulty for 2, 3, or 4 players and called it a day. For reference, at least Halo 5 made use of it's 8 Spartans and gave them a unique look and voice to each character, which made co-op a blast.
After a while, it just seems pointless and tacky, especially compared to Shadow Warrior 1, which played much better with a deliberate pacing to its linear levels vs. the "open world hub" design behind Shadow Warrior 2 with its poor attempt at adding a Borderlands-style loot system.

When I first encountered Warbands: Bushido fostering a sense of mindfulness was certainly helpful.
The game doesn't have a plot as such, but it takes place around or after the Warring States period. This means that you get access to gunpowder units, too! And if you want some semblance of a story, there are scenarios that can be purchased for in-game money. In fact, the miniatures and orders cards are also purchased for in-game currency, albeit in a CCG-like random booster packs.
To fight in Warbands: Bushido, you need to build a warband. Those are split into several categories: gray (for multiplayer), green (for non-random multiplayer), blue (scenarios) and red (arena). All of them have some limitations on the level and amount of troops used. For example, the size and strength of your gray warband depends on your level. Getting better means both increasing the amount of miniatures you can take into battle, and the limit on the sum of their levels.
A warband is made up of miniatures. A miniature has a quality level (in how many levels it can reach), price, as well as battlefield stats: armor, health (which equals striking power), agility, passive and active abilities. They also have abilities that are unlocked via levelling up! Levelling up – via honor points earned fighting other players – also increases the agility stat, which not only determines the move range, but also the position in the initiative queue.
Leveling up (as a player) also increases the amount of order cards you can give to your warbands. Order cards are special abilities that you activate by spending morale points (earned in battle). Those range from increased move to increased attack to making a miniature skip it's attacking or maybe even move back. Each miniature also has an ability card that is used like an order, in that they also cost morale points.
But how do you get said points? Well, once you are in your hex-grid battlefield, your miniatures act one after the other according to the initiative track. To determine the outcome of fighting, the game uses special D6 die that have X's (misses), skulls (hits) and banners (hits that also earn morale) on the sides. In a regular melee attack, a soldier will roll all of his (or her, there's at least one female warrior type) dice vs. all of the enemy dice, with hits canceling each other out. Any un-canceled hits result in damage. Meanwhile, the amount of dice rolled is strictly tied to the health stat – one health means one dice, two means two, and so on. It's a system that we have already seen in Banner Saga, but more streamlined or refined, as luck also plays a part in it.
So, much like in Blood Bowl, you will want to throw the maximum amount of dice as well as more dice than the enemy. That is why Kensei is my favorite unit, which I think I got randomly at the start of the game – I certainly haven't seen anyone else use it! On a glance, the Kensei is super expensive at 5 war points (as expensive as a unit gets) while only having one armor and two health, like some starting peasant. However, he's what you could call an “organic glass cannon” for his sword mastery ability gives him +3 dice to any roll. A healthy Kensei will roll 5 dice on attack or defense, which is just obscene. Even at half health he's roll 4, which is a respectable amount.
That said, Kensei is not impossible to overcome. Heimin, the cheap peasant that everyone gets, is basically made to kill Kensei, as its “Jump Back” ability lets it make a one-dice attack with no retaliation before jumping back a hex. Considering that Kensei only has one armor and two health, three such attacks – if they connect - would be enough to kill him. Archers and arquebusiers can use ranged fire to kill a Kensei without fear of repercussion. And there are other powerful units that can deal no-retaliation attacks, too. Just lock a Kensei up with some beefier dudes, only attack with no-retaliation guys and you can grind him down. And if you manage to both outflank (meaning you put miniature on opposites sides) and outnumber him (meaning that you have three miniatures versus a single enemy one), that’s even better, as such maneuvers decrease the amount of dice that the unlucky miniature can throw.
So building a good warband is more than just putting some beastly warrior surrounded by some chaff (though Kensei can solo people for ages) – especially when said “chaff” isn't that throwaway W:B. And if you can match the order cards – randomly drawn to your hand during the match and only useable once – to your warband, you will go far. I'm a big fan of “Confusion” to neuter enemy powerhouses or shooters for a turn, for example. And if you somehow manage to maneuver well enough to get equipment cards (they appear in a random hex during the late part of the battle), you'll do even better.
Fighting skirmishes (and in campaigns, too), you will earn achievements, which in turn earn you gold coins, which you then spend buying miniature and order booster packs. Campaigns are also purchaseable (the game has three of them now, and they're cheap). Any order cards or miniatures that you don't like can be reduced to dust, which you can then use to craft. Cards have a stable crafting price that depends on rarity, while miniature price depends on quality: no matter how expensive the miniature is in warpoints, a common quality (meaning only levelable to level 3) unit will cost less than 20 dust while a legendary quality digital plastic soldier man will inevitably cost 600 (a whole damn lot).
You also get paints when leveling up, but the customization system isn't that deep. You can determine the headgear, armor and pants colors for you warband, but how pronounced that will be depends strongly on the model. Sometimes, you'll only change the color of barely noticeable headbands or belts, which isn't that impressive.
I do adore how the game looks, though. While the visuals of the menu give off a fain whiff of a mobile game, it has a well crafted theme of a Japanese miniature gaming table going. On a match, you even can see that there's a table outside the bounds of the map. This reminds me of seeing the war room outside the maps of Ruse or Wargame. Meanwhile, the miniatures are all neat, though it sometimes is hard to judge the quality of a soldier at a glance. The bamboo sun hats are hard to distinguish from the jingasa helmets of the ashigaru, for example. On the other hand, you can always right-click on any soldier in the field to see their full stat screen.
Warbands: Bushido only boasts simple visuals and audio, but it works out well enough. The miniatures aren't that animated, with attacks and dodges momentarily changing frames from idle to attack, but it works well in conjunction with accompanying sounds. I only have problems with the way the miniatures die: they crumble on the spot, which looks a bit off to me, but the developers probably didn't want to animate miniatures falling on their side or being lifted off the table.
All in all, I am surprisingly happy with Warbands: Bushido. I'll start this out by saying that this is best Samurai-movie tactical game I've ever played.  It's not historical, and it's not a typical tactics game, but it's good at what it does.   Combats play out more like a series of swift single combat exchanges between colorful characters.  It's simple model of attack, defense, and counterattack effectively conveys dynamic fight-sequences with next to no animation.
It's not a perfect game.  If you like building collections it's great, especially as it's one of the relatively few offerings in that field without micro-transactions.  The battles themselves are short and you can go through a few at a time.  The game has some obviously Hearthstone-inspired aspects, but they're much more tolerable without micro-transactions.  The daily-quests, for example, refresh endlessly and thereby reward playing successive matches as mentioned above.
In terms of a single-player experience it is again, similar to heathstone.  The single-player is supplementary and you probably won't beat the first scenario until you've levelled online.
The matches, at a low level, can seem a bit unfair at first.  I find that this is minimized by more conservative play.  The deck and miniature systems aren't all immediately apparent, but after a couple hours they become more or less intuitive.  Sometimes you get screwed by RNG, but the game rewards kills even if you lose.  You can go down in a heroic last stand and it will be more than waste of time.  Even if you have a really terrible snowball of a game, they don't last very long at all.

The game is clearly meant to be a simulator for the real life MTG trading card game, but for the price that it offers, the things you can do in-game is way too limited. You can earn some free packs by doing the main campaign/story mode, and admittedly it is enough to make a semi-decent deck that will let you progress through the story mode without too much difficulty. However, the cards that you work with in-game (at least when you're staying F2P) do not represent the actual TCG very well, i.e. your choice of cards are far too limited. Any extra booster packs which you want to obtain in-game will have to be acquired through micro-transactions which doesn't exactly come as cheap, so the store price also doesn't accurately represent the actual cost of enjoying the game to the fullest. Lastly, the game's campaign mode doesn't feel like a true campaign (in addition to the campaign mode being really short). It is simply me vs-ing against AI after AI, without any actual, prevalent story that is expected of a true campaign.
Conclusion: If you're a new to MTG, and you want to try out the game, this game is a good way to get familiar with the card game, as it's most likely cheaper than buying a physical deck that works. If you're an MTG player looking for a good online simulator, don't buy this game. You're probably better off spending the money to buy a real life booster pack.

A lot of people try to defend this game as being "dumb fun" or say stuff like "It's not supposed to win awards", but in order for a game to be dumb fun, it has to be fun at all in the first place. What we have here is a game that completely disregards the concept of pacing and instead makes you slog through dull chores and sit through unfunny comedy sketches more than it makes you shoot aliens to death.
Duke Nukem is supposed to be an action game, and yet it takes a good 40 minutes before you get a gun, and even then you're not really in any kind of significant battles. In a game like Half-Life 2, where you actually care about the worldbuilding and are trying to convey a certain theme or message, this would be compelling, but Duke Nukem's world is inherently shallow, it exists solely as a delivery mechanism for crude jokes. Duke Nukem is a simple character by design, so forcing us to learn about him and his world for almost an hour is a terrible way to start a game. For comparison, Duke Nukem 3D has you blowing something up in the first seconds of the game. The game continues in much the same fashion, you're usually navigating an empty environment or trying to solve some kind of puzzle. In one section, you get shrunk down and have to drive an RC car, which sounds really creative on paper, but you aren't actually doing anything in this scenario. You literally just drive the car down a very long hallway and don't fight anything or try to navigate anything other than "go forward". When you finally do get into a gunfight, it's usually with only two or three enemies at a time and then it's back to the slog.
Most of the actual individual puzzles would be fine, and even very clever in many cases, if they were breaks in the action instead of the main action itself, but you're really left with a game that feels like it's constantly leading to something, only to never get there. This game didn't need to be groundbreaking, it didn't need to have the best graphics, or the best animation, or the best story, it just needed to give you lots of things to shoot at and fun ways to kill enemies, but it fails at the most basic action of a first person shooter, which is that it needs to have lots of shooting. Overall, if you want a fun, over-the-top first person shooter, try Bulletstorm, Serious Sam 3, Shadow Warrior, Doom, or even the original Duke Nukem 3D. Only play this game if you want to actually sit down and academically study what can be bad about a game.

After a few attempts of trying to make a professional review introduction, I've decided to say "F**K IT!" and just be perfectly blunt about my opinion of this game:
It's a waste of time, money, and computer memory.
Now, I understand a lot of issues occured during this games making; numerous delays, downsizing, and even a lawsuit between two developers. That being said, this game took 15 years to make! That gives a developer plenty of time to look at their product and say, "Hmmmm... Is this a good game, and if not, how can we make it so?" Allow me to point out The Good, The Bad, and The Ugly things on this game.
The Good: The humor is fairly nice and well-timed for the most part, and reminded me very much of Robot Chicken, Famliy Guy, and it even has hints of classic TV shows like GI Joe and Popeye. This was almost enough to carry me through it.
, being the key word here. I also enjoyed the enemies; a combination of wordplay and mindless minions which made me grin a little every time I remembered their names.
Now for The Bad: The combat is trying to be a mix of Call of Duty & Halo, and while it is acceptable most of the time, it can get repetitive and boring. New weapons and gadgets try to freshen things up, but they can get a little boring as well after making a Pigcop explode for the tenth time. In addition to gear, Duke can increase his overall Ego (or rechargeable shield; pick your poison) by doing "manly" and "badass" things like lifting weights, shooting three-pointers, making popcorn, using the bathroom, looking in the mirror... Just a lot of ways to do it; maybe too much.
Let's get The Ugly: F**k Duke. F**k him and his sh*t-eating grin wearing, dark sunglassed, cigar-smoking, beer-chugging face. He's tolerable at first, but over time, I grew to despise him. He's only good in small doses, personally. It doesn't help that he insults various games like Halo and Gears of War, and (spoiler):
Then there's the bosses: uninspired, boring, cookie-cutter bullsh*t. The physics also don't help things; the aforementioned Ego system uses the game's physics a healthy percent of the time, and these Ego challenges can range from stupid to nearly impossible.
In short, Duke Nukem Forever is an excellent example of how even big-named icons can take a big tumble when handled poorly. Oh, and fun fact: a month after the game release, it was estimated that less than half a million copies were sold but there was enough sold to make a profit. That says a lot, doesn't it?

Considering how many of these reviews reference "peer to peer" as a reason to leave a negative review, or "balance", I figured I'd throw in my opinion here and why I think this game is fun and worth playing.
Peer to peer sucks, I won't defend that, but a lot of the problems people are having with it can be partially solved on their end, by forwarding ports to allow more stable connections, a lot of people don't want to put in the effort.
Second, the game might have balance issues but not as extreme as the people with <2 hours (Steam refund much?) seem to make it. You can play arguable the worst characters in the game, and easily beat arguably the best characters in the game, with only a small difference in skill.
This leads me to my final point, people like to compare this to a fighting game, though I don't agree with that comparison, and they also like to compare it to Chivalry or Mount and Blade. That being said, just like those genres and games, For Honor isn't something you can jump into and immediately become the king of. Your skill at say, Street Fighter, wouldn't translate to skill in this game the same way it would if you played Killer Instinct. BUT, if you put in a couple hours and actually TRY to get better at the game instead of just mindlessly button mashing, you'll find that a lot of the imbalances you thought you were dealing with are actually fairly easy to counter, things that you were getting beaten by consistently will become something that you counter consistently.
Pros:
Solid gameplay
Interesting characters that play very differently, with only a few feeling like they play a lot alike
An attempt at a progression system that doesn't feel like being low level means you lose by default (I've played fresh characters and easily beaten people that are high character level)
It tries to be something new and different, which it somewhat succeeds at, by combining elements of a lot of different genres
Cons:
Peer to peer servers are truly, truly terrible
There are some bugs, though they're uncommon (Things like stabbing the air during a grab instead of actually dealing damage)
Daily missions are dumb because everybody gets the same things, so you see people playing the same classes in the same mode in order to finish the same daily
The single player campaign felt tacked on and rushed, in the last 1/3 of the game you play the same map at least 3 times in 3 different missions.
Overall:
I recommend it, it's fun, you should try it, but you shouldn't get angry because you lose a lot to start. This isn't the kind of game you'll pick up and be the master of immediately, if you go in with that mindset you'll probably be able to enjoy it until you get better.
