So after 2.5 hours of playing this game, I requested a refund. I thought the matchmaking was sh*t, and by all standards it really was. But I did some searching around and found a page on Ubisoft community forums talking about the ports on your router that needed to be open to have an open NAT with Uplay. Before I received my refund I did what the guide said to do, and voila - Open NAT. Searching for matchmaking went from 2-5 minutes to (honestly) 5-10 seconds. Getting dropped mid-match dropped from occuring 50% of the time to only once in the last 3 hours.
If you can get an Open NAT, this game is a ton of fun. The main complaint myself and a lot of others share is the fact that a) the matchmaking is garbage if you don't a closed or moderate NAT, and b) that you even have to forward a crapload of ports to play this $60 game. I thought a lack of dedicated servers would be a major issue (and on principle it is), but the game runs just fine with P2P.
It's hard to recommend this game. I was definitely♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off for a while after I bought it as I was only able to play about 3 complete matches in 2.5 hours. I thought I got ripped off, and to a degree I still do. So, my positive recommendation for For Honor is ENTIRELY CONTINGENT ON YOU BEING ABLE TO GET AN OPEN NAT. If you cannot get one, return this game and save the headache. If you can, enjoy it, because I know I definitely am at this point. 1v1, 2v2, Deathmatch, and Dominion are all great game modes. The 12 playable characters mean you'll typically not see the exact same classes used match after match. I got my refund today and immediately re-purchased the game because it is honestly a night and day difference with the matchmaking once you configure your router. Again, it's BS that a $60 AAA title requires that, and if I could give this game a score it would only be 7.5/10 with an Open NAT. I don't forsee myself dumping hundreds of hours into this game, I see it getting old in a few months, but for now, I'm loving it, and I hope if you get it you take the time to get matchmaking working properly.

Solid game, not worthy of all the bashing reviews it received. Actually the game reminded me quite a bit of the Half Life series: 1) first person shooter 2) aliens come through portal to invade Earth 3) lots of non-shooting portions with puzzles 4) platforming 5) driving sequences 6) some similar levels like the factory
SOUNDTRACK
One advantage it has over Half Life is that it actually has a soundtrack (and a pretty good one) during gameplay. The trend of games without music needs to stop - other big names are also guilty of this such as the Bioshock series. Also the music is in MP3 format in a folder in the game directory if you'd like to copy it onto your computer before uninstalling the game. Most games hide the music and make you use 3rd party tools can be hard to find and/or difficult to use, so this was a nice bonus.
GRAPHICS
They're decent but even on my very powerful i7 4790 with GTX 750 TI, there were framerate and performance issues for 10 to 15 seconds when  starting or restarting a level, and then the problems resolved automatically. On this system I was hoping to play at 3840 x 2160 resolution but performance was too poor.
GAMEPLAY
Boss fights were the best part of the game - challenging but fair and well designed. For the non-shooting segments, which are fairly plentiful, sometimes I wished the game would just move on (mostly during the first half of the game). But I solved everything myself without any help. If you want an all action game all the time game, you should look into the Serious Sam series. But even the original Duke 3D was not all action. Also, the underwater levels were not my favorites. Finally, the game gives you the option of carrying 4 guns (I believe default is 2) - take advantage.

tells the story of a man who appears to be trapped in a cycle of life and purgatory, where the final choice to break this cycle is determined by the player. There is a heavily atmospheric, psychological horror theme throughout the game, represented by contorted characters, dark set pieces, and abstract visuals.
The standout feature of
is its graphics. This doesn't feel like a standard Unity engine game. There is some great lighting and shader work going on, the textures are of a high quality, and the character design is excellent. The soundtrack is also befitting of the themes present throughout even if they may not be original compositions. The only issue I take with
is the limited amount of voice actors, whose dialogue (and subtitles) often don't make too much sense as they are filled with grammatical/typographical errors and sound all too similar, even with pitch-shifting applied to various characters.
There are some severe frame-rate drops, especially in highly foliage populated areas, where I could easily tell the game was dropping below 30 frames per second. I also found a number of issues in regards to clipping through geometry and coming up against invisible walls. The in-game settings are also oddly worded and could be further fleshed out.
is a very short experience, about 1.5 hours, with two endings. I believe it's worth the price of admission due to the level of detail and consistent aesthetic throughout the experience. It is a simple game, there is no combat, no inspecting items, but where
lacks in gameplay it definitely makes up for in visuals and an intriguing story.

"What did you think of the game, Duke? Was it good?"
"Well after 12 ♥♥♥♥ing years, it should be"
It's hard to get something unique in gaming nowadays, with dozens of military shooters, this game definitely offers something different and something new.
The gunplay actually feels pretty good, very retro. I suppose it being dated gives it a bit of an advantage, but I just felt that the gunplay felt impactful.
It definitely takes you in, obviously not story wise, but the game is pretty entertaining and will keep your attention for a while, I played it for a few hours straight and I'd say I enjoyed the hours that I played. I think I will be coming back to it to at least finish it.
At its core, it's still a Duke Nukem game, and the Duke character is pretty amusing (most of the time, we'll get to that in the cons) The game is generally funny with a good amount of humour, but I think there's a lot of games that do it better.
This isn't really a pro-point, but seriously, this game is not a 2/10 or whatever the hell they were giving it on reviews, and this is talking from a perspective 5 years later, the game isn't as bad as you'll read, but it's definitely got downsides.
Cons:
Plenty of game breaking glitches, such as a scene where you fall off a crane and get stuck in scaffolding, and it was impossible for me to get out, took me around 5 retries before it'd actually work. The game is not even close to perfect, just realise that
I don't want a game to completely hold my hand, but I've had to look up a couple walkthroughs during this game, because some of the puzzles are so obscure and not remotely obvious, as I say, I do not want hand holding but I don't want to be thrown into something where I have NO idea what I'm doing. Having to work puzzles out every few minutes or so isn't really what I expected in a Duke Nukem game.
Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥this is bad, platforming in an FPS... DOES NOT WORK, it's just completely boring and I don't see why they'd put so much of it in the game, platforming is not remotely entertaining in a first person shooter
Game feels dated:[/b] The 12 years in production kinda show, because it doesn't feel like a 2011 game, it feels like some remaster of a early 2000s game, the game is hilariously clunky (which doesn't help the platforming) the graphics are borderline horrendous, considering this came out the same year as BF3 and Crysis 2... Even playing it 5 years later, it feels like a game that's 15 years old, and that's not acceptable. And I will reiterate that I am playing this MAXED in 1440p, my PC is perfectly capable of running anything I throw at it and it'll look good
I love offensive humour, but it can get really too far and immature. Two naked girls being sexually assaulted by aliens and Duke going "Looks like you got... f***kd" It's just bad lol. I don't see why anyone would find cheap sexual assault jokes amusing, if you're gonna make these jokes, make them witty and clever, offensive for offensive's sake is cheap. The humour is generally pretty good but it just goes down a slope sometimes, as proven in this segment. It can just feel like they're trying too hard and like it's been done by a 12 year old who's heard some pub jokes, and it definitely does feel like that in a lot of parts. I had a scene where I have to look for a sex toy and a condom for a stripper, like wow,, hilarious...get it? Because sex toys are funny ha ha ha. So then I had to sit through an awkward lapdance, which I'd like to say has extremely poor graphical fidelity and is just a little bit..... cringey?
Like... what?
You'd think on an i7 4790k and a GTX 980, I'd be able to run a game that is comparable to the PS2 era, but apparently my constant 200fps can just drop off a ♥♥♥♥ing cliff whenever it wants to, there are a lot of drops and stutters, maxed out at 1440p anyway
Overall, unless you can get this extremely cheap (like a dollar) I don't recommend this at all, the humour is childish at times, the game is shockingly bad when it comes to feeling dated and it's extremely glitchy. But I literally paid like £1.50 for this game, so it's worth it for me

4 hours in.
While it does not have the oppresively frightening and foreboding flair of Amnesia: The Dark Descent, SOMA builds an impressively immersive world with a well-written, if chilling, story, backed by a mostly well acted script (there's the occasional narmy sentence, but nothing serious).
Gameplay wise it's more of the same formula: explore the abandoned surroundings while looking for clues and ways to progress, which works perfectly given the mood and setting of the game. Sanity meter and effects are gone, I'm sad to say (replaced by a sort of interface screw in case you're badly injured), but they are not as missed as they were in Amnesia: A Machine For Pigs. The puzzles for the most part involve fiddling with mechanisms, computer options, and the occasional item to pick up (you do have an inventory this time), with less focus on physics-based contraptions. Both stealth segments and frantic escapes make a return, and the game even gives you a modicum of choice regarding how to proceed from time to time (do you activate this button or throw this lever? both have their consecuences, some immediate and game changing, some morally based)
Technically speaking, the game looks polished and runs mostly fine (there's the occasional framedrop, particularly when loading a new area; nothing gamebreaking, though) and controls as tightly as past Frictional games. There's even an FOV slider for people who suffer from simulation sickness.
All in all, while it lacks a certain "punch" in the scares department, the setting is engrossing and its story solid (assuming you're into sci-fi, that is).

This game has something more to it than any simple tag or review could attach.  It provides an atmosphere that is almost safe in nature (meaning its kind of hard to die) while at the same time it makes you grip your controller in fear for your life.  They mastered the ballance between the repeatitive nature of horror games where you die and restart, then die again and restart, and finally you master the pathing of the enemy and continue on ward.  They found the balance of making it seem like a desperate attempt of survival while not destroying the horrific atmosphere.  Because of this continous sequence of horrific events you will never feel like you are beating a game, rather you are surviving the atmosphere.  It's movie like, and because of that this is the first game I have ever played where you can feel horrified and continue on feeling like every fight was a "close one".
The story behind this game cannot go without notice either.  It revolves around an idea that has been hinted at before. but never truly exposed and explored in such a manner that it will make you horrified and interested at the same time.  It brings to the table a new philosophical debate as to what is life, and what does it mean to be.  Without going into spoilers and what not, there are parts in this game that will simply make you shiver not from the hyper-active monsters but from the circumstances and choices your character will be put through.
So for me, this game was exactly what I was looking for.  A fun weekend game, with a lot of atmosphere, some horror, and a mystery mixed with thoery that will keep me thinking for a very long time.  This game is worth the money, and more.  I can't wait to see what Frictional Games will come out with next.

Let me get this out of the way: This is a masterpiece. It is beautiful, awe-inspiring, and eerie. The sound and level design is top-notch. The "sanity effects" are jarring (as they should be). The story is enthralling and sucks you in. Overall, it is a unique piece of horror sci-fi evoking feelings of Event Horizon and Alien and worth some mulling over.
I enjoyed my time playing it up until the last stretch of the game. When I discovered it was winding down, I felt myself becoming more and more disheartened. After the final ending scene, I went to see the alternate endings I had surely missed... but there were none. At that moment I realized no moral decisions I had made during the game mattered, and that was what I felt was the most profound aspect of SOMA. It is meant to be ambiguous. You're meant to stress over your decisions and wonder if you had done the right thing, but when you are not rewarded with even a hint of consequences for your actions, they become meaningless. Especially when the endgame is not affected whatsoever and is very black and white.
It is SO HARD not to compare the game to Amnesia when the whole schtick of the enemies is exactly the same. Although, it seems whatever interactivity that was in The Dark Descent has been thrown out. SOMA is a glorified walking simulator akin to The Dark Descent's "sequel" (developed by The Chinese Room) A Machine for Pigs. Although after my experience, I have a newfound appreciation for the latter. There is no game to play here. Only fetch quests and back-tracking in-between reading, reading, listening to audio, reading, and more reading.
You are not rewarded for exploring. Hell, you're not even rewarded for uncovering more of the story. There is no inventory. You heal by shoving your hand into an alien sphincter and while it seems there was an idea that it would be consequential (as it seems the main character becomes "addicted" saying, "I NEED IT"), nothing actually happens. And if you get caught by baddies, you are respawned exactly where you were attacked. If you die, you return to the last checkpoint and there are so many it hardly feels like a punishment.
Those are the major beefs I had with this game that I can describe without spoiling. The minor issues I had were:
1. Screen tearing even after installing new drivers - I have a very high quality rig so this was very strange
2. Some textures never loaded (even ones on the main character) - again, strange considering my rig
3. Main character walks underwater like he's on land, but jumping doesn't have the same physics??
4. Weird physics - easily ignored, but annoying when noticed
5. Game crashed at the same point before Steam forced a patch on me - shouldn't this have happened before I booted it up??
6. Window minimized itself and interrupted play - I gather this is more of a problem on my end, however
Anyway...

Great game if you like 8-bit style games and side-scrolling beat-em-ups. It's not reallya beat-em-up because you rely mostly on firearms, but the gameplay is similar.
The combat in Dead Pixels is fun, but what really makes the gameplay engaging is the huge variety of weapons, items, and upgrades, combined with randomly generated layouts so you'll find different gear at different times and no two games will play out the same. Each firearm has damage, range, rate of fire, and penetration stats, which  makes different weapons work well for different situations. Maybe you're digging the range and power of a bolt action until you run into mobs and then you start blasting away with the double-barrel. Maybe you try to focus on shotguns and keep that going for a while until you run out of shells, then switch to a carbine and find you're liking that better. Maybe you have more fun setting everything on fire with dirt-cheap flares, maybe you're rolling in dough and cackle as you blow things away with $700 sticks of dynamite.
I don't think this will hold most people's attention for 40 hours, but it's a lot of fun and even better if you can find someone to play coop with you.

UBERMOSH is around version 0.02 of a finalized game, even by the listed patch notes. That full game could be awesome, but this is just 90-second snips of a trash arena. Lacking in graphics and variety, the solid combat isn't enough to justify multiple dollars and barely hours of gameplay.
Story time: I picked up UBERMOSH early in development, mostly because I was one of many that got Gearcrack Arena for around $0.09 USD with a coupon. It was weird, confusing, obtuse, and somehow deeper than UBERMOSH. Reaching level 3 in Gearcrack Arena was quite a feat, mostly because the controls were so confusing. The music was great at least, and worthwhile for nine cents, so I jumped on UBERMOSH with the hopes that Walter Machado would improve. The core gameplay was improved and actually worked really well. However, UBERMOSH still has the content variety of a tech demo, and feels like a test for something bigger.
There are a few issues at play that are forcing me to restrict my recommendation. Firstly, the Gearcrack Arena game I mentioned is no longer on Steam. It turns out that Walter Machado stated somewhere that Gearcrack Arena was only a year-long experiment (for sale), and after that year, he removed the game completely. There's no store page to confirm if this was stated to customers, and I don't recall any notice of the game having time-limited availability. Owners can still download the game, but bugs and issues will never be fixed. I can't confirm the dates, but it seems like the game disappeared after Steam Refunds were enabled. Walter Machado doesn't seem like a bad developer, but I have to worry. There's no real reason to remove the game, other than not bothering to fix it. If it was intended to be a temporary trial, release it for free.
Ignoring concerns of shady behavior, UBERMOSH is just too shallow. Arena generation is hard to notice, as the environment is just a big square with random blocks of brown walls. Enemies and guns are varied but feel the same. Class mods are just challenges imposed for a specific playstyle. The hitboxes feel very large, reflecting bullets 10 feet from your sword and getting hit from 3 feet away. After a few 90-second rounds, you've seen everything.
UBERMOSH can be fun for a bit, and has great potential. The shooting and swordplay feels great, but it needs a full game behind it. I was eagerly watching patch notes, and immensely disappointed to see the game go from version 0.014 or so to "Final" by adding cards. It's an alpha still. Walter Machado's games have charmed me, and I want them to be great. But this isn't finished, final, or even worth a few dollars currently. Although he may suddenly remove the game when he starts the next one, I really can't recommend UBERMOSH until it has more than 90 seconds of neon on brown.

This game has a really unique style that I've never seen in a game before. I'm not even sure how I'd describe it but I really enjoyed looking through the smaller details as I moved from screen to screen. Honestly, the art was a massive part of why I bought this game in the first place and if you're put off by the visual style then you may want to pass on Tormentum.
The puzzles in this are pretty standard adventure game fare. You've all different kinds of sliding tile puzzles, a rush hour puzzle, a puzzle with tetrominos, and a handful of others. They're enough to keep you busy and engaged with the game but nothing that's going to make you think too hard.
To the developers' credit, I didn't feel like there were any puzzles that fell into the trap of "adventure game logic". The riddles and other similar puzzles were written well.
The overall story isn't anything groundbreaking but I enjoyed it for what it was. I think mentioning Demon's Souls in the game's description might be a little off though. The tone and atmosphere of the game certainly evoke the Souls series but I didn't feel that the story was similar at all.
You make some choices throughout the game that I found pretty interesting. They're nothing groundbreaking but they gave me some agency over what happened in the story and I enjoyed thinking about what to do in each situation.
I really enjoyed the soundtrack for this game as well. The ambient music that plays as you wander around and solve the puzzles does a great job setting a mysterious and slightly creepy mood. I also really enjoyed Slippin Away by Matt Naylor that played during the credits.
I definitely recommend Tormentum - Dark Sorrow to anyone that looks at the screenshots and wants to see more. The game took me about 2 hours and 30 minutes to finish the first time through if length is a concern for you. My second playthrough (to get the ending I missed the first time through) took about an hour.

This game had been sitting on my wishlist for quite some time before I decided to take the leap and take it for a spin.  I was not disappointed!
As is immediately apparent from the screenshots and trailer, Tormentum's most notable quality is its hideously gorgeous art design.  A hybrid of H.R. Giger and Hieronymus Bosch, revealing each new area was the greatest force in motivating me forward.  The visual design is consistently excellent, and excels at creating a vibrant, absorbing and disturbing world.
How engaging the gameplay is will depend on how obtuse you like your point-and-click adventure puzzles.  Some may find its puzzles simplistic and easy, but I found it very enjoyable.  The game presents enough puzzles and riddles to keep one engaged, but doesn't make things so enigmatic as to grind the pacing of the story to a halt (no chicken-pullies or inflatable-duck-tongs-band-aid-rope things here).
What's more, the game does a good job of allowing those "ah-ha" moments by keeping player knowledge and character knowledge in balance.  One of my greatest pet peeves in adventure games is when I've determined the solution for a puzzle, but the game won't let you progress until the character has had the solution spelled out to them via dialogue or a diagram.  Fortunately, that never occurred here.  The game moves along at a steady pace, and is very hard to put down.
Either way, you probably won't have to worry about putting this game down, as it can very feasibly be completed in a single sitting.  My playthrough took about 4 hours, which is fine for me because it means the game didn't overstay its welcome.  I didn't feel like the game was lacking in content, and believe extending the running time to a full 8 or 12 hours would have caused the setting and tone to grow tired.  In this case, each setting was consistently fresh and fascinating.
Throughout the game, there is a heavy emphasis on moral choices.  It is true that the game is monitoring the things you do, and there are two endings based on the choices you make.  This is, unfortunately, where the game stumbles.  While the choices you encounter are very clear in their binary good-vs-evil quandaries, they tend to exist in a vacuum where you are judged regardless of the larger context of the situation.  Expect to forgive and free everyone you meet if you want the good ending, even if that person is a dangerous murderer or tyrannical overlord.  On top of that, it is very easy to make some "bad choices" by mistake in the beginning due to the nature of the choice not being particularly clear.
Be warned: you may want to play through this game multiple times to get both endings -- don't.  The difference in how things play out is one line of text and the end credits music.  It's fine to just watch the ending you don't get on YouTube if you're curious.  I can see myself playing through the game again just to see how the different choices impact the world overall, but I would not expect any difference if you were unsatisfied with the conclusion.
Overall, I really enjoyed the game.  The style and story were outstanding overall, and the gameplay was engaging enough to be entertaining throughout.  If you're a fan of point-and-click adventures and some existential horror, check it out!

I remember playing this game years ago as a child, so finding it on steam was a pleasant surprise.  Great graphic style and music still hold up to this day, although some things are a tad dated (I'm looking at you, resolution).
The game has a fairly steep learning curve, with 3 starting difficulties (I went with hard and the first few levels were brutal until I got the hang of the game).  Shooting down ships earns the player precious credits, so depending on how OCD the player is, this may lead to an easy or difficult late game, although I think the game generally tends towards being slightly easier (especially leading up to the brutal last boss fight); if you're really stuck the game also lets you cheat fairly easily for the price of being branded a cheat and presumably disabling steam achievements.
For most of my hard mode playthrough, difficulty rose at an appropriate level to keep me challenged without being unfairly difficult, although some weapons are noticably better/worse than their counterparts.   You could take this as a positive or negative thing depending on your outlook; most weapons have a clear use for at least one difficulty setting/level and beyond that player can intentionally downgrade to flashier (and weaker) gun as a handicap or the cool factor.
It can be difficult to see enemy projectiles at times, but this is only really an issue when the player has lots of flashy weapons shooting at the same time, which I only really found a problem on the second playthrough, at which point you're pretty much invincible anyway.

For me, the game only stopped being enjoyable when it became too easy and I had time to be bored; this really only happened in my second playthrough where I cleared the hard waves instantly and then had nothing to do or dodge until the next wave spawned.  For this reason I'd suggest trying the game on at least normal or hard difficulty for maximum enjoyment and replay value.
Overall I'd recommend this game if you're seeking a fun shooter that doesn't take itself too seriously and (mostly) challenges you in a fair way.

The idea behind this game is great. At first its great fun, learning the different operators, maps and guns. The recent ranked map pool changes are honestly one of the best things to happen, meaning ranked is actually a measure of skill and games arent decided before the game even begins due to some maps not being balanced at all.
But there are simply way too many problems for me to recommend this game, and the more you play the more obvious this becomes.
The biggest one is pingers and the frankly ridiculous lag compensation. Server hopping is really easy, so someone from NA or BR will simply server hop and play aggressive, so they'll shoot you before you even see them. Also, if you peek them and miss, after you're back behind hard cover you'll die because they've just seen you which is really infuriating. It doesn't help that ubisoft servers are absolutely terrible with a good ping being around 60, which is more then double what I get in other online games. The hitreg is noticeably worse and has been for a few motnsh too, despite ubi claiming to have upgraded their servers.
Then there are the bugs, like the valk cam bug on bank where you could spot the entire enemy team, the ranked elo glitch which meant the winning team got nothing from winning, the doc glitch which meant you always fought an overhealed 3 armour who would tank a ridiculous number of shots, or the hibana bug where here pellets don't activate which was there for months and even affected pro league an embarrasing amount. I could go on, but these bugs show how bad they can be. Now this wouldn't be so bad if ubi rolled out hotfixes, even if it was only on pc seeing as it doesn't cost them a penny, but instead they waited a whole one and a half months to roll out a ptach which is absolutely ridiculous. How can you let bugs that bad and game breaking stay in there for so long?
And finally, I cannot make sense of the recent balance changes at all. Ever since mid season where they gave an operator with a sniper the ability to see through smoke making him ridiculously overpowered for 3 months before they nerfed him. and even then they screwed up so bad they had to change operators with a high pickrate to try and stop him from being so op (taking smokes away from Ash and Thermite, and then giving them to Jackal when they really don't fit his playstyle at all). Then theres the acog removal from Jager and Bandit (yes I'm a salty Jager main), and the Scorpion they've given to Ela which has a ridulously large mag, really high fire rate, really low ads time and virtually no recoil at all. I honestly don't know what they're trying to achieve with these changes, and it seems more and more that ubi want to cater to low level players instead of just having them learn the game. What this means then is more powerful ops are abused to hell at higher ranks because people know how to play the game, making these ops just no fun to go up against.
Now don't get me wrong, I really want to like siege and have put a lot of time into it, but at this point I am honestly incredibly tired of all the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t I have to put up with. I'm a season pass owner, have elite skins and plenty of playtime, and really enjoy watching pro league, but it honestly just feels like ubi don't care at all. I mean if they allow game breaking bugs to last for months and directly affect pro league (Hibana bug) or let completely op operators dictate a completely ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t meta throughout the pro season (Glaz), how much do you think they care? Every time I want to play rainbow one match reminds me why I'm starting to get tired of all the same old♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ because someones playing with high ping, or someones abusing a glitch, or someones using a completely op operator.

My suggestion is probably something you've already heard: Get 2014 instead.

If you've made it to the Steam reviews, you know the basic premise of this game; I'm going to focus on how the game communicated to the player (player-context, mechanics, multiplayer matches, game economy, and game community), and how that determined the state of my recommendation.
Player-context:  What I mean by this is, when first starting the game, can a player intuitively understand what the game is, what they have control over, what that control means according to gameplay, and the impact they can have as a player on the the state of the game?  This last facet is particularly important for a game focused on multiplayer competion.
This is the worst area of the game.  Players are thrust into anoverwhelming series of menus throwing out faction information, game modes, character selection (9 of the introductory 12 character types are initially locked, with no immediate information about how to unlock them), training, and control options with little context for what any of it means, why it's meaningful, and the lasting effect these choices have on the player as they play the game.  Some general options aren't even able to be accessed or changed until the tutorial is completed, and this isn't communicated in the game.
Mechanics:  I chose to play the game with a gamepad, as Ubisoft Montreal led development for consoles, and the PC version is a port handled by BlueByte.  Camera and character movement is fast, responsive, and comprehensible (even when surrounded by enemies).  Control works better outdoors, in wide spaces, but this is nothing new for a third-person action (TPA) game.  I didn't like having light and heavy attacks bound to the right button and right trigger, respectively, since the majority of TPA games have those tied to face buttons.  With the thumb of a right-handed person demanded to be on the right thumbstick by having that input control where attacking and blocking originate from, however, I can see why button mapping was made this way.  Specific directionality of attacking and blocking, by the way, felt 90% intentional and under control; rarely does a player feel their character (or their opponent) go rogue and launch attacks or abilities out of nowhere.
The mechanical system is intricate and complex:  skillfull play necessitates environmental awareness, tactical understanding, and quick and careful execution.  In other words, stick-flailers and button-mashers will be summarily identified and disposed of.  This isn't a pick-up-and-play style of game.
Multiplayer Matches:  Given the poor player-context defined above, it's difficult for a new player to understand the match options available to them.  But for all the♥♥♥♥♥♥this game has been getting relative to connectivity and stability, I had no issue joining or starting a match, or feeling knowledgeable and in control once a match was underway.  There were two instances of lag I experienced; one during a respawn, and one during a duel.  Both were minor, and neither resulted in me screaming "Come on, what the ♥♥♥♥, game?"  Given the less than diamond-tier status of my network connection in general, I was pleasantly surprised.
Game economy:  If nothing else, I appreciate the lack of mystery or subtlety; it's a $60 base game, $40 season pass, microtransactions, and slave-to-the-grind pacing of advancement for those who say ♥♥♥♥ that♥♥♥♥♥♥to anything except the entry fee.  It's greedy, disrespectful of player time and effort, and nothing new within the multiplayer game space.  My advice is to understand what you're in for; if you're willing to throw your wallet at the forehead of a French game developer so your Samurai can have Lavender Dream Mega Sex armor before your hated Viking rival, then you have nothing to worry about.  For the principled (or cash-strapped), unlocks will proceed by the micrometer.  The good news is,  none of the unlocks I saw were a pay-to-win button; instead, the focus was on cosmetic customization.
Game community:  For Honor has an astonishing lack of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s!  This could be due to my muting and not participating in voice chat at all, but when I played, team mates were focused on objectives, duelists didn't shatter the enticing gladiatorial dream launched by the aesthetic of this experience, and no one was racist or sexist.  It helps that the heart of the game comes down to one player focusing on and defeating one opponent at a time--even in team modes--with some exceptions depending on the quality of play in a given match.
So, For Honor isn't a bad game.  It's an answer to the question, "What if The Watchers on the Wall episode of Game of Thrones were a video game?"
This is the type of game you must commit to if you really want to feel like it was worth your time, attention, and money; you need to patiently and completely understand each faction, warrior, and moveset if you want to spend all of your playing time as anything besides a decapitated corpse.  For Honor makes this difficult to follow through on, due to poor player-context and a very fat 'n' strict bottom-line-oriented game economy.  If total commitment to the systems and subtleties of a complex and demanding game is your thing, then have at it, friend; I've yet to meet someone who dove into an ocean, only to complain it was too shallow.
ETA:  I slept on it, and it turns out, I feel like going for a swim.  My last piece of advice for those on the fence:  Use your refund window (depending on when you read this, you'll see that I spent exactly 1.9 hours playing For Honor before deciding to keep and recommend it)!  This is especially true if your network strength is iffy; jump into multiple game modes and matches at the outset to see whether play is smooth and acceptable.  Yes, you'll get killed diving into the deep end at the word go, but the point of the refund window is answering this question:  Can the game be played, functionally and enjoyably?  My answer is yes.  If you're in the same boat, feel free to reach out to me in-game, player name Dream_Sequence.

Interesting premise but lacking in execution. As of yet the game is very short in content. One can spend roughly 3 hours in it before one has seen everything and a feeling of "this needs more time in development" settles in. The only reason I personally spent more time on this was from coming back for matches between patches to see what they added (and it wasn't much, mostly balance adjustments and bug fixes). The developers consider the game "feature complete" and in doing so crush any hope of new game mechanics to broaden gameplay.
Would rate the experience 4 out of 10, in particularly in hindsight of the the high price for the small game one gets in return.
Offworld Trading Company has the complexity of a typical smartphone or board game with a tedious buy/sell minigame in the form of juggling various goods around. Player influence on total econonmy or pricing is negligible - you can not corner a market or establish a strategic monopoly as it's always possible to buy resources from the market, even if nobody supplies them. A single match is roughly 30 minutes in duration but can take up to 40 in rare cases. Gameplay is heavily streamlined to remain within tight confines.
To illustrate a few mechanics:
Upon starting a match one has to scan the map to uncover its limited resource fields, quickly slam down a base building and then build extractors on resource deposits. Automated NPC ships haul the harvested resource back to the HQ once the extractor building is full. Those units can not be interacted with directly (except for a very rare piracy action card one can win in a random auction to steal enemy supplies for a short duration) and merely exist as a visual way to see when the next resource-"tick" happens. They are the only units on the map, everything else is just buildings.
There is a limit over how many tiles of the map you can build on as building on a tile consumes "claims" - you start with a handfull of those and only get a handful more for upgrading your HQ, which in return only has 4 steps and stops at level 5. A few screenshots on the Store page show how small the fully upgraded "base" will get. As buildings give an output adjaciency bonus one just builds a cluster of similar buildings and spreads out the other clusters of different types to avoid getting targeted by expensive sabotage actions players can buy (with a cooldown), such as EMP strikes.
The match itself is won by buying out the competition. This starts by acquiring "shares" of the enemy company - the total amount of shares each company has can be adjusted with difficulty settings but is typically 10. The more shares one owns the cheaper will be the final takeover - that option simply becomes unlocked once all shares have been bought by someone (no matter if a company bought its own shares or someone else did) - there is no way to prevent takeover, even if the company is doing well financially, as long as the enemy has enough cash on hand to buy one out. This means one could lose if an enemy simply stops spending cash very early to rush a buyout while one would rather upgrade and then have the stronger income/economy to win in the long run. This sounds more complex than it is but at its core feels unrefined and gets boring rather quickly.
In technical regards the game is very simple and seems to be made in the Unity Engine 4 - as such it only supports single threading, has greatly limited scale of maps and environments, medicore visual fidelity and tacked-on UI. At this stage the UI seems extremely clunky - I'd have hoped it's a placeholder but as they are adjusting and updating it while adding new buttons I somehow get the feeling they'll keep it this way.
The current voice files are text-to-speech placeholders with awkward pronounciation but are the most memorable feature of the game - sentences like
from a creepy robot voice are simply hilarious.
All in all it feels like the designers behind this project had a nifity idea but no great vision with merely a few simple game systems in spirit of a board game in their heads - the blanks have been filled with convoluted mechanics. I do not believe the developers will give it a complete overhaul between now and release and as such can
recommend a purchase.

Only the greatest CRPG of all time! No, really.
Well, maybe if you value things like 'not having bugs' or 'balanced gameplay' or 'not being rushed out the door for Christmas'. But, what classic CRPG (Bioware aside) isn't filled with these little character flaws? Frankly, it still feels more polished than Alpha Protocol, which, while remaining one of my favorite all-time games, doesn't have the 'rushed out' excuse so much.
Despite being a licenced game and sequel, the story of the Jedi Exile and her companions (oh, did I mention the player character is canonically female?) manages to have the best narrative I've seen in any video game I've ever played, one which still sparks debate over its true messages and intent. Without giving too much away, you'll be touching on the nature of good and evil, the scars that remain from war, the struggle against objective morality and appointed fate, and the very real consequences that come from being a video game character. (No, really.)
Also, this game both stands up to repeat paythroughs and doesn't make you hate the vast majority of the supporting cast. (LOOKING AT YOU, BIOWARE)
More importantly, thanks to the good people at Aspyr and the dedicated mod community, the game has both the content it deserved to ship with and a slick control and graphical update for the modern gamer. Fully playable using a 360 controller, widescreen without stretching or patch hacks, and on whichever operating system you fancy most. (IN YOUR FACE, BIOWARE)

(Also, I love other Star Wars games too, like the original Battlefront titles, so don't get too uppity.)

4 hours in.
While it does not have the oppresively frightening and foreboding flair of Amnesia: The Dark Descent, SOMA builds an impressively immersive world with a well-written, if chilling, story, backed by a mostly well acted script (there's the occasional narmy sentence, but nothing serious).
Gameplay wise it's more of the same formula: explore the abandoned surroundings while looking for clues and ways to progress, which works perfectly given the mood and setting of the game. Sanity meter and effects are gone, I'm sad to say (replaced by a sort of interface screw in case you're badly injured), but they are not as missed as they were in Amnesia: A Machine For Pigs. The puzzles for the most part involve fiddling with mechanisms, computer options, and the occasional item to pick up (you do have an inventory this time), with less focus on physics-based contraptions. Both stealth segments and frantic escapes make a return, and the game even gives you a modicum of choice regarding how to proceed from time to time (do you activate this button or throw this lever? both have their consecuences, some immediate and game changing, some morally based)
Technically speaking, the game looks polished and runs mostly fine (there's the occasional framedrop, particularly when loading a new area; nothing gamebreaking, though) and controls as tightly as past Frictional games. There's even an FOV slider for people who suffer from simulation sickness.
All in all, while it lacks a certain "punch" in the scares department, the setting is engrossing and its story solid (assuming you're into sci-fi, that is).
Hey, at least your character doesn't have amnesia this time!

This game has something more to it than any simple tag or review could attach.  It provides an atmosphere that is almost safe in nature (meaning its kind of hard to die) while at the same time it makes you grip your controller in fear for your life.  They mastered the ballance between the repeatitive nature of horror games where you die and restart, then die again and restart, and finally you master the pathing of the enemy and continue on ward.  They found the balance of making it seem like a desperate attempt of survival while not destroying the horrific atmosphere.  Because of this continous sequence of horrific events you will never feel like you are beating a game, rather you are surviving the atmosphere.  It's movie like, and because of that this is the first game I have ever played where you can feel horrified and continue on feeling like every fight was a "close one".
The story behind this game cannot go without notice either.  It revolves around an idea that has been hinted at before. but never truly exposed and explored in such a manner that it will make you horrified and interested at the same time.  It brings to the table a new philosophical debate as to what is life, and what does it mean to be.  Without going into spoilers and what not, there are parts in this game that will simply make you shiver not from the hyper-active monsters but from the circumstances and choices your character will be put through.
So for me, this game was exactly what I was looking for.  A fun weekend game, with a lot of atmosphere, some horror, and a mystery mixed with thoery that will keep me thinking for a very long time.  This game is worth the money, and more.  I can't wait to see what Frictional Games will come out with next.

Let me get this out of the way: This is a masterpiece. It is beautiful, awe-inspiring, and eerie. The sound and level design is top-notch. The "sanity effects" are jarring (as they should be). The story is enthralling and sucks you in. Overall, it is a unique piece of horror sci-fi evoking feelings of Event Horizon and Alien and worth some mulling over.
I enjoyed my time playing it up until the last stretch of the game. When I discovered it was winding down, I felt myself becoming more and more disheartened. After the final ending scene, I went to see the alternate endings I had surely missed... but there were none. At that moment I realized no moral decisions I had made during the game mattered, and that was what I felt was the most profound aspect of SOMA. It is meant to be ambiguous. You're meant to stress over your decisions and wonder if you had done the right thing, but when you are not rewarded with even a hint of consequences for your actions, they become meaningless. Especially when the endgame is not affected whatsoever and is very black and white.
It is SO HARD not to compare the game to Amnesia when the whole schtick of the enemies is exactly the same. Although, it seems whatever interactivity that was in The Dark Descent has been thrown out. SOMA is a glorified walking simulator akin to The Dark Descent's "sequel" (developed by The Chinese Room) A Machine for Pigs. Although after my experience, I have a newfound appreciation for the latter. There is no game to play here. Only fetch quests and back-tracking in-between reading, reading, listening to audio, reading, and more reading.
You are not rewarded for exploring. Hell, you're not even rewarded for uncovering more of the story. There is no inventory. You heal by shoving your hand into an alien sphincter and while it seems there was an idea that it would be consequential (as it seems the main character becomes "addicted" saying, "I NEED IT"), nothing actually happens. And if you get caught by baddies, you are respawned exactly where you were attacked. If you die, you return to the last checkpoint and there are so many it hardly feels like a punishment.
Those are the major beefs I had with this game that I can describe without spoiling. The minor issues I had were:
1. Screen tearing even after installing new drivers - I have a very high quality rig so this was very strange
2. Some textures never loaded (even ones on the main character) - again, strange considering my rig
3. Main character walks underwater like he's on land, but jumping doesn't have the same physics??
4. Weird physics - easily ignored, but annoying when noticed
5. Game crashed at the same point before Steam forced a patch on me - shouldn't this have happened before I booted it up??
6. Window minimized itself and interrupted play - I gather this is more of a problem on my end, however
Anyway...

Bejeweled Twist is a great puzzle game. It has a good amount of variety and gamemodes. And like all good puzzle games, it has unlimited replay value. It can be a relaxing game. It can also be a difficult game. It’s a game that requires you to think, observe, and pay attention. It’s a game that can be enjoyed whether it’s played for a few minutes or a few hours. Bejeweled Twist brings in a new form of gameplay compared to the other Bejeweled games. Unlike the other Bejeweled games where you swap two jewels with each other either vertically or horizontally, in Bejeweled Twist, you rotate four jewels (two on the top and two on the bottom) clockwise (to the right). The only thing that’s kind of odd is that you can only rotate the jewels clockwise. You can’t rotate the jewels counter clockwise (to the left). Regardless, if you like puzzle games, I definitely recommend Bejeweled Twist

Tormentum - Dark Sorrow is a descent into beautiful, gory, agony. Prepare your gaming soul for the short but powerful ride wherein an unnamed and conveniently amnesiac protagonist finds the brakes on his dead-man's ride cut.
We have such sights to show you, oh yes.
It has to be said that there is a thin line between a homage and plagiarism, and Tormentum is skillfully dancing on that fine edge. Still, if you want to know what HR Giger's artwork would look like in Hell, look no further. Tormentum is a visual tour de force, a hauntingly beautiful marriage of monstrosities, mythological beasts, archetypes, and desolate wastelands. The soundtrack is subtle, never overly present, but packs quite a punch nonetheless. The slow, melancholic tunes, combined with the phantasmagoria played out before you might just affect you harder than you were prepared for.
As for the puzzles, they are rather typical of the genre, but fun nonetheless. However, a major flaw that most of them have in common is that you'll probably be able to solve them on the first try. Aside from the lack of challenge (and thus satisfaction), this also drastically cuts short the play-time, as you'll find yourself solving puzzles at a pace that is simply unreal for the genre. Most people spend less than six hours on their first play-through.
As for the story, this may not be the game's strong point. Though there is a history behind this dark night of the soul, it's not really worth repeating. Some moral dilemmas present themselves as the story unfolds, but considering how little emotional attachment you’ll have to the cast, none of them feel particularly pressing. It's hard to be upset about the fate of characters who were introduced mere minutes ago, no matter how sorry their plight.
Rather, you should sit back and revel in the flow of gruesome images, the spot-on symbolism, and the melancholic sounds. Familiar as the themes and style may be, Tormentum is something you probably haven't seen before.

If you've made it to the Steam reviews, you know the basic premise of this game; I'm going to focus on how the game communicated to the player (player-context, mechanics, multiplayer matches, game economy, and game community), and how that determined the state of my recommendation.
Player-context:  What I mean by this is, when first starting the game, can a player intuitively understand what the game is, what they have control over, what that control means according to gameplay, and the impact they can have as a player on the the state of the game?  This last facet is particularly important for a game focused on multiplayer competion.
This is the worst area of the game.  Players are thrust into anoverwhelming series of menus throwing out faction information, game modes, character selection (9 of the introductory 12 character types are initially locked, with no immediate information about how to unlock them), training, and control options with little context for what any of it means, why it's meaningful, and the lasting effect these choices have on the player as they play the game.  Some general options aren't even able to be accessed or changed until the tutorial is completed, and this isn't communicated in the game.
Mechanics:  I chose to play the game with a gamepad, as Ubisoft Montreal led development for consoles, and the PC version is a port handled by BlueByte.  Camera and character movement is fast, responsive, and comprehensible (even when surrounded by enemies).  Control works better outdoors, in wide spaces, but this is nothing new for a third-person action (TPA) game.  I didn't like having light and heavy attacks bound to the right button and right trigger, respectively, since the majority of TPA games have those tied to face buttons.  With the thumb of a right-handed person demanded to be on the right thumbstick by having that input control where attacking and blocking originate from, however, I can see why button mapping was made this way.  Specific directionality of attacking and blocking, by the way, felt 90% intentional and under control; rarely does a player feel their character (or their opponent) go rogue and launch attacks or abilities out of nowhere.
The mechanical system is intricate and complex:  skillfull play necessitates environmental awareness, tactical understanding, and quick and careful execution.  In other words, stick-flailers and button-mashers will be summarily identified and disposed of.  This isn't a pick-up-and-play style of game.
Multiplayer Matches:  Given the poor player-context defined above, it's difficult for a new player to understand the match options available to them.  But for all the♥♥♥♥♥♥this game has been getting relative to connectivity and stability, I had no issue joining or starting a match, or feeling knowledgeable and in control once a match was underway.  There were two instances of lag I experienced; one during a respawn, and one during a duel.  Both were minor, and neither resulted in me screaming "Come on, what the ♥♥♥♥, game?"  Given the less than diamond-tier status of my network connection in general, I was pleasantly surprised.
Game economy:  If nothing else, I appreciate the lack of mystery or subtlety; it's a $60 base game, $40 season pass, microtransactions, and slave-to-the-grind pacing of advancement for those who say ♥♥♥♥ that♥♥♥♥♥♥to anything except the entry fee.  It's greedy, disrespectful of player time and effort, and nothing new within the multiplayer game space.  My advice is to understand what you're in for; if you're willing to throw your wallet at the forehead of a French game developer so your Samurai can have Lavender Dream Mega Sex armor before your hated Viking rival, then you have nothing to worry about.  For the principled (or cash-strapped), unlocks will proceed by the micrometer.  The good news is,  none of the unlocks I saw were a pay-to-win button; instead, the focus was on cosmetic customization.
Game community:  For Honor has an astonishing lack of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s!  This could be due to my muting and not participating in voice chat at all, but when I played, team mates were focused on objectives, duelists didn't shatter the enticing gladiatorial dream launched by the aesthetic of this experience, and no one was racist or sexist.  It helps that the heart of the game comes down to one player focusing on and defeating one opponent at a time--even in team modes--with some exceptions depending on the quality of play in a given match.
So, For Honor isn't a bad game.  It's an answer to the question, "What if The Watchers on the Wall episode of Game of Thrones were a video game?"
This is the type of game you must commit to if you really want to feel like it was worth your time, attention, and money; you need to patiently and completely understand each faction, warrior, and moveset if you want to spend all of your playing time as anything besides a decapitated corpse.  For Honor makes this difficult to follow through on, due to poor player-context and a very fat 'n' strict bottom-line-oriented game economy.  If total commitment to the systems and subtleties of a complex and demanding game is your thing, then have at it, friend; I've yet to meet someone who dove into an ocean, only to complain it was too shallow.
ETA:  I slept on it, and it turns out, I feel like going for a swim.  My last piece of advice for those on the fence:  Use your refund window (depending on when you read this, you'll see that I spent exactly 1.9 hours playing For Honor before deciding to keep and recommend it)!  This is especially true if your network strength is iffy; jump into multiple game modes and matches at the outset to see whether play is smooth and acceptable.  Yes, you'll get killed diving into the deep end at the word go, but the point of the refund window is answering this question:  Can the game be played, functionally and enjoyably?  My answer is yes.  If you're in the same boat, feel free to reach out to me in-game, player name Dream_Sequence.

While still in development, it does have a lot of potential. I do believe the Espionage tactics need to be a bit rarer, and there needs to be a tutorial added into the game. Over all, enjoyable, but it still needs some development.
Some suggestions:
Diplomacy. Not all corporate dealings are hostile.
Upgrades that provide proof against certain espionage tactics. (EMP Shielding, Armed Guards, etc.)
Claim purchase / upgrades. Some buildings should not require a claim.
Zone of Control Limit. As of now, youcan build anywhwere on the map. Should be limited to a small area around your HQ, which then expands with HQ Upgrades. I'd also say that anything built within that zone should not require a claim for the owner, but upon purchasing stock in the owners company, allow an opponent to build within it.
Different paced game modes. Some of us like to take things slow (This is why I don't to Online Strategy Games, it becomes an all out blitz). Being able to set the pace / hostility of the AI might attract more players.
Solo mode - just a way to build and get familiar with the game concepts without worrying about other opponents.
Over all, its nice to have a strategy game that doesn't involve blowing things up all the time or building a balanced city.

I have never played anything like it before. Someone wrote, it compares best to the classic M.U.L.E.
The basic idea is, that you found a venture on mars to grab ressources, manufacture goods, and sell them for a profit.
There is a dynamic price mechanism based on supply and demand. This is nothing new. But it plays out in real time and feels like an RTS. (Sidenote: One of the designers mentioned Company of Heroes when talking about OTC! The game is totally different, but it "feels" as action packed as CoH while being all about economics).
So you have to make decisions all the time - and since it is real time, there is a cost for not deciding: Do I claim a nice tile of land on mars to put a new factory there? Or do I make my existing stuff more efficient? Do I buy up someone elses stock? Or do I pay back my debt to prevent someone else from buying me out? Do I want to produce something that will guarantee small profits, or do I take a risk and switch to a potentially more profitable strategy? And .... WHO THE HELL has sabotaged my power supply again?!?
The content and scope of this game is limited, but beautiful. Thats why I think, this game should set for a price of about 25 USD. The mechanic is fresh, the presentation is nice and the playstyle is rather unique.
And I love the music. It will probably change a lot of times... I hope they include most of it in the final soundtrack.
My impression:
- Single Player: Skirmish and Daily challenge are nice play modes. The campaign mode feels like an addon - but it will need a lot of polish if it wants to compete with games like Anno 1401.
- Multiplayer: Intense! Currently you might have to wait a few minutes to get a game going. This will get much more popular the closer OTC gets to release date.
Good points:
- Fresh playstyle and interesting scenario.
- Nice and fluent visual presentation and music.
- Cutthroat multiplayer robberbaron capitalism.
- Music and sound.
Not so good points (yet!):
- Statistics will need more work. (I assume it gets it)
- Almost no storytelling. (I don't expect too much changes here)
- You win by clicking a button. This isn't the most exciting way of a finale (yet!)
I would not expect a huge package that offers anything near the variety of a Civ V. If you are ok with the limited but exciting scenario, then you should grab this game now!

A deceptively fast-paced economic, base-building strategy game with no military units.
Offworld plays very well in a FFA environment, and I enjoy 6- and 8-player games regularly. It keeps you on your toes as players react to changing prices, trying to make profits. You need to be constantly asking yourself, "what resources are the other players neglecting?"
It can become quite frenzied in the end game as you buy up a couple other players and suddenly you need to manage ~60 structures, trying to gain cash faster than your rivals, who are trying to buy out your company.
Every game is different with randomized maps and resource distributions. Black Market (aggressive abilities and other utilities) is also switched up. There isn't really a build order; need to look at the map and the other colonies to figure out the best overall plan, which will definitely change several times during the 20 min game.
It's fun.

Different game, same [Lo]wang. Now new and improved with Borderlands-style loot!!
The original (classic) Shadow Warrior was pretty action packed and epic for its time, putting a different spin on the Duke Nukem formula and though similar to that series, managing to create something entirely unique. Flash forward to 2013 and with the release of the reboot within that year, it was obvious that Shadow Warrior was now an established series and not just a run-of-the-mill shooter but one that had a level of action and performance that rivaled the biggest/AAA title shooters of that time; an overall presentation that perhaps even surpassed those other titles. The humor from the past game returned but it matured, managing to be more intelligent while its tongue was still firmly planted in its cheek, which is something that couldn’t be said for Duke Nukem Forever. Also, the graphics and mechanics were face melting-ly gorgeous and fluid, making the game run as smoothly as it looked with virtually no performance issues.
Now enter Shadow Warrior 2. The same level of performance and action you’d expect from this series is back and even better than before. Graphically, this game is perfect in my opinion. The physics and weather effects paired with the colors and environmental details within the areas you explore are, in a word, gorgeous. This of course just makes the violence that much sexier :D
But now more on that mention of Borderlands. It’s true, just as many others have said, there is now Borderlands-style loot drops when you defeat enemies and there are even a number of different weapons to acquire and upgrades to acquire/craft (yeah, that’s also true – you can now craft in Shadow Warrior!). These upgrades can be inserted into slots for your armor and weapons and they may have an elemental effect, like shock or fire, or they may boost your damage amount or HP, etc. There are of course skills to acquire and upgrade as you level your character and the missions (side, bounty and story based missions) take place in the same geographical regions within the game, though you may start out at a different place and there will be different enemies each time, as the missions are somewhat open-ended and non-linear and there are even achievements to unlock that pertain to beating a certain ‘named’ enemy within a particular mission, essentially like a mini boss. The enemies, not unlike some of the upgrades, also have status and/or elemental effects.
Bottom line: Shadow Warrior 2 does so many things right that it would be hard for Flying Wild Hog/Devolver to ever do anything wrong with this series. It basically just keeps getting bigger and better with each new entry and they have also managed to capture the true essence of a 3rd person hack/slash action game and combine it with the frenetic energy of a bullet hell shooter.

This review is an early access one and even within days of me buying the game some significant changes were made, so I expect lots more changes to come.
This is one really good concept and whilst there are issues with it (especially in teaching a new player how to play and how the systems and concepts work), there is soooo much to like here. The game does away with military conflict and the necessity to be able to hotkey or mouse-click quickly to win. Instead, it requires forethought, palnning, deception and a little luck to do well.
I'll admit, it took me ages to get my head around some concepts and I'm not sure I'm there yet. I have yet to play a multiplayer game (this is my major criticism at this stage - no-one online at this point but hopefully numbers will grow) and have only just started a campaign, but I've already put in 14 hours at the point of writing this in skirmishe and doing the tutorial a couple of times.
There are some really interesting game features too, such as being able to play a single player skirmish while you wait for a multiplayer lobby to fill (which helps avoid the hwole thing where people log on, check for ten seconds and then leave), a team based multiplayer option and a single player mode that works differently to the multi and skirmish modes.
Pros:
- Great amount of tension within the game
- Replayablility Every game is different
- Accomodates various playing styles (with 4 different bases/classes that are reasonably balanced at this point)
- shrewed tactical gameplay
- Various gameplay options across all game modes
- Games last for between 15 minutes and half hour. Not a Civ styled game at all.
Cons:
- Tough to learn. The turoial is pretty much non-existant and many finer points that will have you scratching your head will not be answered without visiting the internets and YouTube
- No-one on multiplayer yet
Overall: I feel like I am only at the beginning of this journey with this game and  with updates that make the game a little more unique on each play, the game will go from strength to strength. It is fair enough to say that I am a fan!

Quick story recap: a long time ago, in 2003, prior to KOTOR release, LuasArts already wanted a sequel, but Bioware was unavailable at the moment and offered Obsidian instead. Then two things happened: 1. LA were greedy and patientless enough to demand the game be done by Christmas 2004; and 2. Obsidian were optimistic/desperate enough to agree to these terms without even seeing the first game. The end result was a glitchy half-cut but potentially great game.
I used to hate it and left after ~5-8 hours into the first playthrough. It seemed boring and I got stuck on the very first planet… but then it got a new life on Steam, with high-res support, achievements, and the Cut Content mod already on Workshops. And I loved it. KOTOR 2 is worthy of the first game, adding a little more ambiguity to the classic light/dark dichotomy, and offering more action and independence to playable characters than the first game. The Exile story is probably not so personally dramatic as the one of the first game, but it's just different and delivers no less.

I don't really like humans, I'm not a social person and don't really get along well with others. Not really one for "hoping for the best" or caring about our children's future either. I guess you could say I am a cynical and sadistic person. But SOMA changes everything about how I look at our existence. This game is smart and incredibly UNSETTLING, not just from a horror standpoint but from a scientific standpoint. SOMA shines, glitters and glows at the very realization that it is not so much Science Fiction, as it is a plausible Science Fact. I have to admit right now, that I hated the Amnesia series. The hiding under beds and in lockers of other horror games, was what I was afraid SOMA would cookie cut into the mold. But Frictional Games knew better going into this, and the outcome is phenomenal. You won't be hiding, so much as sneaking. And there won't be jumpscares, so much as tension. These changes make the game feel unique and more immersing. The game looks gorgeous despite the Twitch community thrashing the game before it even hit release. I played the entire game in full 4K at 40-50fps no stutter. The environments are breathtaking and entrancing. I loved SOMA's design from the moment I saw it. I went in thinking it was going to be Bioshock meets Dead Space. I did not realize it was going to outshine them both......at half the price. Speaking of price, seeing as how both Amnesia games were sub $25USD, I felt a big risk spending $26-30 going into SOMA. That risk is way worth the price of admission. The genius script and harrowing plot will not only give meaning to our existence but maybe a little more faith in our survival as well. The game has no tutorials and will only hint at where to find the next hidden item or difficult puzzle. 10 hours may seem short especially by today's massive games. But if you have ever spent 10 hours on an anxiety roller coaster, I'll have you know that this game makes you feel uneasy even when nothing is around. You cannot play this game expecting to be thrilled; It is a slow paced and incredibly intelligent plot. You wont be getting any cheap scares or fighting any monsters with Plasma Cutters and Power Loaders. SOMA will be giving you a message to think about...........a message to think about for a long, long time.

It's a Mount and Blade game. Need I saw more? This entire series is a masterpiece. Great story, amazing gameplay, easy to learn - hard to master. Almost everything in this game is perfect. I prefer the 1600s setting over Napoleonic Wars. But like other great games - it's only good because the positives overlay the negatives. By god, there's a lot of them.
- Crashes: The game crashes often. It's not really a graphics issue, it happens when interacting with an NPC. Even still, without crashing, clicking dialouge options often drops FPS waay low.
- Hit Detection: Guns are the main selling point of this game. And they suck. More often than not, bullets go straight through enemies. Trying to hit anything below the abdomen is a surefire miss.
- Siege: Sieges 'glitch" out a lot. Once you've pushed pass the wall, you head down to engage the enemy... and there's an invisible wall! The AI just sits back behind this wall - none of your soldiers can hit them, they don't charge, and you can only use what's left of bullets/arrows to take them out. Then retreat, loose morale and have your soldiers suck even more.
- AI: They can be stupid sometimes. AI is hard to program - I don't blame 'em.
- Music: The music is buggy as hell and likes to-o r-r-r-re-n-n-ot-t-tesic-c-ch is an-n-n-nin-ng as h-e-e-e-ell. (to repeat notes which is annoying as hell)
Don't let these cons fool you - this game is amazing. However, some players may get annoyed by these glitches, so be cautious

What is it to be Human? Are we more than our thoughts? Is there some intrinsic quality about the combination of mind and body? Can one still be defined as human without a their organic body? What would happen if you copied a mind and put it into a computer? Would that mind be human? Would it be alive? Would it be the same person? And what would happen if you copied the copy? Dead Pixels is a "Grindhouse" side-scrolling zombie shooter with some survival elements planted in it, as well as RNG. Dead pixels is your typical zombie survival shooter, but does it VERY well for the price.
DP has you running from one end of the street to the other, killing zombies, looting some houses for items/weapons/ammo, trading with merchants, and trying not to die. The number of streets you must traverse all depends on what difficulty you choose or what gamemode. You have 3 different gamemodes. You have a "Story" mode that consists of you getting to the end to escape the city and win, a survival mode, and a time attack mode. All will pit you against the hoards of zombies which vary from the common slow moving zombs, to acid spitting, to commando zombs, to mutant zombs, and the rare chance of "Boss" zombies.
Don't fret though, as you also get a large arsenal to help you. The most common weapons you will find are shotguns, rifles, and pistols. The farther you get in the game (and the harder difficulties,) you will find more powerful weaponry, such as flamethrowers, mini guns, plasma rifles, freeze rays, and even chainsaws. You will also get an assortment of throwing items, like frag grenades, pipe bombs, molotovs, flairs, TNT, and much more. Don't forget about the med kits!
Aside from the items, you can also upgrade your character with the money the zombies drop. You can upgrade your max health, run speed, gun skills, melee skills, carrying capacity, bargaining skill, and luck. This adds in the slight RPG aspect to the game which is nice. In the "Original" story mode your character starts with nothing for stats, but in "The Solution" story, it has all pre-set characters that have different stats and different starting gear.
This game presents it's self like an old retro "Grindhouse" movie game, and using old pixel style graphics to give it the old school look. All the graphics look great and all feel like they belong in the game, and fit in very well. Each type of zombie all have their own look, the backgrounds look good, and the blood all looks good.
There is a few glaring issues though with this game. The biggest one being it has Coop, but it's local coop only. As someone that doesn't have friends, I didn't have anyone to try and complete the game in coop with. I tried to do it myself, but I wasn't very coordinated to do it. The other big problem is Melee. I found once you maxed out the melee skill, you can cake walk the entire game without having to shoot one bullet. I beat the hardest difficulty with no effort because of this.

I've been playing this game for years and it's still one of the best shoot em ups I've ever played. What truly sets this apart from others like it are the weapons. And each weapon feels different, whether it's in the weapons speed, style of destruction, or type of combat. Most of the fun you have will be from trying out the different weapons and finding the most effective ones to use. But beyond the weapons, everything else is top notch for an indie shooter, which is what has made the game such a classic over it's many years of being around. The art is great, the gameplay animation is excellent, the game is long with many levels to give you hours of entertainment. Of particular note are the writing, story, and music. The story and writing are silly, parodying most sci-fi, space operas, but it's still well written and entertaining to follow. And the music is one of the big standouts of the game. Created by Swedish metal band Machinae Supremacy, it's probably one of the best soundtracks for an indie action game I've ever heard, crafting a professional, well produced metal and electronic soundtrack. If you're a shoot em up fan and you haven't given Jets N Guns a try, you're missing out on a truly classic indie gem.

I had a hard time deciding whether this game is worth recommending or not. Ultimately, I decided I might recommend Tormentum in much the same way one might "recommend" eating at McDonald's: it's cheap and quick and can be passingly satisfying if there's nothing better around.
In fact, Tormentum might feel more enjoyable if played by someone with little other experience in point-and-clicks or puzzle games, as its biggest sin is having gameplay that is wholly unoriginal. The game begins in an entirely typical escape-the-room scenario and, while the world does open up and get a bit more unique as it goes, the game never really escapes its use of cliche level design or textbook cookie-cutter puzzles. That's right, sliding tile puzzles, pipe minigames, memory card games, they are all on display.
The writing is similarly trite, feeling a bit in the realm of an emo nineteen-year-old trying terribly hard to sound "edgy." This cringe-inducing neutered darkness extends into the game's art, which seems to be the entire point of it's existence. The game is often little more than a series of static, lovingly-painted stills with little-to-no animation and very little thematically connecting them beyond an apparent desire to look "hardcore." Indeed, the game comes out feeling a bit like someone's artistic portfolio.
Also worth mentioning is the game's hackneyed attempt at imposing a moral choice system on the player, which is predictably obvious and binary and yet at times frustrating as early on the game does a poor job of telegraphing when such choices are taking place, and how the game ends up deciding whether the player recieves the "good" or "bad" ending feels curiously arbitrary.
That being said, the game is functional and pretty, and if you're in the mood for some old-school Newgrounds-style escape-the-room tomfoolery, then this game is plenty adequate.
