This game is gawddamned awesome!
Inspired by legendary SHMUPs (read: Tyrian), Jets'n'Guns is an explosive action horizontally scrolling destroy'em'up with a splendid soundtrack by Machinae Supremacy.
It's based around Tyrian-like structure of progression, where you complete levels and upgrade your ship between them, with an option to pick up extra upgrades (and secret stuff!) during the levels. There's also an occasional boss you'll have to fight, as well as several unique levels where you zip around in your spacesuit instead of being in your ship. Also like in Tyrian and Raptor, you have a rather ample supply of armor (and repair options), so it's quite a bit more comfortable to play than the Japanese-type 1-hit-and-you-dead shoot'em-ups.
The story is wacky and rather nonsensical, as are the weapon, level and enemy designs (there's a gun that literally shoots Superman clones, you pick up secret duckies along the way, and there's the borg-like alien race which is literally beer) and the game doesn't really take itself very seriously, but it creates a strangely interesting atmosphere which I really liked.
It's hard as nails, too! Don't expect any hand-holding, and expect to die and restart levels- or even the entire game, because you CAN screw up your ship build and it WILL turn out to be impossible to complete later levels if you don't know what you're doing. I recommend playing on a lower difficulty level to begin with and get familiar with the game mechanics (which boil down to "kill as many things as you can because you really need all the money you can get").
I'm really glad this game found its way on Steam- it has my full recommendation!

Having Rainbow Six Siege's multiplayer matches divided up into short rounds, there's often a pressure to rush towards the objective as an attacker. Even though the time restriction prevents a stalemate between teams, the 3 min. period is more than enough to take your time and consider the strategy behind your approach. Some of the game's greatest moments thrive off playing mind games with players, letting the tension if the moment throw off the enemy's insticts. Holding back and executing your strategy from afar can often contribute hugely towards this; making sure to pick off any lone wolves who venture away from the objective. When breaching the objective room, keeping your distance from an entry point is often a great tactic. Keep picking off enemies for as long as possible, until a final rush towards the objective once time begins to run out.
Peeking is one of Ranbow Six Siege's main differentiators from other 1st-person shooters and contributes hugely to its unique gameplay. It provides the ability to ease around corners and be wary of potential threats. Leaning is an indispensable tool for all operators. Triggered by clicking in left or right stick while ADS, leaning can be quickly used on the fly when navigating around dangerous corners. This can be a great way to aim your barrel into hostile terrirory, without the risk of fully exposing your whole body. However, by doing so, you'll be exposing your head as a prime target to any skilled marksman. By using the lean ability in Rainbow Six Siege, you'll also be able to take advantage of a commonly used exploit referred to as the "Peeker's Advantage". Used by a majority of high-skilled players, this abuses the game's net code to give peeking players a small advantage when moving in and out of cover. To utilize this tactic, simply strafe in and out of cover while leaning, making you almost untouchablefrom an onlooker's perspective.
In many of today's popular 1st-person shooters, there's often a reward for finding a loadout that suits your playstyle and rolling with it. In Rainbow Six Siege there's often little drive to stay with a single operator, aside from amproving your personal skills with their unique equipment and weaponry. When getting started with Siege, it's best to experiment with a small selection of operators as soon as possible. Try to choose a varied range of operators when doing so, considering how they perform at different ranges and how they pair with other operators in use by your teammates. This also diversifies your in-game skill set, making yourself more adaptable on the field.
Environmental destruction is in no way unique to Rainbow Six Siege, with recent Battlefield games taking the crown for large-scale demolition. However, it's rare to see this reflected so clearly in gameplay - carving out the fundamental flow of multiplayer action. Each of Siege's maps offers wide-scale destruction, featuring fully destructible walls, floors and ceilings. With operators available to counter any fortification, it's key to take advantage of these abilities and push through their defensive efforts. Taking advantage of destructible hatches and walls, breaching charges should be used as frequently as possible when entering fortified rooms. Reinforcedwalls can also be countered in a similar manner, using Thermite's exothermic charges. In a majority of multiplayer encounters, walking straight through the door is the most dangerous route. Make sure to consider your options before breaching, while considering the enemy team's placement. If you're not destroying the map, you're doing it wrong.
During the pre-planning phase, drones are a vital toolfor gathering enemy intelligence. Providing information on the objective's location, enemy operators and fortifications in place, this can give attackers a huge advantage when it comes to infiltratingthe building. However, once the action phase commences, all players are forced out of their drone's POV and encouraged to pursue the objective. Single press "Deplay Drone" button, you can easily jump back into your existing drone and continue where you left off. This can be used to continue scouting the objective room while the action is underway, without the need to use up your second drone. For some extra help with surveillance, remember to use the inbuilt security cameras for an extra angle of the battlefield.
Tightly locking down the objective room is a common mistake made by new players, in an attempt to offer the best protection. You might be protecting the objective by barricading yourself inside the room with your teammates, but this leaves a single major choke point for the enemy team to exploit. When piling into a room like sardines in a can, a single grenade can instantaneously finish the round. To avoid this rookie error, try establishing a perimeter around the objective, potentially stretching to additional rooms to cover a wider area. Creating a more complex maze of barricades will give the attackers more angles to consider, making it easier to catch them by surprise. Barricades and reinforcements in certain locations can also be used as bait to lure attackers into an ambush.
Each of the operators on offer in Rainbow Six Siege come with their own unique equipment and weaponry, bearing varied performance on the field. While your choice of weapon has a huge effect on combat performance, weapon customisation adds a whole new level of fine tuning to your personal playstyle. Finding youe perfect setup for each operator can definitely take some time, with each attachment requiring a repurchase between different firearms. From my personal experience, I've found Reflex sights for Defenders; Red Dot sights for Attackers or Holo sights for both are among the most used attachments, alongside a grip for increased stability. Also make sure to add your own personal flair while you're at it, with a range of skins and charms available to purchase!
Situational awareness is also a key skill to adopt in Rainbow Six Siege, with gameplay requiring more precision and addition to detail than your traditional FPS. While fast-paced twitch gameplay is still present, the varied pacing means you can easily let your guard down. From the moment the Action Phase commences, make sure to be on the lookout for the smallest movement on your screen. Between the game's quick time to kill and required precision, the slightest movement can expose your position, resulting in an instant death. Make sure to check every angle before pushing forward, while also looking into the distance for any potentional threats.
Like any competitive multiplayer title, teamwork helps hugely in Rainbow Six Siege's multiplayer mode. Strategy and forward thinking have the potentialto overthrow the strongest of players if executed correctly. Assembling a team of five helps hugely with coordination, with the ability to choose an effective combination of operators and the best angles to attack from. While true in any shooter, Rainbow Six Siege's reliance on tactical gameplay makes this much more beneficial than your average twitch FPS.
By default, Rainbow Six Siege's brightness settings make some of the game's darker levels almost impossible to play. While this makes for a more atmospheric experience, this is far from ideal in a competitive scenario. It might seem cheesy, but cracking up the game's brightness slider not only helps with navigatingdark hallways - you'll also get a clearer view of enemies potentially hiding away in the shadows.

I've played quite a few of the Duel of the Planeswalker games over the past few years (2012-2015) and this one is my favourite of the bunch.  They finally added the option to fully customize your deck from scratch from a pool of over 1000 cards.  The cards are unlocked by playing the game and hitting up exploration nodes once you've gone through the campaign.
I've played quite a few different deck builds (as well as building decks going for achievements) and they've all been pretty fun and unique.  You get to choose a starter deck that has a theme but by no means are you obligated to stay with it.  You can freely add or remove from the deck, or change the focus as you will.  Or create a bunch of decks for different situations.  The flexibility is huge, and far better than previous DotP iterations where you only unlocked a card at a time with each individual, pre-customized deck.
A couple fun things are missing in this version though.   I hope they add challenges to expansions that were in previous games (i.e. one turn before you die, find the cards/combo that will save you).  The missing elements are more than made up for by the customization though.

This is a very fun multiplayer economic strategy game.  It feels like a spiritual successor to MULE, though with quite a bit of added complexity that I welcome; in MULE you had just three (technically four) resources:
- Food, which gives you time to work during your turn
- Energy, which is required to operate your MULEs so they can produce resources
- Smithore, which is required to build your MULEs in the first place
- There was also a fourth (rare) resource, Crystite, which was purely valuable as a commodity to sell when the price randomly fluctuated to a high level.
Despite being very simple system, the three main resources worked well together and a shrewd player could, at great risk to themselves, potentially corner the market in one resource and leave all the other players out to dry.  Offworld Trading Company allows similar risky maneuvers, such as cornering the silicon market and preventing other players from producing glass and electronics, or cornering the water market and preventing other players from producing food, fuel, and oxygen.  While MULE was a local multiplayer game (it was the 1980s, online wasn't a thing), Offworld Trading Company is online, which allows for large player counts and real-time play instead of turn-based.  There are a lot of other differences, many of them positive, a few of them negative.
There are still a few things I think need to be worked on; the ability to collude with other players to cooperate against another player by directly trading resources instead of putting them on the stock market would make a tremendous improvement and is one of the few vital game mechanics I really miss from MULE.  I'd suggest adding a new building which gives the ability for players to directly trade resources with each other with the caveat that like in the original MULE, the other players in the game should be made aware that these players are colluding.  It wouldn't necessarily say what specific transations took place, just that they made a transaction. Quick story recap: a long time ago, in 2003, prior to KOTOR release, LuasArts already wanted a sequel, but Bioware was unavailable at the moment and offered Obsidian instead. Then two things happened: 1. LA were greedy and patientless enough to demand the game be done by Christmas 2004; and 2. Obsidian were optimistic/desperate enough to agree to these terms without even seeing the first game. The end result was a glitchy half-cut but potentially great game.
I used to hate it and left after ~5-8 hours into the first playthrough. It seemed boring and I got stuck on the very first planet… but then it got a new life on Steam, with high-res support, achievements, and the Cut Content mod already on Workshops. And I loved it. KOTOR 2 is worthy of the first game, adding a little more ambiguity to the classic light/dark dichotomy, and offering more action and independence to playable characters than the first game. The Exile story is probably not so personally dramatic as the one of the first game, but it's just different and delivers no less.

I don't really like humans, I'm not a social person and don't really get along well with others. Not really one for "hoping for the best" or caring about our children's future either. I guess you could say I am a cynical and sadistic person. But SOMA changes everything about how I look at our existence. This game is smart and incredibly UNSETTLING, not just from a horror standpoint but from a scientific standpoint. SOMA shines, glitters and glows at the very realization that it is not so much Science Fiction, as it is a plausible Science Fact. I have to admit right now, that I hated the Amnesia series. The hiding under beds and in lockers of other horror games, was what I was afraid SOMA would cookie cut into the mold. But Frictional Games knew better going into this, and the outcome is phenomenal. You won't be hiding, so much as sneaking. And there won't be jumpscares, so much as tension. These changes make the game feel unique and more immersing. The game looks gorgeous despite the Twitch community thrashing the game before it even hit release. I played the entire game in full 4K at 40-50fps no stutter. The environments are breathtaking and entrancing. I loved SOMA's design from the moment I saw it. I went in thinking it was going to be Bioshock meets Dead Space. I did not realize it was going to outshine them both......at half the price. Speaking of price, seeing as how both Amnesia games were sub $25USD, I felt a big risk spending $26-30 going into SOMA. That risk is way worth the price of admission. The genius script and harrowing plot will not only give meaning to our existence but maybe a little more faith in our survival as well. The game has no tutorials and will only hint at where to find the next hidden item or difficult puzzle. 10 hours may seem short especially by today's massive games. But if you have ever spent 10 hours on an anxiety roller coaster, I'll have you know that this game makes you feel uneasy even when nothing is around. You cannot play this game expecting to be thrilled; It is a slow paced and incredibly intelligent plot. You wont be getting any cheap scares or fighting any monsters with Plasma Cutters and Power Loaders. SOMA will be giving you a message to think about...........a message to think about for a long, long time.

Ubermosh is an immediate, punchy, addictive arcade thrill. You have a sword. Your enemies have guns. Your sword doesn't just cut people - it also cuts bullets, redirecting them back towards where they came from. So you slice an enemy and take his gun, and then you shoot and slice until either you've succumbed to the increasing numbers of enemies spawning in or you manage to survive for 90 seconds. Then you start again.
It sounds simple because it IS simple, but that simplicity is in no way to its detriment. UBERMOSH may have a limited scope, but within that scope it's pretty much functionally perfect. That rapid gameplay loop - spawn in, kill, die, restart - proves immensely satisfying, recalling games like Hotline Miami and Luftrausers in its immediacy. Extra wrinkles are added by class mods that place limitations on your loadout and an extra-tough Hardboiled game mode.
It's not the prettiest game in the world, but personally I like the bleary-eyed, neon-lit 80's VHS presentation, and the colourful pools of alien blood that soon decorate the arena floor add some much-needed brightness. The music is spot-on, adding immensely to the sense of pace and urgency.  You can play using mouse and keyboard or twin-stick style with a gamepad, although personally I found myself preferring a hybrid control method where I aimed using the mouse and moved around using a controller balanced on my knee; it sounds unwieldy, but it's how I got my highest scores and survived the 90 seconds for the first time.
I can't see many people playing UBERMOSH for long periods at a time, but then that's not really what it was made for. I've been having sessions of about fifteen minutes, and what's notable about that is that it always feels like I've been playing for longer, which I think is a pretty good recommendation. With its chunky pixels, copious amounts of screen-shake and immensely satisfying gameplay, UBERMOSH feels like the best game Vlambeer never made, and I can't think of a much higher complement for an arcade shooter than that.

The Basics: Retro Art zombie survival with RPG elements
Previous Time Spent: 10 minutes
Expectation of learning Curve: low
Why I bought this: 2011 zombie craze?
First Impressions: This game is in love with a sort of grindhouse aesthetic, and opens with a film-grainy, retro looking production company logo, before settling into a sort of top down, zombie shooting/beating action rpg. This was clearly released at the height of the low-res/retro indie craze of the early 2010s, so all of the zombies and the main character have a blocky vibe remniscent of something from the NES. And my first 10 minutes gave me a sense of comforting, gory and fairly stupid fun.
My 3 hours: I played through the intro campaign for my 3 hour test-run with the game, consisting of 20 levels in a forgotten and zombie plagued US city in the 80s or 90s. It opens with a standard-issue b-movie explanation for the zombie apocalypse and gives the main character a clear goal, reaching an encampment of survivors who are 20 streets away. In the parlance of the game, a street is a level, which appears to take up some 5 or 6 city blocks , and includes a slowly escalating zombie threat, houses to loot, and a trader who sells weapons, ammo and medical supplies. Additionally, the trader seems to be the only place you can save, so reaching the trader in each level feels like a bit of a milestone.
The main challenge in the game comes from resource management and crisis aversion. Much of the time, you'll be encountering small groups of zombies, but as levels go on, they form larger and more dangerous mobs. Knowing when to slowly take them out with melee attacks, and when to use firearms to take out larger groups more quickly seems to be the key to success here, and it provides a pretty satisfying sense of continuity to the longer campaign. I found myself constantly tempted to use melee, and by the end of the game had a crazy stockpile of ammunition (but had taken a pretty large number of hits). I think there are probably other legitimate strategies to be used.
Character advancement adds an additional layer here, and allows you to figure out styles that work fairly well for you over time. Based on my playthrough, a player earns enough points to upgrade several, but not all skills up to their maximum. The upgrades that I took early on significantly changed the way I played the game, allowing me to be quicker, and better at melee takedowns. When I reached the waves of zombies in the final level, I felt like I had earned the ability to blast my way through hordes of zombies and reach my eventual goal.
High
My Highlight: The game really came together for me when I had a huge stockpile of ammo, the ability to move quickly, and a shotgun with a high rate of fire. Being able to decide to shred my way through hordes of the undead and then mop up with melee felt pretty satisfying.
My Verdict: This is pretty satisfying for mostly shutting down the brain and getting out some violent urges in a cutesy retro world, so I'd recommend it for a steam sale purchase.

I really wanted to like this game. It was enjoyable for the most part, but there is one huge black mark against it that keeps me from recommending it. Aesthetically it's great. The art is absolutely gorgeous throughout and the sound design is on point. The puzzles aren't really anything to write home about but they're passable and do a good job of slowing you down enough to take in the artwork and music without keeping you stumped for so long you get frustrated. I have no problem with the gameplay or atmosphere.
The reason I can't recommend the game, though, is the writing. Setting aside the frequent grammatical errors and stilted, unnatural dialogue, the game sets up an interesting mystery in an intriguing world in its opening minutes, and promptly squanders it by ignoring what it started and throwing on more and more plot threads that go nowhere. By the end, the entire plot is completely dropped to make way for the most disappointing ending I've probably ever seen in a game.
Throughout the plot you're given a series of moral choices, usually pretty obvious but sometimes rather ambiguous. Predictably, these decide the ending you get, but at the last second the game turns into a Chick tract, rejecting any moral nuance and judging you as either good or evil based on weirdly Christian standards of right and wrong, right down to an awkward and uncomfortable "suicide is cowardly and dishonorable" moral. The game opens with a quote by Kant which is supposed to prime you to make the right choices, but considering the ending's utter lack of subtlety it might as well have just said "What would Jesus do?"
If you're just in it for the atmosphere and don't have your hopes up for the story, this could still be worth playing, but if you're not in the mood to be preached to, you should probably skip this one.

Simply put, J'n'G is a fantastic side-scrolling shoot-em-up, featuring no needless or pretentious ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t and just giving us what we
want from the genre; a no-holds-barred opportunity to destroy things. Lots of things, with lots of weapons, resulting in lots of rewards for every ounce of destruction you cause to anything. Even stuff like scenery yields destructive profits.
With all sorts of customisation and upgrade options available for your craft, and no penalty for selling off bits and swapping things around, you'll never reach a point which is technically unwinnable through a shortage of resources -- you just reshuffle your eqiupment setup a bit and go at it again, and that's where the game truly shines; you're given the absolute freedom to mess around and combine all sorts of hull/weapon options as much as necessary to see which combination suits you and the situation best, without having to worry about actually losing credits each time you do so. Furthermore, you're able to mount multiple weaponsets on a craft and switch between them on the fly (at the press of a button!), further improving your chances of success (and ability to destroy everything in sight with it).
It's often difficult, it's frequently unforgiving, it almost always requires patience and practice, but holy hell it's just so much constant fun. The only real issue is that with so much chaos going on at times with so many explosive effects everywhere, you'll often be hard-pressed to spot the difference between chunks of wreckage from your recent victims, and actual enemy fire. Beyond this though, there's little to complain about. J'n'G harks back to the glory days of relentless 'shmup' action all while being something fresh with a somewhat unique approach, so if you're a fan of the genre this is definitely one for you. At such a bargain price you'd be a fool not to get involved.

I played the original Gabriel Knight back in 1995, having been a fan of Jane Jensen's work on King's Quest VI. It was an award winning game back then too and had high scoring reviews, which made my decision to purchase the game very easy! So here we are 20 years later and I was more than happy to give the 20th Anniversary edition a go. It does not disappoint.
If you're not someone who played the original, then honestly it's hard for me to know if you'll enjoy this. It is a game from a different era, dependent on writing, suspense, atmosphere, logical puzzle solving: basically, the kind of game you'd want to take notes as you're playing (although there are hints available in Gabriel Knight's journal - more on this later.)
The less you know about the game's plot, the more you'll enjoy it as you play, so I won't say much except for the inital setup. Gabriel Knight is the owner of St. George's Books, a bookshop located in the French Quarter of New Orleans. He is a failed author and his only companions at the start of the game are Grace Nakamura (who looks after the bookshop) and Mosely, an old friend who is a police detective (who Gabriel jokingly calls 'Mostly'). Gabriel is writing a book based on the Voodoo Murders, a series of killings which have recently taken place in various locations around New Orleans as the game begins.
And so this brings me to the game's greatest strengths: it's characters and story. It was a joy to play it back then when Gabriel was performed by the legendary Tim Curry and Mosely by Mark Hamill. The 20th Anniversary Edition wisely sticks to the original script, narration, one-liners and humour of the first game with only a handful of minor edits. Unfortuantely the recordings of the original voice cast have been lost, so a new group of voice actors take centre stage for the 20th Anniversary. The results are... ok. Well, how do you follow Tim Curry? Others have complained about the voice cast, personally I found them to be variable: the exchanges of dialog between Gabriel, Grace and Mosely are the best performed because I think the actors are having fun with the material, but unfortuantely the performances drop sharply in the game's more dramatic moments.
Fortuantely this does not detract from the story of the game, which is well-researched, detailed, enjoyable, addictive and brings out the best in it's characters. Gabriel is a fantastic game character: a down-on-his-luck type but witty, resourceful and loved not by many but by a few, deeply. He is the classic white cotton t-shirt, jeans and leather jacket type (his bedroom wardrobe contains only MORE white t-shirts, which he jokes to the player about) and his typewriter gathers cobwebs while his waste paper basket is overflowing with failed novel-writing attempts - and just don't ask what's in his fridge! He has vivid and terrifying nightmares when he sleeps and heads straight for coffee when he wakes up, usually wearing the same clothes he wore the day before. He's a classic character in the sense that he is a guy who is lacking an identity/purpose and struggling to find it, reveling in disposable pleasures along the way (writing, women, his motorbike and lots of coffee) while he searches for meaning in his life. As he becomes entangled in the Voodoo Murders, he slowly discovers a sense of doing what is right which he didn't know he had.
Gabriel's relationships with Grace and Mosely are very important to the game too - the highlight of the game's opening interactions is the verbal sparring between Gabriel and Grace, which has exactly the right balance of genuine annoyance mixed with mutual enjoyment. But from the very beginning it is evident that they care deeply about each other - note that Grace continues to work in Gabriel's bookshop despite having been unpaid for three months. Their relationship is not overtly romantic or sexual (despite Gabriel's best efforts!) but more like Mulder and Scully: mutually beneficial personalities who come to realise their dependency on each other, but never speak about it! Gabriel and Mosely have a similar dependency but a more practical one: Mosely is in charge of the Voodoo Murders investigation and assists Gabriel wherever he can, while getting in as many insults as possible. There are many other character moments throughout the game's timespan, I hope I've given you a glimpse of how well it works.
So onto the gameplay and graphics. The game serves as a beautiful advert for the great city of New Orleans - vibrant, atmospheric and beautiful and with real locations such as Jackson Square and St. Louis Cemetery #1. It isn't just the locations, it's the way they are used: imaginatively. Sometimes the character's animations/movement seems to be very stiff and you wonder if some motion capture work would have helped, but it isn't a big issue. The interface is much improved from the original game, with a quick tutorial at the start which seems a little confusing at first but becomes second nature very quickly.
The gameplay is enjoyable for the most part, although some of the things that the game asks the player to do require very precise solutions - this is sometimes a big stumbling block to the game's enjoyment. The 20th Anniversary Edition acknowledges this with the addition of Gabriel's journal, which contains insights into his thoughts and hints on what to do next. The hints have levels: a Level 1 hint will give you a general idea, and a Level 2 hint a more detailed tip, and so on. It is a huge improvement over the original game in which all of Gabriel's interrogations were recorded on tapes. However, a few puzzles in the game can still frustrate and confuse, and it's easy to overlook something said by a character which seems irrelevant within all the dialogue yet becomes crucial later on. Another thing to mention is the game's cutscenes which are in the format of animated comic panels appearing one-by-one. They're really cool to watch, but unfortunately the voice acting doesn't always live up to the action, as mentioned before.
So how to sum up the Gabriel Knight: 20th Anniversary experience?
If you've played the original: this is an excellent remake and an essential purchase, preserving everything (except the original cast) and even adding to it with Gabriel's journal, bonus features and a few extra scenes, mechanics, puzzles and better pacing. Just don't get hung-up on the voices and you'll love it.
If you haven't played the original: they don't make 'em like this anymore - and you might be glad about that, but if you're chiefly interested in characters, relationships, storytelling, solving mysteries and leaving no stone unturned, I'm confident you'll enjoy your time in this classic adventure.

I'm new to Magic, so I picked this up in the Humble Bundle to have some time to practice.
To start with, the tutorial is great. It walks you through all the steps of battling and lets you jump right in from the beginning with a pre-made deck of your choice. You go around the different planes battling monsters and other enemies to advance the narrative. The story is primarily a justification for battles, and is told through text before and after each campaign. You can choose to do practice battles against any deck you want and also play against other people through matchmaking. One drawback is that you can't see how many cards your opponent is holding like in a real match. I honestly don't know why this game isn't integrated with Magic Online. It seems like a perfect fit.
Deck making is straightforward. You can choose a few key cards and have the game fill out the rest or choose each card yourself. There's an option to have lands automatically added based on the mana you're using which can be helpful for new players or experienced ones who don't want to bother with it. If you choose to do land yourself you have access to unlimited amounts of basic land letting you do whatever you want. It rates your deck's strengths and weaknesses and gives you several metrics such as mana distribution which is handy for balancing.
You get new cards either through battling in the campaign or buying them from the in-game shop. You can also buy foil effects and apply them to any card which is a neat addition but purely cosmetic. I would like to see an option to enter the cards you own in real life like in the old Yu-Gi-Oh games and use your own decks. Perhaps an option to use a custom back? The game is also very limited in terms of available cards.
This game was originally made for tablets, and it shows. It controls well enough with a KBM or a gamepad but I would have liked to have seen a better UI specific to PCs. Being designed for mobile devices definitely holds the game back from its full potential.
For anyone who wants to play casual games of Magic and build decks without dropping loads of cash into real cards, it's a great tool.

Honestly the melee combat in the game is great. It's one of the best parts of the game and it feels very satisfying to go head to head with players to see who will come out on top. Of course it's an Ubisoft game so there's negatives out the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
1) Dominion - This is the standard "capture the poitns and hold" mode but this is the mode where you see melee combat go out the ♥♥♥♥ing window. Fights quickly become 2v1, 3v1, and sometimes even 4v1, and if it's not a gank spank then you're very likely to be thrown from a cliff or ledge into an instant kill.
2) Connectivity - It sucks, the game will constantly try to put you into games that are full for some reason. You'll just straight up not find matches sometimes and then even when you do find a match you'll probably be disconnected once the host leaves
3) Matchmaking - The matchmaking here is god awful, probably because of their connectivity but hey. You will very likely find yourself in games with players who are far above your skill rating simply because if the game can't connect you to another person within .3 seconds of searching it immediately switches "Skill Range: Strict" to "Skill Range: All"
4) Story - If you've ever sat down and looked over a 3rd graders "Plans for wurld Domination" essay then congratulations you've seen all the story has to offer, the only real reason to play it is the rewards they give you for completing it. Other than that you're treated to a bland story, forgettable characters, and super easy fights for 18 whole missions (which can be done in like an hour)
No review is complete without the postives though so lets get into that
Positive 1: Melee combat: Like I said, it's super fun to go toe to toe with someone to see who's the better fighter, the melee combat here is super tight and the executions that go along with it really help add that sort of pizzazz to the game
Positive 2: Customization: If it wasn't for this I wouldn't have nearly the amount of hours in this game that I do, the customization will give your hero a different look and stats and you'll only look cooler as you level up that hero. Customization is pretty limited right now though and the stats are only really effective in the worst game mode (dominion)
All in all if they just remade the game without the story, removed stage/enviromental kills, and added less incentive to gank then the game would be super solid it's a shame that the game has to function like it does.

This game came as part of a humble bundle I purchased.  I wasn't expecting much from it because I was under the impression that online magic games were pay2win crap, but I was pleasantly surprised to find that most of the cards can be unlocked just through playing.  If you are impatient and hate money you can pay a certain amount to get everything immediately.  I usually feel cheated when people play cards against me I don't have access to (e.g. when I play in a casual modern tournament and realize the guy sitting across from me has a $800 deck), but the pool of cards in this game is fairly small and you will be able to make a decent PvP deck very quickly.  I actually enjoyed trying to find a way to turn a handful of bad cards into something usable when I first started playing this game.  It's like playing a draft.  I can't imagine why other reviewers are complaining about the starter decks being weak, do you really need Black Lotus to beat a laughably stupid AI with a deck full of 2/2s?  It took me maybe a day to run through the campaign and I've been only playing PvP since and I find it strange how easily I can get a match, even when I play at odd times in the middle of the night or very early in the morning.  One thing I like about this game is that Wizards seems to have hand-picked the cards available in it.  There are still cards that are much better than others, but it makes the meta unique to just this game.  The graphics in this game are a bit buggy, but overall the interface is nice in an dumbed-down Apple product kind of way.
All in all, it's a cool game if you like Magic.  Cockatrice is better, but this is still a nice change of pace from playing the same worn-out netdecks over and over.

One big thing this game is lacking is an actual supply and demand.  I can debt materials out of thin air.  At least they could make all resources actually match the surpluss (or shortage) of stuff in the game.  For example.  If no one built power, stuff should just go unpowered, instead of debting power from some magical source that produces it.  This thought can be carried over into every other resource.  If I want to buy iron, the market better have a surplus of it, such as another play sold 200 iron "to the market" so that now any other player can now buy that 200 iron at some market price and if it is gone, welp its gone (till someone else sells some).  THIS IS THE KEY PART OF THE GAME PLAY THAT I EXPECTED WHEN I STARTED PLAYING.  Sadly this game is more about "get the most money" from selling♥♥♥♥♥♥to the aether instead of economic warfare.
Debt is really meh in the game, especially if you dont have TIGHTER DEBT rule on.  My friend -- when he played with me -- had to get over 300k debt from an auction (that apparently can go onto infinity) before it started to seriously effect his stockprice.
Stocks dont do anything other than protect (delay) you from losing or to take control of another player.  There is no reason to really do anything with Stocks till later in the game.  Realistically it should yield dividends (if you owned other people's stock) for example.  It should be a risk/reward factor -- do I keep my stock in this player to yield dividends and I black market this other player to keep them down while I build up or do I sell now from this guy so I can outright buy this other guy.  This thought process never happens the way stocks are used in this game.  It is always "I will just wait to get more money (from selling stuff) and buy this guy outright".
While the developers have some odd understanding that a minimap and/or player distinction (EVERYONE LOOKS THE SAME) is not imporant, I am left clueless at to this Warcraft 3, Starcraft 2 and Age of Empires "RTS" they have played without a minimap or such distinguishing features between players.  Very irritating.
Races are pretty much unimportant and do little to change the way one plays the game.  "Exanpsive" has the most advantage by default because Claims are so imporant for every aspect of the game but that doesnt mean they automatically win either.
I could go on in detail about a lot of other small aspects of the game that are bad but that would be a waste of time for both you and me.

Was hesitant to pull the trigger on this game due to the reviews. Grindy? Yes, but there are higher-rate servers if you prefer. I feel like it has been worth every penny. Constant communication and updates are great from the developers.

–

For young aspiring entrepreneurs, Earth has grown much too crowded to do business. The vast openness of the barren planet Mars calls to explorers and investors alike. Once the colonies have been established, the entrepreneurs see the potential for profit. Businesses start popping up on the Red Planet – this is where you come in.
Offworld Trading Company is a fast-paced strategy game all about manipulating the Martian market, producing goods and buying out other businesses. Natural resources are limited and competition is brutal for control of the richest veins. Placement of mines, extractors, and other resource-producing buildings is critical to amassing enough materials to purchase new structures, upgrade your headquarters and get more claims. Each claim allows you to place one structure – use them wisely.
Price values of the thirteen types of resources fluctuates with market activity. Is someone selling off their entire aluminum stash? Expect to see prices nosedive. You can also buy stock in your opponents’ companies. If all stock gets purchased and you have enough money, you can buy them out, causing all their buildings to come under your control. The goal of the game is to be the last man standing by buying out all your opponents.
The only bad points this game has so far are its high retail price ($40) and the black market feature. The black market in this game makes investing in buildings risky. Found a high (level 3) water deposit? Someone can purchase an Underground Nuke for a paltry $1000 - $3000 to knock that deposit down to low (level 1)
. It seems an unnecessary element in an already risky business environment.
I haven’t explored deep into this game, still in Early Access at this point, but it’s been both challenging and rewarding. You may ask “Is it really worth $40 in Early Access?” No. Wait for
25% off, preferably 50% or more. If you’re a dedicated economy gamer (Railroad Tycoon, Capitalism series), this might trip your trigger. Pick it up if it goes on sale.

SOMA is a great game but it has its limits and some poor design choices. For the majority of the game it's an intruiging philosophical endeavour questioning existence and humanity, but unfortunately it rather shows its cards too quickly then loses its way.
There's an initial premise here which goes beyond intriguing, and in truth the 'resolution' (which is given in a throwaway piece of dialogue) is clever and makes sense - but the problem is it's given far too quickly and leaves the game feeling slightly lost.
The premise is completely wasted in this game with a bad plotting pace - storywise the game is superb, but the choice to 'reveal' the truth so quickly into the game makes for a mild anti-climax.
My other major design issue with SOMA is with the Slenderman rubbish. Sorry, all that style of running away from the monster garbage has been redone time and time again, and to resort to such an unoriginal style (which totally ruins a section or two in the game) really detracts. It's as if the reveal happened too early, Astronauts realised it, but rather than redesign the game's structure they elected to add running away from monster section.
It's boring, infuriating, and utterly contrived.
I know this review sounds like I'm slaughtering the game and hate it - far from it, this is an excellent game from a well-respected developer. I'm just frustrated by some of the choices they made which reduce this from being an absolute zenith game we'll remember for years to 'a very good game which is let down by bad decisions'.
EDIT: having now completed the game it most certainly picked up. The choices remain questionable and there was definitely a frustrating lull in quality and originality in the middle, and that plot choice wasn't well-advised, but this is a stellar game and one of the best of the year.

Starting at the top - I'm not an expert, and you should vet any software like this independently. I’m only reviewing this because I could barely find any information myself, so consider all of this anecdotal at best. Also, apparently the developer provides trial codes - I didn't realize this myself but I did buy it in the Steam Summer Sale at half the list price.
EDIT: The playtime apparently only refers to the installation, which says I have 0.1 hours - at the time of writing I've used this for exactly one week, so take that into account. I'll update this review if anything changes significantly going forward.
I had excellent success with both the "PC Security" and "Gaming Accelerator 2" elements of this package. The security element is more or less an automated "whitelist", allowing you to SPECIFICALLY allow or disable individual programs and processes, and will let you run programs or processes in a "sandbox", thus preventing them from accessing most other elements of Windows or your storage devices. This may or may not be what you, personally, are looking for, so be aware of that going in. It's not a traditional antivirus utility, and won't scan your PC in advance. I personally ran Malwarebytes in combination with an antimalware/rootkit boot disc, in addition to keeping Windows Defender updated; as best I could tell, I went into installing with a clean system, but someone with more experience might know of a better approach.
The "Gaming Accelerator 2" element, as far as I can tell, disables any non-essential startup programs and Windows processes, giving you more headroom for games (or any software, actually) to play around with, and was very Steam-friendly.
In my case, I used this software on three different systems - an older HP Pavilion desktop running Windows 7 64-bit Home, a Lenovo Thinkpad T430 running Windows 7 64-bit Pro, and a very old desktop running Windows XP 32-bit Home. In each instance, running the "Max Boost Preset" option (which requires a reboot) in the Gaming Accelerator gave me slightly better framerates, less CPU usage, and less stuttering. Just for fun, I tried intentionally infecting the old XP system by downloading and trying to run obviously dangerous junk, and the security element blocked everything from launching or running processes. I wasn't gutsy enough to try that on my "good" systems, but Seventh Knight does have a video on their Youtube channel which appears to be a successful block of an instance of "Wannacry".
Both desktops booted to Windows and launched programs significantly faster (10-30 seconds as opposed to up to two minutes; neither has a particularly clean install of the OS). On multiple occasions the Seventh Knight menu would launch several times on boot, and need to be manually closed. This only happened on the desktops I tried - the Thinkpad had no issues at all.
tl;dr - If you already know how to configure Windows to eliminate bloat and use another sandbox utility, then this software might not be what you want, but I found it to be extremely easy to use, and it appears to do what it says it does. Hope this information helps others trying to get a better feel for the software!

I loved nearly all of this game. Not since Bioshock have I been so absorbed in an in-game world. It's meticulously detailed and sublimely creepy. Pathos-II is a place that just begs to be explored. It's lovely in the most disgusting way possible. However, this game truly succeeds as horror not because of gore/creepy visuals, but because of the concepts within the story. I don't want to spoil them in this review, but let's just say it constantly pushes you to ask some important questions about conscience. (Not unlike The Talos Principle, strangely.) Additionally, you are forced to make numerous difficult decisions throughout the game that deal with this topic, and many of these have stuck with me long after completion. The biggest flaw I can think of in the game is the integration of the monster encounters. They're occasionally frustrating and aren't ever quite as scary as they initially seem, and a lot of them occur in spaces too restricted for the player to feel lost and "hunted" so to speak. (There are a few notable exceptions to this.) I feel that these encounters are greater than the sums of their parts though, as without them, I don't think the astonishing sense of dread would have been as effecting. But still, I feel like they could have been improved.
Ultimately, I urge anyone who likes horror or sci-fi to try this out. It's one of the most powerful gaming experiences I've had in awhile.

*DISCLAIMER - I never received this for free, and I definitely won't be getting a t-shirt!
So I decided that as I was upgrading to a new SSD, and a clean Windows installation, I wanted to try this software out as an alternative to the blunt hammer that antivirus software has increasingly become.
I couple this with Malwarebytes Anti-Malware, just for an extra layer of protection, as I do install and uninstall a lot of different software.  So far, it's been 100% rock solid, with only a couple of irritations that are quite easily dealt with;
* Some software, especially Nvidia drivers, don't play nice with SKPC and requires to be turned off before reinstalling.
* It can be frustrating to accidentally block something that is called via rundll.exe, as SKPC will block EVERYTHING that uses it - and as I couldn't find a way to unblock it (the usual methods didn't seem to work), on the advice of the tuys at SK, I had to remove SKPC, reboot, and reinstall.
Currently, I have not tried the Gaming Accelerator, as my current system has no need for extra FPS.  I purchased this solely for the security system.  Judging by other reviews, I would suggest if you have a mid-range PC, you will very likely benefit from it.
Negatives?  None really, I think I would prefer a nicer, more professional looking UI, the huge black and orange window does the software itself an injustice.  I would much prefer a smaller, cleaner interface without the orange.  It is professional software... make it look like it!
That's about it.  I personally recommend allowing SKPC to act as UAC, this just stops extra clicks and so far is working very well.  Recommended for those who start with a fresh Windows installation, are comfortable with basic Windows file systems, and understand this is not an active scanner, but a passive guardian.

I generally try to avoid security based applications such as Virus Scanners and Firewalls. Not because I don't believe in them in principle; a secure computer system is always a preferred ideal.
Through experience though I found most to be unreliable, expensive and in some respects outright deceptive and malicious. I tend to keep my own computer safe through common sense and caution which for the most part has helped keep my computer virus and trojan free... for the most part.
I came across Seventh Knight PC Security not by any attempt on my part to seek a security based application but honestly as just a bundled accessory that came with Gaming Accelerator 2. I wasn't really that interested in Seventh Knight in itself but the discount for both of them at the time was very appealing so I accepted it way.
I didn't place much stock in it, I didn't expect it to work 100% of the time, and I wasn't really going to put myself in situation to truely test it. But I was curious for some reason so I installed it anyway. And there it has been, running, scanning, monitoring... for the most part siliently in the background since that day I first started it. To be honest, I had tend to forget that it is even there the majority of the time.
I am though periodically reminded of its presence when I try to install some new application or game, it intervenes as intended as a safety barrier between new software trying to just run themselves unexpectingly - much like Windows built in UAC. I have had a couple of instances where I've had to disable the security system to allow some installer to run without error. But that isn't unexpected, there is actually an option right there in the given dialog to do that very thing for that very purpose. The Seventh Knight designers obviously had enough forsight to forsee that.
I'm going to be straight up and say, though I can't speak 100% of Seventh Knight, I do now feel alot more confident of my computers security with it there and for the most part I haven't realised any performance issues or unwarranted disturbances by it while its been on my PC.
The great irony about all of this, is I bought Seventh Knight to get Gaming Accelerator 2. I've used GA2 only a handful of times and have practically abandoned it. I did realise some small performance increases in some games while I used GA2 but nothing worth the time and effort of a full reboot of the system to achieve it
I'm content and very satisfied with Seventh Knight at this point. I have no qualms about it being on my PC and it hasn't done anything to make me question it or feel the need to remove it (ie. performance issues etc). Actually quite the opposite. If your looking for a security package seriously consider this application - atleast research it. I can't speak for other solutions that are available, I tended to avoid them out of habit, driven through bad experiences in the past. But I can say for the most part SK does what it says it does - and at the very least it gives you a catch point for any unauthorised application trying to run. If you don't trust something you can prevent it starting right then and there.
Security is an important concept in computing so I recommend you do your research and decide for yourself what will work for you. There are many applications available and I personally consider SK to be an honourable candidate for that role in an otherwise satuated and at times deceptive security based software market.

Well, what else is there to say about this game?
Sins of the Fathers, 1993, was one of the first games I ever played, and it hooked me. So, since then I’ve played it several times. It is like that pocket book you love so much that, even though you now know it by heart, you can’t stop re-reading it and enjoy it as much as the first time.
The plot is set in New Orleans and the story revolves around some very strange murders and voodoo (♫♩You Do Something To Me ♬♪). I always found that, for a 1993 game, the plot was unusual, and the story very well told as it goes along. I still do, for that matter.
As for the remake – because that’s why I’m writing this and NOT to reminisce the “good old days” – there are some good things and some not so good.

For instance, because I own the game, I had the opportunity to play it by installing it directly on my PC and I had no technical issues with it. On Steam, or maybe my PC is faulty, Gabriel seems a little sticky – ex.: when opening the gate at the police station he stops, freezes, hiccups and THEN he opens the gate.
The other issue I’ve noticed is when the narrator, or Gabriel, makes a comment on something and the game freezes for some seconds (I always expect to be kicked out to my desktop and I know very well what a seasoned point’n’clicker feels when something like this happens (I can feel it now ARGGHH)).
Putting that aside and you have an exceptional game, wonderfully remastered.
Everything is clearer (anti-pixel lovers this one is for you) and well defined; the characters are very well done (Gabriel looks more like the one described on the book (minus the curls) and YES I have the book 😊); the voice-acting is very good and the resemblances to the original are uncanny, but I still prefer the original ones (call me daft if you want) - Tim Curry was exceptional.
The soundtrack is beautiful. That piano sounds so nostalgic. I could feel it, even when I played it for the first time.
Finally, for those who played the 1993 original game, there are some differences on how the story progresses: gramma appears much later in the game; new outdoor set at the police station and different solutions on 1 or 2 brain puzzlers…
Overall, I LIKED IT very much. So, I say, go for IT!
PS: To this day, I’m still waiting for GK4 :((
PPS: I just realized that this review will not count for anything, viewing that the game was bought in Humble Bumdle and not from Steam. Well, I hope it helps you even if this is the case :)

Jets'n'Guns is a shoot 'em up with a very clear purpose: carnage.
In this game, you basically go from level to level, absolutely obliterating everything. And it does that well enough!
I'm left with 2 minds about it, though, which I believe boils down to 2 things: communication, and progression.
Between levels, you have access to the game's shop, where you can buy and sell weapons, ships, upgrades, etc.
You never lose money by buying something and selling it afterward, or upgrading and degrading it, etc. The money you earn from missions is permanent. Which means that, if you want, you can completely change your weapons between each mission, if you have enough "total money".
While the game tries to communicate this, it didn't really seem apparent to me, when I first started. It took me a while to realize it... at which point it was too late.
The main problem might be how cheesy and busy the presentation is -- most information seems to be lost, for me. Too many flashing things and rough edges at once.
Anyway.
The game was bloody hard, in the beginning! It was almost impossible for me to beat any mission. I was playing on Normal, at the second level's Boss. Having a looot of trouble, and I didn't have enough money for a decent load-out, it seemed, to me.
So I checked the forums: apparently, the game would be really hard to start on Normal! So, I lowered it to Easy.
That was... much better. Some level were still quite a challenge, but it was doable.
So, for a while, I just kept gaining money, with a fairly challenging campaign. Then, there came a point when I had enough money to get a pretty good set of weapons and good defense. At that point, I was unbeatable. Every level (a bit after the halfway point, I believe) was just steamrolled. It became really easy!
The game also has a looping system -- if you beat it once, it goes up one difficulty level, and you get to keep all of your money/weapons. I beat Normal... much easier than Easy Mode, since I was all upgraded. Then Hard... same deal. Almost impossible to lose.
After I beat the game for the third time, I decided it was enough.
Level and weapon variety is really high, and while some enemies are just reaskins, there are still a lot of distinct enemies to encounter. There are gimmick levels, secret levels, lots of weapons... The problem was the difficulty. If I had kept playing on Normal, maybe I would have had a much better experience! Instead, the game offered my a Great Wall when I first started, and eventually removed it, making the rest of the game rather pointless.
Some levels take away your ship for another, weaker, one. They limit your numbers of weapons, and things like that. Those were the harder levels, on my 2nd+ runs. But they were good! Why? Because they required experimentation.
The ship carries a Heat element. Weapons firing generate heat. And so does getting hit.
If you're overheated, you can't shoot. So, you sometimes have to balance how much you fire.
There are also both mechanical and energy weapons. The latter generated a lot more heat, but are also much more powerful.
As you can see, the element of experimentation is certainly there! Unfortunately, the game decided to be hardest at the very first missions, where you don't have money nor experience to experiment... Which lowered the rest of the game by a lot.
One simple aspect that I think would benefit the game a lot would be a system of replaying past missions to get a bit more money. It would make experimentation a lot easier, with players replaying missions, while trying different weapons, getting a feel for them, and gaining a bit more money to invest in the process. Sure, it could snowball out of control -- but it already has, for me!
Perhaps each time a player played a mission, he would gain only a lowering % of the total money. Or, maybe he could only gain money for the enemies he hadn't killed before, or the secrets he hadn't found.
Something along those lines. Encourage experimentation, while keeping the challenge present at all times.
As is... I was discouraged at the beginning, and eventually the game just became too easy.
Despite all this, the game does one thing really well. It offers a huge array of weapons to try out and upgrade and just blast everything with. It's mindless, crude, and very rough around the edges, but there's still something quite unique here! So yeah, if it seems appealing, definitely give it a go!

Rules of Magic (especially stack) are very complicated. You have to know when during a turn certain abilities can trigger or will trigger and AI doesn't f**k around when playing against you. For this reason alone I would recommend any newbies to try Magic 2014. Predefined decks are well balanced and give you easier learning curve and fighting chance against AI. Amnesia is an amazing psychological horror game that should be tried by anyone who has even the slightest interest in this genre.

Great atmosphere

First and foremost, Horror games always tend to follow a set format to make them good. Like the fact that RPGs will be very story and dialogue based, Horror will focus on suspense, sound, and visuals – along with a jump- scare or two, and maybe some heads exploding. These are all utilised to have you squirming in the grip of fear and guts, should the game be any good.
Now Amnesia – it's an amazing horror game. It doesn't rely on jump scares and gore. Amnesia is different in the fact that it focuses on the staples, which are sound, atmosphere, and shadowy rooms. The spin here is that your main character does not have a weapon. So instead, the purpose is to be able to survive with your very vulnerable character. The fact you have no weapons is what makes this so pulse pounding – because you can't kill what is chasing you. You have to run, and hide. The whole play-style is based on surviving passively. You're eventually always running away from something. This helped to spawn a whole new sub-genre of horror games, when previously, they weren't so popular.
The graphics are simple in that they don't use anything outstanding, quality wise.
They give you exactly what you want without any awe inspiring effects. You have a range of different environments within this one place, going from church like vibes, to libraries and creepy subterranean cellars.. As for the visuals, for example, the scariest two things about the graphics is the distorted blurring when your character loses sanity, and the invisible monster where you can only see their splashes in the water. Alone, these things are not so terrifying, but combined together … it's amazing. The signature monster itself is also considered not so scary. If you Google it, you're not going to be so impressed by it. The game MAKES the monster scary – with the sounds, the shadows, and the sanity meter. If your character sees too much scary♥♥♥♥♥♥ they lose sanity and can pass out. You don't want to pass out when something is chasing you. Nope.
A minus for this game is that if you suffer from motion sickness, losing sanity is the worse thing that can happen to you since the blurring out is slow, and spins the camera.
When you consider traditional horror movies, I think Amnesia is scarier, because with a movie, you're just watching and witnessing what happens. In a game, everything happens to you. You're the one running away to not die. You're the one who feels helpless and scared without protection, so you have to be smart and practical. There are mods that can add mechanics that help you kill the monster, though honestly I prefer to play it without them – even though some of them are actually well designed. It's cool that Frictional Games allowed modding to happen, and brought these out themselves. Unfortunately, maybe the mods were added too soon for this horror game, since they can take away the suspense behind everything if people want to play with mods. Some will even add the mods before they've completed the game. Turning the main monster into a MLP creature is not quite as … intimidating.
Looking at music, it changes with the scenario. If it's an open, quiet area, it sounds calm, albeit with the slow, minor tune that can pick up and make your spine tingle. If you're moving faster, it increases, you hear a heart beating faster. If the monster is nearby, the music changes again, becoming louder. If you're being chased, it adds to the fear factor by becoming more pulse pounding. Without the music, this game would not have had half the impact it does. The game affects your brain as well as your eyes. In most horror games, you can predict what is going to happen based on the music. However, Amnesiac beats this by tricks like changing the music on the moment, rather than giving you a long build up. They also change the music even when nothing happens – so it screws with your mind. You can't rely on the sound to tell you about the monster all the time. The music itself could be considered the game's main jump-scare.
The voice acting as well is quite important. Your character Daniel is a scared and possibly insane man trapped in a dark story. You feel his madness in his words. The breathing, the panic, the sadness, the anger – it brings Daniel to life and creates tension, since when your character gets scared, it's easy to get scared with them. The monster's growl makes your skin crawl – and possibly would also make you alt F4/tab out the game if you happen to be a nervous type. The voice acting is great. His breathing,  his panicking, all adds to the effect.
The story-line is not complicated. You start off without understanding much about what is going on, and you learn through progression and past segments what the plot is. I won't spoil anything, but the slow progression, along with the atmosphere, the music, the voice acting, the losing of sanity – you'll follow a descent into madness. The story isn't pushed into your face. It comes in moments, it comes slow, so you're able to take your time to look into it. You could choose to play flashbacks or not, which is good for people who want to follow it, or skip and go into the game itself. The one thing I disliked was that with some flashbacks, it gives you a white screen – triggering out like a flash-bang. The intensity can hurt your eyes. They could have maybe dampened that a little to make it less troublesome for your eyesight.
There are small bugs within the game, such as accidentally falling through the floor. Although they worked on these bugs, sometimes if you go too deep into a corner you will still fall through, and probably die. The monsters can bug out too, sometimes they will appear behind you and there's nothing for you to do except to try turn to face it.
Honestly though, anyone who has ever shown an interest in the horror genre, or who wants to dip their toes into it, would be well worth off getting this game. Even after the years that it's been released, it still holds up as possibly one of the best horror games of all time. It's had so much attention and dedication from people inspired by the music, inspired to make lets plays or stream on Twitch, it ended up becoming popular, and helping to spawn a whole new pathway for horror.

Awesome game, can be slow to get started, recommend you find a group to have the most fun. The strength of the game is the attempt of realism... You start out with essentially nothing. Go to a tree, break off a branch, get a rock and some weeds.. and poof, you have an axe. You have to work for everything and all though its time consuming, its not difficult. When you get hungry you dont have to take on a wild boar or hope to find a carcass to devour, just dig in the grass for an edible root, or go to an apple tree and pick some apples.
You wont be a master at everything in one day. You need to actually choose what direction you want to go. Want to focus on farming? Find a settlement that needs your crops to make armor and have them make you armor... want to be a carpenter? Trade your chests and furniture for weapons etc.
You wont need to do meaningless quests, there are none. The game exist as it is, the story is what is actually happening, the bandits you encounter are real people that want your stuff... the alliances you form are with real people, the items you may find actually were made and belonged to some poor soul that met his demise by nature, or another player.
There is no "leveling up". You dont need to reach level 25 to ride a horse... Gather some apples, find a wild horse and tame it. Build a stable, mate the horses and sell the offspring. If this all sounds tedious and boring then you probably wont like the game...
The only complaint I have is the server wipes... I am eagerly awaiting the MMO with a persistent world because having you progress erased is the one total killer in this game. But still totally worth the money and time.

As the name would suggest, this is a security program. However, it's not a scanner - it does not search your computer for existing malware. What it actually does is it prevents new software or files from being able to harm your computer unless you specifically allow it access. For example, you accidentally download "totallynotavirus.exe". With any other security program, it may scan this file and match it to a database of malware. But if this specific malware isn't in the database, it's going to declare the file clean. On the other hand, Seventh Knight will see the new file and ask if you want to put it on the whitelist. The nice thing here is that most programs don't need to be whitelisted to run properly - non-whitelisted programs will still run, but they won't be able to do any harm to your computer because Seventh Knight will run it inside a sandbox. This means that Seventh Knight can actually protect you against Malware that we don't even know about yet. This also means that if you already know a specific file is safe, you don't need to worry about the false positives most anti-virus software will throw against clean files.
Note that Seventh Knight assumes your computer is clean upon install, and thus will place everything already installed on your PC in the whitelist.
However, something I don't like about Seventh Knight is the rather clunky UI. First, there is no way to see everything you've whitelisted on... well... a list. While Seventh Knight does store that information somewhere, it keeps it well hidden, and there actually is no way to know if something on your PC is whitelisted or not. If you want to change the status of an existing program, you have to click "reset a program" and then launch that exact program - which will cause the Seventh Knight to ask if you want to whitelist it as if it were a new program. This is rather awkward and I hope they improve this in later versions.

Seventh Knight does actually give you extra security that free products (or even other paid products!) cannot give against malware so new that it's not in any anti-virus databases.  It also grants you the ability to use potentially harmful software in the sandbox rather than simply bypassing it. But Windows Defender actually does a good enough job against more malware at keeping your computer safe, and there are lots of free products out there if Windows Defender isn't enough. True, they can't protect against as of yet unknown malware, but that extra security benefit wouldn't be worth paying for if that was all Seventh Knight did.
Simple - Seventh Knight only needs to run when you open new software for the first time. It doesn't have any kind of scanner, and that includes real-time scanning. This is important because real-time scanners scan every file you're working with, constantly to see if they are in the malware database. This means that your computer is using a lot more processing power to work with these files than it really should.
With Seventh Knight protecting the computer, you don't need real-time scanning. You can get rid of all real-time scanning on your computer
and still be safe. Ultimately, the reason to get Seventh Knight is not the extra security, but for the resources you'll save by replacing real-time scanning. Well, than and the fact that you don't need to buy it again next year, and the year after that...
Gaming Accelerator has a rather misleading name. Not that it doesn't accelerate games, but in the fact that unlike similarly named products, it actually works.
Most similar-named software are actually optimizers, meaning they change windows settings or mess with the registry or  otherwise mess around in your computer in an attempt to make your computer and/or games run faster. It's possible that some of the changes they do may cause an improvement, but they don't do anything you can't just change yourself. They also tend to make changes that you may not want, such as disabling services you actually use (If one more program tries to turn off Superfetch...) or in the worst cases actually cause more problems than they solve.
Gaming Accelerator doesn't do anything like that. It doesn't change a single setting. What it actually does is it reboots windows in "Gaming Mode". This should prevent almost everything from running other than your games. You are supposed to be able to allow specific programs to load even in gaming mode, but Gaming accelerator has the same UI as it's sibling and it's awkward to use this feature.
Since almost nothing else will even load at all (not just at startup, I mean PERIOD!), the games will have far more resources available to them. You know how DX12 and Vulkan are trying to get the games to talk directly to the graphics card without drivers getting in the way? Gaming Accelerator tries to get the games to talk directly to your hardware without *WINDOWS* getting in the way.
If you're running a game on a PC that just barely meets the minimum requirements (or even falls short), than the difference in performance may very well be night and day! Granted, they likely wouldn't run perfectly, but they'd be much better than without this software. For example, my old peice of crap (TM) actually reached double digit FPS.
However, most of you reading this review aren't using the crappy PC I got at Walmart in 2011. You'll likely be using a machine with far more resources available and high-end GPUs that cost more than low end PCs. And truth is, the gains on a high-end machine are far less noticeable, at least in terms of maximum possible FPS. However, depending on the game you may see a decent increase in minimum FPS, meaning less stuttering or stalling. Heavily modded games might be able to get more usage out of the extra resources though.

Bejeweled as a series is mostly about updating the graphics- Bejeweled, Bejeweled 2 and Bejeweled 3 are more or less the same Match3 game with tiny tweaks and prettier gems. Bejeewled Twist is the only game in the series that breaks some new ground, and it's well worth checking out.
On an 8x8 grid, you match gems by twisting a group of four, clockwise, so that three or more like-coloured gems line up. Those gems are removed, new gems drop into the grid, you score some points, and that's the basic premise. It doesn't get much simpler- everyone can pick up Bejeweled Twist and play a little.
Unlike classic Bejeweled, the game ensures that at each time, you have at least one possible move on your board. That's a generous gesture if you remember classic Bejeweled where running out of moves was an instant game over. But just because you always CAN make a move doesn't mean each game is endless. Par for the course you fill up a "progress meter" to advance in levels, and as you advance, all sorts of assorted nasty stuff is added. Locks make it impossible to move gems, and as they start to fill your grid your control over the board is heavily impacted. Bomb gems detonate after a couple of turns- you need to match them so they disappear. Should they trigger you get an increasingly smaller chance to still defuse them, but that's mostly based on Lady Luck and we all know you can't trust her. Simply put, the further you get the harder it gets to keep moving on.
A couple of neat mechanics improve your score. Each time you make a match a small counter goes up, eventually increasing a score multiplier. Max it out to 10 and you get a chance to trigger the insanely awesome, over the top Fruit Bonus (dancing fruit gems, anyone?). From Lvl 2 onwards, you get a Bonus Sequence of colours to match, filling up the multipliers a little faster. And just like the classic Bejeweled games you get to make matches of 4, 5 and 6 gems to create flame, lightning and hypergems, all of which are designed to clear up the grid more easily.
In terms of game modes Twist is a bit sparse. You get the classic mode where you try to surpass your highscore and a danger-free "relaxed game", which is the same without any nasty bomb stuff. There's also a timed mode, challenging you to get a high score in 2 minutes, which tends to run out of challenge quickly: There's only so much you can do with the mechanics and sooner than later you will have "maxed out" your score. A bit more interesting is the challenge mode, where a couple of different tasks in increasingly harder variants are available: This really is an interesting bonus and you may find some rulesheet there that really tickles your fancy.
But ultimately, the meat of the game is classic mode. Without time limit, with always calculated risk and a wide variety of  valid tactivs this really IS the "Twist" game, and for the moderate price, any fan of Match3 should give it a try.
