The Arma series is a great series if you like beautiful graphics, practical sound effects, and realistic gameplay. However, it has been butchered by Bohemia with their constant DLCs.
I got into the Arma series from playing the DayZ mod for Arma 2. Then I started playing Wasteland exclusively on Arma 2 because of just how insane and frustrating the game experience was. When I saw Arma 3 and how beautiful it was, I bought it for I believe $35 during early access. I played a bit but it was buggy and took over two years for it to be a fun experience for me, but even so, it lacked a lot of content compared to Arma 2, even when Arma 3 left early access and was fully released. Then they started to release DLC on top of DLC on top of more DLC and it has been going down hill since.
The real gameplay of Arma 3 is in multiplayer games with King of the Hill, Wasteland, and a few others, but that will cost you a pretty penny; over 10,000 penies for that matter to fully enjoy the experience.
With the additions of DLCs for Arma 3 there have been several issues I have ran into:
1. The DLC is downloaded and installed automatically regardless if you have not purchased it.
2. All major populated servers, which have now been steadily decreasing due to what I believe is due to cheaper games such as PUBG, require these DLCs. Worry not, my robot friends, you can still play on these servers you just cannot use the content you have not purchased: some weaponry, gear, vehicles, aircrafts, and so on.
3. Due to the content being restricted, you will be presented with a box that tells you that you cannot access this content and you will either need to click cancel on the box or purchase the proper DLC. Because of that, I have been left behind for missions and died many times when in a pickle while playing and I cannot drive away or pickup weapons.
4. The whole DLC thing is a mess, serious WHAT IS ARMA 3 DLC BUNDLE 1 AND 2? DO I GET ALL OF THE DLCs IF I PURCHASE ALL THE DLCs? Seriously, it is a little confusing for me but I understand it... maybe I do not. Imagine being someone new to this game and looking at the store front. It is confusing and a serious mess.
5. The complete game experience, thus far as of the writing of this review, costs $124.93, if I understand the store front correctly. No bananas PUBG is taking the player base when it costs $29.99.
I do, however, digress. Arma 3 is a great game:
1. It is graphic intensive that can run very well on a moderate setup. However, if you have a beefy computer like me than bask in that glory of being a PC gamer!
2. The sound effects are so real that it pulls you into an incredible immersive experience that no other FPS can beat; 5.1+ highly recommended for a true experience. The sound of bullets will scare the bananas out of you.

SOMA is Frictional Games doing what they do best - creating immersion through atmosphere while telling a story that, just when you think you know what's going on and what is likely to happen next will twist and turn and catch you by surprise.
There are plenty of occasions on which SOMA is reminiscent of Frictional's previous releases, the Penumbra series and Amnesia: The Dark Descent, but it never feels like old ideas are being rehashed. Rather, the developers have taken the strongest features of those games and expanded on them.
The one exception to this is the voice acting. Who could forget Red's inane cackle or Clarence's furious howls from Penumbra? Or Daniel's pathetic blubbering? Or calm, well-spoken Alexander whose voice carried such unspeakable menace? And let's not forget Agrippa's continuous, demented encouragement "You're a good boy, Daniel!" While they all had relatively little dialogue, their voices were so unique, so haunting in their own right that they added a dimension of depth to the characters that remained long after they had spoken. SOMA's voice actors, unfortunately, have a rather generic quality, and while their delivery can't be faulted it does not add to the characterisation or the atmosphere - a shame, as Frictional has proven in the past that it is capable of doing much more with dialogue.
Outside of the voice acting, however, the sound design is outstanding, adding to immersion and cleverly manipulating the player's emotional responses.
The number one question that seems to keep coming up in regards to SOMA, however, is how "scary" it is. Is it scarier than Amnesia? Just as scary? The answer is both yes and no. Where Amnesia terrified, SOMA disturbs. It does so through constantly exposing the player to dichotomies such as human vs machine, sterility vs decay, order vs chaos. Viscous liquid drips from machinery like blood from an open wound. A stuffed toy abandoned in a locker is a much more sinister sight than a razorblade lying on a bed soiled with blood. I agonised over cutting off a machine's power supply, yet did not stop to consider alleviating the suffering of human beings, unable to communicate or interact, yet alive and breathing and clearly in great pain.
All in all, SOMA is a very special game, something unique in the way it deals with its themes and the post apocalyptic context in which it is set, cleverly picking up ideas previously explored in works such as the first ALIENS film, Harlan Ellison's "I have no mouth and I must scream", and Jules Verne's "20 000 Leagues under the Sea" to deliver a gaming experience that stays with the player long after each session.
Highly recommended to those who enjoy intelligent horror and dystopic themes - my advice: DO NOT RUSH THROUGH THIS GAME! Take your time to explore, read, interact, and think about things to get the most out of the story and atmosphere.

SOMA is the 5th game developed by Frictional Games,  and as a huge fan of Amnesia (and slightly less so Penumbra),  I was really looking forward to diving into this game.  Underwater settings are a huge selling point for me, and it looked like this one would be chalk full of atmosphere.
I was not dissapointed.
The environments and ambience of the game immerse you in a dark, damp, world full of malfunctioning machines and abandoned sea labs.  It's visually stunning, and it sounds even better than it looks, with  constant creaking and rumbling that you could swear wasn't even coming from the game.  Headphones are a must!
There is also a rich story here, about a man with brain damage, an apocalypse, and a cancerous AI.  It is told to you through a combination of audio recordings, and audiovisual clues in the environment. (notepads, old TVs, etc.).  It does a good job of showing you *just* enough to keep you interested without telling you the whole story.
But then there's that burning question,  which all of us horror fans will be asking -  Is this a good horror game?  And the answer is : No.  No it is not. In fact, I would go as far as to say that Soma falls more in to the category of 'psychological thriller' , than horror.   For a number of reasons -
1.  The enemies are more annoying than frightening.
Visually, they look sort of disturbing.  But that's about it.  They have incredibly predictable AI patterns, and avoiding them is just a matter of exploiting their particular AI flaw.  Some monsters respond to sound, others to line of sight, etc.  They are a far cry from the truly horrific creatures we faced in the Dark Descent.
2.  The voice acting is totally at odds with the situations your character finds himself in.
Your chipper Canadian protagonist responds to mutilated bodies and biomechanical horrors with a casual "Gosh! What was that thing?"  It would sound more at home in an episode of Scooby Doo than a dark horror game.
3.  The game heavily implies that your circumstances are imagined,  so the feeling of risk is out the window.
At multiple points throughout the game , your character will randomly teleport from place to place and suddenly find equipment he didn't know he had.  A horror experience relies on putting you in your character's shoes and creating a concern for his or her well being.  In SOMA, it is impossible to care about the fate of your character because you are all too aware that he may be simply experiencing a hallucination.  And yes, I am aware that this can be a horrifying situation if done correctly - see 'Layers of Fear' if you're looking for psychedelic horror of that nature.  Cuz this aint it.
So, with all of that being said,  is SOMA a good game?  Well .... yes, and no.   Can it create a compellling and atmospheric world and suck you into it ?  Yes.   Can it tell you a mind boggling story that will have you questioning what you see ?  Yes.   Does it have good gameplay?  Sort of.   Is it a good horror game?  Hell no.
If you are looking for an intriguing story in an atmospheric world,  SOMA will satisfy you.  If you want to be frightened, look elsewhere.

SOMA is one of the most intense experiences i ever had the pleasure of dipping into and it's undeniably s brave videogame; it boldly challenges the current market tendencies without the fear of crafting a product that won't be appreciated by the masses.
It is a title that should be played by those who believe that videogames are not capable of conveing deep messages and that they should only be considered as mindless entertainment.
The game showcases Frictional Games' growth as a developer, moving from the "scary enemies" induced fear, to a more refined horror experience, relying on feelings of oppression, hope, sadness, humanity, claustrophobia, loneliness, identity and decay, rather than simply exploiting dark alleys, scary monsters and cheap jump scares; this aspect of the game is what will make it less popular, but more worthy of the "Masterpiece" label.
SOMA puts you inside a society in decay and on the brink of extinction, because of a natural disaster that forced the very few surviving people to live underwater.
This aspect might feel close to the "Vaults" idea (made popular by the "Fallout" franchise), but where the Bethesda games deal with a feeling of "rebirth" (society starting from scratch after a catastrophe), in SOMA we see the humanity on its last days, and you can feel the depression of mankind knowing it can't save itself.
I'm tempted to say more, but it would spoil the story; let's just say the whole narrative universe feels very well grounded and indeed real and connected (not to mention very engaging).
SOMA is a game in which the environment and the enemies rarely pose a thread, but it still manages to be more stressful and horryfing (in a good way of course, considering it's a horror game) than such titles as "Amnesia The Dark Descent" or "Penumbra".
The horror in this game is awakened by the player identifying as the protagonist, and what you'll imagine while playing can be scarier than what you'll actually see; It's a game which speaks to the player and scares him on a sub-concious level.
Knowing that the world istelf and the story have the major roles inside the experience, the developers didn't have to rely so much on enemies, like in their previous games, so the encounters with them are pretty rare, but each foe has its own "set-piece" and really shines through as a character of the story, rather than a "trash-mob" to simply avoid.
The rest of the gameplay really carries on what the previous Frictional games were made of, mostly physical puzzle-solving and exploration.
The world is very well characterised and you'll genuinely care about the storie's progression, making each chapter a step closer to the "grand finale".
The most amazing thing SOMA has going for itself, though, it's the ability to leave you with something after you have completed it.
The game will make you think about life's meaning and significance, will make you question morality and what it means to be human; it will even make you go through sleepless nights thinking about what you just witnessed, and it will also make a very interesting conversation starter with friends who played the game as well.
The graphics are surprisingly great for a game with this sort of budget and audience.
There are not many fancy effects or shaders, but the levels are so original, well designed and detailed that you won't care about the not 4K textures and so on.
The sound design is even better, adding an insane amount of atmosphere to the macabre depths of the "Pathos 2" underwater station (the setting of the game).
I still think the game is a masterpiece, but of course it's not perfect; the main issue can be found in its difficulty.
The few enemies you encounter are scary because of the design, but can sometimes be easy to exploit, and that might take a little away from the whole experience.
You never feel like there's a terrible hidden menace lurking around that might catch you at any time (like in Alien Isolation, for example); you'll be relieved to know, though, that the game is jumps-cares free, which is always a good thing.
That said, SOMA remains one of the best games i have ever played in my life, and one of the best narrative experience i have ever had the pleasure to dig into, considering every possible medium (books, films, comics, ecc...).
It's a must buy for people who aren't afraid of dealing with somehow depressing themes and really want to see what a masterfully crafted environmental narrative experience can provide to the player.

As a fresh face to the Mount & Blade series, and also a fairly seasoned veteran at the Elders Scrolls series, I had *some* difficulty learning this game. Whether is be from the fairly complex battle system, to the robust and dynamic economic system, all the way to just not having my hand held. The reason for me being, initially, overwhelmed, was that there isn't really any direction given to you (so, for all of you players who hate linearity, take a look at this). Essentially, you're thrown into a huge world after you complete the short tutorial, and with only two towns to note, you have no main quest line (at first), no grandiose story (also, at first), nothing. "Why?" you may ask. The answer is one that, albeit cliché, is simply because it's up to you.  With literally no bars to take note of, you can: make a living learning all of the best trading items and locations, be sure to spend a ton of money on mercs though; plunder every poor village you see, using the money and supplies to further expand your small band of unruly thieves; play the noble boot-licker, and live a virtuous and honest life as you win further glory for your lord. As the parenthetical phrases have said, the lack of a story is only in the beginning, when you're not a particularly notable character. Though, you could completely ignore that story, and still fully enjoy every aspect of the game.
Aside from the story, the combat system is something to take note of. There are speed multipliers that aide or detract from damage done on horseback, range and reach modifiers that take note of how much damage point X on a longsword does compared to point Y or Z, guns that can literally change the tide of any fight (I've been one shot so much while prancing around on my pony...), and fun archery, crossbows, and throwing weapons, all affected by range of the shot, location of impact, and all that nitty gritty stuff. As a side note, it's a fun little challenge (and I use that term loosely) to find a band of 10+ looters, or similarly weak enemies, and fight them by yourself, I've taken grenades into those fights, and run circles around the enemy to herd them, in a sense, and then just toss a grenade ;)
The characters are rather lackluster unless you're dealing with specific, named characters, who all have their own sets of morals and values. For an example, a more noble character may leave your party if you're constantly bullying small villages, whereas the more violent-loving characters may shun you from running from a fight - yes, even if it's your 20 man squad of peasants, versus a noble's 100 man squad of elite soldiers. Named characters also have their own skill sets, so finding the proper balance of brain and brawn, or just pure brawn, is all a matter of personal taste and is affected by your long-term goals for a character. The political aspect of each faction and character is something that I find incredibly amusing as well, blindly taking quests from the nobles of Sweden may land you as the enemy against whomever they're currently at war with, thus losing a key trading outpost (I say this from experience, be careful).
This game hasn't won any awards for its graphics, they can be buggy, low res, low poly-count, and all of the above at one time. And, speaking of bugs, there can be a lot. Tearing in a lot of terrain, a complete lack of rendering in the overworld, and just flat out moronic AI, the pros outweigh the cons, immensely.
Multiplayer is something that I didn't bother with much, but I have dabbled. From what I've played, the classes seem fairly balanced, and the 'kill to coin' system if very reminiscent of CS.
In the case of Warband vs With Fire and Sword, I'd have to take WFaS. Overall, the game feels slightly more immersive with the landmass being real geographical locations, cheaper costs for mercenaries (which actually did take away a lot of frustration from a lot of my merchant characters), and guns. Guns are incredibly amusing to play with since the game takes place in the period of time when gunpowder just began to be utilized for firearms and explosives. There's also some quality of life improvements with the guildmaster from warband being replaced by the mayor, who's accessible from a town menu, there are also more towns you can actually visit, rather than large amounts of fortresses that only house nobles. Sadly, though, I have yet to see tournaments in any of the towns, and that was a major point of fun for a lot of my playthroughs.
All in all, a fantastic game, with a lot more than you could hope for. Don't judge a game by its graphics: 9/10

I originally bought into this game back in the original 2011 buy-to-play release, planning to play this with several friends in an alliance. The devs are a small indie team that promised a lot of innovation and unfortunately were not able to quite deliver all of it. Naval combat with boarding and 2 more promised factions never made it in. Multiplayer combat stability was unreliable enough that my friends quit, and the devs never seemed to figure out a good way to monetize the MMO side. However, instead of completely abandoning it and turning the servers off like many other studios would do, they did a major update and converted it to free to play. I have to give them credit for that. I paid for it, and even if I don't play it frequently there are still enough things for me to do playing solo that this is a better outcome than having a server required game with no server stuck in my steam library. I recognize this may not matter to people trying it for the first time as a free to play game, but for me it is an important point.
Former rare developer event units and pvp attack protection can be purchased for Crowns. Crowns can be obtained in exchange for the standard gold resource that is mined or pillaged.
While there is a map editor for scenarios and a single player component available, they mostly serve to familiarize you with mechanics and the layout for the primary player fortresses. The meat of the game is the hybrid MMO campaign map where other players can attack you. There is still a small campaign story and NPC towns there - you can easily raid NPCs for gold to keep attack protection up and just play solo there in a form of pseudo-singleplayer as long as you want. I am glad that the devs never took this option away - pvp stability was frustrating enough years ago that I have never bothered to drop attack protection to go back and see if they fixed it.
If you are a gamer on a budget, this is a real mass combat RTS siege game that can be played for free, no MOBA, no Combat Card Decks. All the parts of it that matter are accessible for free, and as a single player game I think it is pretty good. Just building up your city and skirmishing with NPC settlements can be quite enjoyable in itself for a good 10-30+ hours, and there are 9 cities, 3 each for humans, elves, orcs, for you to cycle through. I have no idea if PVP/Co-op has improved, so your mileage may vary if that is what you value most. Look to other reviews to see what people are saying about that.

Like Punch-Out?  This isn't like Punch-Out.
Beast Boxing Turbo does not use the usual 3 K.O. for a TKO.  This game uses the fighting formula for winning a fight(I.E. 2 KO's).
You and your opponent have regenerating health bars and stamina.  Taking a blow reduces the maximum amount of health you can have indicated by the red bar.  Stamina dictates your power and how many punches you can throw before you tire yourself out.  Tiring yourself out is not good because your speed will drop, making your punches and movement slower.
The story has 4 leagues from the easy to beat to opponents that are able to react faster than you.
For those looking for a bit of a challenge normal difficulty does not give that.  I beat all my opponents with some relative ease on normal.
After each fight you get coins which are used to purchase equipment and upgrading your stats.  Once you beat an opponent they are available on exhibition.  This mode allows you to farm for less coins but still a good way to grind for them should you need coins to fight the next opponent.
I really find this game to be very fun.  Kinda short on Normal but fun nontheless.

Tormentum is fun. Some puzzles definitely made me think for a little bit, but overall this game is on the easier side of point and click adventure games. Besides just being a series of puzzles to solve, morality is at the heart of the game. Frequently, you will have to decide on whether to kill people or show them mercy. That's something that wasn't necessarily obvious when the game first began. The game's best feature is the interesting art style. For some reason they didn't even make the game run in full 1080p.  It's like any screen shot would make a good cover for a death metal album and the excellent art style is dampened by the low resolution of the game. The animation in the game is really sparse too. A lot of the time it feels like the background is just a static picture. Any movement at all is welcome and really punches up the visuals. It really makes scenes look exciting and dynamic because the art style is so strong. Even some of the more poor animations still look cool because of the art style of the game. The aesthetic is very similar to the Shadowgate remake from a couple years ago. But, that game was way more difficult to beat than Tormentum. In fact, I'd recommend Tormentum to those just dipping their toes into the point and click adventure genre for the first time. This game would be perfect to play on tablets. The game play is simple and it's not very hard. It took around four hours to finish the game for the first time. I collected all the achievements so I had to play the game a few times. It took about four and a half times to finish the game to get them all. Subsequent playthroughs were really quick because puzzles are really simple after already knowing the answers.  It was still fun to replay the game, though.

I'll keep this short and sweet.  Amnesia: The Dark Descent is without a doubt one of the greatest horror experiences you can have.  The story is pieced together by the main character Daniel who awoke with amnesia and after that you begin understanding his objective throughout the game.  Gathering information on this beautifully crafted and immersive little world involves finding notes scattered in all sorts of places.  Exploration is important.
This is not your traditional horror game where you can fight back.  Your only means of survival are hiding, running or distracting enemies then progressing to the next area which is done seamlessly thanks to the  automatic save system.  While you explore you will encounter instances where puzzles must be solved in order to progress.  You solve them by interacting with objects in the world, be they rocks, boxes, gears, etc.  Some puzzles are simple, others require a little more thinking outside the box.  Keep in mind that if the solution is too obvious, it's actually very likely the correct one!    You can also throw objects to cause distractions.  All of these things combined makes for an incredibly immersive experience.
You have two forms of life, standard health and sanity.  If either one depletes entirely you're dead.  Thankfully you can find items that will heal both of these. You start off with a lantern and must search for fuel to keep it lit.  Another means to help you are tinderboxes which are used on various light sources such as torches.
I don't really have a negative thing to say about this.  It's unique, terrifying, creative, immersive, gorgeous, with a brilliantly written story.  This is one of those games that will age greatly.
Oh, and one more thing, there is only one way to play this: in complete darkness with a set of decent headphones and the volume cranked.

I missed out on a lot of classic adventure games by not returning to PC gaming until the late 90s. The Gabriel Knight series was one that I missed completely, which makes me doubly thankful for remake efforts such as this. Through a fresh layer of polish, it's very clear to see why Gabriel and his cohorts were so widely acclaimed in the genre. However, it's also clear that this remake might not be the best way to experience the series.
Gabriel Knight, if you've never met him, is a bookseller and aspiring novelist in the French Quarter of New Orleans. He's a listless Lothario, a fact that his charming assistant Grace and punchy police pal Mosely are not hesitant to harp on. Despite his appearances he soon becomes entangled in a murder investigation that leads into the darkest corners of New Orleans, where voodoo and ancient curses hold sway. There's an interesting mix of historical and kitschy voodoo to delve into, which helps give the game a more grounded feel even when things start getting crazy.
Unraveling this mystery is done in the grand old tradition of classic point-and-click adventures. You can travel by map to a number of hotspots around the city, each with features to examine, items to pocket, and colorful characters to question. It's important to note, though, that this being a traditional adventure means there's some antiquated design to contend with. Puzzles are logical and items have real-world uses, for the most part, but identifying exactly where or when to do something isn't always clear. In fact there are more than a few points where you'll find yourself wandering aimlessly because you need to stumble across an unforeseen event to progress. The remake does try to punch up the gameplay past traditional pace, though. There's not a lot of clutter in these scenes so important elements are usually easy to pick out, and dialog options that move the plot forward are highlighted for uncultured knuckle-draggers who don't want to bask in the game's fully-voiced dialog.
I'll be honest, I wasn't sold on the voice acting at first. It's a big deal for Gabriel Knight; even without playing any of the originals myself I was aware that the cast was remarkable. Whereas OG Gabriel was voiced by Tim Curry, remake Gabriel is someone I've never heard of, who effects a ridiculously thick Louisiana accent for every line. But it wasn't long before he and the rest of the cast grew on me, assisted by the excellent script. Grace gets some vicious burns on Gabe throughout the game, Mosely pals around like a dopey high-schooler, and even some of the minor characters like Hartridge get incredibly memorable lines.
Between the entertaining dialog and the gripping story that steadily builds in intensity, there's plenty of reason to work your way through the old-school puzzles. However, the remake is marred in a few ways that sometimes make it feel like a step even further back. The 3D models for characters are attractive but suffer from stiff animations, making them look more like Sims than people. You'll also spot a number of glaring (and sometimes hilarious) bugs like heads spinning like tops and torsos contorting wildly. In dialogue both parties get animated portraits that are detailed, but move like rigged portraits... the effect is a little creepy and reminds me of the Begun of Tigtone, if you've seen that. You can skip dialogue by clicking but sometimes it only drops the voices, and continues animating silently. And if all that wasn't enough, the thing has crashed on me a few times during long play sessions.
The bottom line is that Gabriel Knight - Sins of the Fathers is an excellent game that isn't particularly well-served by this remake. And it isn't in the ways you might expect, because the new voiceovers are great in their own way and the modern amenities really do help with the pacing. No, it's just a technically weak product, beset by rough animations, visual glitches galore, and general instability. You absolutely should experience the game for its story, its moments of horror, and its contributions to the adventure genre. But as long as you're not put off by pixel art and slower pacing, you might just be better off with the original.

Oh, Amnesia: The Dark Descent. Where could I begin? Coming from somebody who often frequents games in the horror genre, I can safely say this is the most terrifying game I have ever played. The thing about Amnesia is that even when there is no danger, the game still manages to install a feeling of dread into your mind for roughly 95% of the entire experience. The notes that can be read in the game, while not necessary to understand the story, add so much to the atmosphere. This game does not rely on cheap jumpscares, but when the moments of danger do come, they are presented in such a way in which you do not just jump in your seat for a second and laugh it off, but rather your heart starts to pound as you run down corridors and try to find a place to hide. Another great aspect of this game (which has unfortunately been copied, and badly, many times now) is that you have absolutely no means to defend yourself from the monsters, and you can only hope you can either outrun them (You can't) or hope you can't be seen in your hiding spot.
All in all, I would say that Amnesia delivers a great story, near perfect atmosphere, and scares that will leave you crying for your mommy. Amnesia: The Dark Descent represents the best of the horror genre, and is a mix of great pacing, atmosphere, storytelling, graphics, and pure, bitter dread. I would recommend this game to basically anybody who loves the thrill of being scared, or anybody just looking for a new experience that differs from other games in general.

First if you want to see something hilarious, go online and look up PC Gamers review of this game. It is pretty funny. They gave it a 80/100 which is a huge joke. If anything, because of that mistake, their editorial license should be permanently revoked.
Buy this for $5 or less in a sale or not at all. I'm giving it a sideways thumb only because the combat is satisfying enough to be enjoyed for one playthrough. As far as the game sucking goes, people are not wrong. It has good sound, the enemies are recreated well, and the weapons are all decent. One of the biggest problems in the game is level design is lazy and just sucks. Basically, the whole game is a diservice to the Duke Nukem franchise. The graphics are not great and there are sections where your fps will drop randomly from 60 to 50 for no reason at all other than bad coding. But it doesn't happen often so the game runs smoothly for the most part. It is a run of the mill decent time if you get it for $5 or less like I did because that is about all this game is worth.
The gameplay could have been done much better, more specifically the level design and interaction in the game. The level design is amatuer at best and feels forced, like they were on a time constraint (which they were). The levels are bland and boring at best. Interacting with something usually consists of pressing E to start opening a door then tapping spacebar repeatedly a few times to pry it open. This mechanic has always been totally pointless and barbaric in games and does not need to exist anymore because slamming a key on a keyboard is not considered actual gameplay, so stop using it devs. Pressing E once is all it should take, like in DOOM 2016. Other kinds of interaction include being able to pee in toilets, look in the mirrors to trigger one-liners from Duke, and some other things, all feel pretty pointless and extremely juvenile. Not that the original Duke 3d was sophisticated or anything, it just seems like they took extra pains with this game to make it embarassingly juvenile and goofy. You can also be shrunken down and have to navigate a section of a level while tiny, figuring out what to do, or even drive a RC car at one point while shrunken early on, and none of the gameplay while driving or being shrunken is very well done or very fun at all. One thing that helped ruin the game was its unfunny self-awareness. It starts up with Duke playing his own video game then the camera pans back to show two hookers raising up as if they had been sucking him off and they say that the game looked like fun or whatever and Duke quips "after 12 ♥♥♥♥ing years it better be!". Oh the irony. If Duke could have actually played this game he would have kept his mouth shut. The game constantly refers to the original Duke Nukem 3d and all that does is make us wish we were playing it instead of this mediocre game. Duke also says quotes throughout the game taken directly from several cool movies, but it is not funny and is just awkward. The timing is really bad and it just feels juvenile and does not fit the situation. I could just see the writers for this game sitting and snickering like two 6th graders in class talking about boobs and weiners and laughing. Unlike Duke Nukem 3D, nothing he ever says in this game is funny or feels like it even should have been said at all.
The main reason this game failed is that if it were another title rather than using the Duke Nukem name, it would be a solid lesser known game, probably even a cult hit like the game Bulletstorm was. Well, probably not. Like I said this game is just average at best. But the fact that they slapped the Duke Nukem name on a only average-at-best game was a slap in the face because the original Duke 3d was so awesome. Doom was the reason I got into PC gaming back around 1997 and then I discovered Duke Nukem 3d and was instantly blown away and it left a lasting impression on me that I will never forget. Then they released this♥♥♥♥♥♥and I was mortified.
It is certainly not worth the $20 price tag it normally has but if you can catch it on sale for $5 like I did and just forget about it being anywhere near as good as Duke Nukem 3d, then you can have a somewhat enjoyable playthrough. Comparing it to Duke Nukem 3d which is easily a 9/10, it would only be a 5/10. Or a low borderline 6.
BORDERLINE 6/10 not recommended unless you can get it for $5 or less

It is time to update the review, as it's been more than two years since this early access text:
You'll tell me that I have a few minutes in the game. True. But well, from what I've played, I was really charmed by it. Old-school arcade shooter with a punching soundtrack, simple as hell (well to understand) and that idea that the blade can send back bullets... I'm already in mode trying to send them all.
Walter Machado listened to us, people used to arrows for moving or AZERTY users used to ZQSD (which is our equivalent of WASD for QWERTY). He updated the game so that we can finally play with more ease (try to do WASD on AZERTY and you'll be killed after a few seconds). And well, since that, I've confirmed my first impression that UBERMOSH is a little gem. For the price, you'll not be robbed.
While the graphisms are clearly influenced by retro-gaming and what we used to have before, I can still see that huge blade, that nice characters and well.... Yep, completely charmed by it.
Keep doing the good work!
--------
As you can see, I was really enthusiast for the game and if you look at my library, I've bought the soundtrack and the sequels, despite the fact that it could have been DLC, but hey, Walter's choice and I'm supporting it as UBERMOSH is really worthy of being bought.
Yeah, I've spent less that 8 hours in the game, in the two years I've begun playing it. But UBERMOSH isn't done to be played hours straigh, it's done to play 10 to 20 minutes, as a break from other games.
Walter Machado really listened to the community, as I've said, and I must say that I'm quite proud to have achieved 100% of achievements, as the game isn't as easy as it seems.
There is no real plot apart that you're in an arena, without guns but with your sword that can reflect bullets. Enemies are coming and the goal is to survive 90 seconds of them, with limited lives and by picking up guns (once you have the most powerful, it stays on). The arena is randomly build: you have rocks that can serve as a cover or obstacles. It's also limited by flashy inscriptions: cross them and you're finishing the round.
There are different modes:
- Normal one which is the No Class
- Kensai: you can only your sword, no gun can be picked but you have six lives
- Gunner: you can only use gun, but they're firing automatically (you can keep your finger on the left button of your mouse)
- Warlock: you have already the better gun, but it's not firing automatically (you have to keep clicking to make it work) and you have two lives (unless I'm switching games in my head).
Like I've said in my earlier review, the game is clearly made with retro-gaming in the head: graphics are quite reminiscing of an early era of video games. But I love the colors changing at each new rounds.
The soundtrack is also very great: guitars for a sci-fi feel. Yeah, that's how I will describe it.
I have only one problem: the fact that I'm sometimes running in ennemies when going down or up that are spawning or firing from outside the screen. It's just annoying but well, it's part of the life in UBERMOSH.
Seriously, go ahead. And given the fact that I'm also playing BLACK and Vol. 3 mean only something: the whole series is a gem and really addictive.

The Story is mediocre at its best. But that is definitely not the focus of the game, because the gameplay and the cheesy humor is the prime element of the game.
The movement system allows the player to dodge a lot of enemies and bullets, because the character "Lo Wang" is super agile. You can dash in all directions and do double jumps. If you combine these while you are in combat then you really feel like a badass ninja that dashes across the map. As a PC player this feels highly satisfying when you have good aim - but I absolutely can't imagine how this should work with a controller as you need good aim at this high speed of the game.
The weapon variety is excellent! There are over 70 weapons in-game that all feel very different. The game still has the standard weapon categories like shotguns, smg's, bows, swords but it differentiates from there on. I for instance got a smg weapon drop that consumes no ammo but has the worst iron sights i have ever seen in a video game - which implies that it should only be used in hip fire. The sword variety is also very interesting because you can get some very exotic looking weapons but also viking style axes or some future neon looking laser♥♥♥♥♥♥
Shadow Warrior 2's combat is extremely similar to the DOOM (2016) style of combat. It plays awesome, is very fast and precise. For me this is the style of combat that I enjoy the most in FPS games.
In my opinion the gem system is not at all fleshed out and is the opposite of compelling.
The minor upgrades with 1-5% increase in a stat feel not satisfying and the rare legendary drops give a huge stat boost but lowers some other stats, which feels quite odd and not as rewarding as other lower tiered gems.
The gem system could have been replaced with another system that would have suited the game much better for example a talent system to give you new ways to play the game as you could play the game with a new "class setup".
Because I had to play with the gem system or else I would have had a significant damage loss I made the best out of it. An example of a fun way to mess with your weapons was what I did with a revolver pistol: the revolver had six rounds in the chamber. Then I added a gem that gave the gun two additional rounds making a total of 8. The other two gems were that a shot consumes double the amount it would usually use. So in the end I had a pistol that shot with 4x its strength, which felt extremly pleasing when you land a headshot with this weapon as it was most times an instant kill.
This was the best and only "creative" way I came up to make a weapon feel much more fun to play than the vanilla weapon - the other weapons that I played with were equipped with minor stat boosts, which as I mentioned were not really fun to play with, compared to the revolver.
The comedy of the game may not be suited for everyone as it is has this really cheesy humor and just blatantly bad jokes - which in my opinion are very funny if it suits the situation. The protagonist also is an expert in lightening the mood with a pun or a funny way to behave in a more or less serious situation.
One example would be at the beginning where you want to untie
where he says: "OK, so this is probably a terrible idea, but I'm sort of out of options here. I'm gonna untie you. When I do, please don't eat my face. I'm a friend, OK? Frieeeeeend. Alright, here we go..."
The hub area was in my opinion a thing that slows the game down. It is where you can buy new weapons, craft new gems or get new quests. In my opinion it is a thing that I just had to tolerate because I didn't like it but also didn't despise it.
It makes perfect sense to use a hub area in a coop game as both players spawn there and can go on a mission together, but in the single player game it just feels kind of odd.
The inventory management in shadow warrior 2 is a nightmare. It is just horrible to search for a stat in a gem as you can not sort it by their stats. What is especially strange is that they don't have a group for only "more attack speed" or "more damage" - it is just a mishmash of gems in one bag, sorted by its rarity. This just rips you out of the action when you want to change the gems in a weapon before you move on to the next fight.

The Duke is finally back, but should we hail the king or blow it out our asses? Aaron checks out Duke Nukem Forever...
Alright, I admit it. Back in the day, I was a bit of a Duke Nukem fanboy. Duke 3D was amazing, and it was, in my option, the best FPS of the time, beating even id's Quake. So, it goes without saying that, when the next Duke Nukem title was announced after Duke 3D's release, I was very excited, indeed.
As the months and eventually years rolled on, this excitement started to wane. Setback after setback, no-show after no-show ate away at my enthusiasm, until I was left, much like every other fan, with nothing but a bitter taste in my mouth. Duke soon became vapourware and we'd all but given up on his return.
After the fiasco of 3D Realms' closure, the final nail was, seemingly, hammered into the coffin. Did I care? No, not really. By that time I couldn't care less if Forever ever arrived. Sad, but true.
When Gearbox Software announced it had resurrected the title and that it would finally see the light of day, I hardly jumped for joy. In fact, it was more 'meh' than 'yeah!' Still, if only for nostalgia's sake, I had to play it, but I was hardly pumped.
So, why then, despite the fourteen year wait and the heavily unoptimistic outlook of the title did I start to grin like a five-year-old when I finally fired up the game?
Yep, even with nothing but cynicism in my noodle, as soon as the familiar drum hits and guitar riffs of the Duke theme rocked out of the speakers, I was instantly ready to kick♥♥♥♥♥and chew bubblegum (and yes, I was all out). I was a very happy chappy, and memories of 1996's frag fest soon drifted back.
Sadly, though, this feeling didn't last all that long.
As we all know, Duke Nukem Forever has been in the kind of development hell that no other title has ever faced. Over the years, the project has seen several game engines, redesigns, staff changes and more. It's amazing that anything coherent came out of the development process, even after being hammered together by the talented guys over at Gearbox, and it's not long after starting the game that you begin the see the results of this tortured evolution.
You immediately notice that, visually, Duke Forever is a bit of a mess. To say that this looks like an original Xbox title may be a bit of an overstatement, but it's not a statement that's all that far wrong.
There's no antialiasing to speak of, leading to jaggies everywhere, texture pop-in is rife, and although many textures look great, there's a shocking amount of amazingly ugly, low res decals strewn about the world. Object modelling is often basic and notably rushed, and the overall feeling is very unpolished and disappointing.
Duke Nukem Forever can, at times, look fairly decent, and although not a patch on today's cutting edge graphics engines, it still packs in the character and feel of the 90s titles. It's just a shame that it looks so dated technically.
Still, graphics aren't everything, and you can overlook a lot, if the game underneath is a winner. Unfortunately, this isn't quite the case.

The core FPS gameplay in Duke Nukem Forever is as straightforward as it gets, and there's nothing in the way of complex game mechanics or originality to be found here. It's full-on run, gun and kick, and nothing more, really. Duke can interact with the environment, solve a few rudimentary puzzles and even drive a couple of vehicles, but for the most part, the game is basic shooter fare.
Enemies are as dumb as their Duke 3D counterparts, and many of the advancements we've come to expect in today's FPS releases are missing, right down to polish, silky smooth controls and buttery aiming. Duke is often clunky and sluggish, which is a bit of a problem when many foes zip around the screen at high speeds.
The vehicle sections are decent enough, but controls are iffy, often leading to untimely deaths or bouts of wall-kissing as you get hung up on scenery, and load times are excessive, leading to prolonged pauses if you die and have to reload over and over, something you'll be doing a lot on higher difficulties.
Even with these flaws and lack of TLC, Duke Nukem Forever's gameplay is solid enough, and a couple of enhancements have been made. Duke no longer has a health bar, but instead packs an Ego meter. This functions like everybody's favourite Spartan's shield, and as you take damage, it's depleted. Once it's gone, take too many hits and you're dead. Stay out of harm's way and it'll recharge. Simple, if wholly unoriginal stuff, but welcome nonetheless.
As you explore you can increase the size of Duke's ego by performing certain actions, such as lifting weights, winning at slot machines, signing autographs and even smashing a blatant Christian Bale-alike in the face. You can even play a fully functional pinball table to earn more ego.
This time Duke can engage foes in hand-to-hand combat, and can perform executions on wounded enemies. There's also a few QTE-style button mashing events to open doors, finish off bosses and the like. The inventory system has been mapped to the D-pad, making it easier to access items, and you can use a nifty ‘Duke-vision' system to see in the dark. These may be very basic changes, granted, but every little helps.
The problem is that, despite these few simple additions, Forever's a game that's never quite made it out of the late 90s, and it's painfully obvious that this game was conceived over a decade ago. Simply put, it shows its age.
Shake it, baby!
Luckily, even though it was released many years ago, the original Duke 3D had some unique ideas that have stood the test of time, and have returned here. Most notably Duke's arsenal of weapons still packs an enjoyable punch (even if the weapon models are some of the ugliest I've ever seen), and the shrink ray and freeze guns are as entertaining as ever, as are pipe bombs and trip mines.
These lead to some cool moments, and the varied alien horde make for some interesting foes, if often stupid ones. Titanic Battlelords, floating commanders and deadly Octobrains are just a few of Duke's memorable cast, and each has been beefed up for this outing.
The many interactive environments and items add to the enjoyment, too, even if most are nothing more than frivolous detractions, and environments throughout are interesting, taking in such locations as opulent casinos, the burning ruins of Las Vegas and alien-infested hives.
There's also the simple, basic fact that Duke Nukem Forever is just plain fun, in a stupid, over the top way. In a time when we find ourselves wall to wall with ever more unimaginative and downright dull real world military shooters, Duke Forever is a breath of fresh air, and that alone will make the game worth it for some, even if it's nowhere near as good as it should be, and is more guilty pleasure than classic blockbuster.
Then there's the 'humour'. Duke's trademark misogynistic ways and crude style are back in force, and may or may not hit the mark, depending on your appreciation of schoolboy humour and poorly modelled cleavage. It's all a little childish, really, but this is a Duke Nukem game, so it's to be expected.
There are a few pokes at pop culture in there too, such as the aforementioned Mr Bale, and even a dig at Halo's Master Chief. It all adds to the fun, but is hardly a substitute for polished gameplay.

is the sequel of the 2013 game which is a remake of the 1997 game. It's an FPS game in which you play as smart-mouth Lo Wang, a modern ninja warrior with special powers and an arsenal of melee weapons and firearms, fighting your way through demons and mercenaries out to destroy the world one way or another.
As a game Shallow Warrior 2 (not a typo) is pretty fun when it wants to and pretty dull when it tries to take itself seriously. The main story was uninteresting, annoyingly convoluted and felt like a tedium in which you progress through the fun aspect of the game, the gameplay itself. The game is famous for its cheap but albeit funny at times, mocking and filled with
jokes. Sometimes they work, sometimes they feel... forced but most of the time is a cheap comedic relief. Some people will appreciate them more than others to be sure and truth be told Lo Wang really shines in the positively ridiculous adventures on your side questing. Which is a shame really. The game felt interesting and funny when you did the side quests, that is not to say that the main quest didn't have its moments, but I found the game most enjoyable when it didn't take itself too seriously.
When the game tries too hard it shows and it removes the premise of ridiculousness and goes for a serious note which is frankly not what the game is supposed to be.
The gameplay is nice, you have a variety of weapons to choose from, each with some different mechanics and passive bonuses. You have lots of mods to choose from and this is where the game excels. You can mod just about anything into any weapon to create your own personalized tool of destruction. Elemental damage, critical strikes, reduced missed attacks on ranged weapons, bows, arrows, grenade launchers, the game has it all.
Of course this is a double edge sword (HA!), which means that on higher difficulties, elemental immune bullet (slash?) spongy enemies, will cause you switch to different weapon every 3 minutes. It's is annoying to switch constantly but that's the nature of the game. Although I did find myself to breeze through the game with a very few weapons, I can imagine on max difficulties, weapon switching is a must do in order to succeed.
Slaying enemies nets you XP and you can spend the points to improve on your skills. The majority are passive bonuses but you can also make any of your 4 primary skills better. There's no level limit so theoretically if you play enough you can get all tiers of all skills on the different trees. There's lots of useless loot and I do mean
which makes inventory management a nightmare to go through. However you can 'recycle' them for something better but that costs resources and it's not very money efficient.
The game itself is quite short, just about 15 hours to do all main+side story missions, there are also a few trials added as a free DLC which grant access to several blacksmith weapon improvements. Gameplay is the saving grace of the game and the only reason which this gets a thumbs up. It's entertaining, it's fast paced and it's feel really good to slash demons with your sword. It's what the game does best and I kinda wish there was more of it and less elemental resistant enemies which turns this fun aspect of the game into a chore.
I'm giving a slight recommendation for this based on the fun gameplay alone but with a caveat; get this on a discount. There's not plenty of issues with game, it's fairly straightforward but it's really short and there's not really any replayability unless you're really into the game. Higher difficulties mean that you get more resistant enemies and you're playing the same dull story again and again. The developers did a solid job but the game has glaring flaws which take away from an otherwise fun experience and that's a shame. I certainly hope if there's a sequel for this in the future that some, if not all, of the issues will be gone and the game can truly shine.

So having now finally completed the game not 5 minutes ago, I think I can safely say: to those of you who are looking for a game with lots of interaction, large amounts of exploration, and ahappy relaxing game. Yeah well... this one's not for you. For those who are looking for what anygood amnesia recipe game should contain; a deep thought provoking plot, but a linear course of objectives, and what is essentially a lot of masked levers, levers in denial, actual levers, button that are kind of like levers and door levers, then bingo. You've found yourself a nice tastily lengthy game with a pretty ♥♥♥♥ing heart-wrenching story at points and some pretty decent voice acting.

Hope you like context menus. Everything you do in this game requires right clicking on something, navigating over to a dropdown menu, and selecting the appropriate action.  Sometimes there are nested menus that you need to navigate through. Since most basic tasks need to be repeated many times such as gathering resources, or leveling terrain, expect to be clicking through the same menus over and over again. This is partially alleviated by an "auto craft" feature which will perform a task repeatedly after you've clicked on it through the menu, but you will still need to go back to the menus each time you want to change a task, and the auto-craft feature doesn't work for everything.
Every time you want to access a menu, you need to stop moving and enter mouse mode. Mouse mode lets you move your mouse around and click on things. Then when you want to move around in the world again you need to switch back to move around mode. There's also a separate "combat mode" which you need to switch to in order to do combat.
There is a way to set a default action for a tool, so for example you can set it so every time you click with a shovel it will dig the earth instead of navigating through the menu to select "dig earth", however you will still need to constantly go through the menu to change the default action between digging and filling since inventory space is limited. And if you want to switch tools, you again have to go back to mouse mode then to context menus. Basically there's a lot of clicking for even the most simple tasks, despite a few little short cuts.
When you are working with terrain you need to constantly go into "observe mode" which lets you see whether the terrain is level. But again, instead of a quick key for observe mode, you need to stop moving and go into mouse mode, right click somewhere on the ground and navigate through menus to get to observe mode. Once you're in observe mode however you can't actually perform any actions and need to go back to move mode so you can use your tool.
When you're gathering resources the UI doesn't tell you how much more weight you can carry, so you have to keep clicking until your inventory is full. However it will still make you go through the digging animation even if your inventory is full and then tell you that you can't pick anything up. Things like digging and even eating are not instant, you have to watch a timer count down. Watching a timer just to tell you that you can't carry any more is frustrating.
The interface is poor, the control scheme is poor. The game itself is repetitive which can be forgiven for a building game, but not with the painful menu system. There might be a good game somewhere under all the clunky menus and clicking, but I can't be bothered to find it.
Another side note, there's these electronic birds chirping constantly while you're playing, it's a pretty annoying sound. If you try to turn it off in the audio menu it turns off all sound effects. There really needs to be a separate setting for "ambience".
All in all this game might be a good concept but poor implementation. It feels more like a proof of concept for a game than a completed game. Currently, it's not worth my time.

Given the oft and loudly proclaimed provenance of this game I expected a 4X-RTS experience, except with markets instead of militaries.  I imagined hours of playing vast, sprawling games across the surface of Mars, replete with complexity and grand strategic depth.
That's not what this game is.  In fact OTC is a scion of the great RTS's of the late 90s, and it operates on that same tense, refined, match-oriented, competitive level- in which the genre name becomes an anachronism, because the actual gameplay is so tight and focused that it would be best described as tactical rather than strategic.  Matches are fast-paced and relatively short, demanding a combination of quick clicks and quick thinking to stay on top.  Resources, tech, and production are all tied up with each other in a single intertangled "tree" of progression.  You can buy or sell any resource or product at any time if you have the money, and one of the key facets of playing well is using this ever-market to drive up the value of your surplus goods and drive down the value of your opponents', while still making sure you are keeping your levels where they need to be to avoid halts in production or debt accumulation.  There's a moment sometimes in a match where suddenly you see a way that you can make the market perform for you like a puppet- a few minutes and some well-placed clicks later and your stock is way out on top  (assuming, of course, your plans aren't deflected by your opponents' own devious machinations).  Victory in OTC occurs when one player owns all the stock of all the corporations in the match.
During the best matches I experience that same sort of premium-grade thrumming that I used to get from a good game of Starcraft in college, complete with peculiar blink of bewilderment at match's end as my brain powers down its High Alert protocols and returns to normal functioning.  I find it interesting that the devs keep emphasizing how not like Starcraft this game is, and yet my gut-level experience has been very similar for the two games.  It's interesting as well that the devs were so worried about multiplayer catching on without any combat outlet for players.  And yet this game shines most brightly in the cutthroat multiplayer arena.  I think they underestimated our creativity when it comes to eradicating our opponents.  The markets of OTC can be just as disruptive and violent (and satisfying) as any zerg-infested terran marine making a bee-line for your base.
Overall 7.5/10
Pros:
+original concept with a classic feel
+elegant, streamlined gameplay
+relatively short matches
+rewards creativity and decisiveness
+compelling soundtrack
You decide:
+/-quick clicking can be a major factor in your success
+/-limited options in terms of tech and production
+/-the differences among the corporate classes pose some interesting market problems for players but ultimately gameplay is pretty much the same for everyone
+/- Early Access...sometimes you find a diamond at the end, sometimes it's a lemon.  I do tend to trust Stardock though.
+/-high tension gameplay
Cons:
-high, inflexible price point (a side effect of Kickstarter)
-graphics and glitches need a lot of work before they are polished
-occasional imbalances
-game doesn't prepare you for its experience (watch some LPs, it helps a lot)

Summary:  This is an excellent sandbox game with a poorly designed multiplayer experience.
Pros:  The sandbox part of this game is wonderful.  You're just some peasant in the Feudal Age trying to get by via primitive tools / shelter.  You need to use the resources around you to find food, make tools, and build shelter.  There are specializations you can go into, skills you can level up that let you create increasingly more complex items, and skills that let you become master over nature.  The depth and thought behind the crafting and building system is wonderful.  I could play this for hours on end with a small group of friends just building stuff.  Along with that the game is very pretty.  Graphics are superb and I find myself enjoying the view very often.
Cons:  We'll skip the obvious "it's buggy b/c it's in alpha testing" because that goes without saying.  I'll instead focus on the outdated multiplayer system.  To give you a brief overview, you can be killed by anyone at any time for no reason.  They'll take all your stuff, you'll lose skill points (levels / experience), and this could set you back days in terms of resource gathering.  It works both ways as you can go and kill people as well, but good luck.  The established players are armed to the teeth and are quite bored begging for newbies to show up so they can raid the camp.  This is something you'll find across many servers.
Now the issue here is not the PK system, but rather the lack of safe zone.  You're not safe in your camp, in your claim, or in your building.  Not even if you get walls up (good luck getting those up in time) as those can be destroyed.  The PK system also claims to punish those with low alignment (killing friendly players) but the punishment is negligible and can be countered very quickly.  Sure this is more realistic, but last I checked, living in the Feudal Age wasn't "fun".  Neither is getting chain killed nonstop for no reason.
So how to do new people join existing servers?  You don't.  You join, build something, and get raided.  That's it.  Join a friend who has a guild with a well established set of walls.  Join with a ton of friends on a new server and race to get your base set up.  Or just get killed repeatedly.  This game will eventually release an MMO beta.  It'll get some attention, maybe even make it to release.  But within 1-2 years of release, the servers will shut down due to low population.  The multiplayer system will be sure to kill any fun this sandbox can provide.
This is a game worth passing on (especially for the ridiculous price of 40 dollars for this garbage).

Interactivity in this game - as in all the games of Frictional Games - is superb! They’ve also made huge leaps in level design and character development since Amnesia: The Dark Descent.
Do yourself a favor and don’t watch or read anything about it, to avoid spoiling this awesome experience, my candidate so far for GOTY 2015.

You *might* like this game if :
You are into very simple economic games
Like short games
Are into realistic sci-fi themes
You won't like this game if :
You like to sink your teeth into empire / engine building
Find economic games boring
You like direct in your face interaction between players
In the notes for this game the designer states it was his goal to create a short playing economic RTS - Starcraft based around trading not fighting if you will. A New Kind of RTS.
Uh huh. Well, they've certainly succeeded. But does it work ? And is it actually new ?
In the main it does not work and is not actually new. When you stop and look at what it's doing you realise it's not that far away from any of the Railroad Tycoon games - except there is no railroad building or locomotive managing here.
So that comparison bears some inspection. In RT you ship goods around to make money, buy stocks, bid on auctioned inventions, buy industries all in a goal to buy out your opponents.
In OTC you ship goods around to make money, buy stocks, bid on auctioned things all in a goal to buy out your opponents.
Sound familiar ?
The difference here ( apart from one being set on a green playing field and one being set on a red playing field ! ) is that whilst in RT the shipping and management of that shipping forms a large part of the challenge in the game, in OFC its abstracted - build your resource producing building, and you're done. The shipping just "happens".
With the shipping abstracted the challenge in the game for a player lies elsewhere. But. Uh. Where ? Choosing what building to build next ? That's it ?
What's left is a very thin game - one which comes down to cracking the (simple) puzzle of what build order you should build buildings in - whether to skip some, concentrate in others and so on. In fact this is pretty much the economical part of the RT games. There's literally nothing else to do in OTC however - apart from a bit of sabotage, which by and large comes down to paying X dollars to knock out Y building for Z seconds. Call it an EMP blast. Dynamite. An uprising. The upshot is largely the same.
Given a relatively simple resource / building tree in the game ( it's a short game ) there is no complexity there either in figuring out what sneaky specialisations you can bust out or great economical wizardry you can pull off. This is definitely at the lighter end of the resource manipulation gaming tree.
Also, because of the target of the game design to make a short economic RTS based game, you are never going to get into an empire building, economic engine developing kind of position that world building and economic building players typically like. This is all about getting in, making your fast bucks, and buying everyone else out in quick order. So for those that *like* those kind of economic world building games,  this game isn't going to float your boat either.
There is much made of "every game being different" and amazing replayability, which boils down to the map being random, resources being strewn around the map randomly, and depending what small build orders people build, the price of some goods being different. Think random map creation in Railroads. Or Civ. But. It doesn't actually have a huge impact on your gameplay here - because the bit where you interact with the world is largely abstracted - you just choose what to build where. So no matter the world, or the players, you will still be sitting down every time and making a quick decision about which 3 or 4 key buildings to build in which order. Sure others can impact some of those decisions, but really, it's not going to have you in knots of chess like deliberation. It's going to have you reaching to spam the sabotage and buy shares  buttons.
Despite all that I've enjoyed my time with the game, I appreciate the attempted design of the game, I like the martian theme ( which is just fluff ) but it really at this point strategically, tactically, whatever has no legs at all - its an interesting experiment, its largely met its goals, but it doesnt make for a great replayable game.
If you are into the board game sphere, then this game is like a super light and simple Euro - and probably wouldn't hold your attention for more than a couple of games.
One last point, the price of this game is wayyyyy too high for what you get. No way is this a premium price game, and I would say unless you either don't care about how you spend your gaming bucks, or have a desperate need to buy this game, I would avoid.

The Story: I expected nothing less from the creators of Penumbra and Amnesia: The Dark Descent. I have been waiting for this game to be finished for YEARS and I am so glad it went above and beyond my expectations. I was impressed with the storyline and character development, I really felt for Catherine and Simon, and I found myself rooting for their survival throughout the game. Also the sense of immersion was incredible. The world while there are a few loopholes, is very immersive and well-done. It had a very Penumbra feel in regards to the storyline, but SOMA was far more upbeat. Rather than having a completely depressing outlook like Daniel in Amnesia where it's hard to find redemption, SOMA takes you to the lowest lows in regards to human survival and morality and gives you a very compelling shred of hope, and sense of awe when it comes to the wonders of being a human being. It also leaves you with some major philosophical questions in regards to, "what is a soul?" and "what defines human consciousness?" After beating the game I kind of just wanted to go lay in the grass somewhere, stare at some clouds and take a moment to say "Damn, it's great to be alive." Not many "horror" genre games make you think, and for that I think SOMA will take it's place on a pedestal as one of the best horror games out there. It's not just the scares, it's the overall experience that sells it.
The Gameplay: One of my biggest concerns was whether or not it would be like Frictional's other works and have only one or two enemies, but SOMA has loads of 'em, and some of them had me damn near peeing my pants. Really felt like they did some great improvements with the AI. As someone who's played hundreds of hours in Amnesia and custom stories, let me say that damn one of those last enemies really will NOT GET OFF YOUR♥♥♥♥♥ Like you really have to be sneaky as all hell to get past these guys and I enjoy that challenge. Also makes the game very re-playable. The blur mechanic when you're close to enemies is pretty useful, but it can be annoying when you're trying to see. Mostly when your health is low, it's almost better to just kill yourself and re-do after a certain amount of blur. Otherwise, runs great, beautiful game. Minor lag on loading screens but very worth for the visual results.
Overall: 10/10 loved it. Can't wait to see the mods.

In light of the recent patches to the game, I'm going to have to stick with my very ambitious but flawed gem answer. It's Obsidian doing what they do best, setting lofty goals for their projects and just barely missing the mark because they bit off more than they could chew.
The Peragus mining facility goes on for far too long. It could have been cut in half or just cut entirely with you starting off on Telos. The fact Peragus/Telos is so long makes replaying the game unappealing solely because of how much time you have to sink into the game before you're finally allowed to explore the other planets. Many story arcs and companions are woefully underdone and stand in stark contrast to the ones that are well written and very fleshed out. Another minute complaint is that Handmaiden and Disciple are not very well balanced against themselves, they shouldn't have had identical stats and feats.
All that aside, I like the more somber tone this game has over it's predcessor. The few story arcs they did finish are interesting, the few companions they did flesh out are really well done. The skills are balanced against themselves, no one of them is so bad it should never be taken by the PC. The crafting was very well implemented. The amount of customization allowed for with your companions and the flexibility of the Exile leaves you for a lot of room to mix and match, something I really enjoy in games like this.
Warts and all, I still think the positives of this outweigh the negatives. Look into the Restored Content fan patch, it adds a lot of interesting things and implements some of the content that had to be left on the cutting floor due to time and budget retraints.

Super Punch Out!! always seems to be forgotten by people when listing off the SNES's best titles. To be fair it's up against some stiff competition, but to this day SPO is still an incredibly fun and polished gem that has sadly faded from most people's memories. The developers of Beat Boxing Turbo clearly remember it though, with their game being clearly and highly inspired by Nintendo's boxing puzzle game, with a bit of Fight Night mixed in for a colorful arcade feel that reminded me why I miss SPO so much. It's in no way a perfect replacement, but it's an admirable effort and a surprisingly fun time!
So you want to box? Well tough luck, human, there's no place for your kind in the ring! Under a disguise though no one would stop you, and thus you enter the world of beat boxing in an attempt to make a name for yourself and prove humans have a place in the sport.
As the name suggests, this isn't straight boxing, but somewhere between the over the top feel of the before mentioned Punch Out and a simple arcade recreation of the sport. Your collection of moves is small and the way to utilize them equally limited, but you're given just enough variation to be able to plan out various moves, and counter the attacks of your beastly enemies (which true to form all have their own special attacks and fighting styles). It's easy to learn and honestly pretty easy to master as well, which actually becomes an issue after a point as fights become cake walks and the CPU's way to counteract this is to rely on cheap hits and forcing you into corners that never feel particularly fair. It's disappointing the difficulty fluctuates from such extremes, but when it's not beating you in the face without remorse the ease of conquering your opponents never became hugely unsatisfying.
As a budget priced game there have been some obvious cuts and as a whole the amount of content here is slim. Perhaps most disappointing is the absence of any multiplayer mode, which seems an obvious addition that could have extended the hour or so story mode a lot further. Other issues arise in the clunky combat, that isn't a problem generally but on higher difficulty levels leads to a lot of cheap KO's. Some recycled character models/frames are a bit tacky as well, but the cartoon artstyle mostly makes up for the corners that have been cut off the presentation.
Irregardless, Beast Boxing Turbo is worth recommending if only for how unique it is to the platform, and for how fun it is while it lasts. It's far from the classic that is Super Punch Out!!, but as that is a sequel itself perhaps it's only a matter of waiting for Beast Boxing 2 for it to reach that point.
In the meantime I'll be over here punching pigs in the face.

Undoubtedly this is probably one of the most controversial games on Steam right now. The game features some very strong sexual content and nudity, which would probably result in the game getting an AO if rated by the ESRB. In addition, some of the scenerios (pariticuarly the blackmail quest) results in you doing actions in the game that border on sexual assault.
However, despite the obvious ethical boundries the game crosses, it is still relatively fine as a point-and-click RPG. I also like the option to create your own storylines for the game and I hope later versions of the game moves past being merely a pick-up simulator.

There are redeeming qualities here. The seasons change and the way that affects food production is interesting. Little touches like wolves hunting deer packs in the countryside of your kindom is endearing and immersive. The way terrain effects unit behavior, archers having to get on top of a hill to shoot enemies on the otherside of it and getting a range boost from having high ground for instance, is really cool. The weather effects obscuring your vision be it from rain, darkness, or fog and how those conditions effect units, archer's accuracy for instance, presents an immersive challenge I really like. Using workers to loot the corpses of your battlefield for spoils is awesome. And leveling up your units, and customizing their battle strengths by how you spend their level up points is great. All of these qualities set this game above any other MMORTS I have ever played
The actual gameplay however is glitched to hell, AI is very disobedient making micro management extremely frustrating, I got into a PvP match it didn't load my army and when one of the enemies left it loaded my army with the remaining enemy's army on top of mine which is not supposed to happen, you're supposed to spawn on opposite corners of the map. Customization of unit formation, stance, and garrison status do not stick. Units that you didn't garrison are randomly assigned garrison status for no conceivable reason, and the developers have said they're not going to work on the game anymore. So as much potential as this game has it may never be realized. Perhaps since the game has gone free to play in the last couple months will save it. For now I don't recommend it.
