Right when you begin the game, the title screen tells you that it is "the ultimate fiery and bloody experience". That would be a nice way of describing this game.
It's "ultimate" because it is a really fun game with really cool mechanics backing it. It's "fiery" because the graphics are incredible for what it is, with enemy craft swarming you mercilessly, shots flying and explosions covering the screen in fiery death. It's "bloody" because the pilots of such enemy craft will pop out of their ships and explode into bloody gibs when you shoot them down and ram your own ship against them, laughing like a maniac. And to top it off, the soundtrack is pure high octane awesomeness courtesy of heavy metal band Machinae Supremacy, whom you may know from other awesome soundtracks like Giana Sisters: Twisted Dreams.
All in all, a game that no shoot 'em up fan should let pass. This is, with no room for doubt, the best western shmup made in all of videogame history.

My old review was critical of vehicle handling.  I played an updated version and am still not recommending this game.  The reason is simple.  There is no content and handling still sucks.  It's a crash simulator with a handful of scenarios, and downloadable scenarios that are just more of the same.  The car physics are fun, but the handling is still unrealistic.  I don't care what the fan boys or devs say.  They haven't raced REAL cars.  There isn't much to do either.  No story, no career, no reason to play the game other than crash your car, or someone else's crap AI car.  Yawn.
What's good?  Graphics are good.  Sound is improved, but the engine noise seems generic, like, muscle sound, truck sound, car sound, and tuner sound.  Still, the sound is better than what is was, and the graphics were never a complaint.  Car physics are cool, and hitting those trees or walls really teaches you that crashes are bad for cars.  There doesn't seem to be too many bugs.  Game runs good.
What's bad?  Handling.  If you want a racing sim, go elsewhere.  The crash physics in this game are great, but if you want a racing game, this game sucks.  Down force just doesn't apply.  There is good physics for turning, like when you pick the sports cars, the suspensions still do not push the cars down hard enough on all sides, and the spoilers don't push the car down at high speeds, you will tire skip the imperfections of the road frequently, and not turn those hair pins, even at 20 mph.  What a fraud.  I have to slow the best sports cars / rally cars to sub 10mph to turn a hair pin.  A fully modded sports car can do 20+ on a hair pin.  The suspension and down forces compensate for the G-forces and allow you to shoot into those turns.  Beam.NG still sends you barreling off the road like a missle because tire physics are the only thing that matters.
Summary: Some cars are fun to drive.  Though, I had to learn specifically how to handle those cars, and what speeds I had to be at to take on certain turns, like real racing, however, the difference is that the speeds are far lower that what I would expect.  A lot lower.  The best sports cars still seem to drive like missile bricks.  The brake forces and down forces do not feel realistic, and I have raced REAL CARS.  I also play racing sims frequently, some of which have cars that I have driven, and are somewhat accurate with the look and feel of driving, and the speeds I need to handle the corners.  BeamNG has potential, but the racing simulation takes a back seat to crashing physics.  And it's boring after about 10 minutes.  My 3 year old laughed for about 5 minutes, then ran off to play with action figures.  That's about how much I want to continue playing until I can hit the turns like a real race car, hell, have a reason to play other than 1 minute scenarios with crap AI and no purpose.

It plays NOTHING like Punchout.  As a Punchout sucessor, it fails miserably.  The control style is totally different, there is little focus on attack patterns, there are no specials, and you run away to dodge instead of actually watching your opponents moves.
Putting that comparison aside, it's a fun little romp, if you enjoy arcade style boxing games.  Personally, I love them.  Even bad games in the genre can be pretty fun, and this one is pretty decent with a unique personaility.  The emphasis on chains over countering is a decent, if unprefered, twist, and the RPG elements keep the game escalating in its early stages.  Controls are responsive, and beating down an opponnent with no mercy is satisfying (a redeeming feature in a game where you can easily be overleveled).
It's biggest fault is that it relies too heavily on it's RPG elements to manage progression, so your foes will quickly go from being too hard, to just right, to way too easy.  Other complaints include a limited number of opponents, and a lack of advanced blocking / dodging strategies.
So it's kind of fun and a little lacking, i.e. it's a $5 game (SRP).  I can easily list off a dozen games I've payed more for on sale and enjoyed less.

I was afraid something like this would happen when playing a 20th anniversary edition... Gabriel Knight: Sins of the fathers was the first adventure from Gabriel (the Shadowhunter) in 1993 and the first game created by Jane Jensen.
At the time it was a fantastic game, it was one of the first games to include a dark subject, not exactly suited for kids, not because of the violence or blood (that was something that other games always had) but also because of the dark, dramatic, almost ghotic nature of the main story and characters. Something different at the time (and still to this day) was the research that jane did for these games, mixing historical facts, real places,  with of course a good dose of fiction to create her own story, and not just an historical retelling. It was always fun (and amazing) to go looking for these places after finishing the game, and see how much of the real world was put into the story. For me the most amazing story of all that jane had created was the one for Gabriel Knight: the Beast within, the second game, about the legend of king Ludwig II and Richard Wagner.
This game, Sins of the fathers, was the first story of the series, and has all the great elements that were expanded in the later adventures of Gabriel. The 20th anniversary edition keeps this story , but at the same time tries to update the game engine, the graphics, sound and even some gameplay elements to make it more accesible to the current generation of gamers...
This is one review where i'm having a difficult time with the steam system for reviews...you can't always either recommend or don't recommend a game...there are gray areas...and to recommend a game is not the same as liking a game...
In this case, for Gabriel Knight, i will say that i like the game, meaning, i like the original game back when i played it 20 years ago and what it meant to me and to players at the time it camed out... That same game (the story) is still here in this 20th anniversary ed, and i'm glad i have a version compatible with current systems and accesible online (installing the old CD version is a pain...)
But...aside from that, to be honest this new version is... while it looks better than the original that camed out in 1993 (of course!)...the one from 1993 was more polished and had greater graphics and sound (for that time) and this version from 2014 actually has worst graphics (for a 2014 game). So the problem here is that, what the creators of the game tried to do was (i think) do a new version with updates that make it more appealing to "current generation" of gamers but at the same time not changing too much and keep enough things to still make it appealing to the "old generation" of gamers that played the game in 1993...and the result is one game that it's not really appealing to either one of them...
The graphics for this version are updated of course, they are better than 1993, but they are pretty bad for a 2014 game, and even though they are noticeable improved from the previous game of the company (Moebius) they still have several problems: the animation itself is low quality, badly animated and there are bugs like the spinning head problem (where a character in game starts spinning the head like a possesed doll) and it happens all the time, also the characters appears and dissappear when closing a door or leaving a room..the backgrounds for the game are nice...and just that, but they are far from scary or moody or anything, they simply are sterile.... The characters closeup portraits are fare better in comparison, but honestly the 2014 Gabriel version... (the most important character) seems more like a teens pop star than a shadow hunter. His hair still has that 1990s volume that was so common back in the day... but now by today standards it just seems wrong (and funny!)... that's precisely one of the things that has to be changed in 2014 if you want your character to be taken seriously...
the dialogues....and the voice actors...the dialogues are too much for a 2014 game....meaning too much lines of everything...yeah...for me it was interesting to have all (or most) of the original dialogues...as a collection curiosity...but for 2014 is overkill, (even if the important dialogues are being colored in yellow) the world has changed, people has shorter attention span, and also the way stories are presented today has changed...it's not worst, it's just different, you can still put a big story like the one from Gabriel Knight in 2014, you just have to make some changes to make the thing work...it's not about caring or not caring for the original game, it is about making something that has better flow of narrative, (and again, you are trying to make a new game that will appeal to current gamers)
About the new voice casting, they are doing a fine job at that...but it's not at the level of the original cast of 1993 with Tim curry, Mark Hamill and Leah Remini. Of course it would be impossible to get the original actors for different reasons (too expensive!) and also the low quality recordings (as for using the original material) so it's no surprise there but that's one thing you have to consider if trying to redo the original game...
The only "updated" element that i think is actually better on this version, is the music, wich is done almost all over again by the original composer/producer of the game, Robert Holmes, and it is great, even if it just sticks to the original themes, it does show and advantage over the old version and it sounds great.
So my review for Gabriel Knight is that,
, because of the original one that i played in the 90s, the story is still there,
because i don't see this being interesting in 2014.
The problem is if you are going to do a new version of an old game...you have to make it attractive for 2014... and make all the necessary changes...yeah...the fans are gonna be mad...well, this is not for the fans, a new version is for the new players.
As it is, this version is only appealing to the original players of the series, like myself, but no so much to current generation. If you are doing it for the original players of the game only, then just make minimal changes, update only the things that can be updated without changing the core of the original, the things that make the game be what it is (like the Another World 20th anniversary ed wich is nice) and be clear that you are making a product that its more an historical piece of gaming than a "new game" wich it isn't.
I know by now many people that love the game must hate me, but i will say that, there's no point in redoing and old game from another era if there's no possibility of doing it right... The translation from 1993 to 2014 in this case, and for different technical/artistic reasons had many elements lost in the process (or changed for worst), and i very much prefer to see a new game by jane jensen and a new story than a 20th anniversary edition....

If you want a tl;dr of this review, I would say this: don't buy this at full price. Wait for a sale; it's fun, but not worth full price.
The good:
- Freeform deck construction. It is nice they finally added this, and it is pretty fun to come up with your own deck and add cards as you get them. If you're like me and get a rush out of cracking boosters, this is a nice plus.
- Multiplayer is decent if you're up against an experienced opponent.
The bad:
- Terrible UI. It was obviously designed with controllers or tablets in mind, so you'll do a lot of pointless scrolling in menus if you're using a mouse. I had to plug a controller in just to change video settings because it wasn't obvious how to change the tabs in the menu... is it so hard to let us click to change them? Another gripe I had with this is that it takes a bunch of scrolling or clicks just to change your deck, when a simple dropdown before a match would've sufficed.
- Going on the last point, the deck building interface is horrible and slow. I'm on a 1920x1200 monitor, please use my screen real estate better.
- Small card pool; it's as if you're playing constructed with a single set. Though you think "oh boy, I get to make my own deck!", there are actually only a handful of viable archetypes that you'll probably end up sticking to. This is compounded by the fact that you can only have 4 of a common, 3 of an uncommon, 2 of a rare, and 1 of a mythic in each deck. This feels artifical and limits the amount of possible decks.
- AI opponents get a bunch of fun and interesting cards that you'll never get to play.
- Sealed mode removed. Though I understand the entire game is a pseudo-sealed mode, it's stupid that they built up the infrastructure to make this possible and then removed it.
The ugly:
- Stupid AI, and I played on the hardest difficulty. It's painfully bad in this one compared to others. I've never seen an AI cast a combat trick actually during combat, and the AI that had them just used them to trigger Heroic on their second main phase (even when casting during combat might've killed one of my creatures). I've also seen the AI cast removal to destroy the wrong creature, and it's not very satisfying to win against someone who has basically misplayed.
- Tokens seem overpowered. Removal is limited and costly in this game, so if you can token flood, there are only a few viable answers to it. Planar Cleansing and Anger of the Gods are the only two mass removal spells I can think of, and since they're rare, a deck can only have two of both. I swung for 300 with a token deck against an opponent who had no recourse for it. If Brimaz, King of Oreskos hits on turn three and your opponent can't remove it, it's basically game over.
- Damage still seems to use the stack for some reason. I blocked with several tokens and a creature that had P/T equal to the number of creatures I controlled; when one of the tokens died in combat, the other creature lost toughness and then died when it blocked. Combat damage is supposed to be simultaneous.
Overall, this edition of DoTP took one step forward and two steps back. If you want to know why this is gimped, it's because Wizards doesn't want to make a product that competes with Magic the Gathering: Online. DoTP products are intentionally limited so that people won't just play them instead of spending money in their actual pay to win service. But, if you haven't played much MTG recently and want a decent amount of fun, grab this the next time it's on sale.

Alright now that the ending of the game rage haze has passed *Spoilers, the ending is hot garbage*
So I can better point out the problems with this game.
Story/Writing
I played the first one, and I had a horrible time, understanding what was going on.  I recognized the characters, but didnt recognize their motivations, their personalities.  The story felt like the writers had no idea what they were doing, that they ran out of time, and at the mid point of the game, random things just happen.
The world itself, is a tragedy when it comes to writing.  What is going on since Shadow Warrior 1?  Is demon invasions a common thing?  What is life like in the universe now that we have super Chi tech and the shadow world constantly mucking with it?  The answer is... IDK.  I only played through the game, and it is not explored, explained, because there is no explanation.  The world is nonsense, it is a paper thin place mat holder for the gameplay.  By the end of the game, I didnt know what I was doing, or why I was doing it... and by the time the end credits were rolling I was to mad to care.
Characters
Ok like I said with the writing, the characters are terrible.  Their motivations confusing, not in a "Oh gods and criminals are fickle" kind of way, but a "You never really know or understand them by the end of the game" kind of way.  It doesnt help that the animations and movements of said characters in the cutscenes are laughably bad.  They flail around, they twist their faces into shapes the animators never intended, they make poses and expressions that dont match the context of whats being said around them, its very ugly and amaturish, and it gets worse and worse the longer the game goes on.
Instead of Hojo, we have a new head partner, whatever you want to call it, and they are just plain... obnoxious.  She's not funny, she's not cute, but she will try her hardest to convince you otherwise throughout the game.  #BringbackHojo
Wang himself is a cool guy bad♥♥♥♥♥sure, but he seems so random, so chaotic in who he respects or blatantly disrespects to the point of being a hinderance.  Even Wang was on my nerves towards the end of the game, and he truly is the only character I liked.
The other characters are nothing memorable, in fact Im forgetting most of them by the time I got around to writing this review a few days later, thats how memorable they are.
Weapons and modifications
Here's another massive set back that has nothing to do with the terrible writing.  The game showers you with weapons, but many are worthless.  Many are given to you, when you have already recieved better weapons from previous quests.  Add a cluttered, messy mod system to that... and you spend 5 to 10 minutes shifting through mods and muttering to yourself, while your trying to play a 2 player game.  So instead of all these weapons with beautiful animations and effects when you shoot them, to which I have to give credit, that only get thrown away or worse, NEVER USED AT ALL, why not balance the weapons a bit.  I would have prefered far less weapons, if only to to affect the balance, making the actual weapon improvements and upgrades more meaningful and impactful.  I didnt use 3/4th's of the weapons I picked up in actual combat.  Why would you, when it takes minutes shifting through mods to find out which one increases the damage or other stats you want to shove into it?
The Ending
Cliff hanger, that... made little sense.  Go to forums, and you will find that no one really knows, no one has any real theories... why?  Because it was just a stupid, cliff hanger to set up a sequel or DLC... there is no reason behind it, and if I'm wrong, I dont even feel bad for declaring otherwise, because the game didnt explain it.
In closing... buy Shadow Warrior 1

After a few years of development limbo hell, we finally get to see World of Speed on paid Early Access. While it'll still be several months before full release into free-to-play, there is a lot of potential for a great free online racing game that many are eager to see. For the moment, it's only quick online races and a practice mode with more features to come, especially looking forward to seeing how team racing will be like once it happens.
While there is a small active online player base (AI cars with random real names fill empty grid spots), it is fairly understandable because of the current pay to access model and a lack of in-game community features (only text chat in pre and post race). It can also feel rather grindy after a while, achieving the hard bet objectives being the best way to earn credits (even then can be risky unless you have high confidence and some aggressive driving). Also keep in mind the rather funky online driving physics that can mess with your race, particularly when trying to achieve the bet objectives. That might be a deal-breaker for some, but the quirks don't really bother me that much. Your experience would vary by control type as well.
At the moment, there's a fairly decent car and track selection, with more cars and tracks being planned in later updates, Customization is somewhat limited and there's no tuning aside from tires and upgrades. A few cars are locked behind the premium currency wall, which could be a bother if you like a particular car that is behind that paywall. Will have to see how things go when it comes to that.
So far, I've been personally enjoying the game. I'm just happy that World of Speed is available in a playable state, having dropped nearly $40 for the Gold Cup Bundle for the exclusive cars and extra currency (also to support developers on top of that). If you don't mind the paid Early Access state, go ahead on and make your purchase. It's also worth waiting if you rather play it for free once it hits full release.

With the release of Magic 2015 it seemed like Wizards of the Coast had finally been able to release a fun and functional piece of software.  This, sadly, is not the case. Although the graphics are highly polished and there's a huge selection of cards to build your deck with, these are the only good points drowning in a sea of bad design.  To start with you're forced to choose a starter deck which is anemic at best.  In order to fortify your pathetic deck you fight AI opponents with vastly superior decks seemingly designed to irratate you into forking over more real money just to make your deck competitive. Didn't shell out money and yet somehow still find yourself winning the game?  No problem. Stainless games thought of this eventuality.  The AI cheats.  Constantly. Especially on higher difficulties. Drawing the perfect opening hand every game, knowledge of what's in your hand, and drawing the perfect card the AI needs, everytime.  On top of all this, the frustration engine that is Magic 2015 is actually missing features from previous versions.  Stick with the old Microprose developed Duels of the Planewalkers.  It's far superior, even after 18 years.

From the developer of GEARCRACK Arena (the game infamous for the reviews that read "Buy it for pennies, sell the cards, make a profit, listen to the music.").
I enjoy GEARCRACK for what it is, and now with UBERMOSH, hopefully people will realize what Walter Machado strives for when developing games (thus nullifying the undue dogpiling and (")nit-picky-ness(")): Simple Arcade Diversions.
For the money, it is truly appalling just how vehement other reviews have condemned GEARCRACK, especially when some other games in the “Bargain Bin” that cost more than thrice it aren’t as commensurate at entertaining. UBERMOSH is already leaps and bounds better than GEARCRACK (I say with an attempt at a sympathetic-to-the-consensus viewpoint), though I’m hoping that one of the new game modes planned for UBERMOSH will be reminiscent of GEARCRACK in having little to nothing explained (which was a throwback to games from the ‘90’s (a la System Shock 2, perhaps)).
The only legitimate criticism of GEARCRACK was that nothing was explained; go to the forums to discover that a lot of variables are determined by RNG. So people concluded that the (")hardcore(") aspects of the game were simply (")unfair(").
I thought that was half the fun of GEARCRACK – I feel those who complained forgot just how much they paid for the game (not to suggest that price absolves a game of criticism, as Walter knows).
UBERMOSH plays much like GEARCRACK but in a much more refined and simplistic manner. There are (at this time) really no discernible nuances. You run around an arena with hordes of enemies pursuing you. You can deflect enemy fire; you can directly melee the enemies; you can pick up their weapons.
GEARCRACK had enemies with shields that required you use certain implicit tactics to destroy them; limited ammunition; an incredibly short time-limit that assaulted you along with unbelievable barrages from the enemies
you took an action.
I've little doubt that UBERMOSH will have more complex features added later - it will not be nothing but a "serviceable diversion," as I called GEARCRACK - but, to be sure, (it seems) that is Walter's goal.
People can complain about GEARCRACK and it's possible that the basis for those qualms won't necessarily be baseless.
The only complaint (thus far) that can be recorded of UBERMOSH (besides just how early of a version the game is in (clicking on "Extras" (where I would assume some sort of Options would be) does nothing but remind you "Non-final version")) is that "there's nothing to it."
This is a simple arcade game. Your goal is to beat your previous scores. The action is incredibly hectic and very fun. As it is, it isn’t necessary to have a levelling system, a customizable arsenal, a level select feature, etc.; the basic gameplay is such that progression driven by the self is enough to ensure fun (not to suggest "Good game Walter, we're content, you can be done with updates," lol).
there's always room for you to get better at the game.
...I actually regret buying this game while it is discounted. I just saw it and immediately bought it because I have hope that Walter Machado will continue to be a great indie developer and that he’ll achieve success.
Walter is worthy of your support; the flak that GEARCRACK received is not applicable to UBERMOSH (and I contest that, though the criticism of the former wasn’t undue, GEARCRACK did not deserve the
of criticism it received – those “Mixed” user reviews).
I recommend this (and Walter’s previous) game.
DISCLOSURE: I posted a screenshot of UBERMOSH on my profile. I like to show discounted games however I can on there - my Game Collector showcase was full - took a screenshot of my score just to have UBERMOSH shown on my page.
That screenshot has had 1 upvote; my review has No ratings yet.
Walter Machado sent me a friend request. I have to assume it was... because of my screenshot? Or perhaps he has read my review and, in the interest of integrity, just did not vote either way on it.
Say all that to say: I wrote this review (as with all my reviews) according to my own opinion - it was not endorsed in any way by Walter.

You *might* like this game if :
You are into very simple economic games
Like short games
Are into realistic sci-fi themes
You won't like this game if :
You like to sink your teeth into empire / engine building
Find economic games boring
You like direct in your face interaction between players
In the notes for this game the designer states it was his goal to create a short playing economic RTS - Starcraft based around trading not fighting if you will. A New Kind of RTS.
Uh huh. Well, they've certainly succeeded. But does it work ? And is it actually new ?
In the main it does not work and is not actually new. When you stop and look at what it's doing you realise it's not that far away from any of the Railroad Tycoon games - except there is no railroad building or locomotive managing here.
So that comparison bears some inspection. In RT you ship goods around to make money, buy stocks, bid on auctioned inventions, buy industries all in a goal to buy out your opponents.
In OTC you ship goods around to make money, buy stocks, bid on auctioned things all in a goal to buy out your opponents.
Sound familiar ?
The difference here ( apart from one being set on a green playing field and one being set on a red playing field ! ) is that whilst in RT the shipping and management of that shipping forms a large part of the challenge in the game, in OFC its abstracted - build your resource producing building, and you're done. The shipping just "happens".
With the shipping abstracted the challenge in the game for a player lies elsewhere. But. Uh. Where ? Choosing what building to build next ? That's it ?
What's left is a very thin game - one which comes down to cracking the (simple) puzzle of what build order you should build buildings in - whether to skip some, concentrate in others and so on. In fact this is pretty much the economical part of the RT games. There's literally nothing else to do in OTC however - apart from a bit of sabotage, which by and large comes down to paying X dollars to knock out Y building for Z seconds. Call it an EMP blast. Dynamite. An uprising. The upshot is largely the same.
Given a relatively simple resource / building tree in the game ( it's a short game ) there is no complexity there either in figuring out what sneaky specialisations you can bust out or great economical wizardry you can pull off. This is definitely at the lighter end of the resource manipulation gaming tree.
Also, because of the target of the game design to make a short economic RTS based game, you are never going to get into an empire building, economic engine developing kind of position that world building and economic building players typically like. This is all about getting in, making your fast bucks, and buying everyone else out in quick order. So for those that *like* those kind of economic world building games,  this game isn't going to float your boat either.
There is much made of "every game being different" and amazing replayability, which boils down to the map being random, resources being strewn around the map randomly, and depending what small build orders people build, the price of some goods being different. Think random map creation in Railroads. Or Civ. But. It doesn't actually have a huge impact on your gameplay here - because the bit where you interact with the world is largely abstracted - you just choose what to build where. So no matter the world, or the players, you will still be sitting down every time and making a quick decision about which 3 or 4 key buildings to build in which order. Sure others can impact some of those decisions, but really, it's not going to have you in knots of chess like deliberation. It's going to have you reaching to spam the sabotage and buy shares  buttons.
Despite all that I've enjoyed my time with the game, I appreciate the attempted design of the game, I like the martian theme ( which is just fluff ) but it really at this point strategically, tactically, whatever has no legs at all - its an interesting experiment, its largely met its goals, but it doesnt make for a great replayable game.
If you are into the board game sphere, then this game is like a super light and simple Euro - and probably wouldn't hold your attention for more than a couple of games.
One last point, the price of this game is wayyyyy too high for what you get. No way is this a premium price game, and I would say unless you either don't care about how you spend your gaming bucks, or have a desperate need to buy this game, I would avoid.

So having now finally completed the game not 5 minutes ago, I think I can safely say: to those of you who are looking for a game with lots of interaction, large amounts of exploration, and ahappy relaxing game. Yeah well... this one's not for you. For those who are looking for what anygood amnesia recipe game should contain; a deep thought provoking plot, but a linear course of objectives, and what is essentially a lot of masked levers, levers in denial, actual levers, button that are kind of like levers and door levers, then bingo. You've found yourself a nice tastily lengthy game with a pretty ♥♥♥♥ing heart-wrenching story at points and some pretty decent voice acting.
The plot is very moving, it explores the idea that consciousness is what makes us human, not our bodies but our "being". This being said, it's pretty bovious your going to be doing a lot of body-swapping. It also broaches on the idea of mankinds actual downfall and how this can be averted through digital means in conjunction with the first idea (basically in one easy sentence: if you shoot me, and shortly before I die, someone transfers my consciousness into something/one else before I pass.... am I really dead? If that's not confusing enough, you're also going to be put in a lot of situations where you will be given the choice to end "human" lives, and the game even makes you go through the process of being at the side of someone as they are dying, So if you're already not great with sadness... this also might not be a healthy game for you. Trying playing with a kitten after, spending time with your family. Loving life after. It helps.
"The baddies" don't relly exist, like amnesia, there are creepy horrible looking-things, that will occasionally or frequently (depends which bit) try to nibble your bottom of or just curb stomp you, if that happens too frequently inside a couple of minutes and you day and it's back to the last checkpoint you go, which are nice and frequent, so to play the game there's not an awful lot of skill required. Try playing this drunk, with headphones on at night only and .... well then it's another story!
Plenty of room for mods and custom maps for those who care to make such things, sequel? Hmn. Interesting idea, not sure how it'd fit, but I'd buy the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of it, because this is my Jam homie.
Voice acting can tend to be a little clunky, with emphasis at points where there's none needed, but sometimes where there's a bit more emotion needed there' just blank hearted ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ everywhere. It's all well and good saying the character is nerdy and socially awkward but that screams lazy. I can totally ship the main Character and the "girl" he finds along the way however, but more fluff needed. The game makes it out to be a whole load of fluff, but apart from the events on Pathos 2 we find little out about the outside world... with good reason but this is a little annoying all the same..
The ending is ♥♥♥♥ing beautiful. It's one of those "OMFG YOU ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥S how could you leave it at that?! .... If there isn't more after the credits I am negative reviewi- oh wait there is?!" moments. And it's pretty adorable....
So all in all: allright voiceacting, limited gameplay, fantastic story, little replayability, Good Immmersion, Nice graphics and needs a sequel.

As you continue to play the game it becomes apparent though. Most of the "survival" genre fanbase is looking for something they can call "realistic" without having to put in the effort this game requires. Most gamers these days are all about instant gratification with minimal effort. Everything in the game takes time to build and to become proficient at. Couple that with a fanbase where 1/2 or more of the players come from games like DayZ or Minecraft, where important items are found at random on the ground and crafting is simple, and it shouldnt come to anyone's surprise that there would be enough bad reviews on steam to turn heads.
All that being said, this game is a community effort that is made more enjoyable by either a small group of dedicated players or a larger one all pitching in for a specific goal. For me, its been a great experience with very few things to complain about. I have put a good chunk of time into it so far and plan to continue doing so. To be honest, it would be a disservice to the devs not to give them credit for what they have accomplished with this game, which is why i felt the need to write this in the first place. Hope this is helpful to some fans of the survival genre on the fence about buying the game!

I never was one for these MMO FPS games, but Nether is something unique in terms of a post-apocalyptic based game. Instead   of the world ending through nuclear war, alien invasions or economic collapse, the planet was struck by a massive barrage of solar flares. This version of the apocalypse strongly reminds me of a book I read but the only with mutated, teleporting monsters and a more interesting urban envoirment that's based off of Chicago.
This game really is visually pleasing and the consept of exploation and scavanging for supplies does feel rewarding when an hour of searching pays off in the form of locating a gun or a large stash of food and ammo. Also, being an alpha game there will be many different add-ons and improvements, the most recent being a driveable dirt bike. But aside from these plus points, the game is incredibly buggy and full of unfair surprises along with very xenophopic and violent players.
One of the first major problems is with the Nether, the game's main enemy force. Now, there are a few different types of Nether with different EXP for killing them but fighting them comes down to a hack and slash with something that basically has no-clip enabled. You can barely land more than two strikes on them because they teleport constantly. What about running from them and hiding, you ask? I'll put it simply, you can't. Nether teleportation allows them to jump alarming distances and close the gap very quickly, which, if you don't have a gun and a lot of ammo, will result in your death. Death brings another massive problem with this game; if you die, you lose all of your collected items and experience points and accumulated skills. This isn't limited by just death by Nether but by other players, accidental deaths or glitches. Such as when I have been killed by a random player and lost over three hours of items and experience. These incidents can range from annoying to infurating and have made me second guess about playing this again. But I went back in order to try and find the game's newest addition: the dirt bike.
Luckily, I managed to find one hiding in a building and was eager to try it out. Even though there was a few known bugs, I mounted up and got going. But getting the bike to turn around was one of the hardest things I have ever done in this game. The basic controls are W to go forwards, S to reverse, and the mouse is used for changing direction. From experience, this isn't a very good control scheme. When I use a vehicle in a FPS, I want the directional keys to be used for movement and the mouse to look around. When driving the bike in Nether, your vision is restricted to looking over the handlebars, because of this it will be incredibly hard to pick a route and then take off down the streets in order to escape Nether(the bike generates a lot of noise and therefore will alert Nether and other players). The bike also lurches distances constantly, but I expected it to do this. It's also a bit of an annoyance to get on it if it's lying down, press E to stand it up again is the key but it will fall back over again so you have to time it properly in order to get on it. The bike is very weak as well, hitting something at five miles an hour can take off a lot of health. Now I know that this is a new thing and will be buggy but in all honestly, the controls should be changed to the WASD keys for movement and the mouse to look around, with a snap-vision feature that puts you back to looking at what's in front of you.
In conclusion, I do recommend this game. Aside from the bugs and sometimes unfair gameplay elements, if you find a decent server and have a few friends, it's worth playing. By yourself, it does come down to a survival horror type of game and it can be entertaining at times. Hopefully, once this game becomes fully compleated, it will be fixed and stand along side DayZ. But until then, it's a what-you-see-is-what-you-get game. But it is worth the buy.

As a fan of RTS game, Offworld Trading Company has definitely been a refresher for me. It feels very different from the conventional RTS (examples: StarCraft, CnC), but it still plays very solidly as a game in the genre. While it may feel bland at first to know that there is no martial combat aspect in the game, it compensates for that empty space very quickly by bringing pressures in macro decisions.
As the name of the game suggests, this game puts you in the position of a decision maker for a trading company on Mars, with range of actions from claiming different plots of land on Mars and trading the goods, to tampering the markets to your advantage (or your opponent's disadvantage). Your goal is to buy out all of your opponents and become the monopoly on Mars's resources.
The game is fully focused on macromanagement, which may make the game feel a bit slow. However, that does not mean that it is not exciting. Game gives you a lot of options with very limited number that you can actually choose, so you have to really plan a bit ahead on how you are going to work things out. As time progresses, your choices grow, but you will see that you will constantly be hassled by your opponents and may start facing the danger of being bought out. Your only friends will be your wits and your guts, as you make your own moves to press down your opponents and take control of what they own once and for all.
While the game is enjoyable in many aspect, I feel that the snowballing effect may become an issue as people become more familiar to the game mechanics. I guess that will be another thing that will be countered, either by evolution of player strategy or developer intervention. I am just bringing out the possibility.
Overall, I would give this game a 9.5/10. Half point off for not enough music. =D

Игра находиться на Бета тестировании, поэтому сложно что-то хорошее и плохое говорить о ней. Эта игра только для экстремалов, кто любит приключения и поистрепать себе нервы. Именно, вам придется долгое время ходить одному в заброшенном городе среди пустых районов, заброшенных домов, магазинов. Кроме ножа в рюкзаке у вас ничего. Так что вам придется хорошенько попотеть, да бы пройти сквозь заброшенный город и найти еду, патроны, оружие и т.д. Поверьте это не так легко и не сразу вы все находите, как в некоторых пост-апокалипстических играх (вы их знаете). Но в городе вы не одни. В нем обитает полчища монстров, которых лучше обходить стороной. Так же стоит избегать игроков-одиночек. С ними дальше не пойдешь, они тебя убьют, заберут твои вещи и пойдут дальше. На счет этого я хочу сказать, что доверять здесь нельзя никому (если вы не играете с другом). По поводу местности хочу сказать, что поиграв хотя бы 5 часов, ты привыкаешь и чувствуешь себя уже намного "комфортнее", чем раньше. Уже знаешь где и сколько монстров обитает в том или инном районе, знаешь где что лежит и сколько. Немного хотелось бы поговорить о различных запасах для выживания. Как я уже писал об этом, что вам придется бродить по городу, вам так же скидывают припасы (Loop Drop). Хватайте все что можно и тикайте во все стороны иначе вас убьют другие игроки. Стоит отметь что есть магазин. Там можете купить товар как за реальные, так и за игровые деньги. Но за реальные деньги я только видел фонарь, свечу и одежду. В этот магазин можно зайти только в Safe Zone, Riverside, Westview, Musem когда появляется надпись в верхней части экрана. Наверное мучает вопрос " А где же достать деньги?", деньги можно заработать передавая товар с одной safe zone на другую. В каждой такой зоне лежат ящики к примеру: LSZ-MTO, MTO-RTO, RTO-WTO. Возьмем во внимание последние 3 буквы, они обозначают местность в которую вы должны перенести товар: LSZ (Lakeside Zone (Safe Zone), MTO (Museum Outpost), RTO ( Riverside Outpost), WTO (Westview Outpost). Вам дают за это не мало денег и так же получаете опыт. Тут довольно легкая прокачка героя и каждый навык придуман не просто так для "галочки", а дает какую-то пользу. Но, когда вы умираете, вы теряете все и имеете всего лишь 1 жизнь. В принципе я поделился своим мнением об игре. Несмотря на некоторые баги, недостатки, игра стоит внимания игроков, любящих "игры - песочницы". Она полностью оправдала 12 долларов.

While i really like this games art and the puzzles are good, i cant recommend it.
The story is amazingly vauge, right up until the end.
SPOILERS BEYOND HERE
At the end, you learn this is all basiclaly a test in the afterlife for whether your soul can change. This is kinda crap but i could forgive it if it didnt act like the moral authority on some of its more complex questions.
An example, should you give a crown rumored to give large ammounts of power to a lizard man who just appears racist to bird people and is kinda a demanding jerk? Or your rat friend you saved from prison (or killed earlier, idk what happens then) so that he can protect his family? The rat also eats people, but the lizard really seems like the kinda guy to abuse that power.
The right decision is to give it to the lizard supposidly, because the rat goes into war and dies if you give it to him. How are you supposed ot know beyond a slip in one of his drawers about an offer for him to join an army? Why is it your fault that you didn't know that the crown only works for those pure of heart?
Another example, at the beggining there is a  jailer who only lives to torture people mercillessly, and was going to kill you. About halfway through the first level your given the option to spare or kill him. The right answer is to spare him because "who are you to decide who lives and dies?"
It has some ok moral quandaries, like whether or not to kill the rat guy early on who has only been nice to you, whether or not to ruin some blind guys paintings just to save time getting a blueprint, whether or not to help someone who is living in constant agony, whether to kill or save the guy the rats were going to eat, etc. This is all Stuff that you can morally go to and say "yes thats good, no thats bad" to most people because its so brain dead stupid what the right choices are.
I don't directly blame the devs for this issue mind, having any complex answers with a black and white morality system is incredibly hard to do right. No, I blame it for using these complex situations at the end for measuring the ending you get. It should have been left to the player to decide whether they were right or wrong, else it just comes off as condescending, biased, or based in religious beliefs.
I won't say that you cant have a game with these kinds of opinions, where the idea of what is "right" is one of the three i said earlier. It just needs to be handled better, a good example being the beginners guide. While the beginners guide asks some far different questions, they are just as complex as the ones in this game. It never answers them, or uses your choices to determine an ending. No, instead the beginners guide ends with hinting at the writers idea of what is "morally right," without ever outright saying that he IS right.
Either way, in the case of this game, the ending prolly shouldnt have relied on these morality questions. Instead, it should have just had a singular ending that leaves everything grey. You dont need to write every interesting part about a characters story, just to where it needs to end.
In my opinion if the game ended 5 minutes earlier i woulda said its amazing, even if the game never explained itself itd fit the artistic style and world so much better. If it ended at that point, it would just be you riding an elevator down for what seems like eternity, remembering a phylisophical idea about what youve experienced and require the player to answer the questions on their own. They could expand that and hint at their ideas of what was right and wrong, maybe having the character just remembering his life and why he was there, and what the stakes were. If they did that, it would have had just enough hinting at the bias the writers had without slapping it in my face.
Overall, amazing art, good puzzles (few head scratchers but no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t,) and overall a nice well optimized game with decent story. The ending just felt condescending and religiously focused, and i cant overlook that.

The first adventure game I recall playing was Adventure and Zork on my Atari 800XL. I sucked at both, and don't recall I ever completed either, or even got pass the first or second rooms! By the time I got my first PC I'd missed most of the golden age of point and click adventures and didn't really buy any until a few years back when GoG first got started. Since then I've bought and played quite a few, but this is the first "remastered" game I've played.
Gabriel Knight is a pretty ace game. I think I'll have to buy the originals from GoG so that I can check out the second and third games as they (currently) don't have a remastered version. It will also be interesting to see how the original voice cast works (Michael Dorn is always a favorite of mine). It will also be interesting to see the old graphics - the Anniversary Edition content doesn't really show much, bar some very very low res images of the different locations.
As for the remake. Well. At first I thought I was going to hate the game as I didn't like Gabriel's voice at all. Fortunately that passed and I got used to it. I thought the voice acting was well done, and the audio overall fit nicely.
Graphically, the game is pleasing, often with photorealistic textures and subtle animations. But at the same time, the 3D feel of the game is decidely "off". Scenes look flat with 3D characters just plonked on top. Hard to describe but readily visible. Mind you, it didn't detract too much from the game, and the fact that the backgrounds were more subtly coloured than interactive objects meant that it was easier to see things to pick up etc, without the asinine "glow" effects that modern games have embraced. The comic book style cut scenes were nice too.
The story was pretty cool and kept me interested all the way through.
There were some minor bugs though, for example at once point my journal got updated with an entry. Fair enough you might think, the journal updates as you progress through the game. Unfortunately it updated with an entry which had nothing to do with the puzzle I'd just solved, but instead with a piece of information that was a bit of a spoiler for part of the game I'd yet to do. Slightly annoying, but nothing too serious. More humourous were the occasions where the characters perhaps thought they were Beetlejuice, and their heads would rapidly spin around. Happened a few times and got a good chuckle each time.
Some of these adventure games are hit and miss with me, and are either incredibly easy, or so difficult I just end up following the script from a walkthrough. GK was inbetween this, I did have to revert to a walkthrough two or three times (although it has a built in hint system I never activated it), but on the whole the game was logical (albient occasionally bizzare in said logic) and not to taxing on the old noggin.
Final game score 360/362... dammit Jim!

A modernized edition of the one of the greatest adventures ever made. Not much was changed, and that's probably for the best. It's enjoyable whether one did or did not play the original (I would imagine much more for the latter category).
Pros
- Better graphics. You do not have to stare at pixels anymore to experience one of the best stories in PC adventure gaming history.
- A pretty faithful rendition of the original puzzles. Not much "remaking" done.
- Some of the cutscenes beat the original even.
- Voice acting is surprisingly ok all things considered.
- Some interface improvements (like ability to highlight all the hotspots).
Cons
- Occasional graphics bugs and animation blunders. Not nearly as bad as in Cognition though.
- A couple of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ puzzles added that were not in the original game. Minor issue.
- Some people (like Kotaku reviewers) might find the game lacks atmosphere somewhat. Though I do agree with the statement, it wasn't game breaking for me pesonally.

I'm one single starfighter versus a legion of troops, tanks, AA turrets, fighters, interceptors, frigates, gunboats, carriers, and dreadnoughts.
Those legions don't stand a chance.
------------------------------------------------
This game starts you off as a "Federal Hero", in a galaxy that is no longer at war. You are unemployed, down on your luck, and left with no choice but to be a hired gun for the scum you were fighting against not so long ago.
Your ship, if you can call it that, is all but falling apart. You have barely enough money for lunch, let alone a better gun... but if there is one thing this cesspit of a galaxy always needs, its a mercenary.
So off you go, doing what you can to get by, only to stumble upon a threat so huge it will literally destroy reality itself. Not only that, but it just so happens to be masterminded by the one target that got away from you and your Federal Hero allies all that time ago. Its time to go hunting.
------------------------------------------------
JnG is a sidescrolling 2D shoot 'em up, kinda like MetalSlug, but you are a spaceship, so... you can go anywhere on the screen. The screen itself will always be moving, except for a few boss fights.
The soundtrack of this game was pretty much entirely done by the awesome metal band "Machinae Supremacy", and is pulse pounding from start to finish.
The BRRRT, and ZZZZZTTT of the guns & the BTOOM, and KRAKOOM of the explosions are spot on.
The crazy light show you will be offered by your gigantic arsenal of weapons is beautiful in its own twisted way.
The universe you are thrown into is bizzare, but feels plausable. It is diverse and insane. One minute you are fighting your way out of a Dogman starport, the next you are busting through an insane perfectionist's persoanl spacestation/wardrobe, then you are jetting over a magma spewing fireplanet.
As you progress through the missions and even the playthroughs of the game (it auto puts you into a newgame+, you keep all your weapons/upgrades/etc) you unlock more and more tools of mass destruction, almost all of which can be upgraded in some way, from adding more barrels to your chaingun, to adding additional energy shielding to your ship, and many more inbetween.
This is the perfect game to blow off some steam, and to make you feel like an absolute badass.

As you can see, didn't play the game very long and that's purely because of the gameplay, fps, and physics. Even on medium settings for the more taxing graphical options (like shadows, particles and density) fps still feels very low and the cars seem sluggish to respond to controls like there is some sort of input lag or delay.
Physics for collision, especially against other cars needs HUGE improvement. The two races I played vs bots were already annoying, I can't imagine playing vs other actual players. Bots can be very aggressive and completely uncaring about positioning of you and others' cars, they're perfectly fine ramming the crap out of you even in straight sections of the road, they may straight up ram you in the back or side if you're in their way. If you or another car hits you, it's like you get stuck to their car and can be hard to get away depending on what the AI feels like doing. Doesn't seem to be any actual damage to cars, even if you crash into a center divider straight on not much happens, you just kind of bounce off or get pushed to the side of it after slowing you down and you continue on.
The worst thing that put me off from keeping this game is that there are mobile-game type "waiting" mechanics thrown into it. Every race your cars durability goes down by 20%, fine I get it. But it takes 45 minutes to have it repaired OR you can use in-game credits to repair it. Initially it doesn't seem like a lot of money, however, I fear that it will get worse later on in the game as most games that employ this sort of mechanic tend to do. There are upgrades you can purchase for your car obviously, not sure if there is waiting thrown into that so check other reviews.
Physics of the actual driving are very... grippy I guess you can call it. You can take corners extremely easily even very sharp ones using keyboard by just holding down left or right. Typically you would have to just tap on a direction (for keyboard) let go of gas, or brake before corners or a combination of all 3 most of the time. In this game unless you're going max speed you can just hold a direction without doing anything else and your car will take the corner perfectly fine.
Honestly I would wait to purchase it. For 10 dollars I mean you might enjoy it, but I don't know how many people are playing this, the two races I played were vs bots, you have to wait about 2 minutes then it throws you in a game with bots. So for each race you have to wait 2 minutes if it doesn't find people to match you against which can be annoying if it happens frequently. It's not open world either so you can't even drive around or do anything while you're waiting, it's a lobby type of system you would find in fps games. I don't think people fans of sim racing would like this and even people who are arcade racing fans, I dunno, the physics are just too wonky and unsatisfying for me.
You can do MUCH better at 10 dollars no matter what you're looking for. Sim racing? Pcars and Assetto Corsa when they're on sale have been 10-13 dollars. More arcadey? NFS Shift 1/2 or GRID 1/2 or the numerous other older racing games you can buy around that same price range. If this was f2p maybe I would have recommended it, maybe, but even then I would wait to play it.

So, after all those years, it has finally come, although under another dev's wings.
TL;DR: physics is a combination of the ol' NFS World and Drift City, car balance needs a lot of work, but the races online seem to be straight out of Initial D, which is great if you got some Eurobeat blasting. Overall I've really enjoyed the game, win or lose.
The matchmaker waits for a bout 2 minutes before filling up the rest with bots. There also are bets and well, they're bets, dont take a bet you cant win, dummy, but it's hard to progress without winning bets, but if there are a few bots in the game the medium bet should be pretty easy to complete. If you got 8 players on the other hand...ohboy. If you got 5+ bots? try to complete the hard bet, which still can be tough but very rewarding.
The physics: No, this is NOT a simulator, nor a simcade, this is proper arcade. With FWD cars you cant properly drift though, but with the RWD cars you actually lose a bit less speed on corners than with grip driving, but always drifting isnt viable on technical bits as drifting needs "settling time": No grip-no grip-grip-GRIP-GRIP. Dirt actually slows you down, a lot, so thats good.
The customization: there's like 3 choices each for every bit of the car, the game is lacking some rims, but those could very well come in the nearby future, and liveries are "coming soon". Overall I'm pleased.
The cars: 3+ choices every class, but some are most definitely better than others, as the car specs are realistic, and the 0-200 time matters the most on the tracks you'll drive as a beginner.
The tracks: you get about 3 tracks as a rookie, but as you progress into faster cars you'll also get more technical tracks, like the Nordschleife, road California, other sections of existing areas... The races are short, about 2-3 minutes, so this game doesn't suffer from Dota2-itis where you have to cancel all arrangements just to play a single game.
WARNING: from class B to D the GT86/BRZ is by far the best car at the moment, purchase wisely. Although you may have to spend some diamonds to unlock the right car for the next class, which is a huge annoyance. Either that or youll have to grind a bit with a car you dont really want.

The game is quite fun, but it's not without issues, so I shall list all the problem spots that I have found...
- First off, the anti-ram system is pretty bad, you can try all you like to avoid colliding with other players but a massive crap storm will happen as a result. I have gotten spun out from random lag and there was nobody around me but I get spun around 180 degrees for no reason at all... The best option is to turn off anti-ram entirely because it’s much easier to deal with a rammer yourself than have a computer do it for you.
- Second off, the game is a massive farming fest. Nothing completely wrong with that, but it would be nice if you could get a lot more credits for completing races. Right now it’s near impossible to buy and upgrade your cars while you’re progressing through the levels. You either have you play with stock cars online, or not have enough money to buy a higher level car when you unlock one. A single player mode that works the same as multiplayer mode (with bets and dealership points); but not allow you to earn XP; would be a great addition. That way you can work towards upgrading your car to the highest level before embarking to play multiplayer mode, then unlock a higher level car and play single player mode to max it out.
This was the only issues that I could think of right now; this list will be updated whenever I think of other issues with the game. But overall the game is quite enjoyable and I recommend it.

Remake of the of one of the most iconic Sierra Online adventure games.
To those who haven't had the chance to play the original 1993 game, the anniversary edition offers rich and captivating story and interesting puzzles in fairly current graphics cloth.
To those who played the original, the remake may prove to be a dissapointing experience as a lot of the original charm has been lost in the translation to the contemporary cloth and may be better off to setting up the game from original cd-rom in dosbox.
GOOD:
Excellent story woven into a detailed and captivating background of voodoo, mystery, murder and horror which is just as good today as it had been in 1993, when it first came out.
Interesting puzzles and great dialogue
BAD:
Conversion from original 2D to 3D is bit underwhelming. While technically there's nothing much complain, the 3D reimagination lacks stylization and atmosphere of the original. As a result, the 3D art feels very sterile and soul-less, as if it had been entirely outsourced to an external company moving mechanically through the motions, having very little involvement in what they had been building.
Voiceover is well done and asides from a few kinks acceptable to the ear. Performances of individual actors are quite agreeable, but fail to fill the huge shoes of the original cast of Tim Curry, Mark Hamill, Michael Dorn, Virginia Capers and others.  Particuarly the role of Gabriel performed by Tim Curry was so excellent that lack of it in the remake is quite off-putting.
On a personal note, i'd much rather see a remake of GK3 which was really interesting story-wise but features horrible 3D graphics.

I have over 100 hours each in the three previous versions of Duel of the Planeswalkers, but after hearing the awful reviews, I waited until I found Magic 2015 on sale to pick it up.  And after only an hour, I'm about to give up and go back to the 2014 version. The earlier versions were fun because completing each deck build was a minigame, without having to worry about the literally hundreds of different builds that the actual game has. So for this revision, they've decided to limit your starting deck and then make you work for expansion cards that you thenexamine to seet if they fit with your deck. It's like someone said "Let's make a system that combines the complexity that some players hate in our the full Magic game with the constraints that the people who like original Magic hate!"
And the UI was designed for tablets by someone who clearly just hates the human species. Each option kind of rolls along the screen, so you can only see the description of each option one at a time and they added sound and graphics to menu choices. If I want to flip over from a match to increase my screen resolution, for example, I have to wander blindly through two sets of menus with several seconds of CGI whooshing effects to tell me that I'm entering the options menu. Imagine the previous versions' menu system with its vaguely annoying side swiping function, but redesigned by someone who thinks players don't want to know what choices are available, where those choices might be located, and don't want to get there anytime soon. I guess if you think discovering the sound options is a minigame, you might enjoy it.
I'm not sure I would recommend this game to anyone, since I've got over 300 hours in various versions and am gritting my teeth.

It's funny, before I played Hearthstone I used to think that the interface in DotP was pretty okay.  It's still better than Magic Online, but it's basically crap.  It feels like it's made for consoles and the Steam version is an afterthought.
I'll pick one small example of why this game is designed poorly.  I'm a longtime Magic player, and have played other DotP games, so I picked Planeswalker difficulty and went right to the end of the tutorial, and then onto the first game of the campaign.  At some point in the game, I wanted to cast a spell using certain mana.  I knew that this was something previous games wouldn't always let you do.  So I hunted around in the options for a check box related to it.  I tried one marked "Auto Lands" but that didn't do anything.  Anyway, when I cast the spell, a prompt came up saying "Press the mana choice key to choose how to cast this spell".   Sounds easy, right?  Well I have no way to know what key that is.  I hunted back in the options for a "Controls" setting, but there's none there.  Before I could locate a help page or something that might tell me what key it is, the game crashed.  When I restarted, my progress in the game was lost.  The 20 minutes I had just spent grinding down the AI's zombie deck while I was mana screwed was for nothing.
How could this have been prevented?  Simple!  The prompt should have said "Press the mana choice key (KEY NAME) to choose how to cast this spell".  But instead of getting a useful prompt, the game persists in presenting me with the "continue" button even when there is no game action I could possibly take.  I'm not going to bluff the AI! The game should really be run in the equivalent of "F8" mode from Magic Online, or at least have the option.  "Auto-continue when no actions are possible" it could say.
Okay, whatever, I've already wasted more time with this than I shoud have.  I'll go back to playing Hearthstone now.

Excellent game, expansion of Mount & Blade: Warband that includes guns, grenades, and more. If you haven't played Mount & Blade: Warband yet, I highly suggest you go there first. This game serves more as an expansion on Warband.
Pros: interesting and indepth war based in central and eastern europe, at the outbreak of gunpowder warfare. Firearms add a new depth to battle situations, and allow for more strategy when controlling your units. Seige mechanics have been greatly improved (mostly in the fact that not everyone is trying to cram themselves onto ONE ladder to seige the castle), including more diverse town and fortress layouts. Multiplayer is improved again with better seige battles, and the popular survival-squad type game mode.
Cons: Does take a while to get going and have a decent sized army. Certain units are greatly overpowered (looking at you Swedish Reiters). Unable to buy stores and businesses in this version, and weapon diversity is down from the last game.
Overall, excellent niche game for those who have played games such as Total War or Age of Empires, and have wanted to experience personal action on the battlefield, or if you like Chivalry, try your hand at commanding your forces.

For Honor.
TL;DR: 5/10. Not really worth it.
---The good.---
Singleplayer: I was expecting this game to have the same situation Brink had, where it was literally just multiplayer with bots. This game has its own singleplayer, with only two of said maps converted into multiplayer maps. There's horse chases, assorted siege weaponry and a well voiced narrative to go with the ample amount of cutscenes in the campaign. The cutscenes aren't too long, and don't overstay their welcome, yet still explain the story of the game well. The singleplayer got ample amounts of love.
Ambience: It's very rare that an art department fails to impress, For Honor's art department was no exception. The ambience is beautiful, even if you run the game at minimum settings like me. There's a lot of fitting decorations for the characters, scenery and environments. The environments even change, depending on what faction is currently winning the faction war in that area. The armor is believable and isn't 'John Smith' levels of generic, with a surprising amount of things you can do with it.
Balance: I will have more to say about this when we get to the 'bad', but first, I will say good things about it. There is no 'one class beats all'. While some strengths are best applied to other classes, you are not doomed to lose every time because you're a Conquerer pitted against a Orochi.
Gamemodes: The gamemodes are fun. Dominion is the traditional conquest mode, a 4v4 setup where there are points to capture and a constant tug of war between the two armies that must be influenced by the player in order to hold. Brawl is the 4v4 deathmatch mode, where there is no respawning and no armies or objectives to hold. Lastly, there is 2v2 and 1v1 duels, which disable item levels entirely and allow you to fight to the death for the best of 5 rounds. All fun, easy to get into, easy to get out of.
Optimization: EDIT!: This is no longer applicable! The newest patch has ruined its performance!
Animations: The animations in this game are very well captured. They're all very believable (though those with interests in HEMA might cringe from the hollywood-like actions they take) and flow like water.
DLC plans: It actually makes me happy that they're following Rainbow Six Siege's mode of DLC, where all of the in-game content such as maps can be accessed freely, and the characters and items that come from it can be purchased with in-game currency (albeit at an expensive price).
------
---The bad---
Balance, an addendum: There is a lot of frustrating class designs which I truly do not understand why they thought it was a good idea.  Peacekeeper? Nobushi? Why commit to a fight when you can just put a bleed on someone and back off? Orochi? Just guard break and get a free overhead heavy attack, you're so fast at literally every attack you get. Afraid that the fight might not go your way? Oh well! Just sprint away until you can find a ladder to cheese your opponents to their death on, or until help arrives. Shigoki? No point in trying to trip them up. You can't shove them, you can't knock them down with any charging attacks from the Raider, Conquerer, Warlord and other classes. Their heavy attacks also cannot be interrupted by simply attacking them, and they have a back breaker attack, which, if you are just a little less than 40% HP, will just flat out kill you.
Mechanics: Item levels (that you can just buy with real money, no need to unlock them fairly, and they're only disabled on duels). I can stop right there. No competitive game should ever give you a way to get a leg up over your opponent. All rewards should be cosmetic, in my opinion. Guard breaks punish you for being good at parrying, and the current meta is to land as many guard breaks as possible to ensure free hits. Ladders can be dwelled on, there is no knocking you off unless you have a ranged ability from the berserker or orochi and if someone climbs up to punch you off, you can just drop yourself on them and send them to their deaths. There are an /abundance/ of environmental kills, from lava, to water, to cliffs, to spikes, to pits. They are /the/ most unsatisfying way to die in this game, and yet the developers think that it's just fun to add instant death holes everywhere in a meta that strongly encourages guard breaks that can be used in shoves. Revenge mode. Put yourself in a bad place where you are about to die? Just get revenge mode, and get un-interruptable attacks and extra health to weather the storm with! And lastly, parrying weakens the attacker, not the defender. It allows you to play patiently, and there is no pressure you can apply to the enemy.
Controller superiority: This game was designed for a controller. No PC game should be designed around a controller instead of a keyboard and mouse. Not even Castle Crashers or Dark souls got a pass on this.
'Dis'honor: There is no respect in this game. If you wanted good sportsmanship, you will not find it here. It rewards you for being a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to strangers.
Peer to peer hosting: Ubisoft, you have not done this in any of your other games, why on earth do you think this was a good place to start? With frequent disconnects, failures to join lobbies and poor connections to people from across the sea, peer to peer hosting is perhaps the biggest shot to the foot this game could have suffered.
Microtransactions: You can buy your way to glory. Forget earning all of your stuff. Want to be item level 80 before the game reaches its 72 hour mark? Start spending. It has literally allowed people to do 3v1s in deathmatch games.
-----
For Honor, like most games, has good things about it, yet has squandered so much potential. It could have been so much better. Chivalry, War of the Roses and Mount and Blade Warband did a lot of things that avoided these pitfalls that this game hit along the way, and deep inside I ask myself; why didn't they just look at their competitors and take the best from each game?
It is, at its core, an 'okay' game. It just barely passes. But this game will be buried and forgotten by its worthy successors next year.

What I like the most of this game is the skill cap. If servers are set up properly, players have a skillcap so they cannot master everything in the game. They have to chose what they want to do. This gives a real reason to teamup with others and play together as everyone will specialize in his own path. This skill cap applies for the combat as much as the crafting part of the game. So you have to make choice and stick to it. You cannot be a two handed master and at same time be the best archer. You have to chose or make 2 different characters and then raise them separatly which is just amazing and way more realisitc. Indeed, it's always possible to FORGET what you learned and learn something new. But then you'll have to swap the sword for the bow, etc.
The building is different than those Minecraft block style games. All those games like 7DaysToDie, ARK, etc... You have to craft some materials then put them together the shape you want. Not in Life Is Feudal: Your own (abreviation: LIFYO). LIFYO, you already have the blueprints. All you need to do is prepare the land to place the blueprints. Then you have to gather materials and build. Indeed, you cannot access all the blueprints as they are part of the progression system. So you have to be a builder in order to place blueprints and then build them. This said, everyone (or close to that) can gather some materials to help like cutting woods or digging for stone). So it's always possible to help build your village without being the carpenter or doing any masonery.
It's also fun that there is a weight system. You cant carry a mountain and fly like a light bird. Since stone is awfuly heavy and you will carry not much and be fast as a turtle while carrying, they introcuded the cart. So yes, you can fill a cart and then pull it which is far more realistic than those games where you carry a forest, a zoo and/or the entire minerals of the planet in a little bag. That's what make the game heavy grinding but also very fun and rewarding. Building a house is hard. But when you manage to build a small village, after hours and hours of work, you feel happy. Way more happy than building a tower 1000000 feet tall in Minecraft where there is absolutely no building challenge as physics don't exist and it's easy to gather bilions materials and roam around with them to build. Minecraft is for people that want to build very fancy huge customized structures. If you want more simple one but very hard to build as in real medieval life, LYFIO is by far a better choice.
The game offers various way to entertain ourselves. Yes you can gather ressources and build stuff. But you also can tame animals, have a farm, go for hunting or fishing... and hunting is about setting traps OR chasing some wild animals to kill them and get their meat and skin. And those weapons you need to hunt, well, you have to unlock them! They are part of the choices you have to do. Indeed it's easier to be hunter with a bow but you cannot be a two handed sword master and an archer at the same time. You have to make a choice (assuming you are playing on a server applying those skill cap limitation).
The materials you gather also have quality. Sometime, you have to hunt for quality and try various spot before starting to gather. Higher quality materials will give better crafting results. The buildings will have more hit points, the armors/tools/weapons will last longer while using them, the food will resplendish more hunger, etc.
What I dislike is: they wanted to make a real game.. the grinding mimic the reality alot.. it's painful to build something.. just as it was in real life.. but the only survival stats is the HP (as every game where you can fight) and hunger.. nothing else.. for such a realistic game, they could have cared of more.. like thirst? like need for sleep? like sickness (that would give a reason to the healer to exist cuz else, it's only useful when 2 folks wanna beat each others to incrase they skills.. meh)? or the fact a human being as to keep warm (especially during winter)? This game lacks those things. It's realistic on gathering and building. Why not pushing it a bit further for the characters needs too? Would have been amazing.
Again, this is a very good game. Dont be fooled by the bad reviews. I played close to 30h and I felt I have done nothing yet. And I'm just excited to reconnect later with friends to play more. It's very addictive.

Unreal-Based Games tend to be good, this one is absolutely beautiful. A hand sculpted map leads the way as one of the absolutely best features, with the unique play-style and leveling system coming close behind. The Nether themselves are improving, and still can make you jump, but unless you're quiet and sneaky, expect to die often early on. PKers can ruin your day, and Phosphor has under-preformed on the curbing of Kill-on-Sight tactics. Clipping in the map kind of kills the immersion, but the collision meshes are a steadily improved feature. All in all, this game plays well as any, if not better, than most survival games on the market today. I'd wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of the genre.
