Quick Summary – Amnesia is an “immersive horror” game with emphasis on creepy atmosphere and puzzle solving. Don’t go in expecting an action packed fight for survival. If you don’t enjoy running from enemies and sneaking around in the dark, you may want to look elsewhere.
You play a man named Daniel in the 1800’s who has chosen to erase his own memory, and wake up in an unfamiliar deserted castle, looking for a way out. Unfortunately, the only way out is to descend into the cursed innards of the castle as your sanity slowly drains away. As you progress, you find notes and diary pages detailing some of the events which have led to your current circumstances. The darkness is not your only enemy.
The game is played in first person perspective and while this is familiar to most gamers, keep in mind that you cannot fight enemies. All you can do is run and hide if you run into a monstrosity in the halls. To make matters worse you don’t just have limited health, you also have limited sanity, which is drained by witnessing disturbing events (objects moving on their own or unworldly environments) or by standing too long in the darkness. When you are unfortunate enough to run into a monster, don’t just run and hide, don’t even look at it. The more you look at a monster the more likely it is to become aware of your presence. Yeah, the monsters aren’t really roaming the halls chasing after intruders, but if they notice you, they’ll definitely squash you.
As mentioned before, a large part of the game is puzzle solving, such as trying to unlock new areas to advance by manipulating levers or mixing ingredients together in your limited inventory. If you’re used to games spelling out mission objectives or quests, you’re going to have a hard time.
Pros:
+Immersive game story with some genuinely tense and terrifying sequences (water monster…)
+Some challenging puzzles to get your brain working
Cons:
-The game can be frustrating since the solutions to a lot of the puzzles are not obvious, and you have the added pressure of working in the darkness under threat from monsters.
Overall, the game is not for everyone but if you like games such as Outlast, you should enjoy the horror element of Amnesia. Just bear in mind that the puzzle solving can be a real pain for first time players.

I have been waiting for this game to come out ever since NFS World servers were shut down because everyone said that this was its replacement and I am disappointed to say that it's NOT. Not even close. That said, I'm not saying that it's a bad thing, because this game is more of a replacement to Auto Club Revolution (ACR) by Eutechnyx than to NFS World, or at least right now, the bare bones of it.
The PROS:
- Graphics in this game look really nice. Everything to the sky, the surrounding buildings (if you are on a street circuit), the trees look stunning.
- Queue times for multiplayer races last up to a maximum of around two minutes. If the timer comes close to two minutes and has yet to find anyone, the game will just drop you in a "singleplayer" race against seven AI, which will pretty much give you an easy win if you don't mess it up or the AI are less aggressive (see CONS for details about the AI)
The CONS:
- Track list thus far is very underwhelming. There are only five locations to race at (Côte d'Azure, California Highway, Nürburgring Nordschleife, Moscow and San Francisco) along with their sectors being individual sprint races (Moscow and San Francisco have modifications to them because they are street circuits). I would have expected more, like Spa, Silverstone, Hockenheimring, etc.
- AIs in this game are both too easy, and very aggressive (and/or dumb, I can't tell). If you manage to get a lobby by yourself with seven other AIs, get to first place immediately and leave them to there own activities because they will ram you into a wall.
- No ghosting option (as of yet), meaning there will be a lot of collisions.
- No manual transmission as of yet.
- Visual and miscellaneous bugs/glitches
The IN-BETWEEN:
- There is customization in this game, albeit not NFS 2015 level customization, but customization is there nonetheless.
- Car list is decent, but is very outdated and not very large.
- The physics are mostly based around PROJECT CARS, with a small hint of NFS into it in drifting because it's not too difficult to master it. You will have to manage the car's steering and throttle while drifting, but it's mostly tap the handbrake and control it.
- Premium Cars are cars that are maxxed out and have free custom parts already unlocked that increase XP, Credits and Dealer Points by 50% after races. They can be bought using Diamonds, a secondary currency that uses real money to get more of. These cars are optional if you don't want to spend countless hours grinding at the game.
If you want(ed) a replacement to NFS World, this is not the game. The Crew (both the first one and the upcoming second one) and Forza Horizon (1, 2 or 3) are better options for that because they're both open world and you can do whatever you want with whatever car you choose. However, if you want(ed) a replacement to ACR, then this is it, or at least the start of it. Not perfect, but it's something.

I like the game concept, but I feel as though the black market is detrimental to it. You are meant to outfox the other companies, by speculating on price and going after the resources that will be needed. It's like playing MULE or Settlers of Catan. Imagine Microsoft, instead of competing for market share with Apple based on innovation, could just nuke one of Apple's manufacturing plants. That's not how it works. I try not to give meaningless reviews, so I put some time in the game before deciding to recommend it. Perspective: I have played the original Magic game in the 90's, and I did get the 2012 edition of the game. I do not play IRL Magic.
Pros: 1) DECK BUILDING! I despised that I could not actually craft a meaningful deck in any of the prior games like 2012.
2) Multiplayer seems relatively stable in 1v1 duels, which is what I usually play online.
3) The AI is reasonablystrong, although it does get a bit predictable with extended playing.
4) I am disappointed that WOC seems far more interested in their pocketbook than customers' enjoyment. The  pandering to buy DLC is rather demoralizing. The good news here is that if you just PLAY THE GAME through,  and are willing to go win a few duels online, you can get all of the cards that are available in the DLC for free.
Cons: 1) The fact that some of the higher end decks you fight in the single player mode have cards that you are not  allowed access to again speaks to the fact that the game is more about filling WOC's pocket than providing an experience that is as good as playing the IRL card game. That said, I still feel it was worth the $10 or so I spent on the game and the expasion. It would be nice if these cards were added to the player pool at some point.
2) Again, you (don't) get what you (don't) pay for: the single player game is bereft of almost all semblances of a  single player game: animations, cut scenes, etc. There may be a total of 25 seconds of unique graphics in the entire base game, including the intro animation. The original 90's game had a significantly better developed plot and GUI for travelling and having random encounters/duels.
3) Others have complained that the multiplayer lacks certain 3- and 4-player options that were present  previously. I cannot comment on this, but you can read others' reviews for the details.
In short, the game is not perfect, but few games are. I find it a good way to blow off some steam playing online 1v1 or vs. the AI, but it is not a game you will spend 100 hours or 100 dollars on. Get it for cheap on sale, and enjoy what is there.

As a person retaining a rank of honorary SGT due to having been the first to join my current Milsim (that is still growing with 20+ members that I consider as good friends) unit during its times of getting its legs up in February of 2016, and with 2k+ hours, I feel like as though this game deserves a rounded - if not biased - review with my personal views on this game.
Arma 3 is a game that has - with addition is renown for - its many very kinks or visible flaws such as Desynchronization lag, Low FPS, occasional crashes, impossible deaths, and with all that other jazz. But however, it all doesn't boil down to those small kinks that judge your decision out of the box, rather when the gameplay draws and sucks you in.
Whether you like systematic, logical, as well as analytical thinking or planning, or just, "♥♥♥♥ it," going in there with no plan. Or if you're just looking for an adrenaline rush from a slow paced, but also fast-paced feeling game of which engagements can be taken or affected in many ways ranging from terrain features, engagement distance, time of day, opposition count, available vehicular support, and so so much more, this game with all of its game modes and casual or sim communities can very much provide you with that. I can talk to each and every person in my Milsim community, I'd know they love this game very much due to the experiences they've had in this game from beginning to end.
Arma 3's combined arms add more to it as well with the 3 main militarized factions containing vehicles from both air to ground that's specialized to a task and with their own feel. It's just spectacular as well to engage in large-scale combat or to just spectate furthermore watching it unfold with heavy tanks maneuvering together engaging methodically with scary precision, helo's going low and slow to avoid anti-air, or just regular ol' combat infantry tracers at night. This is also not to include the new amount of new vehicles still approaching or have arrived from DLC.
Arma's Multiplayer aspect and Modding Capability is the main focus on here as well being the selling point of the game. The multiplayer can range from a small group to a hundred or more people. Each mission can also be pre-configured via Eden editor or file editor outside of the game. Based on the editor's skills it can range from a simple mission to a very complex and in-depth mission. Or even a game mode like the famous KoTH, Wasteland, or original PUB: G based playerunknowns game mode in Arma, "Battle Royale."
I'd also like to add that single player is really not recommended and that I recommend you play with friends or just random people. It will make it a better experience I guarantee you. However, I'm not forcing but just suggesting you do so for a better experience.
Lets also not forget the modding facet as well. It is a major part of the community of which allows Arma's flexibility with increased depth. Hundreds to thousands of mods on and off the steam workshop ranging from a Parkour mod, Combat environment enhancements, custom maps, along with even an abundant more. Each and every mod is different/special in a way adding their own spice of life to Arma's already spectacular environment.
I personally loved looking at flying aircraft since I was small. Flying in this game though makes me feel free like a bird from doing near impossible scary looking maneuvers in either combat or non-combat areas that could only be accomplished with learning from millions of crashing and deaths that caused much embarrassment. Crashings and deaths that were, of course, the learning wedge of the game.
Arma's learning core is very much to say a huge one if you were to play it as a military tactical or sim shooter. Each player will feel very overwhelmed with the number of controls in-game but I assure you it is not that scary. Taking it slow will very much help, as well as learning very basic navigational tools if you haven't already.
This game very much requires you also to think about each action before acting upon it, albeit sometimes also requiring you to also have fast reflexes as well in certain situations. I can, however, tell you that even then, a player with barely 5 hours can still wreck a player with over 2k hours I assure you.
Arma's graphics are of course nothing to gossip about but they're acceptable. Sound wise I would say it's not better but okay, sometimes muted. They're good enough to immerse you into the gameplay. The sound is not perfect but it replicates life close enough. There is a delay of sound from distanced sounds so sound takes time to travel. Albeit from personal experience, sound is not affected by the environment.
The four current maps, however - Stratis, Altis, Malden, and Tanoa if you have Apex - are greatly crafted maps to explore being real "based on" islands with small towns and urban city areas.
Tanoa is a new but great South Pacific based tropical map with dense jungles in addition to bustling industrial life, it greets new or old players with tropical and urban combat along with hidden ruins.
Bohemia Interactive or BI releases DLC based on their roadmap and are known to not lock basic systems from each DLC (Like aircraft sensory systems from Jets DLC) behind a paywall. I can list off every DLC but I'll cut it short with the majors being Jets; Apex; Laws of War; Eden; and Zeus.
The latest DLC released being the codenamed Orange DLC, "Laws of war," focusing on a different perspective on the civilian side of war and relief efforts. With the major DLC having released a campaign as well focusing on such perspectives. This also applies to one other such as Apex, of which has had a 4 player Coop campaign released on the island of Tanoa.
The main campaign, however, is not much to talk about. I haven't personally completed it yet but I am looking to completing it soon. Tanoa's story adds much more to the main campaign but not too much to the point of where you need to finish the main story to know what is going on since it focuses on a bit more of action. Laws of war is completely different but focuses on a story of an IDAP (International Development Aid Project) explosive specialist who is tasked with defusing and explaining the story behind a bomb-riddled town of Oreokastro.
Arma 3 continues to grow and grow with its many player experiences and achievements. I have played the full game and this review contains no spoilers.
SOMA is not your typical half made jump scare game. Its a true experience where the story and atmosphere creates a believable world. The environments instill fear even though there might be no threat. Moments of the game actually were stressful to experience(fear). The story line is much more immense than most games out there; it will actually get you thinking about the subject yourself; making you more involved in world the game creates. The story and atmosphere will give the feeling of being truly alone. There are a variety of threats. Incredibly detailed environments play perfectly along with the events and story line. Graphical quality is great. Interactions with objects bring you further into the game. There are actually a few choices you can make during the story. There are survey's scattered about the game asking you how you feel about things giving you a glimpse of how your opinion might actually change throughout the experience. Controls are responsive and very easy to use, For the first time ever leaning is actually a useful feature that you should take advantage of. Sound is amazing in this game; ambient, music, and triggered sounds blend together well increasing the depth of atmosphere even more.
There is still a great deal more I could say, but I just finished the game and my mind is blown over how great this experience was.
The only way you could not at least like this game is if you were to make a big deal out of the few glitches or it isn't jump scary enough for you. As always to make sure you get the most of it, you need to play in the dark with a headset fairly loud so you can hear everything, to pay attention to all details, and observe and search as much as possible.
This will go down as one of the best games ever made for me and I will remember it for a long time.

105 Hours in-game at time of writing
Life is Feudal: 6/10
Pros:
- Terraforming makes the ability to modify the world and grow your city around you fantastic.
- Being able to ride horses.
- The "Quality" system where everything you do, make, or grow relies on the quality of everything used.
- Attacking Training Dummies/Archery Targets increase your related weapon skill.
Cons:
- Combat is clunky, slow, and oafish. Fist fighting throws your fists way left/right to where you don't hit what's right in front of you. Archery Is... the worst I could imagine. The longer you hold the arrow, the worse your shot gets, but your arrow goes almost nowhere unless you hold it for several seconds.
- The skill trees have no sense to half of the progression lines. (e.g. to use a bow you have to get 60 leather armor skill then 30 crossbow... because crossbows are worse than bows in this backwards world?... and... to use chainmail armor which is the very first heavy armor... you have to master riding a warhorse...)
- Crossbows are terrible in this game. You can't reload and move at the same time and it takes 3-4 seconds to reload (While anchored in place as someone/something attacks you). This makes hunting with a crossbow useless. Then, to fire this crossbow, you have to hold LMB for several seconds to charge the shot enough to make the bolt go more than a few meters... For a game that says "realistic medieval" they failed that right here because I have never heard of a crossbow that you have to draw and hold like a bow. You load them, you point them, you pull the trigger.
- Melee weapons. The combat system had potential here. The problem is that they made it feel clunky. To clarify, imagine that you were to pick up a stick and swing it like a sword. Good. Now make it to where only the blade part does damage. Fantastic. Now weigh your arms down with weights you can barely lift and swing... Welcome to Combat is Feudal. It's literally a game of stand there and slash each other with this oafish attacks until someone drops. (Notice I'm using oafish a lot? I've played ogre games where the ogres were actually more graceful than this).
- No sharing allowed. You can trade items easily enough but you cannot share your house. If you are playing co-op with a friend and want to share a house with your ONE friend, you have to establish a guild for the two of you and the house must be within the claim boundaries of the guild monument.
- Guild monument... This dumb thing will expect you to feed it your items every day (In-game day not real time day) for "maintenance". Then, it will continue to demand more and more items of better and better quality and refuse anything beneath its demands. It will continue to do this so it can continue to grow and claim more land and, eventually, be upgrade eligible. There is no "Stop growing" or "Quit eating everything you angry wood sword in the ground thing!" button. At first it is easy to keep the maintenance up with two-three people groups but soon you'll find yourself needing to give it items you are barely able to get for yourself just so it doesn't "decay" until it destroys itself.
Overall, the game is fun for a while and the more people you have the more fun you can have with a lot of things in it. But it isn't for me because of the reasons listed here and because I don't like it, I won't be recommending it.

This isn't Amnesia 2.0 and that's a good thing. This is an evolution of the template laid out by Amnesia to tell a kind of story that hasn't been explored this well in the medium before. It's not perfect, but it feels like a true step forward in the slow crawl toward the maturation of videogames.
There are no "Renegade" or "Paragon" black and white moral choices. In fact, they have little to no effect on the story. But you feel them nontheless. Your choices can haunt you.
The game, like most, leans on the trope of audio and text message logs to help fill in the story. In this case, I felt they were *just* long enough to not wear out their welcome. There is also a lot of environmental storytelling that encourages you to let your imagination run wild.
I'm usually pretty bad at traditional adventure games but I was able to complete the game with no outside help. This really helped keep me immersed in the story.

"In the Beast Boxing Leagues of Beasthalla, the strongest monsters fight for fame and fortune."
You are Char, a great fan of Beast Boxing. You dream abotu one day becomming a beast boxer yourself. But there is one problem: you are a human from the slums and humans are not allowed to compete. So you buy a monster costume and trick your way to a qualifying match for the Bush League, the lowest league there is.
And that is where the game starts and you start to jab, cross, hook and uppercut yourself to fame and fortune. And eventually realize that youa re fighting for more than just your dream, but human rights and the place of humanity in a beasty world.
The controls are fairly simple, be it controller or keyboard, requiring only either an analogue stick and two buttons, or the arrow keys and two punching keys. As you progress through the game, you are tought to block, dodge, counter and preserve your stamina through a series of optional tutorial fights.
There are 12 opponents in total to unlock and you can do exhibition matches against any opponent you have defeated. Every fight nets you cash. I am still making my way through this one. Not a bad game by any means, its actually quite enjoyable. The sniping mechanics are well done and fun to play with. You'll have to adjust for distance and wind depending on the difficulty. There are custom difficulty settings which is nice, you can choose which assists you want, but you only have a few choices. For instance, I would like the game to tell me the distance of my target without showing me where to shoot but the custom options do not allow this combination. Measuring distance is one problem I have with the game. On the hardest difficulty, where making the shot is up to you with no assits, it is difficult to measure distance. On most levels it seems that you have a map that will give you a scale you can use to measure (by using your fingers and the screen). On other levels you do not have a scale on the map an you just have to wing it. The game also gives you almost no introduction to the sniper itself. The tutorial will teach you the controls but not how to measure with the sniper scope. This is not a major issue though as there a user made guides and videos that will teach you. I may just be bad but it seems that this is not a stealth game. On some levels you can hide your shots with background noises or sneak around but it seems that nearly every level comes down to you fighting several enemys and sniping at enemys as they rush toward you. I found sneaking very difficult. It is hard to tell when you are well hidden behind an object (when not using the games cover system). It is also difficult to judge the enemys field of view. Perhaps most frustrating is that you can only stealth kill enemys from behind. If they turn just a little so that youre not perfectly behind them youll have to try and kill them with your pistol. Pistol kills can be difficult because the enemies take about 3 torso shots to bing down and each time you shoot them they will stumble to the side making it very hard to get your next shot off before they can put a full clip in you. This is really only a problem when your stealth kill has failed and your up close. A headshot with the pistol will still kill enemies in one shot. You also have to crouch walk (which is extremely slow) if you don't want to be detected. This is not an issue with the game. You can sneak around and kill targets but it seems almost like a waste because before the levels over you'll probably be fighting waves of enemies anyway. In, short if youre looking for a good stealth game this probably isn't it. The game does have good elements though. The sniping is enjoyable and when you kill someone you often get a cool x-ray kill cam. You get to see your bullet travel in slow motion from your gun through your target and it never gets old. If you don't like the feature it can be turned off, or to less frequent, or more if you do like it. You get some cool traps you can set like landmines and trip wires. You can move dead enemies around and hide mines under them so when guards come investigate theyll detonate the mine. Sniper Elite is a good shooter if youre patient, if youre looking for a stealth experience you may want to look elsewhere.

Ahhh.....Gabriel Knight. One of my favorite games of the 90s and definitely one of Sierra's best games.
Gabriel Knight is a novelist and owner of St. George's Rare Books in New Orleans. He's in the middle of writing a new book about the recent string of Voodoo related murders. The writer, Jane Jensen of Sierra fame, did a particularly good job of representing the city of New Orleans and it's vibrant history, and the story itself still holds up well after 20+ years.
It was a little disappointing that they couldn't get Tim Curry to reprise his role as the voice of Gabriel, but I'm sure he was a little too expensive for Pinkerton Road to even consider, let alone the likes of Mark Hamill and Michael Dorn. The actor they got to voice Gabriel in the remake did a commendable job and kept the original style of southern charmer and womanizer, and a few chuckles can be found by using the hand and eye icons on most of the female characters in the game.
While the 3D rendering of the remake brings new life to the game(and it is beautiful), it's a little disappointing to an old school gamer like myself. See, back in the day, adventure games were much more complex and unforgiving. The high resolution textures take the challenge away of having to find a tiny object in the sea of 256 color pixelation of the original.
The puzzles are challenging and require that you pay attention to the information you're gathering from extensive conversations with the various characters in the game. You can't just fumble through this one. if you try, you'll likely be backtracking often or finding yourself using a walkthrough (anyone else remember old Sierra hint books?) in later parts of the game. Fortunately for me, I played through this game several times and actually remembered much of what was required to have the game move forward.
If you want to see where the great adventure games of today got their inspiration from, buy this game and support Jane Jensen's new operation. Then maybe one day the Sierra of old shall return. Nah...scratch that. Just stay small and independent and avoid those buyouts so you can continue to breath new life into the genre.
Now Steam just needs to release Gabriel Knight 2: The Beast Within, but not a remake. It's perfect just the way it is.

REVIEWS DONE QUICK BY MAX TURBO
- Why should you get this?: You're looking for a surprisingly well-written, branching, occasionally emotionally effecting "choose your own adventure" style game that lends itself to playing in short bursts. It also has light management sim elements in it, as you will need to discover the most efficient routes to take around the world, along with buying and selling items to fund your journeys. It also evokes a feel of a fantastic, "bygone" steampunk era remarkably well.
- Why shouldn't you get this?: You dislike reading. There is a ton of reading in this - it's pretty much the main gameplay mechanic, aside from figuring out where and when to leave places from. And speaking of that, I could also see this being stressful to people who don't like to make snap decisions, as you will sometimes need to do as you roll into countries in the nick of time and need to quickly get your bearings to move on to the next area before the local train / car / airship departs.
- Did Max enjoy this?: Yes, very much so. I had heard this game was well written, but I was surprised at how much it ended up digging its narrative hooks into me. I also ended up speaking like an English gentleman for the next couple days, much to the annoyance of everyone around me.
- Similar games to check out: the Sorcery! series, Out There Omega Edition

80 Days is a rich and clever game. The mechanics are both fun and easy to grasp. The minimalist artwork leaves space to the imagination. Above all, the game just has a near endless replayability: this is not only because you may choose new routes and explore different parts of the globe, but because you can completely change Passe-partout's outlook upon the world he encounters. This is of course due to Meg Jayanth's remarkable writing, which goes from being witty to moving, epic, touching, or very dark. The steam-punk world she conjures surpasses its original material, it's vibrant and smart, making us think about different ways in which history could have played out. It's also a model in making diversity work effortlessly in a game. It could have been easy to make this game done-teaf about colonialism, racism, sexism, etc. or engage in the kind of tokenism all too common in mainstream media. Instead diversity and critique are seamlessly woven into the narrative. An intelligent, enjoyable game through and through.

In Short (from my curator review): "Excellent game whose novel Economic-Strategy ideas will hopefully spawn a long lasting genre of this quality. Dispels the notion that strategy=violence."
Longer Form: I am an economics student in graduate school and a sci-fi fan, so as far as I'm concerned OTC was designed specifically for me. The economics & finance in the game is not only fun, but educational and facsinating if you have an interest in those subjects.
I love the strategy genre, and have for years, but having a genre so closely tied to violence: Total War, Company of Heroes, Starcraft, Age of Empires, etc. has always bugged me a little bit. Not because I'm a pacifist, but because it takes away from strategic depth to have such a simple zero-sum mechanic at the core of gameplay. With OTC there are not such clear and basic decisions. In a war game: produce units, more is almost always better. In contrast, OTC can't be won, even on the easiest difficulties, by spamming one type of production. You'll inevitably over-supply that commodity and shrink your profits on each sale down to next to nothing while paying through the nose on whatever inputs are associated with that commodity. Simply put, there's more strategic depth.
The art style is nice, it is simple as of right now and realistically rendered, I wonder whether there is room to convey information more through the art than is currently done. For instance if the ships transporting resources could convey more about their cargo to lessen the emphasis on the ever-present charts.

Note on Early Access: As always, monitor reviews and update logs to note that devs are making progress, but as of the time of writing this review, they are very active and seem to be constantly tweaking and making improvements.
A few minor gripes: 1.) My computer is not a world-beater, but can handle most any games on medium or high, however OTC gives me a little trouble with frame-rate so I've had to go down to low settings, which is a shame for such a pretty game.
2.) In-game UI could use some poish, main menus and what not are gorgeous so I have faith that these will get better.
Recommendation: If you like strategy games you should do one of two things: 1.) Buy it 2.) Wait until it comes out of Early Access, then buy it.

Have you ever played an RTS or 4X game and thought "I wish non-military victories were more viable?"  Well let me tell you about Offworld Trading Company.
In Offworld, you are a company looking to compete with other startups and get rich by mining Mars for as much of the thirteen available resources as possible and drive opponents out of business.  There are NO military units.  Economic victory is the only victory.
There are four factions, but you don't select one until you've had the chance to survey the map.  Resource availability and diversity is randomly generated, giving you the chance to plant the faction you think is best for the environment. APM will not save you, Starcraft fans. Resource tile claims are very limited.  You will NEVER have all thirteen resources immediately.  Some can be extracted on the spot, and others can only be produced by combining resources.  What you can't collect yourself, you can purchase in an always available market where prices fluctuate on your behavior and the behavior of your opponents.
Your "score" is your Share Price.  It is your net worth minus your debt.  You defet other players by buying up massive amounts of their increasingly expensive shares.  When you purchase all of their shares, you get everything they've been building.  Your goal is to buyout all the other players.
The "essential" resources are Water, Oxygen, Food, Fuel and Power.  Will your colony starve if you lack them?  NO!  "Starvation" does not exist, unlike Civ.  You will automatically buy what you need from the market passively and accumulate Debt instead.  Scrambling to acquire them all initially to avoid debt is a beginner's (or Civ player's) mistake.  What good is staving off debt if you grab all those things without producing precious Aluminum or Steel to allow you to upgrade your headquarters and edge closer to victory?  At the same time, you can't ignore them forever, because too much debt reduces your Share Price, allowing players to buy you more easily.
As you upgrade your headquarters, you are provided handfuls of more claims to tiles to help you collect and produce more resources, and build fancier buildings that will help you generate the wealth you need to buyout your opponents.
And then Sabatoge comes into play.  Just because there's no militaries doesn't mean you can't take your opponents down a peg.  The Black Market opens at regular intervals, allowing players to buy EMPs to temporarily disable opposing buildings, fake Mutinies to steal buildings, Dynamite to destroy buildings, or devastating, nonlethal Underground Nukes to permanently reduce the yield of an opponent's production tile.  You can also buy precious claims when you want just one more building without having to upgrade, or Goon Squads that defend buildings from attacks (and then throw them back at opponents).
There are four factions.  Three of them are human and require Water, Oxygen and Food.  The Expansive humans are great if you're hungry for lots of tiles, because they get an extra Claim on a tile every time they upgrade.  They also require less Steel for upgrades.  The Robotic colony doesn't care about Water, Food or Oxygen, but instead require Electronics (the final, most expensive resource) as well as massive amounts of Power.  Scientific colonies have the unique ability to plant production facilities directly on top of a raw resource, therby "skipping" a step.  This is huge if you use it carefully.  My favorite faction, Scavengers, use Carbon instead of Steel and can use the Black Market more frequently.  They are my favorite because while other players are fighting over Iron and spending claims changing that same Iron into Steel, I can just use Carbon for everything (yet they are useless on a map where I can't find Carbon.)  Again, when you play the game, you scan the map for resources FIRST and then choose the faction you think will work best with what you can grab.
As of March 2015 the game is aesthetically rough.  There are only two songs, simple, loud sound effects, and placeholder robotic voices to announce events in game.  Still, I cannot put this game down.  Its positively brilliant and addictive, and it will only get better as the game develops.

To start, this game works.  Almost everything about it is fine tuned and stays refreshingly to it's roots.  I really enjoyed it and have good reasons for it.
Like Amnesia and Penumbra, the SOMA is a survival horror game is told from a first person perspective.  Your character is less mute as other protagonists, but his little quips and lines do not interfere with the horror aspect at all, as they are well paced out and appropriate to the situation at hand.
The gameplay is much like the originals, with a few changes.  The inventory system is back, but not like in Dark Descent.  You collect certain plot-related items and keep them in a small, unaccessable inventory for when they are supposed to be used.  I don't hate this mechanic.  I DO miss collecting consumables such as health potions (laudanum) and oil for my light source because that added another layer of tesion in Amnesia: TDD.  But it isn't all bad.  The light source you have in this game is a head mounted flashlight thay doesn't take batteries, but is rather dim, and if left on for a while it will begin to flicher and get MORE dim.  This makes up for a bit of the lost tension with the light source problem, as you need light, but don't know when or where it'll fail you.  This I welcome and am glad it was implimented.
Again, no weapons as the tradition goes, which leaves a sense of vulnerability to the player.  You can jump, crouch, lean, and run (considerably faster) in this game.  This is to hide from your foes and traverse the environment.  The controls are classic Frictional.  Simple and extremely easy to get ahold of.  As for the enemies, I really love how they are implimented, and how there are more different types than ever before.  Without spoiling anything, hiding won't help you with some of them.  Each enemy has it's own behavior, meaning you need to come up with a new way to outsmart them each time you come into contact.  This was a dire change that was needed, and what ruined Amnesia's replayability for me, that and scripted enemies (which are still here).  I am relieved this was fixed.
There are interesting new gameplay mechanics, such as walking on the ocean floor.  As many know, this was in Bioshock 2, and was more gimicky than anything else.  It is a full fledged mechanic in this game and took me off gaurd when I first played it.  Expect to play 1/4 of the game on the sea floor, and expect it to be wonderfully mapped, and fun to play.  It will literally "immerse" you into the game.  Speaking of immersion, the atmosphere of the game is stellar and unmatched save for A Machine For Pigs.  The sound design is truly incredible and some of the most realistic aspects of this game.  Even dropping something or tripping over an object on the floor is satisfying because of the sounds these actions create.
World interaction is finally back.  Amnesia 2 was notorious for stripping the series of it's gameplay elements (ie: opening doors, the encouragement of exploration and deviation from the main path, interacting with all sorts of dynamic objects, being able to hide in a closet, etc, etc) but replacing them with a truly amazing story and stunning atmosphere that could get you immersed in mere seconds.  SOMA, takes these atmosphereic elements and the gameplay of their previous games and merges them into a single game.  It is revitalizing to see this and realize how hard work and raw dedication can make a game truly astonishing.
There are multiple health regen points in the game to make up for no consumables, but getting health often could change the environment around you a bit due to a plot element.  This leads to interesting descisions.  "Do I want to get heath and risk blocking this door off?  Or do I wait to get health and explore this room first?"  This adds player descions to the many moral choices already in the plot of the game.
The difficulty is not to low, but not too high.  There isn't a seting to which you can change the difficulty, but I don't believe it's needed.  The game is challenging in the correct places and unlike the first Amnesia, you get two "knockouts" beofre you are truly dead.  If you are injured, you need to find a health supply, which are found as you progress.  The game is challenging enough, and some of the puzzles lack a bit of direction, here and there, but most of the "ah HA" moments come naturally after looking around a bit and finding something that was blatantly obvious in the first place.
In addition, this game has a problem the previous games had as well.  The graphics optimization.  The game runs great, but at times I got frame drops that went as low as 40 FPS from a solid 60 FPS.  I had this problem with both Amnesias and The Penumbra games when I had my old laptop.  Now I have a higher end computer, but the lag still comes and goes.  The game is still very much playable, but it can get intrusive at times.
The game only has one loadscreen.  The one that you get when you click "continue" or "new game".  The map changes are seamless and the immersion is held intact because of this.
In conclusion, if you enjoy the themes of Sci-Fi horror and Philosophy in a game's story and a stunning environment and stellar voice acting to boot, pick this one up.  It is one of the best survival horror titles I've played in recent memory.

It’s pretty much a retro Left 4 Dead. Dead Pixels is a 2D, action platformer from CSR-Studios. Let’s get rocking.
The Good
Despite its minimalist approach to the zombie killing genre, DP brings quite a bit to the table in terms of usable weapons and items. There is a good smattering of firearms (most of which have monikers that are nods to other famous zombie franchises), there are several options of throwing weapons (grenades and the like), and there are a ton of items that you’ll find lying around to sell to vendors.
DP keeps it simple all around the board (for the most part). Controls are simple, the story is straightforward, and you can only progress in one direction. It doesn’t get any less complicated.
Dead Pixels, while simple, is actually pretty fun.
The Bad
As far as I can tell, there’s no way to see what guns use what ammunition. I can’t stress how annoying this is.
The Meh
Some of the zombies that crop up in the late game soak up an unreasonable amount of ammunition before they kick the bucket a second time. It can get frustrating, especially when you’re short on ammo.
Verdict: Yea
For three dollars? Hell yeah you should get Dead Pixels. If you hate it, you’re only out three bucks. If you like it, you’ve got a decent time killer waiting in the wings for the next time you get bored. As always, thanks for reading.

Fantastic remake. The graphics are stunning compared with the original game, but of course 20 years of technology help that along.  I liked the new voice-overs too.  They couldn't get the original actors, but if they had, the original actors are now 20 years older as well, so it makes sense to have a new crew.   The music is improved by an order of magnitude as well.  I liked the fact that Jane Jensen did not mess with the original story, although certain theings got moved to happen on certain days to balance out the game play.
There is also a new graphic novel that tells the back-story -- from several hundred years before.  It's available from the game menu.  There's also a lot of additional content available on every scene, comparing the old to new images as well as interviews with members of the original crew.  The additional content is also available from the game menu (in the Archive).
I definitely recommend the Gabriel Knight remake as one of, if not the best, adventure game ever.

After playing it for almost 18 hours, there's one thing I can say for sure... the amount of ramming Russians is TOO DAMN HIGH.
Honestly, every race is either you against AI, you against AI with a russian or two or you against a lobby full of russians. Naturally every single one of them will ram you. Every. Single. One. They may not do it immediately, but they surely will. That's along the other usual tricks, like using you as a brake, wall etc.
Problem is... if this was the only bad thing, you could deal with it. But this ain't even the tip of the iceberg. So let me start with the only positive thing about the game: progression system.
By racing you earn cash, exp and class points. Class points are dependent on the car you use, therefore to gain class points for a given car class, you need to use a car from such a class. You get a free single unlock of a random car in the class upon leveling up (that's how you gain access to other classes). After that you can race and spend the class points on unlocking upgrades for the car or to unlock another car from the class... random again. If you're unlucky, you'll spend a long while driving something you don't like but it's still down to time rather you throwing money.
Now, the bad stuff. This is gonna take a while:
- aformentioned Russians. Ban them all. If cancer would had to take a human form, it would take a form of a Russian. That's how bad the races are because of them.
- server sided physics. This means that even if you don't want to ram... you will still ram, because when you get close to another car, the physics go kaput and you have no control over what's happening. Best thing to do is to stay away from other players... which is difficult due to the issue above. In practice mode (client sided physics) though the physics are pretty much what you'd expect from an arcade racer.
- premium cars. Yes, you have to throw money at the game to get those cars AND they come with perks... so if you want to farm efficiently... you need to have those cars. Not cool.
- GUI is... rather bad. The colours make me want to puke after a while. Not that good.
- did I mentioned Russians?
- Nitrous spam is unreal. You don't spam it at the start, you have no hope of winning. Ever.
- Pretty much every RWD car is drift for the win. Given how crappy the physics in MP are... rivers of cancer. Literally.
- Drifting is awful, no sense of what the car is doing, whether you'll make the corner or not... and... come on... enough with drift for win everywhere. Sick and tired of it. Especially on tracks that aren't optimised for such driving style.
- DLCs at the launch of Early access and... at a price higher than the game itself... or many other games out there.
- I am yet to see an actual response from a developer on the steam forums which is the only way of contacting them provided... not a great start there as well.
There's a few more minor things, like upgrades being exactly the same for every car, not being able to queue with friends or specifically with AI only etc. A lot of things are supposed to be adressed so I'll give it some time. If it changes, this will change to a positive review. There's potential for this game, it all comes down whether devs are making a jump on the money or want this game to actually be something good. Hopefully it's the latter although I am expecting the first deep down inside. Time will tell.

This isn't Amnesia 2.0 and that's a good thing. This is an evolution of the template laid out by Amnesia to tell a kind of story that hasn't been explored this well in the medium before. It's not perfect, but it feels like a true step forward in the slow crawl toward the maturation of videogames.
There are no "Renegade" or "Paragon" black and white moral choices. In fact, they have little to no effect on the story. But you feel them nontheless. Your choices can haunt you.
The game, like most, leans on the trope of audio and text message logs to help fill in the story. In this case, I felt they were *just* long enough to not wear out their welcome. There is also a lot of environmental storytelling that encourages you to let your imagination run wild.
I'm usually pretty bad at traditional adventure games but I was able to complete the game with no outside help. This really helped keep me immersed in the story.

I am obsessed with this game. Normally i get bored easily and will buy a game, play it for 30-50 hours and then move on to the next thing. Not this one. I have put 100 hours into it so far over the past 3 weeks and am more obsessed than ever. I am constantly surprised i still love this game since it seems very grindy, but the strange thing is that i rarely notice the grind when i actually play. Even the seemingly grindy tasks like flattening the earth or fishing for food don't seem to be as tedious because you are constantly thinking about what you will be able to do next once you complete that task.
Things to be prepared for/know up front:
--This game is not quick. You will not build everything in the game in a matter of days. Even seemingly simple things such build a small wodden house will take 30-40 man hours (longer if you have to do everything yourself). If the thought of always having something new to build or something to improve appeals to you, then you will like this game.
--This game should not be played alone in my opinion. I don't mean you have to start the game with a friend, but you better find someone else in game (or more than one person preferably) if you want to have any success. Everything just takes too darn long and never ending if you aren't able to divide up tasks.
--Many servers are heavy RP so if that's not your cup of tea, make sure to find a server that isn't.
Recommendations for enjoying the game:
--Research the available servers thoroughly and pick one you think you might like. Nothing ruins this game quicker than joining a dead server or a server that enforces rules that will ruin your fun (like deleting your character if you die)
--If you are first starting, run around the whole map visiting the towns. Dont just join the first one you see. You will be spending a lot of time with these people so you have to determine what their goals/time commitments/ etc are. I played on 2 servers and the enjoyment i had on one is immensely more simply cuz that one contained people more willing to help, and more people on at the same time i would play.
--Do not play alone. I have already said this, but i cant stress it enough. This game becomes 100x more fun if you are working on something with a group of people and can pass the time chatting with them rather than working by your lonesome in total silence.
Conclusion:
This game deserves more credit than it seems to get, but in the end it all comes down to the server you join. Join a good server and you will love it. join a bad server, and you will play this for 10 hours and never come back.

As of the latest January patch, I still cannot recommend this game.
I will begin by saying that these survival games have a high PvP appeal to it: you fight the nether and you also must fight other players. If you do not enjoy the PvP aspect of this genre, I would not recommend purchasing this game.
The preview photos in the Steam store are quite misleading: they show a group of players who roam the wasteland with you, but it is quite difficult to find 3 or even 1 willing player to join you. The new "group" implementation addresses this slightly, but I have seen Player Killers abuse this to locate less suspecting players.
Now, there are many who think there should be a separate PvE and PvP server, but the anxiety and thrill of losing all your items is all part of the genre. I enjoy this thrill, but there is a major concern that needs to be addressed: campers. In a post apocalyptic world, it is plausible that people would be out there just to hunt you down, but these campers get away easily with killing other players.
Here are my suggestions and suggestions I've heard from others to better address the camping issue:
1. Implementation of aggression counter. Aggression increases as more players are killed.
2. The nether will be attracted to players with high aggression. In reverse, the nether are less aggressive towards players with few or no player kills.
3. One can reset the aggression counter by paying a certain amount of money (or as an extreme example, a total character and global inventory reset).
4. Nether should spawn on roof tops or have the ability to climb building surfaces.
5. Players with high numbers of player kills should have limited (or even restricted) access to their global inventory. For those who do not know what the global inventory is, you can store all your items here and retrieve them at anytime, which makes campers more inclined to camp with available resources.
Here are other suggestions, addressing overall issues:
1. Extend the Museum safezone. Player killers can still hide behind those pesky trees at the front entrance.
2. Nether can still attack and detect you behind walls. I really don't know how nether can hear or smell me behind a concrete wall while I am in prone position.
3. Loot should be scattered much more randomly. People often know where to look for their sniper rifles.
4. Some textures are buggy, like the bridges.
I know this game will improve in the near future, but until then, I would not recommend purchasing it.

A delightful interactive novel that is surprisingly gripping and fast paced, without losing depth. Simple, in a way that really good things are, hiding away a deep layer of complexity under a well-designed and joyful presentation, suffering from a slightly clunky UI and lack of automatic stats.
After playing it through a couple (of dozen) of times, I can say that I am almost as addicted to this as I was to replaying Fallout 1- in its own way, this is an open world game that adapts to your choices and decisions, with many paths through it, offering almost infinite replaybility due to the number of routes through the world.
The world itself also bears comparing with Fallout's- an alternate history, set earlier than the 1950's, and during the preparation for the coming apocalypse, caught in the moment between Empire and Modernity with a Steampunk twist worthy of Captain Nemo. It reminds me of the "League of Extraordinary Gentlemen", as written by Alan Moore (NOT the film), and gains by being described, rather than shown, adding to the personal narrative develop.
It gains depth with every reading and reads like a DIY page turner, growing in every playthrough as plots, twists and characters unlock, enriching the players understanding of the diffeent facets of the world they are traversing by a journey.
To paraphrase: the game is highly replayable, as the player discovers and creates the world for themselves through meaningful choices and encounters in several short-ish playthroughs, summarised in slides at the end of a run. It combines simple, but effective puzzle, trade and planning mechanics, and a few surprising enconters that unlock over time. It is not, however, for haters of inventory management. Permadeath, executed through the mechanic of eastward-only motion, is a highly effective driver of devision-making.
If I were wishing for more, I would ask for consequences in the world over several playthroughs, such as having characters permanently added to your team in Saville Row, adding perks and bonuses over playthroughs and altering the course of the world as Passepartout and Phileas relive the time loop of 80 days over and over, every time making little changes that add to the whole, which would provide dedicated gamers a definitive endpoint to the narrative you can discover within the game- a big, fat "The End".

To start, this game works.  Almost everything about it is fine tuned and stays refreshingly to it's roots.  I really enjoyed it and have good reasons for it.
Like Amnesia and Penumbra, the SOMA is a survival horror game is told from a first person perspective.  Your character is less mute as other protagonists, but his little quips and lines do not interfere with the horror aspect at all, as they are well paced out and appropriate to the situation at hand.
The gameplay is much like the originals, with a few changes.  The inventory system is back, but not like in Dark Descent.  You collect certain plot-related items and keep them in a small, unaccessable inventory for when they are supposed to be used.  I don't hate this mechanic.  I DO miss collecting consumables such as health potions (laudanum) and oil for my light source because that added another layer of tesion in Amnesia: TDD.  But it isn't all bad.  The light source you have in this game is a head mounted flashlight thay doesn't take batteries, but is rather dim, and if left on for a while it will begin to flicher and get MORE dim.  This makes up for a bit of the lost tension with the light source problem, as you need light, but don't know when or where it'll fail you.  This I welcome and am glad it was implimented.
Again, no weapons as the tradition goes, which leaves a sense of vulnerability to the player.  You can jump, crouch, lean, and run (considerably faster) in this game.  This is to hide from your foes and traverse the environment.  The controls are classic Frictional.  Simple and extremely easy to get ahold of.  As for the enemies, I really love how they are implimented, and how there are more different types than ever before.  Without spoiling anything, hiding won't help you with some of them.  Each enemy has it's own behavior, meaning you need to come up with a new way to outsmart them each time you come into contact.  This was a dire change that was needed, and what ruined Amnesia's replayability for me, that and scripted enemies (which are still here).  I am relieved this was fixed.
There are interesting new gameplay mechanics, such as walking on the ocean floor.  As many know, this was in Bioshock 2, and was more gimicky than anything else.  It is a full fledged mechanic in this game and took me off gaurd when I first played it.  Expect to play 1/4 of the game on the sea floor, and expect it to be wonderfully mapped, and fun to play.  It will literally "immerse" you into the game.  Speaking of immersion, the atmosphere of the game is stellar and unmatched save for A Machine For Pigs.  The sound design is truly incredible and some of the most realistic aspects of this game.  Even dropping something or tripping over an object on the floor is satisfying because of the sounds these actions create.
World interaction is finally back.  Amnesia 2 was notorious for stripping the series of it's gameplay elements (ie: opening doors, the encouragement of exploration and deviation from the main path, interacting with all sorts of dynamic objects, being able to hide in a closet, etc, etc) but replacing them with a truly amazing story and stunning atmosphere that could get you immersed in mere seconds.  SOMA, takes these atmosphereic elements and the gameplay of their previous games and merges them into a single game.  It is revitalizing to see this and realize how hard work and raw dedication can make a game truly astonishing.
There are multiple health regen points in the game to make up for no consumables, but getting health often could change the environment around you a bit due to a plot element.  This leads to interesting descisions.  "Do I want to get heath and risk blocking this door off?  Or do I wait to get health and explore this room first?"  This adds player descions to the many moral choices already in the plot of the game.
The difficulty is not to low, but not too high.  There isn't a seting to which you can change the difficulty, but I don't believe it's needed.  The game is challenging in the correct places and unlike the first Amnesia, you get two "knockouts" beofre you are truly dead.  If you are injured, you need to find a health supply, which are found as you progress.  The game is challenging enough, and some of the puzzles lack a bit of direction, here and there, but most of the "ah HA" moments come naturally after looking around a bit and finding something that was blatantly obvious in the first place.
In addition, this game has a problem the previous games had as well.  The graphics optimization.  The game runs great, but at times I got frame drops that went as low as 40 FPS from a solid 60 FPS.  I had this problem with both Amnesias and The Penumbra games when I had my old laptop.  Now I have a higher end computer, but the lag still comes and goes.  The game is still very much playable, but it can get intrusive at times.

However, buyer beware - as of this writing it is fairly buggy while in menus, with a couple of issues that force you to restart your game, as well as some fairly nasty connection issues.  I rarely encounter them, but other players seem to be having difficulty getting into matches at all.  On top of that, its learning curve is basically vertical - it doesn't explain itself particularly well, and given its complexity, that's not good.  Some buyers may also find that it doesn't have enough content to justify the price point - my rule of thumb is one dollar per hour and I'm going to reach that with For Honor without any issue whatsoever, but I can't speak for others.  Last but not least are persisting balance issues - they're not huge, and all classes can be countered, but some are percievably overpowered at the moment.  Hopefully all these issues are addressed soon.
Consider this a cautious recommendation - perhaps wait for a sale, or for it to have recieved a few patches.

An absolutely awesome and skill-based medieval fighting game. In my opinion if you like medieval games and don't mind ubisoft, then you'll love this game. All future dlc is free (maps/content), although new characters will cost a lot of in game money, just like Siege, which I actually liked because it prevents splitting the community. Unlike Siege, all classes can be played for free but need to be bought with in-game money (other than 3 starting Vanguard classes) to unlock appearance customization and equipment upgrades.
The classes are actually well balanced and can be customized how you like to a certain extent. Bleeding can be irritating but theres passives that negate it in Dominion/Deathmatch, or you can block/parry/dodge. The fighting system is a lot more complex than it initially seems in the singleplayer or tutorials. Every class has specific passives (such as the shove allows the Lawbringer to chain into other attacks) and combos that if followed attack faster/more damage. The major gripe i have with the game is the GANGBANGING! Revenge mode builds much faster when fighting multiple opponents, which for 2v1 is great, but if its 3-4v1 like in an Elimination match, then gg. Combat is very skill based, although you can definitely get boosts from leveling up your gear. If you look though, gear level is factored into matchmaking. So far, all the Common items have the same base three stats, but each has a different appearance and normally it will offer one/two of the three skills upgraded, and one that suffers a minor deduction.
Overall, the game is really fun especially if you love medival games and due to the nature of combat seems like it will allow you to continue playing for a long time. Plus there is 30 prestige levels (20 regular class levels) per class and 12 classes to start. It took me about 22 hours for 2 prestige levels. As you rank up you will unlock new Armor paint schemes, higher levelled gear, outfits, executions, class abilities, and emotes. It honestly is kinda following the theme of many games currently with loot boxes for gear+random gear for your class after match. Steel is somewhat hard to earn but not too bad if you do the daily quests and the contract orders like in Siege. This will let you rack in money much faster than trying to complete games only.

Still, maybe we'll see some variant of that and/or proper HD reduxes of KOTOR 1 and 2 in the next few years, especially considering the coming bonanza of new Star Wars movies.
Regardless, this game is still well worth your time if you enjoyed KOTOR1.

I was very pleased to see this game after playing Punch-out! (Mike Tyson's Punch-out!, for the NES), as it's not the type of game you often see.
Don't buy it thinking it's Punch-out. It's actually a significantly different game, with different mechanics, that stands on its own! If you enjoyed it, you'll probably like this one as well, but they're fundamentally different game.
With that out of the way, I'll now say what I like and what I don't like.
The most obvious think here are the graphics. The game has quite a lot of character to it, and the visual style of the game suits it surprisingly well. Although the models are questionable (you can see the polygons clearly in some characters and animations), the textures manage to hide that pretty well, and make the game look awesome!
Personally, I think the game looks great, but it might not be your thing... I guess you can decide that from the screenshots.
As a segway... the music. It's very good! And it's varied enough, each stage giving a different vibe, matching the opponent as well. One complaint I have it that the music doesn't loop very well, most of the time. In combat I didn't really notice it much (maybe because there wasn't enough time to notice), but on the menus it's pretty apparent... and feels awkward. I think there could've been more polish into the ending and starting of the tracks.
Other than that, it's awesome, good job!
SoundEffects weren't really something I enjoyed a lot. I found them a little annoying at times, with some high-pitched sounds, but they're bearable.
Now, a problem I've had with this game was the Interface. The style of the menus were a bit out of place, but that's not the main problem. Navigating through them is slow and unintuitive with a controller. I guess a mouse helps it greatly (since this is a PC), but for a game like this, I prefer using the controller.
Also, key bindings were very awkward with the shared functionalities.
When you change a certain key, it might have 2 functions at once, which you can't change separately... that makes it weird with a couple of keys. I think the game would have benefited quite a lot from having all the keys able to be rebound, and a reworked interface. Ah well...
Options menu was a bit lackluster as well, but at least it had separate audio sliders... That's a plus and some games fail royaly.
So, all in all, presentation was pretty good, despite having a clunky interface.
Now about the gameplay. In this, you have essentially 3 modes: Carreer, which is separated in Tournament and an Exhibition Modes. Then you have Endless.
In the carreer mode, you can upgrade your character by buying attributes, and equipment. Each piece of equipment has its benefits and its downgrades, letting you create your own sets for different situations. I didn't really like this, for the simple reason that it makes for a not as balanced game. If there were no upgrades, you would have to play like in the old days, memorizing patterns, and actually train to beat a game. In this, if you lose a couple of matches, you can just buy your way to victory, in a way.
But... this is a different type of game, so I guess I shouldn't be complaining about that. It works for this game, letting the player create his own pacing in a way, and giving the game some customization, so I think it's good... even if I don't like the notion of it.
In Tournament Mode, you have 4 leagues, each with 3 opponents. Each opponent has his own fighting style and backstory (which I enjoyed greatly, not swarming you with text, but letting their personalities go through small but to the point catch-phrases and fighting style, well done!). These get progressively harder, as one would imagine. You gain currency at the end of each fight, receiving a smaller amount when you lose.
In Exhibition Mode, you can fight whoever you've fought before, for a smaller amount of currency. This was there in case the player was having difficulty defeating an opponent, then grinding a bit and upgrading his equipment/stats. I didn't really need that, but we'll get on to that further.
Finally, in Endless Mode, you find in Rounds of just 1, trying to go through as many opponents as you can. As you fight, coins drop on the floor, which you can use in Carreer Mode, or to buy Health during the Endless Mode, as you don't gain health after each round.
I actually enjoyed the game's structure quite a lot! Although, it was pretty short for me. Either way, for 5€, it was enough... and a lot of fun.
Now, the most important part of the game: the combat.
I have several issues with it. But, it was fun as hell while it lasted! And it's deeper than it seems when you start playing.
You can do Jabs (left-handed fast, but weak punches), Crosses (slightly slower but stronger right-handed punches), Uppercuts, and Hooks as attacks. Your objective is to figure out which ones work the best against the different opponents, and then doing combos with these.
The great thing is that opponents start defending against your combos if you use always the same, so it pushes the player to experiment with different tactics.
And defense, you can Block, and you can walk Sideways (this walking sideways is my biggest complain, instead of a dodge ability). When you Block, you still lose HP, but a smaller amount, and you can lower that by upgrading a certain attribute.
Each fighter has HP and Power (which is essentially a Stamina Bar). Whenever you attack, or Block, you lose Power. If you use it all, you'll get very, very slow, and won't be able to attack nor block appropriately. This makes the player be a bit more careful when to attack and block, creating a good pacing to the fights. However, the slowing part of running out of energy, is often not being able to escape attacks fast enough, even by walking sideways. That sometimes got awkward and frustrating during a couple of fights, but it's a question of being careful when managing attack and defense.
In regards to HP, you have a general bar, you have one that depletes faster, but also regenerates. This creates an awesome dynamic in combos: the bigger the combo, the more impact it may have. You can finish the fights really quickly if you combo your attacks wisely, but they can also end fast for you if not careful. When you're hit, this alternative bar lowers faster, but it regenerates up to a point when you're not being attacked. This was unexpected, but great design, well done!
One big complaint I have with the combat, it the lack of connection. Due to the sideways walk and the animation, punches sometimes don't connect when they feel like they should. If you slightly to the left/right, you can still see the punches hit the opponent, but it doesn't register. This leads to some awkward moves and makes it almost feel unfair, but it's not so bad once you get the hang of it. Still, I don't like it and I think it should be reworked if the developers make a sequel.
Achievements were mainly straightforward, but some were pretty creative, which I appreciate.
Lack of multiplayer is a fault, in my opinion, since you can complete the game within 5-6hours without too much of an issue... but hey, it's 5€! And it's pretty good either way! Maybe more in a future game!
Another thing was the difficulty... I started the game on Hard, and it actually was hard when I started. But once I got used to the controls and developped a tactic, the difficulty has fallen quite a bit. Then there was NewGame+ which was surprisingly easier, with no difficulty options this time. Only 3 fights gave me a fairly hard time (due to very strong punches), but other than that, it was very easy in the NG+.
But, it was challenging at times.
So, if you're curious about the game, I'd definitely recommend it. It has its flaws, but it was a very enjoyable, and at times challenging game. And it's not very expensive, so you wouldn't lose all that much for trying it!

So a few months ago this was one of my favorite games. Easily in my top 10 and i would have recommended it to anyone who likes crash driving style games.
Sadly there are a few reasons (nit picky but do make a difference at least to me) that makes me PERSONALLY not enjoy it as much as id like
Now heres when i wish steam had a different review system, because i would normally say go ahead get this game give it a try and i will tell you that. Buy it, give it a try if you like crash mechanic driving games. But first here me out and maybe if the issues i list are something that REALLY bother you, you may save yourself some money and time
First off the game itself is really good, its fun and its gotten so far and for the most part its going in a good direction. hopefully down the line i can fix my issues
Note im using MPH for my speeds
Now onto why i downvoted this game
The camera angles lets start are absolutely DREADFUL. When you are turning or hit something, the camera switches into weird stupid angles like a down up view or a top view which DOESNT HELP when im trying to DRIVE. And when you attempt to adjust it, well then it gets wonky. So what they tried and failed at is when you back up the angle switches to the back view so you dont have to do it manually (i hate that) and thus makes it much harder to do what would normally be simple manuevers. When you start to drive forward again it puts the camera back, however if at any point you alter it before then it will still re adjust itself, but will adjust itself according to what you did. Bit hard to explain but lemme try in more detail
Say you are facing forward and lets say its North, as you back up the camera switches to facing South, and as you drive it forward switches back to North. Now if you say as you back up turn the camera yourself (while still backing up) and face the camera North while backing up its all fine. BUT once you start to move forward the camera still thinks it facing South, when it really isnt. So as you go forward it switchs to what it THINKS is North but is really South. So instead of all manuel camera switching it just goes all wonky on you. Basically think of it like this, whatever angle the camera turns itself it will turn back the way it came, so if it makes  180 turn it will turn 180 back again to fix it. But if you already turned the camera yourself and its facing where you want it to be facing the game still thinks it needs to turn 180 and does so thus putting weird angles that you have to fix that can and will mess you up alot.
Next is braking/steering
This part is a core part of the game its basically how you drive, and since its a driving game this is incredibly important
The braking in this game is trash. The cars will drift and turn at the slightest brake and can take a long time to brake as well.
Steering. The game was always a bit bad at this but now it seems worse ive got cars going 30 and i turn a smidge and boom drift city. Its annoying and basically makes it to were i cant actually turn without slowing down to a crawl (and in this case that can take 10 seconds to brake)
Lastly crash mechanics
So i sometimes get my car glitched into rocks and other cars which is stupid but happens rarely. I also notice i can scrape a car against a wall going like 40 or so and it says something stupid like "engine malfunction tires flattened) and then i lose all control of my car. Now imagine hitting something going that fast and not scraping it. Ya, really ruins the game
TLDR
The camera angle auto adjusting and actualy car control are absolutely terrible and is the reason for why it takes out of the fun, immersion. and overall satisfaction for me. Im sure many will enjoy this game but i dont and until these issues are addressed will keep my vote at a thumbs down

Tormentum smoothly combines point-and-click adventure with classic puzzle gameplay, a horrific artistic theme, and silent protagonist storytelling.
The game took me <4 hour to beat, and has limited replayability given that you will already know how to solve all the puzzles. That said, I thoroughly enjoyed every minute of gameplay, and never found myself skimming and skipping any element. The world is so thoughtfully put together that within each and every background there is beauty to be found. From the smallest details to the grander scope of world view, the one continuous sense of a living, breathing world will spark your curiosity to dive yet deeper into the miasma.
A common gripe I have with puzzle games is when my post-disbelief-suspended limitations misalign with the programmed gameplay elements (e.g. Why can't I just walk between these gate bars that are clearly wide enough to pass thorugh?) Tormentum weaves its horror so immersively that I found myself intuitively understanding the world around me and how to navigate it.
I overwhelmingly recommend Tormentum - Dark Sorrow.

I have two criticisms of this game. I wanted MOAR, and;
There is a "choices matter" gameplay element that I was a huge fan of all the way up to the very end of the game at which point it lazily falls back on a patronizing deontological ethics lens.

Tries to have its cake and eat it, too.
The spectacle scrolling shooter is a wonderful thing. Beautiful visual effects... missiles on top of lasers on top of bombs on top of fireballs on top of smoke on top of debris. The skill based scrolling shooter is also a wonderful thing. Learning patterns and avoiding death by knowledge and reflex is satisfying once executed to perfection. This game combines the two into an off-putting mush. It's incredibly difficult to determine what will and won't instantly kill you behind all those pretty visuals. The result is that often times you die and are not sure why. Combine this with infrequent checkpoints and it's the recipe for frustration.
Pushing the difficulty down from Normal to Easy is a necessity. It substantially reduces the number of things that will instagib you, but not so much that you won't still end up playing the same five minute segments a half dozen times before completing them. Jets'n'Guns fails the Super R-Type test... meaning you'd be better of playing Super R-Type. Here's a free to play browser version:
The upgrade system is compelling. The humor is compelling. The B-movie sci-fi Di ck Tracy story presentation between levels is compelling. The gameplay is fatally flawed. If instant or sub-second death is a feature, then the threats must be clear, and the checkpoints must be frequent. How odd that Jets'n'Guns makes me want to play more Super Meat Boy....

(SINGLE PLAYER ONLY)
This game is about being a WW2-sniper, it's not a modern sniper game, it's not a future sniper game, nor a pre-historic stone archery game, it's WW2. The game is good for what it is supposed to do, sniping and it allows you to choose different difficulties depending on the level of realism you want in the game. Whenever you shoot someone in a critical spot, like the head, testicles or major organs, you see a slowed-down view of the bullet piercing through said bodypart with x-ray and everything.
The story is very linear, as you go from place to place,being directed by markers on the map. In certain parts the game is too linear as certain enemies only pop-up when you reach a certain point, and even de-spawn when you go back far enough, thus there is no real point in scouting out and really, planning your battle as you won't have full view of all the enemies and you might not even know that certain enemies were there, until it is too late.
The X-ray view of bullets also gets repetitive after a while unless you enjoy watching the animations, which I do, the graphics look quite nice when seeing the special animations.
Once you finish the game there is really not much to keep you going back other than collecting hidden bars of gold in every level, and sniping hidden bottles of wine in every level. If you played the game at a lower difficulty it might be fun to try a higher difficulty to see if you're up for the challenge.
This game is a one-time thing and will only really hook enthusiasts of this type of game to play again,while it is fun and it works well for what it is supposed to do;that is the only thing.
