I am going to be the odd one out here by not recommending this game, despite my playtime.
Pros:
+Satisfying melee combat
+Potty humor
+Gore
+World design
+Graphics
Cons:
-Loot
-Open world
-Progression system
It is to my surprise that after putting too many hours into this game, I finally decided I do not like it. What I loved about Borderlands, I feel brought down the experience in Shadow Warrior 2. Examples:
-Loot: Borderlands has a loot system. Diablo has a loot system. A lot of games have loot systems. A lot of games loot is meaningful. The loot in SW2 is not. You find gems upon gems upon gems that you can spend more time crafting together and socketing onto your weapons than actually playing through the campaign. You are constantly being bombarded by beams of light glistening off of dead bodies. Health, mana, money, gems, gems, gems. Back into the menu, remove, craft, socket again ad again and again. While the gems do help in scenarios, it never feels like it has any meaningful impact to the game, like for them to be removed wouldn't matter. The weapons you can get are only bought from a store, unlocked via story progression, or dropped from very specific miniboss enemies, meaning evry other enemy drops only health, mana, money, and gems. Stupid, pointless gems.
-Open world/levels: You can have a wonderfully crafted level to go through. You can have a wonderfully crafted world to explore. You can have uniquely crafted open levels to experience. Or, you can have SW2s 3-4 levels repeated over and over and over and over again with buildings in a different order and enemies in a different order. Now you can guess the tedium that creeps reeeeaaaalll fast.
If the story was worth suffereing through it all, which it isn't, I could possibly recommend this game, but because of the level design, or lack thereof, and the way the loot is handled, both of which are at the core of this game, beating the game just seems pointless, let alone multiple playthroughs.
Yes, the melee combat is pretty good, but get a lot of enemies around you and suddenly melee isn't really viable because to swing in close is to get hurt. To parry and dash is to not have time to slash your enemies before another enemy tries attacking you. The soldier and drone type enemies are especially unpleasant to face. When it came to the more human+gun type enemies, I found myself just spam-dashing past them so I could finish the game and not have to deal with them. It just became a chore to play the game.
To this games credit, the gore tech is pretty nice. It is an improved version of what you get in Metal Gear Rising Revengeance where anywhere you cut is cut. Want to chop a sliver off an elbow? You can do that.
Do yourself a favor. If you want first person hack n' slash combat, go play Dying Light. You want fun gun toting combat? Borderlands is your game. You want a meaningful loot based system? Go play Borderlands, Dying Light, or several other games at your disposal. Want a world, or levels that are actually fun to explore? There are literally hundreds available. Go play Revengeance if you want cool "I cut you up how I want" tech. This game is a rare instance where it is not worth having all of the components in one not as well done package vs having the components done better, seperately, in seperate games.

Nether is a must have game if you like games that give you nightmares.  Intially, it doesn't look that scary, however try playing it in a dark room with a headset.  My first impression of the game was negative to be honest, it really annoyed me that everytime I died I would reset level wise and lose anything I was carrying.  However, after dying too many times to count, I have come to appreciate this.  In most games, if I die it annoys me and I grumble, but it doesn't actually affect my game in any real way.  In Nether, I'm terrified to die.  I hear the crunch of footsteps, nether noises, and gunshots even after I've put the game away.  This experience is one of a kind, and it hooked me.
In terms of bugs, updates and general technical experience, Nether can be a bit bothersome.  Sometimes it is difficult to pick up items, although moving backwards usually helps.  I haven't seen any serious graphical issues in the game which I am really, really impressed by since it is in its' beta and pretty new.
Normally I like to be sort of friendly in MMOs, but Nether is sort of a "shoot first ask questions later" sort of game.  In most servers, I find people don't really speak much to one another (I didn't even notice there was a chat option for like 3 hours) and its usually pretty hostile if they do.  I suggest pairing up with a few friends when you start this game otherwise the other groups in the game are going to take you down pretty quickly and there is little opportunity to make friends in the game.  People will often just kill you for no reason, however that's to be expected.  I had someone "hunt" me for 2 hours, following me around in map until I finally almost had a nervous breakdown and died of starvation in the subway (a very dark moment in my life).
All in all, I really recommend the game.  The devs are great, always doing updates and adding to the game as well as keeping us all updated with patch notes.  Really immersive, intense and amazing!
I hope you like spending money, because after you buy this game you won't win a duel unless you buy all the boosters packs.

At this point I am only playing Duke Nukem: Forever because a friend challenged me to do so, claiming I can't tell a game is crap by just looking at it, and I need to actually play it first to establish an opinion. So, here I am after
playing this piece of garbage for over 3 hours.
By the time you're reading this review, I am pretty sure you are aware of how bad this game is. It's bland, it has toilet humor kids in 5th grade would find too low to their tastes and it's pretty god damn boring. I am assuming you were thinking to yourself "Well then maybe I should buy this as a joke game?". To that I say: Maybe.
This game came out after what I liked to think was a new era in the video game industry: Mass Effect, Crysis, Bioshock, Assassin's Creed, The Orange Box and others were bringing new ideas to the table - new mechanics were introduced, gameplay aspects renewed for a new generation of both console and PC gamers, new narratives, stories and much more dedication was present in each and every game. I was expecting every game released from 2007 and onwards to be groundbreaking, or I was at least expecting them to follow the same lines.
Unfortunately, I was young and naive.
This game is slow, it features a small variety of weapons and allows you to carry only two of them (EDIT: You can actually mark the option to allow you to carry 2 additional guns... Why?! what's the point?!), it is anticlimactic, sexist and distateful (see: "wall♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; and "pregnant women explosions"), has the level design of a Call of duty game, without the mildly fun parts, and to top it all off, it's unfunny.
If Duke Nukem Forever was a rollercoaster, it would probably have a very slow setting, homeless people posing as monster and strippers waving as you pass by them, and much like a rollercoaster tycoon ride, it will end with either you dying or asking for a refund.
My final score for this game is "You should be paid to play this game" (Which I wasn't, unfortunately).
Finally! After all this ping-pong state with development I can get my hands on this game!

This is fairly standard, it basically acts as a booster to all of the currencies you earn after a match. The catch is that the premium membership in this game buffs your earnings to a fairly reasonable amount. Note; NOT excessive, reasonable as in you can progress without slowing to an extreme grind. The boost is a 150% increase across the board to all currency earnings, after your EA boost wears off expect this game to slow to a crawl, especially when combined with the car durability system.
Whether you are buying one of the mid-tier plus cars with in-game credits, or if you are paying real money for one of the premium currency exclusive cars (of which there are only a few to be fair) the price will always be high. Early on the cars only cost a few thousand in-game credits, but passing the "C" class onwards means that you will be expected to grind HEAVILY to grab cars later in the game, or you can buy one of the Steam DLC packs that as you can see, cost a lot for what you get. The premium currency can be converted into in-game credits, which seems like it will become necessary later on unless you want to deal with a billion races plus the tax of a ton of car repairs plus the lack of premium membership.
Currently you have two modes of play; "Practice" which is by yourself where you will earn no money and find no opponents. Or you can hit the big "Play" button, with no option to join your friends and form a party, no ability to choose modes or tracks or servers, where you will most likely be thrown into a game filled with Russians who teleport around the track in white Toyota Corollas.

This game is fun. I played this with 3 other people on a server, built a small village within a week. The most amount of time I've dedicated to any game. I like it because players can dedicate themselves to specific roles and level up skills related to those roles. For example, I was a dirt flinger. I terraformed the land and was also a lumberjack. So I worked on creating defenses and creating plots of land to build new structures. One person was a blacksmith and tanning expert, so he would make nails, weapons and leather pieces/armor for us. Another was an herbalist/farmer, for food and remedies. The last one was a hunter and forager. Just between the 4 of us, we made a sustainable community.
However, at the end of it all and with the bugs that are present, you leave yourself thinking, "Why am I wasting my time with this?" A week of my life wasted to have a bug completely roadblock progress and features that were not implemented yet. The only way we could get these objects is if we contacted the server admin and he spawned it for us.
It seems like the developers are more focused on the presentation of the game at this point than the actual functionality of it. It's almost as if they had their project lead hijack the functionality process and started prioritizing his "ideas" rather than creating a solid base to work from. They are also talking about an MMO version of it, but why? The game functions really sluggish already on a static map and serverside lag is very bad. As another user pointed out, people that dig below water level causes corruption in the server database, tree stumps and other objects that are laying around cause lag, etc.  And what does a new player do on a large server where there are no resources for them to be productive? To me, it seems like it has a lot of potential, but the priorities are not straight for this game to be successful. Just seems like another one of those games that are selling an "idea" rather than an experience.
I would not recommend this game solely on that basis.

Amnesia: The Dark Decent was focused more on horror. Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs was more story-driven. Here is a wonderful balance of both, though the game overall feels more like the Penumbra games than Amnesia.
Gameplay is more-or-less the same as Amnesia, but that's not a problem. Why fix what ain't broke? Unique monsters for every area, I like that. Unique settings, spooky atmosphere, and intruiging features. The only issue is stuttering between areas, mostly due to the lack of loading screens so each area has to load in-game. As I understand, each area is loaded by progress/pressure chambers rather than proximity, so it has to load all at once causing stutters, which is understandable. The game has only been out for two days at the time of writing so that'll probably be worked on as time goes by.
The story is like something out of Star Trek. You know, those episodes that take the topic of "What does it mean to be human?" and explore it, picking apart philosophies that you probably haven't thought much of. SOMA does that. What is humaity? Who are we? What do we feel? Do robots feel as we do? If we lose our bodies and all that's left are our conscious minds, are we still what we are? Some lines made me pause the game to mull over what was said.
The last ten minutes of the game were some of the most emotionally-conflicting experiences I've ever had in a video game and I feel very torn over the ending. Rarely games affect me in the way SOMA did. Get it. It's worth it.

Ok, I've spent just shy of 20 hours in this game reaching the end. This is without a doubt one of the most thought provoking games I've ever played. The story takes many unexpected turns and tackles quite a few subjects like survival, morality, and what it really means to be human. The horror encounters arent always really as scary as you would expect, I found myself more terrified of the sound design of the environment and the petrifying, bleak atmosphere the game gives you. This is not a happy game, but it doesnt need to be. The writing is good, and the voice acting is spot on. The puzzles dont feel like stereotypical video game puzzles, like the resident evil cranks and whatnot. They actually feel right, like it would if you were just a random guy who didn't know  how to work these strange machines. This isnt a game that holds your hand, it takes some patience to work out where to go sometimes, but you feel a good sense of accomplishment when you do. My problems with the game were fairly small, mostly some performance problems here and there, graphical bugs, fell through the world once. And while there arent very many loading screens at all, they did take a LONG time for me. All in all I definitely reccomend this to anyone interested in either a horror game, or just a very intriguing story to dive into.

Cold. Lonely. Brooding. Hateful. Alien.
Five words that best describe the atmosphere of SOMA, befitting for a storyline about the relationship between reality, humanity and a fast-approaching future of technological progress. Every room felt so authentic and even if you absolutely, positively knew that you were in a safe, story-based part of the game, it still had the feeling that you were being watched by some terrible intelligence. The slower, more puzzle-based sections made the more "active" portions all the more terrifying because you'll be content in a place of certain safety with the full knowledge that you have to leave it again to press on.
My sole issues with the game are that the game chugs from time-to-time (though it may be because my laptop needs a bit of an update), you cannot hide in closets or put up barricades anymore and the monsters have this annoying habit of opening up doors without a single issue.
You'll have a few laughs and smiles here and there in odd places, but remember: You are alone. Nameless abominations stalk the dark hallways. You're trapped on the bottom of the sea and you don't even know if you're even the slightest bit Human anymore.
And nobody on the surface can help you.
Welcome to SOMA.

The immediate comparison that comes to mind when viewing this game is the NES/SNES classic "Punchout", and I'd say that's pretty accurate. There are a few places in which it falls short, though it does shine in a few spots as well.
The art style is a probably a personal preference, but I liked it. The beasts are just wacky enough without falling into the realm of ridiculous. Animation is a little stiff, but it works. Keep in mind that this is a $4.99 game and it is not trying to be AAA. But, hey, Punchout was no "looker" either, right?
Now, where BBT falls just short of "Punchout", in my opinion, is in the gameplay. I played it with a wired 360 pad and it felt great using the two triggers in combination with the thumb stick for movement and punches. I'd have to level my criticism mainly at the lack of complexity in the enemy fighters. While each has a signature attack, it's not hard to win each fight with the same jabs and crosses. Once you defeat the game, a game+ mode unlocks and it does get a little tougher from there, but the action remains pretty straightforward.
One thing BBT does well is that it presents you with many training options that allow you to boost your stats with money earned from fights. Watch out though, because it's fairly easy to overlevel and fights become even easier. You may also purchase new gear that changes the look of your fighter (in-menu... all fighting is done first-person) and gives you even more stat boosts.
All in all, I enjoyed the game. There aren't many games in this genre, so fans will probably want to check it out.

Beast Boxing Turbo is afforadable, fun, has enjoyable graphics, and is humorous. The game mechanics work well, the character design is great, and the minimal storyline is fun. Would I reccommend a playthrough? Certainly. For $5, a game of monster boxing is certainly worthwhile.
That being said, however, there is the frequently mentioned flaw of the game being too short. In one sitting, I managed to purchase every item, max out all my stats and plow through all of the "campaign". It didn't take long to use up the entire game's playability, and the "endless" mode gets boring really fast. I played through it twice and quickly lost interest after that.
My biggest complaint, however, is that the game is painfully easy. I finally stopped playing when the game asked me if I wanted to play through "NewGame Plus 11". The big problem here is that this game can be destroyed using a strategy a five year old could master. In NG+7, which is supposedly the maximum level of difficulty available, I, being someone who is not at all a major gamer, managed to beat the first five characters in a row without them being able to so much as pull off a single punch by doing little more than button-mash jabbing right as the fight started. If a character can't be simply annihilated in five seconds that way and they start blocking, you move off to the side, take advantage of reach with a single hook, and then begin mashing again. Repeat this until you get the fire-glove power, which eventually makes it so you virtually can't lose, and then pummel jab until the fight ends. If you can time this without getting caught in some combo or running out of steam, you honestly can't lose. I was running the entire story mode in under fifteen minutes. It is mindlessly easy to master, and after the NG+1, which was the only time playing the game I felt even mildly challenged, the fun bled out. It was mechanical and I knew what was coming.
Despite this major issue in playability, I would still highly suggest giving the game a run. Perhaps, like all other games on Steam, it would be best to wait until it goes on sale. Beast Boxing Turbo is the PunchOut or Wii Sports Boxing for the PC. It controls pretty much the same way as those games and it has the same looks as PunchOut and actually manages to look a bit cooler thanks to the variety in opponents, even if there are only 12 of them.
The game really is beautifully rendered, but the fact that the backdrops and the crowds are in 2D is a bit disappointing.
You can use the mouse or controller to land your punches and there's an extensive tutorial to help you ease into the game. Except that, by the game you reach the 10th opponent - and at the same time the last tutorial - the game is almost over. Yes, there's a New Game+, but it's still a shame if you're not into stuff like that, or simply do not have the patience to go through it again.
Defeating opponents rewards you with money. Money that can be used to upgrade your character by training at the gym or by buying equipment. By the time you reach the last opponent you're probably already strong enough to take him down the first time. My advice; don't spend your money on equipment, just use the money at the gym to make your character stronger.
I praise the developer for not letting me grind in order to defeat the last opponent. But at the same time I wish it was made more difficult. Because Beast Boxing Turbo is a fun game, but a short one. Two hours and you're done with it.
I really, really, really hope there'll be a sequel, with more opponents, a better tutorial system (or more opponents after the tutorial) and more incentive to keep fighting (or to do rematches).
Even with its 2 hours of playtime BBT has become one of my favorite games.

Was a huge fan of Arma 2, put quite a few hours into it. Preordered this and have only put a review now years after its release.
I want to start off by saying that I absolutely agree with other Recommend reviews, it is a huge improvement on Arma 2, and has a lot of great new features that aren't implemented or even really possible in other games. There are some amazing moments:
-suppressive fire is real and scary.
-Being in a helicopter crash looks and feels cool, especially when it's due to a rotor or engine being disabled.
-Aquatic battles are actually fun and unique. \
-The gunplay has been improved a bit, and it's not AS sluggish and clunky as before. (It's not perfect, but it's far more tolerable, and theres actual fun to be had in CQB engagements.)
-Obviously a plethora of new weapons, vehicles, and other features......
But that's where a huge gripe of my comes into play. Bohemia Interactive has quite literally done one of the worst DLC plans in the history of modern gaming. Theres a DLC for Helicopters, a DLC for go karts, DLCs with short campaigns that include new weapons and vehicles, a DLC for Marksman equipment that includes Ghillies and more powerful and dynamic snipers..
That's the problem.. I preordered this game for $60, got the game when it was an Alpha, played hours with the meager content and Singleplayer campaign that they had included, as well as online.. Then I start to get locked out of really participating in more and more servers, because they utilize these new DLCs.. So while everybody else has the new (and fairly basic) guns, I'm stuck to the weapons that were released in the Alpha version of the game.. People are getting to use M4 style weapons, the AKM, Ghillie suits, DMR snipers.. And I'm stuck with the couple guns in each class that hardly resemble any popular modern weapons, that came with the game, as well as the basic uniforms included for each faction.
NOT TO MENTION the fact that they'll randomly cover your entire screen in an Ad gradient, that tells you to purchase the DLCs that this server is currently using, EVEN IF you're in the middle of a gunfight and nothing that you're doing currently involves any of the DLC.. There is constantly a box on your screen when playing tactically, telling you that you don't have all the DLCS, and you should seriously need to go to the store and buy them NOW. So if you don't want to play with Ads absolutely bombarding your screen, you can pay $11.99 each for the Marksmen, Jets, and Helicopters DLC, and $1.99 for the Go Karts DLC.. OR you can just buy the bundle for $19.99.. Not bad right? $80 to play? Well UNFORTUNATELY that doesn't include the new Arma 3 Apex Campaign and equipment. So if you want all the new guns, apparell, access to the vehicles, etc, you'll have to shell out another $34.99.. So now we're at $124.99 to have access to all the vehicles and weapons used in most servers, and we haven't even gotten thru all the other planned DLC..
Now we've got a new Campaign called Laws of War that brings you a new story, new weapons, vehicles and equipment, and that's only another $11.99. It just keeps going up, and up, and up.. You starting to see the problem?
It's too expensive to actually play the game with all the content without being PUNISHED for not buying ALL the DLC.
So while I payed $20 for Arma 2 and got Jets, Helicopters, Ghillie suits, various snipers, and other weapons, albeit less of everything; at least I got to play the game online and really get immersed without being inherently punished for not shelling out more money every time a new DLC came out.
There was NOT enough content in the base game when you first released this, that's fine, I never cared, I knew it was Alpha.
But then you never really added anymore free content to the game to fill that space and flesh out the $60 price tag. You just keep adding more content with price tags on it. I actually JUST now see that you've lowered the price of the game to $40. Good for people who are just now looking into getting the game, but that's really just a slap in the face to the people who played so much Arma 2 that they instinctively jumped onto the chance to play an Arma THREE..
.... So you're probably asking why I actually recommend the game, since a HUGE thing of mine is content per pricetag..
It's quite honestly just that good.. I hate to say it. I love the game I want to play, the moments are amazing. I just feel like this amazing game took a unsightly turn when the developers got too greedy, too quick.
I still am in awe riding in the back of a pickup truck, while it's being airlifted by a chopper only to have them drop you off perfectly right outside the heat of battle.
tldr: The moments, and the visuals, and the mechanics of the base game are enough for me to recommend it. Just don't expect a fully fleshed out content of a game without buying ALL the DLCs. You will be punished thru annoyance while playing the game without them.

Jets'n'Guns is a mixture of bullet hell, reverse bullet hell (where you build your own insane firepower), ship customization, and your usual side-scroller.  Loud, crazy, brash, with plenty of enemies, guns, and weiredness, it's an extremely satisfying shooter.
You play as . . . well the plot gets kind of bizarre, but sort of a soldier turned mercinary, who goes out to save the universe by blowing up spaceships, trucks, troops, building, jets, monsters, and everything else.  As you play you earn money, unlock equipment, find hidden weapons, and far, far more.  Eventually you're customizing your own spacecraft with all sorts of crazy weaponry as you find new ways to defeat your enemies.
Customization and gameplay is a big part of this.  Pick the right loadout in order to survive, pick your battles, and react fast to survive.  The wrong loadout or bad tactics can kill you - and you may need to replay a level and/or recustomize your ship to get things right.  Fortunately, anything you buy can be traded in for full price, encouraging all sorts of combos.
Pretty much a must-pick up for a side scroller/bullet hell player.  But a few caveats:
1) The bullet hell aspect is also based around enduring attacks and being willing to take hits.
2) At times the game screen can get crowded if you build your own bullet-spewing monstrosity, so don't just think a big loadout saves the day - you might not even be able to see your ship in all the chaos.
3) The plot is utterly bizarre and it's hard to tell how much is parody, throwaway jokes, actual humor, or just plain craziness.  There's also some elements that may be parodies of sexist tropes, but the plots are so crazy it's hard to know.

Gridiron Football is card solitare that attempts to simulate a football game.  After watching a short cute video about the game, you can choose some options then begin.  At the main screen, you will see all of the teams available along with their strengths and weaknesses.  After choosing (and even renaming) your team you begin the game / season.
You are presented with a choice of choosing a running or passing play.  Both options are there regardless if you are on offense or defense.  If you hear "Break" you outsmarted them and the less yardage you have to get / block....if you hear a tackle sound, they guessed correctly and you need to get / block more yardage.  Then you see red & black football player cards of differing numbers (they range from 1 - 13).  Your objective is to take a red (or black) card & pair it with the nearest number of the opposing color.  IOW a Red 3 can take a Black 2 or Black 4...Black 9 can take a Red 8 or Red 10...and so on.  The more matches in a row you can make, the further down the field you go or the more yardage you block your opponent.
There is more to the game, including an offseason mini game to improve stats,  a Big Play button which gives you either another card to help you or an event which can either help or hurt, weather affecting play, home field advantage, playoffs...etc.
Likes
Tension of making tough decisions on plays (do I end the play & let him get the 15 yards or risk a Big Play and hope for a card / action to help stop him.
Big Play button giving you at least one extra chance to stop or increase the yardage
Wishes:
- The 4 NFL league (NFC N & S and AFC N & S (their GFC equivilents of course)) Right now there are only 2 divsions
- When you are able to get a penalty on them / receive one, I'd like to see text of what the penalty was...adds more realism.
I will edit this review with other Likes, Wishes, Cons as I play more & especially as I finish my first season and experience the offseason mode.

WOW am I glad I came across Jets'n'Guns. I got it on a whim after seeing it under the recently released Steam games and knowing my interest in weird SHMUPs. I had never heard of it beforehand so this is a strictly no-nostalgia-goggles review.
To put it simply, Jets'n'Guns is the MOST western, gross looking, and FUN SHMUP I have ever played on PC. I say western because it is the polar opposite of a eastern bullet hell anime Touhoufest. The game is very enjoyable for casual SHMUP players like me who really sucks at SHMUPS, though I had to kick it down to Easy mode the first time through. The game's design is gross... but that's not bad... it makes you feel like you're playing what it is: a Windows 98 game that doesn't give a crap about what it looks like. YES, you WILL see Comic Sans. YES, you WILL not care because you're having so much fun. ALSO: The music is pretty great... prog metal with a chiptune backdrop.
Gameplay all about throwing as much firepower as possible at the enemy ships. You do this by collecting cash from every kill and using it on upgrades between each level. By the end of the game you will have SOOO MANY UPGRADES you won't know what to do with them. Make sure to experiment as much as possible with different combinations: I was not aware it didn't charge you more for selling back weapons for a while.
TL;DR: Get this if you want a gross looking but satisfying SHMUP with a huge upgrade system.

I was glad that they gave the player the ability to build their own decks rather than using just prebuilt decks, like in previous iterations.  That is where my praise for the game ends.  The list of available cards is extremely limited & I found myself praising mediocre 1 drops for winning countless games.  That being said there are a few truly good cards at your disposal, if you are interested in purchasing digital booster packs with real world money.  The deck building rules for the game are too constricting and prevent players from developing decks that are actually fun and interesting to play.  You are allowed a full playset (4 cards) of commons, 3 copies of any given uncommon, 2 copies of a rare card, and only 1 copy of any mythic.  It is important to note that these deck building rules also only apply to players so the ai will be running full playsets of their win conditions at all times, if not more.  The single player campaign is incredibly sluggish and tedious.  You will more than likely find yourself playing the same match over and over again because your bargain bin control deck and limited removal power just can't answer that 5th mythic rare bomb the ai dropped.  This game is terrible.  Save your money.  Play Hearthstone.  Not kidding.

I must begin this by disclosing that I am a long time supporter of Frictional Games, my first encounter being Penumbra: Overture. After that, I was hooked on Frictionals style and story-telling, even if I had to force myself through the scares.
SOMA then.
To all veteran consumers of Penumbra and Amnesia, I am glad to say that this game is an amazing progression in almost every category while remaining true with tone and structure(more or less). The sounds and music are phenomenal; the former is utterly convincing and unnerving, the latter is subtly beautiful but powerful enough to drive across the new exciting tone SOMA has introduced. Voice acting is also nearly perfect. The visuals went far beyond what I expected and especially the underwater sequences were especially impressive. The crafting on the environments is also superb. When on entering a bedroom, a messhall, or a laboratory, one can really feel the people who lived there and the events which took place. While not all the areas are outright oppressive, they feel established and genuine.
I found myself initially missing Amnesia: The Dark Descents inventory system, but it never really hampered my progression abillity apart from times when I didn't really know what my character was holding. Overall, I found the puzzles fun, although getting lost can be frusturating. The puzzle complexity is somewhere between the first Amnesia and Penumbra: Black Plague, leaning more toward Black Plague with the importance of computer terminals and electronic challenges. While hunting around for that one component that will make everything work is not fun, it did not happen often.
This is a scary game. Besides the plot, which I will get to, there are plenty of scares to be found in the bleak visuals, terrifying soundwork and, of course, the antagonists.  I actually found myself initially dissapointed by the levels of terror; after all, both the Penumbra and Amnesia games turned up the horror to 10 pretty speedily. I was soon to realize that this game had a different buildup. Instead of peaking near the middle, the scary in this game peaks near the end. This, along with the fact that I encountered different entities relatively breifly meant that I was rarely at ease in the later half of the game. In fact, I was in such a hurry to evade threats, that I surely missed out on some wonderfully designed environments. What little I saw of the creatures coming at me was very limited, but very effective at increasing my run speed; if anyone knows how much of a monster to show, it's Frictional. Of the sound, however, I got a larger sample. While time spent hoping that the shambling creature threateningly close would just go away was plenty, I never really felt bored due to the horror of their design. As for jumpscares / setpieces, there were two scripted scares I anticipated and one that I really didn't. The game is light on jumpscares, most of the horror comes from the dread of going forward.
Probably the most vivid aspect of an already intense game. As the header indicates, I won't spoil anything, but the story is worth at least a second and third look. In addition to the contextual fright that it adds, it's just plain amazing. The view gleamed in the course of the game seems only like a peek at the massive framework behind it all. Frictional in the past has had problems with ending the story in a way beffiting the rest of the plot, but in my opinion Frictional gets it right here. I will not say any more, but I am already excited to delve into the plot more and more even as I have already finished the game.
As for anyone who is unaware of previous Frictional Games, this game is for you too. If you are a horror enthusist, sci fi fan, or someone just looking for an experience that isn't dull and washed out, an experience that meant something to your mind: I would highly reccomend a playthough of this game made by a passionate studio by five years of work.

I got this on a great deal (less than a dollar) and it was certainly worth it. I didn't understand the game at first, but once I picked it up it was a fun challenge. It's by no means elegant or deep, but it is fun. At first I thought I had to kill all the zombies, but then I realized that the real strategy to the game was much more complex. The supplies are scarce, including weapons, ammo, and medkits. You have to search through houses, buy and sell stuff to merchants, upgrade your stats, and strategically move through each section of the levels while conserving as much of your supplies as you can before reaching the next merchant. Once you run out of ammo it's pretty difficult in the later levels, so build up ammo as soon as possible and avoid wasting it all to kill only a few zombies. In the later levels there are waayyy more zombies than you can possibly hope to kill, so the real strategy becomes maneuvering between waves while shooting down hordes with your machine gun or shotgun, killing many at once in order to get lots of money without using up too much ammo. It's a super fun game! Pick it up when it's on sale!

At the outset, this is a very fun game. Walking around on the ocean floor through delapidated, crumbling buildings is fun. It's largely rail-like in your exploration, but the sights are very interesting. It all feels like a sort of futuristic sci-fi that you can expect the kids who failed engineering and architecture to have created, so you'll feel right at home if you enjoy the Alien movies and their ilk.
I appreciate the game attempting to drive the player to consider the ramifications of sentience and individuality, but it ultimately led me to hating the main character. My only friend was Carl -- and I hated him. You'll probably hate him.
The AI is extremely frustrating. Their gimmick makes it difficult to look at them so it's almost impossible to get around them in the later stages as the slightest sound has them homing in on you to lovingly leave you battered and limping. It seems that most of the time, throwing objects to distract them does absolutely nothing, but god help you if you accidentally bump into a snow cone; they can hear that, you know.
All in all, this is a game best watched and not played. The only real decisions you have are no-brainers and clearly divide players into "practical" and "inappropriately empathic" camps. Your time is largely spent on trying to find which un-assuming bit you can suddenly pick up and what innocuous bit you can now stick it into or just having to avoid the all-seeing monsters. (Hint: locking them in a room is useless.)

This game is amazing. Pure and simple. Play KOTOR 1 first, if you haven't, and then play this one. The story is so well developed, and offers more variation in things you can say to other characters and the responses you will get than in KOTOR 1. The crafting system is very well developed for its time, and the influence system among the characters is an amazing idea, and makes multiple  playthroughs enjoyable. There are more force powers than the original, and they are pretty cool. There are two negative points for this game. One is th lack of interaction between characters. Not very often, at least in the vanilla game, have I been able to hear two characters in my party talk to eachother, like they did in the original. It could be just me, or the game.  The second is glitches. The game, at least for mac, has a lot of glitches. Nothing game ending, but mostly graphical glitches. Ocassionally, you will get stuck walking through a door for a few seconds, or some other minor thing. Just be sure to save often.
If you get stuck, or have no idea what to do, consult the internet. There are some places where quests will be difficult to find and complete. Just be sure to explore every area completely, and if you still have no idea of what to do, search for your problem online. The one place where this occurs most is on Nar Shadda.  Overall, a great game that I would pay 20$ for, and a 9.5/10.

TL;DR;Very nice art, but the story feels unoriginal, there are not too many actual animations and the puzzles are quite unexciting. I would rate it neutral if possible.
Almost all of the puzzles have either really obvious solutions or can be solved by randomly clicking everything. There is barely any moment when you really have to use your logic skills, which makes the actual gameplay experience feel like an afterthought, almost like in a hidden object game. More than once i have solved a puzzle almost by accident, surprised by the simplicity, by doing what i do in other puzzle games just to understand what the puzzle might lead to. This is not meant to be bragging, i am actually quite awful at puzzles so the transparency of those contained within this game surprised me even more.
It also doesn't help that the story really feels like an afterthought as well, almost like they came up with the art and made up a story around it (which could probably have amazing results in a game with more exciting gameplay but here there is not enough to occupy your mind otherwise and it feels like a choose your own adventure game without the choices)
If you are looking for something to relax with and appreciate the artstyle its worth the low price but if you expect some brainteasers in your adventure games it might disappoint you.

4) what a player does on the world map wont affect the world map for others so if someone takes over the entire map it has no bearing for the other players
cons:
1) co-op has the tendency to lag (you can still do everything solo though with little difficulty)
2) doing pvp with someone can be a bit finicky (pvp can also lag)
3) the ai for units is not the best. for example put your units on passive and individual squad members will still chase enemy units across the map which unfortuantly drags the entire squad back in. (although passive greatly helps with unit control the ai needs to be better)
4) a very rare glitch but when it does happen your progress and unit levels can be reseted. this is a connectivity problem though more or less in regards to the server.

I can't even express how happy I was when I saw this 20th Anniversary Edition pop up on Steam.  Sins of the Fathers was one of my very first point-and-click adventure games (I was a whopping 12 years old when it came out) and I was completely enthralled by it then.  I'm pleased that the story lost nothing over the years, and is just as unique and spellbinding as I remember it.
This edition maintains all the wit and creativity of the original, with updated character graphics and location scenes to introduce it to a modern audience.  I was delighted to find that all of the things I loved about the original were retained here, including an absolutely gorgeous soundtrack.
If you're a fan of the genre, and especially if you were a fan of the old Sierra adventure games, this is a must-have (along with its first sequel, which although stylistically different has a story even more engrossing than this one).

I'm pleased to finally have had the chance to play Gabriel Knight since I never had the opportunity to play the series back in the 90s. Being an adventure game fan, I've heard good things about it, and I was stoked.
Let me start off by saying that the theme is really interesting, a welcomed change of pace.
It's rare to find games that feature voodoo, cajun, or New Orleans culture in a respectful manner.
I think in the 90s, Gabriel Knight was hailed as a cutting-edge franchise because it was a modern noir murder mystery story set in New Orleans, featuring POC characters, and it was quite violent for a video game at the time - a point & click, no less.
With that chunk of history in mind, and the 17+ hours I've spent playing the game, it's safe to say that it is pretty good!
But, I do have a bone or two to pick, and I'll explain why in detail.
To be honest, it was really difficult for me to really connect with Gabriel and appreciate him as a character; but, over time, I grew to appreciate the game and other characters, instead, and then it became much more enjoyable.
I feel that the characters, music, and atmosphere is what really made the game for me and it was what kept me from uninstalling the game because I was so frustrated with Gabriel being little more than a womanizing dream boat - who falls in love with a woman after only knowing her for three days!
(And she explicitly told him she was uninterested, at first)
Story-wise, I felt that Gabriel was a flop, in the beginning at least, and I thought the love-at-first-sight and playing hard to get aspects were uncomfortable and unnatural (but it was a popular theme in 90's story-telling, I'll admit).
Also, Gabriel had very little character development up until the peak of the plot, which was disappointing because it made him seem even more of a pretty boy cut-out instead of the formidable hero he was - literally - destined to be.
But, my personal gripe aside, it was a good adventure game; I had fun with the puzzles and I enjoyed interacting with the characters, too! (Mosely and Grace were wonderful, I just wish that they were a bit more involved.)
This was a good remake, and I hope that the other two games will be redone so that they may have a chance to reconnect with old fans, and inspire new fans, as well.

Gabriel Knight: Sins of the Fathers 20th Anniversary Edition
OMG! Was that really 20 years ago? Seems like yesterday when it came out. Back in the days when I was starting out playing PC and videogames. I had so many fond memories that I actually  shied away for long weeks before playing the revamped version on Steam , not wanting to spoil my memories of the game by a bad new version. But here's my two cents.
8 of 10
The graphics made a huge step forward from 1993, of course. I liked the improvement, from dust particles that can be seen when the sun shines through a window, to the sometime kind of 3D backgrounds and characters. Advertised it is as being HD, but well it's not all HD, the story is done e.g. told in comic style. Because truth be told, back in the 90ies the graphics were so ugly, that sometimes you were just clicking around with your mouse, just hoping you hit something that could be useful. Big Thumbs up for the improvement!
8.5 of 10
Even after all this time, the story still feels fresh .Gabriel Knight's humor and dialogues are still fun and feel fresh. The game is an Absolut classic. Voodoo Gods, the New Orleans Flair and the story of the Schattenjägers. The riddles are tricky and sometimes a little farfetched, but the producers added a new hint system in your diary, which should help beginners of the genre. And even though I been playing the game before, it still took me around 14 hours.
8.5 of 10
The 90ies music was replaced by a new mix by the original composer. Very fitting. Nothing against old-school, but 90ies PC music was not that good. I was surprised how fitting the voice actors were. Especially the voice of Gabriel Knight.

Definitely a must buy for nostalgic gamers (like me) , adventure gamers in general and probably the best game for starters of the genre.

"Cabrit sans cor" is all I have to say. Figure out what that means and tell me you don't want to play this game... these words have haunted me for almost 20 years...not kidding.
I fondly remember my days spent indoors, during incredibly hot summer days in Georgia, playing Sierra games. They were such amazing adventure games and something altogether different from my console titles (SNES at the time I think). But stumbling upon Gabriel Knight really has remained as my first discovery of a "sleeper" hit game. Knowing now that the main devs involved were partly responsible for King's Quest and Phantasmogoria makes total sense and a perfect way to describe this game: the gameplay of KQ mixed with the dark and sinister spector of Phantas.
The tale of Voodoo, murder and noir dectective skewed N'awlins style is a true classic. The author of the script really did a great job capturing the flavor of the south (sometimes moreso than the voice actors...), and as a southerner I can tell you that is not an easy thing to do. The dynamic of the characters is well crafted, and the tale is tense and masterful. Morover, I love the film "Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil" and this game certianly has a similar "Southern Gothic" feeling. The bizarre cast of characters, wrought iron fences, the sweet smell of magnolia and gardenia, the heavy wet air of New Orleans, the general ease that the old South did once proffer, and a glimpse into the darkest shadows surrounding some of the best kept secrets haunting the opulent manors and old money that flow in the veins of old surviving Southern towns and cities.
It has depth in both story and gameplay, but some may not really enjoy the point and click play. It can also get a little repetitive; having to travel around and explore places you've alreday been to just to try and find one thing or one detail about one thing you missed...it can bug you. Also, one of the classic faults (if you can call it that) of old Sierra games was the quality of the backgrounds sort of hiding, or at least obscuring, the paths the player needs to find. Also, some gamers may not understand the whole "open the inventory to combine items to equip them all/get them to work" sort of problem solving required to solve some puzzles, if they can find the puzzle to begin with- looking at you clock puzzle... Trust me, if you play this game you'll find it. Truthfully; that's what I love about the games, but I admit that it isn't eveyone's cup of tea- you have to spend time IN the game. Click on everything, explore every corner...and the new option to press a button to reveal all interactable objects is AWESOME... you used to have to click blindly until you got a GUI box to pop up.
It's a great game you 90's gamers may have missed and one newer gamers may never hear of again! Thanks for the reboot, so happy to have it in my library again!

Not sure what tweaks have been done to the game since the other reviewers played it, but this is a definite thumbs down.
Supposedly, you make good yards when the computer guesses wrong, and very little, if any, if it guesses right on offense. On defense it is supposed to be the same. But it doesn't work that way. When on defense, and you guess wrong, the computer opponent STARTS OUT with a 25 yard gain, and it takes solitaire matches to reduce it. But there are very few matches. Even when you guess right against the computer opponent, it STILL starts off with a 12 yard gain that you have to whittle down, again with very few matches available.
Now when YOU are on offense and the computer guesses wrong against you, for a pass, you start at zero yards, and MUST get THREE matches in a row before you gain a paltry 8 yards. Subsequent matches add yardage, but again they are few and far between. When you run the football, and the computer guesses wrong, once again you start at zero yards, and add 4 yards for subsequent matches. Now if the computer guesses right, it is that much harder to gain any yards.
And the computer sneaks a peak at what you choose as well, I purposely ran nothing but pass plays for three possessions, gaining some yards, and figured now I'd start off witha run. Of course the computer 'guessed' right on run, when there is absokutely no possible way it could have, based on previous play calls.
If this game sounds interesting to you, wait until it is at least 75% off, and be prepared for a mountain of frustration. Even at 75% off you may very well regret your purchase.
NOTE: A new update to the game was applied on July 4. It added kickoff and punt returns, plus penalties. Penalties reduced your chances even more of getting matches, and running plays now only gain 3 yards per match, instead of 4. Also, when you guess right on defense, the computer opponent starts off with a 15 yard gain now, rather than the original 12.
I also noticed special teams plays result in TDs (for the computer opponent, of course) more often, plus more turnovers (again, for the computer opponent) when the player uses a Big Play, regardless of weather.
Bottom line: Made an already extremely frustrating game even more so. I now wouldn't even recommend buying it even at 75% off. Save your money and the frustration.

Everything about this game screams greatness. This game has some of the finest side-scrolling, platforming, shmup action that I have played and I go back to the Jungle Hunt years. There is no lack of challenge and once you think it starting to get easier, you get hit with the wake up call that forces you to completely change your strategy. I found myself playing this one again after I beat it on normal, just so I could blow everything up with overly powerful weapons to find out that there is even more content than I thought. I'm currently on my 3rd go though playing it on hard for a new challenge. This game has way more replayability than I expected. The one thing that bugged me about this game is that a few levels had some really cheesy enemies as well as few lame weapons but these a minimal in contrast to the rest of the game. What made this even more character along with the explosions and violence was the humor and found myself chuckling in the middle of battle a few times. There is no shortage of levels, enemies, weapons, secrets and customizable ships. The controls seemed a little sensative at first but easy to overcome in a very short amount of time. Sounds were good with the 80's hair band music that seemed to fit the style of gameplay. The graphics get insane at times and I was amazed at how quickly the screen could fill up with weapon shots, enemies, explosions, etc... that you can easily get lost in the madness. I would highly recommend this to anyone and a definate picker-upper. I give this a 9 out of 10. -1 for the few levels that you are going to say "ooooh gawd, really?"
So for I love it, for 6.99$ the value proposition is great.

You know what separates a good (review) writer from an average one? Adaptability. No genre is left out and no topic is out of reach. It was only a matter of time until I’d accept writing about a video game geared only towards a mature audience. As far as the Steam presence and tolerance for such adult themes are concerned, developer Eek! Games walks a fine albeit thin, red line. Guess that “barely legal” term doesn’t quite have the right ring to it, but for as long as users refrain from posting  directly on Steam, sensitive/explicit screenshots of this game’s action, then all will be well. But who are we kidding? This is the Internet and you can’t swing a digital dead cat without hitting a troll.
Don’t you just love it how hypocritical society can be at times? Ultraviolence gets a free pass, nudity doesn’t of course. Blowing out brains, mashing organic matter into sausages, even turning people into meat pies (Sweeney Todd knows best) has become normality as far as film and gaming fiction is concerned. Flashing skin? A tenth circle has been erected just for you in Hell. I won’t emphasize a lot on this since, nothing’s gonna change anyways. What’s important to understand though, is that adult humor and themes have a niche of their own, along with gamers and fans which deserve the same respect as those which prefer shooting hordes of nazi zombies or jumping over platforms with Italian plumbers.
So just as its name implies, House Party is a fairly straightforward affair. Players control a nameless male hopeful in search of temporary female companionship. One night stands, ok? It’s a house filled with young adults so I hope you didn’t expect it to develop into a “fun” round of Yahtzee or Bingo. The catalyst which would really get the party going, seems to rely on your direct interaction. It's the booze and since the characters don’t wish to re-enact a Prohibition-era party, you’ll be the hero who saves the day. The main “antagonist” is a teetotaler jock named Frank. Since the developers really hate conventions, they roasted this fictional character by making him dumb as a brick, tough as nails (his one-hit knockouts spell “Game Over” for you) and in charge of sheltering partygoers from dangerous vices.
You definitely have to use your wits and circumvent this issue since a dry party is a sad one indeed. I never went to many myself, but I’d hate to be the killjoy of any situation. Frank has to get out of the picture. You can trick him and act friendly, for example. Same tactic applies to the vast majority of female NPCs, but keep in mind that advancing  through some quests will lock out others. Not that I’m complaining. With a small map as it is, replayability is very important. It is Madison’s house and she’s the host of the party, but you can certainly befriend any of her female acquaintances and experience the game from multiple perspectives. Unlike Frank, the girls are not walking stereotypes as far as I could tell and if you think that it’s gonna be a short trip into their pants, you’ll be proven wrong.
Playing House Party I can now finally say that I’ve seen every single gaming genre and subgenre being powered by Unity Engine assets. It is a visually pleasant title, as expected. Stable frame rate. Eye candy plays its crucial role afterall. The house and its immediate surroundings are still a rather confined space for a game world about socializing and then taking steps further ahead. The Leisure Suit Larry series which House Party wishes to mention as inspiration had decently-sized worlds which felt quite immersive at times.
The sounds are alright, even if nothing special. The voice acting lacks enthusiasm and that is something that you wouldn’t expect from a game about parties and having fun. You don’t put the “fun” back in “funeral” here, right? Soundtrack could surely use some diversity. No one dances for hours to the same song, no matter how plastered they are.
At a superficial glance this might just be another “subversive” attempt at showing that alchol and parties don’t mix well and perhaps may even lead to future regrets. Or you might get the wrong idea that in order to score, you need to get her drunk enough until your fugly mug looks almost as presentable as some pasty actor/singer/whatever she desires. This game is as much about adult humor as its graphic simulation itself while proving to be a life lesson if you look deep enough. And yeah, playing the “nice guy” role does have nearly the same results. It’s about patience and creativity, I guess. Look, you don’t need dating advice from me.
So far players can only engage in heterosexual intercourse and it’s not like it bothered me in the slightest. At the same time, I don’t judge what people do in the privacy of their own homes and personal freedom will always matter a lot more than what some book, politician or “holy” figure tells you to do. If you’re playing this, I’ll assume that you’re a discerning adult since it is obviously not the title nor the gameplay suitable to minors. Let those “feast their eyes” on televised violence instead, since nudity would probably cause them seizures or something.
Humorous situations arise from the creative ways in which you either obtain or combine items and how you ultimately interact with the female partygoers you attempt to woo. Cold reading is necessary in the sense in which some of those in-game girls might be feuding with one another and you can play that out to your advantage. Gathering intel before the battle, eh? In anycase, it adds to the fun factor even if most of those jokes fall flat compared to simiar titles from this niche. Skip the dumpster fire known as Leisure Suit Larry: Box Office Bust and just (re)play Magna Cvm Lavdae or Reloaded, if you’re curious about more successful counterparts to House Party.
At the time of this writing there is only one playable story in House Party. It’s just the official “New Game” since I won’t place the Tutorial in the same equation. It’s basically the same map anyways and it gets old fairly fast, especially once you learn what makes each girl “click” into place. The fact that save games only register for as long as you haven’t exited the game, seems like a really bad design choice which forces players to backtrack and replay just for the sake of it. Achievements and a price drop are strongly recommended, so potential players should wait for either a bundled offer or a Steam Sale. And remember this: censorship is far worse than its complete absence.

I think the problem with this game, is that its designed to do 3 things:
1. Cool 90s simulator
From the♥♥♥♥♥slapping humor, the referances, to the usage of Beer and Steroids as items. Especially the action figure levels
2. First person shooting with cool guns
After playing Shadow Warrior, Doom 1 & 2, Heretic & Hexen and some Duke 3D: I think I understand what "cool guns" is. Or how its suppose to play.
3. Filler content
Puzzle platforming, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ short "interactive" cinematics, physic puzzles, lots of "oh we can do this in engine like its 2001-2004!"
These 3 things mesh somewhat. But its also problematic.
I.E The irst 2 things don't really mesh, the way this game is made.
You are controlling a very slow elite solider, who can barely move. The gun's generally don't do anything either. Most of them are terrible in their own ways. And as the level design evolve, you spot another issue: Duke is practically blind. The extreme narrow vision don't work out at all.
While its true a lot of 90s fps features very narrow vision, it worked out differently when you could snap across extremely large rooms, in rapid speed. It works out terrible when Duke is slow, can barely damage anything, can't see anything, and keeps getting flanked.
But that also brings us to the next point on the agenda: Enemies don't really deal damage. They don't feel scary. Fighting them feels like swatting flies, slow flies that poke you.
But generally your guns are not any better. The best weapon might even be the pistol, simply because its accurate and has raw damage. Every other weapon has crippling flaws, and generally feels awful.
"Different weapons do better against different enemies", thats what the hint tells you. Not really. The pistol is the best. Even if something like the shotgun is cool, its pointless when it only works as a melee weapon. And all weapons feel worse than the pistol and shotgun.
But then:
Point 3 of the list comes if, you complete a combat section. Either you have to wait for new cinematic and a enemy bash trough something, or you encounter the dreaded physic puzzles.
You can't just become good, and go really really fast. Instead you have to spend a lot of time waiting around, for the horrible cinematics. Some of them are amusing, but most aren't that good. Its just waiting around A LOT for a NPC to stop blocking door ways.
And at some point, you enter a boss fight. Okay, so you need to use explosive weapons. But explosive weapons have practically no ammo. Often there will be a ammo container on the scene. Or a rocket launcher tucked somewhere on scene, so you can obtain a explosive weapon.
It doesn't feel great at all.
Some of the finishers looks good, as in humoristically good. Thats a plus. But most bosses are terrible to fight. The best boss might even be the final one, because it lacks the obstacles earlier bosses have.
Because instead of camping a ammo chest, rocket pigs are his reinforcement.
Because instead of a gatling gun, he tries to be impressive.
The core problem with this game, is that it fails to understand what a power trip is, fails to understand speed, and simply isn't juvenile enough to do any of the things it wants to do.

Duke Nukem Forever is a game that is notorious for having spent nearly 15 years in development hell.
The finished product is built from the all the assets that were created for the game between 2003 and 2009 (as found in pictures that were released when the game was pretty much cancelled in 2009). What Gearbox then did was patch all that unfinished content together, and create a fairly minimal amount of content in order to obtain a game that they could release.
As far as the gameplay goes, the game is unfortunately way too much of a departure from the original, with a 2-weapon loadout made to facilitate the use of a controller (later patched to a 4-weapon loadout in single player), fairly slow movement speed with the possibility to sprint in very short bursts, and some fairly clunky platforming at times. The gunplay itself is decent, but suffers from annoying reverse mouse acceleration which can't be disabled.
Due to the troubled development of the game, the levels are quite a mixed bag. Some of them are cleverly designed (The Duke burger is a favorite of mine), while others feel quite linear and empty, and the graphical quality varies a lot between areas. Exploration is rewarded with easter eggs and collectibles, and the levels are filled with interactive elements.
The story is actually based on the original one written in 1997, and is a straight sequel to Duke Nukem 3D. Just like in D3D, it is extremely simplistic. The writing can get really cringe-worthy at times, with some dated references and (intentionally?) bad jokes. The voice acting is a bit of a mixed bag too, despite John St John reprising his role as Duke Nukem.
The multiplayer is pretty much dead by now, with very few servers to be found.It is comprised of 4 very basic game modes and 10 maps in the main game. The "Hail to the Icons" introduces 3 more modes as well as 4 maps, and "The Doctor Who Cloned Me" also contains 4 maps. There is a progression system in play, with objectives that unlock hats, glasses and shirts upon completion, and a levelling system that unlocks items in a virtual apartment of sorts.
In terms of graphics, the game is very inconsistent It does have a couple of fairly impressive set pieces, but many levels turn out to be very ugly, plenty of low-resolution textures and a somewhat uninspired design. You can really tell the artwork that was created in 2003-2006 from what was made at Gearbox during the last stages of development.The lighting model is very good, though, with a Doom 3-style fully dynamic lighting system that looks genuinely good in some places.
The biggest problem with the graphics actually comes in the form of a poorly implemented, low-resolution, depth-of-field effect. Not only does it kick in at all the wrong times, but it is also so low-resolution that it just drowns the screen into a pixelated blurry mess. And unfortunately, the only way to turn it off is deactivating all the post-process effects altogether (There is a fix for that however in the form of an older build of the FlawlessWidescreen utility).
The music and sound design are pretty good, with a decent heavy metal score and fairly convincing sound effects.
In terms of performance, the game runs fine on a variety of hardware. Loading times are fairly long, and the game suffers from the typical old Unreal texture streaming issues. There is a fair range of graphical customization available, however the options aren't very detailed, with some options bundled in a single menu entry. There are also only post-process antialiasing methods available, which only add to the already blurry nature of the game.
The single-player campaign can be completed in about 10+ hours, with some hidden collectibles to find. The multiplayer is mostly dead nowadays. The "The Doctor Who Cloned Me"' DLC is very good, and adds an additional 4 hours or so of additional single player content.
In conclusion, while it was a bitter disappointment in 2011, Duke Nukem Forever isn't as terrible a game as most would say. I did have quite a bit of fun playing it, despite its many flaws. However, it wasn't worth its full price at the time, and it still isn't worth its current price either. It's one of those "get it when it's on sale if you are really curious" kind of games, and the price does drop quite significantly when it goes on sale. For $5 or regional equivalent, it might be worth it.

What does it mean to be human? What is life? What is consciousness? Who is to decide the answers to those questions?
I think, therefore I am. Right?
Even after the ~15 hours it took me to see the credits rolling down my monitor, these are just some of the questions that still boggles my mind. It's games like this that may make your head spin, and to question your very own existence.
Even with the above being said, remember that this is a horror game and it may make you s**t your pants.
Oh well. On to the game itself.
Aside from being scary, the game offers an extremely deep atmosphere and story. Combine this with existential questions, horrifying gameplay and breathtaking artistic design, graphics and sound, and you should at least have an idea what this game has to offer.
Without spoiling the story or any plot points, I will just say that if you're a fan of sci-fi, you will greatly enjoy the story and the setting this gorgeous, yet haunting looking world has to offer. It will also force you to make some very morally difficult choices, unless you're a cold-hearted human being that is. This is one of those games that sucks you into it's world, making you not wanting to exit the game until you've reached the credits.
If you ever played Amnesia, the last masterpiece released by the same company, you should feel right at home with the controls and physics offered by this game. Pulling out desk drawers, opening doors, it's all controlled the same way (holding the mouse button down and moving the mouse) and feels just as good.
While there is no inventory screen you can still carry some items around with you that are used automatically in their proper places. There is also no HUD for health, but the game gives you very good visual feedback about how close you are to dying. When really low on health you can no longer sprint and instead are limping around and the screen gets much blurrier etc.
The game ran fine on my GTX970 and I managed to almost always maintain 60fps on the highest settings at 1920x1080 resolution (except when the game clearly loaded the world and it dropped). I found some minor bugs, like places where you could exit the level's boundaries although they required me  to really going out of my way to jump around looking for them (as I have a tendency to do :P ), otherwise no game breaking bugs to report.
So, without dragging this out too long, here are my conclusions.
Would I recommend this game?
If you like great stories and atmosphere where you can really take your time to absorb and interact with the world around you, then yes, without a doubt.
If you enjoyed Amnesia, then yes, this is for you as well.
If you're too afraid of scary games, but still want to experience the story? I'd say stay the **** away!
Is it worth the 27,99€€ steam asks for it?
After completion, for me, personally, that's a "Yes, definitely".
ps. "robots" can be freaking terrifying. Sleep tight...

This game is a unique RTS game where instead of crushing your opponents with armies you crush them with boat loads of money! You might be sceptical at this and think this will make the gameplay lack complexity and make it numb and boring, and this was a sentiment I held until I've played for a few hours and started understanding the complexity of the game.
While the resource amasing in most RTS games is secondary to the warfare aspect and hence simple and mostly automated, this game revovles around its resource system and it works better than I first thought. The reason for this is that there's a dynamic resource market that's central in the game; simply put, if all players harvest iron and aluminum and other metals, the prices of these will drop and further harvesting becomes pointless. If that's the case you want to be the guy that's harvesting the precious food, oxygen and water, and making big $$ while buying the cheap resources the other players conveniently has overproduced. You're a daytrader, buy what's cheap and produce and sell what's expensive. This also means that adapting quickly is the key, and given that's it's played in real time it reminds me more of a high-octane game like starcraft than say the relaxing civilization series.
In essence there's an ever ongoing interaction with the other players that you don't see as clearly in war based RTS, where it's all about big clashes between the armies and each player does their own thing in the rest of the time. This interaction makes the multiplayer games super fun, while the play vs the A.I. ("quick play" and there's some sort of simplified campaign at the moment) is not quite as entertaining but still works well. A comparison with board games like Risk is fitting, and it is perfectly suited for LAN's.
There's some additional strategical elements to the game that adds depth; there are ways to sabotage an opponent and there's four different "classes" to choose from, a you should make depending on your strategy and the map.
It is, however, what I consider to be on the expensive side for a game of this dimension. With some more work done on the campaign, and a proper tutorial (the one in place now doesn't teach you very much), it would be reasonable though, and given that it's in early access maybe that's what will happen.

Knights of the Old Republic II
– The Sith Lords, was developed by Obsidian Entertainment and released early 2005. KOTOR2 is a Star Wars RPG played from a third-person view, and a sequel to the original KOTOR game which was developed by Bioware and released in 2003.
There was an update on July 21, 2015 which dramatically improved the quality of the game, adding in steam achievements, steam cloud saves, native wide screen support, controller support, and best of all the Steam Workshop.
The events taking place in KOTOR2 take place five years after KOTOR1, the Sith are winning the war with the Republic. You play as “The Exile”, a former Jedi Knight who has lost his/her ability to use the Force.
Throughout the story you are given chances to earn “light side” or “dark side” points based on the ethical decisions you make, you also grow closer to your various companions based on choices you are sometimes presented with.
All of this gives the game an extremely replayable atmosphere; because you can go back and choose different dialogue, experience a completely different story, and most importantly deal with the consequences for your choices.
Combat wise, the game is identical to the first KOTOR, you have the same types of weapons: lightsaber, Melee, Blaster weapons, Ion weapons, Mines, Grenades, etc.
You can
pause the game before and during combat to plan out your strategy of engagement, will your companions lay down range fire while you rush to the front lines lightsaber blazing? Or is this a boss and you need to throw all your grenades? First use force lightning, flurry, auto attack, force drain, then power attack? There are countless strategies for combat within the game.
There are Mini games; Pazaak
and Swoop bike racing
. Learning the tricks of these mini games are very rewarding in the game, but a guide would be the appropriate place to learn about these mini games.
Once upon a time there were no achievements for KOTOR2... ...until the magical day of July 21, 2015! This is one the games I always wanted achievements to be available on, most achievements will be earned with playing through the game twice; Once choosing the Dark Side path, once choosing the Light Side path.
There are also several achievements for skill based side objectives, however it's safe to say that all of these achievements are very well achievable. You do need to be willing to go through the story several times to earn them all.
KOTOR2 is priced at $9.99, my first play through was 47 hours. The quality of this game is excellent. Personally, I am guilty of being biased for star wars RPG's and playing the heck out of them, but even for a normal person you can easily squeeze out 20+ hours.
To quickly recap, Story: Excellent, the story changes based on decisions you make throughout the game. Gameplay: identical combat rolling system to KOTOR1. Achievements: straight forward, you will need to beat the game twice and maybe three times
. Price: Extremely fair, if you want an even better price just wait for a steam sale.
I adore the Star Wars universe, and this is my favorite RPG series within that franchise. With the advent of J.J. Abrams, Star Wars Episode 7: The Force Awakens
, the franchise will regain momentum.

From the first time I saw Star Wars Episode IV on VHS when I was 6 I fell in love with it. I have played nearly every Star Wars game ever made, read over 140 Star Wars novels, read hundreds of issues of Star Wars comics, and basically prayed at the Temple of Lucas Arts for years.  I played over 120 hours of this game back in 2006-2007, and after many more years of gaming it is still one of my favorite games.  While it lacked the amazing story of the first KOTOR, the gameplay improvements and the amount of options and replayability value make this game in my top 10.  I usually prefer more light-hearted games, but the gritty and real nature of this game really grabbed my attention.  Multiple playthroughs as both light and dark side characters, gaining influence with different party members and piecing together their backstories (Atton's backstory- holy crap!) and the tie-ins to the first KOTOR really help this game rise above the surprising amount of content that they cut right before release in order to make the deadline.  With the Steam update of this game, as well as the mod that restores the cut content, there is no better time to reinstall this game or give it a try for the first time.  (However, if you have not played the first KOTOR all the way through do that immediately, even though it is a 12 year old game the plot is still my favorite in all of gaming.)
Warning, this game is 9 years old and it FEELS 9 years old. Don't expect the newest Frostbite physics/graphics engine.  But, the story and customization make this game a MUST for me. If you like Star Wars at all, give this game a try-- but play the first Knights of the Old Republic beforehand, it is absolutelynecessary and makes the story 100 times better.
